en: Preface to the *Record of the Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land*:
How sublime is the teaching of the Pure Land! Is it not the very path by which all the sages fulfilled their human form?

Mencius said, "The physical form and its colors are the nature of Heaven. Once one knows that the physical form and its colors are the nature of Heaven, one cannot speak of the mind apart from the land.
To know that the nature of Heaven constitutes form and appearance is to find no room for seeking the soil externally;
to speak of the mind while separated from the soil is to regard the nature of Heaven as having something external to it. What is called "mind" in this case is merely a single, discrete entity.
To seek the soil by means of an external mind is to regard form and appearance as having something external to them. What is called "soil" in this case is merely a single, solid mass.

That is all. These [views] all fail to understand the doctrine of "fulfilling the form" (*jianxing*). In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of the *Avataṃsaka*, principle and phenomena are unimpeded, and phenomenon and phenomenon are unimpeded.
The verse of Samantabhadra says: "Throughout all infinite oceans of lands and kalpas, they are all purified by a single skillful means.
This is the ultimate standard for fulfilling the form. It further says: "When I am about to reach the end of my life..."
"Having completely eliminated all obstacles, one beholds that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face and immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
This is the correct path for realizing the form [of the Buddha]. Some may argue: 'Since Vairocana pervades all places, how can one point exclusively toward the West?

This would deviate from his universal embodiment. Yet they fail to realize that within the Flower Treasury Ocean, every speck of dust and every hair-pore possesses [the entirety of the Dharma-realm]."
The adornments of the infinite vessel-worlds throughout the ten directions are likewise like those of Sukhāvatī.

Thus, by seeing the single Buddha Amitābha, one has already seen all the Buddhas of the ten directions; and by being born in the single land of the Western Paradise, Sukhāvatī, [one has attained birth in all lands].
This has already traversed the Buddha-lands of the ten directions. Why is this? Because it is both one and many, being non-dual and without distinction.
This Dharma-gate alone was proclaimed from the golden mouth of our Honored One, Śākyamuni;

it is praised together by all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, and is circulated and upheld by the great Bodhisattvas, transmitted further and further without end. Since the Great Teaching came to the East...

Aside from those who have been directly enlightened through the single transmission, those among both the monastic and lay communities who have attained liberation through the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) are too numerous to be easily enumerated.

Ji Qing, dressed in plain white robes, followed the Confucian way while concurrently cultivating Pure Land practices. He constantly desired to compile his accumulated learning to serve as a means of self-exhortation;

however, due to the pressing demands of daily life, he had deferred this task until now. It was upon meeting his nephew Xi-sou, who had recently resolved to develop faith, that he wished to complete this work.

I have compiled this record to strengthen the aspirations of those who look toward the Pure Land. To that end, I have identified the essential points of its core principles by consulting the sutras and śāstras, followed by the works of Chinese authors, and further supplemented by what has come to my own ears and eyes.
Having weighed these sources and made appropriate adjustments and additions, I have bound them into a single volume titled *The Record of the Holy and Sages of the Pure Land*.

It is my hope that all who see or hear of it will rejoice and thereby enter the stream of the Dharma; and that through a single thought of sincere devotion, they may together ascend to the other shore.
How excellent! As it says in the *Shijing*: "The warbling yellow bird / Perches on the corner of the mound. Now, the Pure Land is likewise the corner of a mound for the sages and worthies.
According to the purity of one's own mind, so too is the Buddha-land pure; thus, one finds the place where they may rest.
Furthermore, among the efforts of the student, none precedes knowing where to stop. Therefore it is said: "In stopping, know where to stop. How could one be a human being and yet fail to do this?
It is like the birds. The Sūtra says: "In that land there are always white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śārikas, kalaviṅkas, and *saṃjīva* birds.
Six times throughout the day and night, they emit harmonious and elegant sounds.

These sounds eloquently expound such dharmas as the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. The sentient beings of that land hear these sounds."
Thus it is. All should mindfully recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

Whether regarding the mind, the land, form and color, or innate nature, one must directly realize the place of return and sever all frivolous conceptualizations. The seed of the lotus flower resides solely within the person themselves.
Those who peruse this record—do they not delight in the teaching of "fulfilling the form"? To "fulfill the form" is precisely what is meant by rebirth in the Pure Land.
Compiled by the student of Pure Practice, Peng Jiqing, in the first month of spring in the forty-eighth year of the Qianlong era.

Regarding those recorded as having attained rebirth, only works composed in China have been included. As for the origins of the Pure Land teachings as elucidated in the sūtras and śāstras...
This work has been largely produced from abbreviated sources. It is like attempting to regulate the Yellow River without starting at Jishí, or channeling the Yangtze without beginning at Míngshān;
having lost sight of the source, its current will surely become obstructed.

Therefore, this text first identifies the Founder of the Teaching to establish the object of our devotion, followed by Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta to clarify that there are assistants, and then Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī flanking Vairocana, while collectively praising the West.
Together we shall propagate the pure karma. Thus we know that among the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, there are none who do not take the Pure Land as their refuge.

As for the patriarchs and masters of the various treatises in India, although not all of them recorded accounts of their verified rebirth, once they had attained the stage of fruition, how could they be restricted by east or west? Regarding all discussions related to this teaching:
I have likewise recorded these together here, merely to provide extensive support for exhortation and inducement.

In the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*Lokadhātupraveśa-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is stated that the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī, the Householder Vimukta, and the Layman Vimalakīrti all entered the gates of liberation without departing from mindfulness of the Buddha, even for the duration of a single thought-moment. It manifests...
In boundless lands, one beholds immeasurable Buddhas; this is possible only by reaching the source of one’s own mind and exhausting the ocean of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Only then can one personally realize such a samādhi. Those who cultivate pure karma must certainly hollow out their hearts to receive this teaching upon the crown of their heads.

However, as this matter pertains to the universal path, it does not belong exclusively to a single land; its principle encompasses the entire realm of *sāhasra-lokadhātu*, and is not restricted to the West. Should one enter [this practice] indiscriminately...
I fear that this compilation might deviate from the established precedent; therefore, I have abridged the text and marked out only its essential meanings as follows.

Furthermore, the *Yúnqī wǎngshēng jí* (Cloud Dwelling Collection on Rebirth) merely highlights...

As for the verification of his deeds and the details of his practice, they are rarely fully known; thus, one might as well merge Zhang and Li into a single person, or confuse the Zhi and Mian rivers so they share the same taste.
Many who have barely finished reading [his works] grow weary and wish to lie down. This work, however, encompasses even his minor actions and presents his complete life;
it synthesizes a thousand chapters and stands alone as a singular exhortation, much like the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (Shiyi lun) of the Great Master Zhiyi at Mount Zigai.
Regarding the *Treasury of Jewels Treatise* (*Bao wang lun*), the *Wan shan tong gui* of Yongming, the *Tiger Creek Jewel Mirror of the Lotus School* (*Hu xi lian zong bao jian*),
the *Oral Questions of Tianru*, the *Direct Pointing of Ningjiang*, the *Pure Land Verses of Xizhai*, the *Dharma Compendium of Yunqi*, the *Warning Words for Cutting Off the Stream*,

and the various writings of other eminent figures within the realm— though one might attempt to encompass them all in a complete collection, it would be difficult to do so; and how could one possibly grasp their essence through mere fragments?
[Omission]. To serve as a substitute for the edict of the *liú rén* (the imperial herald), it is as if the celestial drum were resounding. I pray that all virtuous ones will listen with reverence.

Regarding those previously recorded as having attained rebirth, their accounts necessarily required corroborating evidence; yet, as such evidence was not heard of, many omissions and gaps resulted. Although...
However, though you do not behold his physical form, I pray that you examine his shadow. Simply purify your own mind; what need is there to wait for rebirth?
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If within the flying mind both merit and wisdom are combined, the mind will naturally open and one shall see the Buddhas of the ten directions."
One will be reborn in all pure lands according to one’s vows.

Thus we know that for the venerable masters such as Zigé, Tiānyī, Zhōngfēng, Tiānrú, Miàoyè, Kōnggǔ, and Hānshān, as well as the predecessors Chén Yíngzhōng and Fēng Jìchuān, there was a hidden cause;
their ultimate fruition was not in vain. To cast off the body and depart is to travel without shifting even a single step—what need is there to wait until the moment of death?

Only through ten recitations can one definitively attain rebirth. It is not appropriate to seek by following external traces, for that would lead further astray from the principles of the teachings. The *Wangsheng ji* (Anthology on Rebirth) regards only auspicious and virtuous conduct as supreme; it generally rejects and omits those who sacrifice their bodies and give up their lives, instead exalting only ordinary practices as being suited to the times. Although this may be considered a strategy of total safety, as for the matter at hand— [The text continues: ...it is like a person who, having fallen into a pit, seeks to escape by climbing out from the side of the pit. This is because they do not understand the principle of the "two gates" [of sudden and gradual]. If one does not know how to enter through the gate of the sudden, one will surely fail to exit through the gate of the gradual. It is difficult to generalize. The "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra" states that from his first aspiration for enlightenment, Vairocana Tathāgata practiced with unflagging diligence, offering up unspeakably unspeakable numbers of his own bodies and lives as alms.

This matter is explained in detail within the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*. Therefore, this record is compiled accordingly. Jing’ai sacrificed his body for the sake of the Dharma; Changmin forgot [his own life] out of compassion.

He rescued beings with his person; his compassionate heart was profound and vast, and his pure vows were firm and steadfast. As I repeatedly peruse his final instructions, I still harbor feelings of awe and urgency.
Furthermore, there were masters such as Shandao, Zhitong, Wenluan, Huicheng, and Chaocheng, who swiftly relinquished their retribution bodies to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
Their spiritual clarity remained settled, neither trembling nor wavering. This was because they dedicated [their merit] through the King of Vows of Samantabhadra.
Turning toward the Dharma-realm of Amitābha, rely upon this fierce resolve to attain non-retrogression in Bodhi. Such an example should simply be followed and studied;
how could it ever be lightly dismissed? One might then ask: "Should one not worry about Māras? It is said: "Māras and Buddhas exist only within a single mind.
If you simply prepare the correct cause, you will certainly achieve the perfect fruit. Understand that the four great elements are fundamentally empty, and the five aggregates..."
It is not existent. At the moment of casting off the body, it is like leaving behind traces or like shedding a cast-off skin;
who is the one that discards, and what is that which is discarded? Thus, the mountain of blades and the mass of fire are entirely the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
the jeweled trees and lotus ponds do not depart from their current location. This mind is the Buddha; this mind creates the Buddha. How could there be anything distant? It is just as in samādhi.

It has not yet been accomplished. Because the grasping at a self has not been transformed, one merely stirs up the emotions of longing and aversion, which incite the actions of acceptance and rejection.
I fear that when pressed by suffering and pain, afflictions will only grow stronger; it will be difficult to hope for the nine grades of rebirth, and Pāpīyān will find his opportunity.
This is precisely what Yung-ch'i feared. Those who practice in the Dharma-ending age should examine themselves with great urgency.

The accounts recorded by various scholars of the past vary in their degree of detail; as the refined and the vulgar are played together without discrimination, they cannot avoid being confused and erroneous.
Herein, I have weighed the old texts, consulted ancient records, and added refinements according to my own standards.
While ensuring that the essential meaning remains entirely consistent with the original intent, I have retained the original annotations from each source to provide clear corroboration.
In various texts concerning the Pure Land, the names of ancient virtuous masters are generally designated by the title "Teacher" (Shi).

However, in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), whenever a person has two names, only one character is cited. This record includes Buddhas and Bodhisattvas at the beginning, and officials and lay devotees at the end.

If names were not recorded, it would be quite difficult to maintain consistency; therefore, for the two groups of the ordained, following the precedent of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, only a single character is recorded.
For those who remain at home, following the examples of previous histories, both names are recorded.
The *Wǎngshēng jí* (Collection on Rebirth) records that Zhōu Xùzhī saw the Buddha at the moment of his death and passed away with palms joined.
However, upon examining various earlier histories and the *Dōnglín zhuàn* (Biographies of Donglin), this account is entirely absent; it must therefore belong to a later harmonization of traditions.

Furthermore, it records that Bái Lètiān, Sū Zǐzhān, and Zhāng Tiānjué—three individuals who were said to have been reborn in the Western Paradise based on an examination of their causes and effects. Now, as for Bái...
Although the Duke possessed the sincerity to dedicate his merit through this painted image, throughout his life his faith and devotion were mostly directed toward Tuṣita.

The textual evidence within his collected works is definitive; following the "Record of the Painting of Maitreya’s Ascent" and the "Record of the Painting of the Western Paradise," he inscribed both with the date of the third month of the fifth year of the Kaicheng era.
Some claim that he first sought Tuṣita and later turned toward An-yang (Sukhāvatī), but this is not the case. When Zizhan was bedridden with illness, he spoke to the Elder of Mount Jing-shan...
The verse of divination says: "To be liberated with such clarity is truly rare. When it comes to speaking of the Western Land, one says that the West is not non-existent;
yet, within this very point, one cannot apply effort. Now, those who cultivate the practice of Pure Land must possess three minds.

Regarding what are called the profound mind, the sincere mind, and the mind of dedication and aspiration—even down to the ten recitations at the moment of death—there has never been one that was attained without the application of effort.
To say that it cannot be attained through the application of effort implies that the three minds have not yet been fully realized.
It is difficult to guarantee rebirth. Layman Wu-jin has delved deeply into the source of the Dharma; his vision transcends the four seas.
Yet, the vow-text he has now recorded resembles that of an ignorant child and is quite like a humble plea for charity; it does not resemble the writings transmitted by others.
These accounts are likewise not to be trusted; therefore, I have deleted them all.

Regarding the various worthies recorded in the *Biographies of Laymen* (*Jushi zhuan*) and the *Biographies of Virtuous Women* (*Shannü zhuan*), I have strictly verified their past conduct; had there been any blemishes, they would not have been included.
For the most part, these matters have been set aside with brief dismissal. Here, we rely solely upon the final [attainment], disregarding past failings.
Thus, those such as Xiongjun and Weigong, or the likes of Zhonggui and Shanhe, once they have entered the lowest grade, are immediately included among the ranks of the sages;
all other cases may be understood by this principle. It is through this that one knows the power of Amitābha’s vows and the adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The great ocean does not reject the hundred rivers; the bright sun does not neglect even a single aperture. Should one but be willing to turn the mind, there is nothing discarded.
All who possess sentience should universally believe and accept this.
The foregoing are several points of my humble view; they should serve as a draft for the initial compilation.
I orally transmitted them to Xi Sou, and as each chapter was completed, I immediately revised and finalized it on the spot. Once the entire volume was complete, its general purport remained unerring.
I have further recorded these notes at the beginning of the scrolls to inform those who come after.
Recorded by the student of pure karma, Peng Jiqing,
from the Verses of the Record of Holy and Sages of the Pure Land,
composed by the disciple of pure karma, Peng Xisu.
How great is the mind of sentient beings! Subtle and wondrous, it is difficult to conceive. Ultimately like space, not a single dharma can be found;
Yet it is universally able to perform the work of a Buddha And bring the fruit of Bodhi to maturity.
In a single thought, one is unaware of oneself; Delusion and ignorance give rise to empty flowers, Sustained by the power of various karmic forces.
Establishing the lands of the ten directions, Within which all regions reside, For eighty-one million eons, Deluded thoughts have been without root or source.
The seven realms of existence revolve like a wheel;
One thoroughly understands that it is but a single mind, Wherein each thought interpenetrates every other, And every buddha-field is distinguished by its excellence or inferiority.
Some are adorned with pure jewels; some are heaps of rubble and filth. Some are brilliantly radiant;
some lack the light of the sun and moon. Some are the dwellings of bodhisattvas, peaceful and with immeasurable life;
some are inhabited by mixed classes of beings, where suffering abounds and joy is scarce. Some are filled with hungry ghosts.
The spirits in the depths cry out incessantly; some are born entirely in the hells, suffering the torments of being ground and crushed.
All Buddhas universally abide there, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
King Amitābha, the Great Vow-King, resolved his mind to take up a pure land and accomplished the Land of Peace and Bliss, which none throughout the ten directions can compare with.

Providing all manner of precious jewels that sentient beings love and delight in, those born from the blossoming flowers of the Perfectly Awakened One who hear the Dharma and realize the Unsurpassed, and those sentient beings from other realms who give rise to a heart of faith and longing—the Buddha’s power protects them all;
at the end of their lives, they attain rebirth there. Alas for those people devoid of wisdom!
Hearing these words, they are utterly deluded, not realizing this is the Pure Land.
Within a single thought-moment of an ordinary being, my mind fully manifests all Buddhas in brilliant clarity. Boundless lands of fragrant water are mutually filled with radiance;
by recollecting the Buddha, one sees the Buddha; by aspiring for rebirth, one is reborn there.
Just as when one takes a treasure from one’s own home, there is no obstruction whether moving east or west;
how excellent are these noble beings, who well understand the true nature of reality!
Knowing all phenomena to be like dreams, they do not hasten toward mere extinction, but in accordance with the sūtras, they adorn and purify the Buddha-lands. I now take refuge in them universally.
Praising and rejoicing with a heart of utmost sincerity, and with a profound heart of dedication, may I renounce this Sahā world and swiftly be born in a pure realm.
The power of the Buddha is ineffable, and the power of the mind is ineffable;
may that defiled and turbid abode be transformed entirely into a Lotus Treasury.

I have now finished speaking these verses; I prostrate to all the worthy sages and saints. May they extend the light from their white tufts of hair to gather in all beings, as numerous as motes of dust;
May their lotuses bloom in the mere snap of a finger, And may they all enter the field of enlightenment.

Section One: The Teacher of the Pure Land.
Amitābha Buddha, Amitābha Buddha. He is the Teacher of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. In the Sanskrit language, he is called Amitābha; this translates as "Immeasurable.

Because that Buddha’s radiance is immeasurable and his lifespan is immeasurable, he is named Amitābha. According to [the *Wu*...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "按無" (according to/consulting the *Wu*...). A full translation of the source text would require the remainder of the passage.*

In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, in the world of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja of the distant past, there was a king who, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, felt great joy in his heart and resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path. He abandoned his kingdom and renounced his royal status to become a śramaṇa named Dharmākara.
He went to the place where the Buddha Lokeśvararāja was and requested the Buddha to preach the Dharma. At that time, Lokeśvararāja...
King Buddha extensively expounded upon two hundred and ten billion buddha-fields, the virtues and evils of devas and humans, and the coarseness or excellence of those lands.

In accordance with their heart’s aspirations, he manifested them all for them to see. At that time, when those bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s description of the majestic and pure lands, they beheld them all and gave rise to unsurpassed, sublime vows; their resolve became serene.
His resolve was free from attachment. For five full kalpas, he contemplated and embraced the pure practices for adorning a Buddha-land.
Having cultivated these in this manner, he went to the place where that Buddha was and addressed him, saying: "I pray that you will listen and examine me;

I shall now fully declare my vows as I have made them. The first vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any beings in hell, hungry ghosts, or animals in my land, may I not [attain enlightenment].

I shall attain perfect enlightenment. Second Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should, after the end of their lives, fall again into the three evil realms, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Third Vow:

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not all be of a true golden color, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Fourth Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land...
If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be differences in physical form and appearance such that beings are either beautiful or ugly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the fifth vow.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not know their past lives, even to the extent of knowing the events of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the sixth vow.

I shall not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the sixth vow. If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the divine eye, such that they cannot see as few as hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the seventh vow.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the divine ear, such that they cannot hear as few as hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas...
Eighth Vow: "If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, there are those among the Buddhas who have spoken the Dharma that I do not fully receive and uphold, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

Ninth Vow: "If, upon my attaining Buddhhood, the devas and humans in my land should not possess the knowledge of others' minds—even to the extent of knowing the mental activities of sentient beings within hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands—may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

Ninth Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not possess the power of spiritual travel such that they cannot, in a single thought-moment, descend to traverse hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Tenth Vow:

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should give rise to conceptual thoughts or harbor attachments to their own bodies, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Eleventh Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood... [text continues]
"May I not attain perfect enlightenment if, upon becoming a Buddha, the gods and humans in my land do not abide in the stage of certainty and are not destined for final nirvana.

This is the twelfth vow. May I not attain perfect enlightenment if, when I have attained Buddhahood, my radiance has a limit, such that it does not extend downward to illuminate hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands.
This is the thirteenth vow. May I not attain perfect enlightenment if, when I have attained Buddhahood, my lifespan..."
The fourteenth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the śrāvakas in my land could be measured—

even if all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to become pratyekabuddhas and together calculate their number for hundreds of thousands of kalpas— should they be able to know that number, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

I shall attain perfect enlightenment. The fifteenth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the lifespan of the devas and humans in my land should not be immeasurable—except for those who, by their own original vows, have mastery over the length of their lives—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. The sixteenth vow: [As stated above].
Seventeenth Vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be even the sound of the name 'unwholesome' heard among the devas and humans in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Eighteenth Vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the immeasurable Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions should not all praise and extol my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Nineteenth Vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions..."
Those who, with a sincere heart, believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land—even if they recite my name but ten times—if they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment;
except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma. This is the nineteenth vow. If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions...
The twentieth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the ten directions who hear my name and fix their thoughts upon my land,
planting various roots of virtue, should not— upon the approach of their death— be surrounded by a great assembly and have me appear before them, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
First, with a sincere heart, I dedicate these merits; if those who wish to be born in my land do not achieve their goal, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

This is the twenty-first vow. Second, if upon my attainment of Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land do not all fully possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
This is the twenty-second vow. Third, if upon my attainment of Buddhahood, the various bodhisattvas from other Buddha-lands...
The assembly of bodhisattvas who come to be born in my land shall ultimately and inevitably reach the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

This excludes those who, by virtue of their original vows, have attained mastery over those they transform; for the sake of sentient beings, they don the armor of great vows, accumulate the roots of merit, and deliver all beings.

They travel through the lands of various Buddhas, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, make offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, and transform and enlighten beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

I vow that all sentient beings shall be established in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, transcending the practices of ordinary stages and manifesting the cultivation of Samantabhadra’s virtues before them.
If this were not so, I would not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the twenty-third vow.

I vow that within my land, the bodhisattvas, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual strength, shall be able to offer worship to all Buddhas; even in the time it takes for a single meal, they shall be unable to reach [the limit of] all... [worlds].
If, after passing through immeasurable billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, I do not attain perfect enlightenment—this is the twenty-fourth vow.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who manifest their roots of virtue before the various Buddhas should have any of their desired requisites for making offerings fail to appear as they wish, may I not attain perfect enlightenment—this is the twenty-fifth vow. If I...
If, upon attaining Buddhahood, there should be bodhisattvas in my land who are unable to expound all-knowledge, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

This is the twenty-sixth vow. If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be bodhisattvas in my land who do not obtain bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the twenty-seventh vow.

I shall not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the twenty-seventh vow: "If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land, as well as all things therein, were not pure, radiant, and immaculate;
if their forms and colors were not exceptionally distinguished, reaching the utmost subtlety and excellence such that they could not be measured;
and if among those sentient beings, even those who have attained the divine eye, there were none capable of clearly discerning their names and numbers—then may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

The twenty-eighth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land—even those of the least merit—should be unable to perceive and behold the immeasurable radiance and colors of the Bodhi-tree, which rises four million *li* high, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The twenty-ninth vow: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who receive and recite the Dharma..."
If, upon reciting and upholding [this teaching], one were unable to attain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the thirtieth vow.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land were such that their wisdom and eloquence could be measured or limited, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

The thirty-first vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, my land is not pure such that all the infinite, countless, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions are clearly reflected within it, as if one were looking at one's own face in a bright mirror—if this be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The thirty-second vow: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, from the ground..."

Thus it is. As for the void, the palaces and towers, the ponds, streams, flowering trees, and all the myriad things belonging to that land, they are all composed of countless varieties of miscellaneous jewels and hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense. They are exquisitely adorned and wondrously beautiful.
Surpassing all devas and humans, its fragrance universally perfumes the worlds of the ten directions. Any Bodhisattvas who smell it shall all cultivate the practices of a Buddha.
If it were not thus, I would not attain perfect enlightenment. The thirty-third vow:

Should I attain Buddhahood, may the various classes of sentient beings in the infinite and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, upon being touched by my light, [all become Bodhisattvas].
[His] body and mind will be supple and soft, surpassing those of devas and humans. If this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

The thirty-fourth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, among the classes of sentient beings in the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, there should be any who do not obtain the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and various profound *dhāraṇīs*, [may I not attain perfect enlightenment].
I shall attain perfect enlightenment. This is the thirty-fifth vow:

"If, when I become a Buddha, there should be women in any of the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who, upon hearing my name, rejoice with faith and delight and resolve to attain Bodhicitta; yet if they should not subsequently be born as men, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
If, after my life ends, those who loathe the female body should again take on a female form, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

This is the thirty-sixth vow. If, when I become a Buddha, the multitude of Bodhisattvas in the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should not constantly practice the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) from the end of their lives until they reach the path of Buddhahood, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the thirty-seventh vow.
If this be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. The thirty-seventh vow:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans of the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds in the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, bowing their heads in worship, and with joyful faith and delight cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva, such that all gods and people of the world do not pay them respect—if this be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. The thirty-eighth vow:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land who desire clothing should have them appear according to their thoughts—exquisite robes in accordance with the Dharma as praised by the Buddhas—spontaneously appearing upon their bodies, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be those who seek tailoring, pounding, dyeing, or washing [of robes], may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the thirty-ninth vow.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the joy experienced by the devas and humans in my land should not surpass that of a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted (āsravakṣaya), may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
This is the fortieth vow. If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not be able to see, at their will, the Buddhas of the ten directions...
Forty-first vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas from other lands who hear my name do not,
upon reaching the attainment of Buddhahood, possess all their faculties [in full perfection]..."
If, upon my attaining Buddhahood, there should be any deficiency or incompleteness [in these matters], may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the forty-second vow.
Furthermore, if upon my attaining Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of other lands who hear my name should all attain the samādhi of pure liberation;

and while abiding in this samādhi, in a single moment of thought, they should be able to make offerings to immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones—[if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment].
"Venerable One, may I not lose my concentration; if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the forty-third vow.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas from other lands who hear my name should, at the end of their lives, be born into noble and honorable families—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the forty-fourth vow. If, when I attain Buddhahood..."

If, when the multitude of bodhisattvas in other lands hear my name, they do not all experience such joy and exultation that they cultivate the bodhisattva practices and become fully endowed with the roots of virtue—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the forty-fifth vow.
Furthermore, if, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitude of bodhisattvas in other lands hear my name and all attain the sameness of universal [wisdom]...

[The Buddha] said: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any lack of clarity; or if, while abiding in this samādhi until the attainment of Buddhahood, I should not constantly behold all the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the forty-sixth vow.

Furthermore, if, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not naturally hear whatever Dharma they wish to hear according to their aspirations—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

[Attainment of] Perfect Enlightenment. The forty-seventh vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitude of Bodhisattvas in other lands who hear my name should not immediately reach the stage of non-retrogression, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. The forty-eighth vow."
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas from the lands of other quarters who hear my name do not immediately attain the first,
second, or third stage of dharma-patience, and if they cannot immediately attain non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas,
may I not attain perfect enlightenment. When the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken these forty-eight vows, the entire earth shook in six ways.
The earth shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down exquisite flowers. From the sky, voices praised him, saying: "He shall certainly and surely attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
After the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had established this vow, he focused his mind single-mindedly on adorning a wondrous land.
The Buddha-land he cultivated was vast and expansive, surpassingly sublime and uniquely marvelous; it was eternally established, without decay or change, beyond the reach of thought.
For immeasurable kalpas numbering in the trillions, they have accumulated and cultivated the boundless virtues of a bodhisattva;

they give rise neither to thoughts of desire, thoughts of anger, nor thoughts of harm, nor do they give rise to perceptions of desire, perceptions of anger, nor perceptions of harm; they are unattached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, and they have perfected the power of patience.
Disregarding all sufferings, they possess few desires and are content; free from defilement, anger, and delusion, they are ever tranquil in samādhi and unimpeded in wisdom.
They are devoid of hypocrisy and crookedness, maintaining a gentle countenance and kind speech, anticipating others' needs before they speak, and exerting themselves with courageous diligence.
With unwearied aspiration, they single-mindedly seek the pure and white Dharma to benefit and bring peace to all sentient beings. They revere the Triple Gem and serve their teachers and elders.
Adorned with great majesty and fully endowed with all practices, they cause the merits of all sentient beings to reach fulfillment.

Abiding in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they are without fabrication and without arising; they contemplate all phenomena as being like illusions and remain far removed from coarse speech. Themselves...
Harming others brings harm to oneself; harming both oneself and others brings harm to both. Cultivating virtuous speech benefits oneself and others; it benefits both self and person.
Abandoning the kingdom and relinquishing kingship, severing attachment to wealth and beauty, one practices the six *pāramitās* oneself and teaches others to do so.
Throughout incalculable eons, accumulating merit and virtue, wherever one is born, according to one’s wishes, immeasurable treasuries of jewels spontaneously manifest.
He should teach and transform countless sentient beings, establishing them in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
He may become a householder, a lay devotee, or one of noble and high-ranking lineage; or he may become a sovereign of various lands, a wheel-turning sage-king (cakravartin);

or he may become a lord of the six heavens of desire, even up to the King Brahmā. Constantly, by means of the four requisites, he provides offerings and pays respect to all Buddhas, as [described above].
These merits are beyond description. His breath is fragrant and pure like the *utpala* flower; from all the pores of his body issues the scent of *candana*.
This fragrance universally perfumes immeasurable worlds. His countenance is upright and handsome, and his marks and signs are exceptionally sublime.
From his hands, there constantly issued inexhaustible treasures—robes, food, drink, exquisite flowers, incense, silken canopies, banners, pennants, and various articles of adornment.
Such things surpassed those of all devas and humans; he attained mastery over all dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Dharmākara has now attained Buddhahood and resides in the West, at a distance of ten trillion *kṣetras* from here.
That Buddha-world is named Sukhāvatī. Since his attainment of Buddhahood, ten *kalpas* have passed. Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"In the past, beyond *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a world named Sandalavana and a *kalpa* named Susthitā."
There was a wheel-turning king named Araṇemin who, in the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, gave rise to the bodhicitta and made a vow to take up a pure land.
The Buddha immediately bestowed upon him a prophecy: "To the west, passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddha-fields, there is the world-realm of the Tathāgata Ghoṣarāja.
After one asaṃkhyeya-kalpa as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you shall enter the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
During this *kalpa*, the world will be renamed "Peaceful Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*). At that time, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named the Tathāgata Immeasurable Life (*Amitāyus*).

With single-minded diligence, I practiced for three weeks. If one possesses merit, they will immediately see the Tathāgata appearing before them;
however, those who have created obstacles through evil karma in previous lives and cannot see him—if they can practice with single-minded intensity...
Exerting effort without retreat and free from other thoughts, one will again quickly attain vision. Why is this?
If there is one who seeks unsurpassed bodhi and practices with single-minded devotion toward even a single matter, there is nothing that will not be accomplished.
It is, for example, as if a person were to drink a single handful of water from the great ocean; they would have thereby drunk all the river waters within Jambudvīpa. Thus it is with the Bodhisattva.
If one can cultivate this ocean of bodhi, then one has already cultivated all samādhis, all patiences, all stages, and all dhāraṇīs.
Therefore, one should always practice with diligent effort and without indolence, remaining free from negligence, binding the mind in single-minded recollection.
One must cause the Buddha to appear before oneself through such cultivation. When first seeing the Buddha, one should reflect:

"Is this the true Buddha, or is it a mere image? Knowing that the image seen arises from mental conception (*saṃjñā*), one realizes that even all the true Buddhas, down to those occupying a space as small as a hair-tip within empty space, are likewise so; they are like empty space, equal and without distinction.
The Buddha is created by one's own mind; apart from the mind, there is no Buddha. This applies even to all Buddhas of the three periods of time:
they are likewise thus, being entirely non-existent and existing only in dependence upon one's own mind. If a bodhisattva can thoroughly understand all Buddhas and all phenomena in this way...

All are but the measure of mind-only. Having attained the patient endurance that accords with reality (anulomikī-kṣānti), they either enter the first stage (bhūmi) and, upon casting off the body, are swiftly reborn in the world of Abhirati, or are born within the pure Buddha-land of Sukhāvatī, where they constantly behold the Tathāgata and personally receive his offerings. According to this scriptural passage:
This is in harmony with the *Sūtra on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha*. Those who cultivate the practice of purity must not neglect it.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva—Mañjuśrī is also called Mañjuśrī or Mañjuśrī; this is translated as "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*) and also as "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Miaojixiang*). He was born...
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the home of the Brahmin Brahmadeva in the village of Tāla, he was born from the mother’s right side.

His body was the color of purple gold; upon touching the ground, he was able to speak, and he subsequently left the household life in the presence of the Buddha (as seen in the *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*).
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* states: "In the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a world in the southern direction named Samatā."
The Buddha named Dragon-Lineage-Supreme Tathāgata is none other than Mañjuśrī.

The *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* states that the Buddha Joy-Treasury-Maṇi-Jewel-Accumulation in the world Constantly Joyful to the north is none other than Mañjuśrī. Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
When Amitābha Buddha was a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), he was the third prince, named Rājasaṃgha. In the presence of Ratnagarbha Buddha,
he resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, vowing that in future lives he would practice the bodhisattva path without limit,
adorning buddha-fields so that worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges within the trichiliocosm would be transformed.
The Buddha-lands of the ten directions become a single buddha-field, filled with great jewels. Furthermore, there is no harsh touch, nor are there any women, even their names do not exist;
nor are there śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the like. It is filled with bodhisattvas who are in their final birth.

The Buddha then bestowed upon him the name Mañjuśrī. In a future age, in a world in the southern direction named Vimala-viśuddha-ratna-sthāpana, he will attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and be known as the Tathāgata Samantamukha-pratyakṣa.
The *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* states: At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished preaching the *buddhanusmṛti-samādhi* for the great assembly, Mañjuśrī...
The Bodhisattva Viśeṣamati again addressed the great assembly, saying: "In the past, during the time of the Tathāgata Ratnatejas, there was a son of a householder named Śīlarakṣita.
While still in his mother’s womb, he received the three refuges. When he reached the age of eight, his parents invited the Buddha to their home for offerings.
As the youth saw the Buddha walking with peaceful and slow steps, flowers sprang up beneath his feet, and a great radiance shone forth."
Having seen him, he was filled with joy and paid homage to the Buddha. Having paid homage, he gazed intently at him, his eyes never wavering for a moment.
By seeing the Buddha even once, he was able to eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas.
From that time forward, he constantly encountered Buddhas as numerous as the sands of ten billion nayutas of Ganges Rivers. All these World-Honored Ones preached in this same manner.
Through the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, thereafter one million Buddhas appeared, all bearing the same name: Candanasāgara.
At that time, the youth personally attended upon these Buddhas without interruption, prostrating to them, making offerings, and joining his palms in contemplation of the Buddha.
By the power of the causes and conditions of this merit from contemplating the Buddha, he further encountered ten million *asaṃkhyeya* Buddhas, and from that point onward...
Thereafter, he immediately attained a hundred trillion *buddhānusmṛti-samādhis* and a million *asaṃkhyeya* *vartanī-dhāraṇīs*.
Having attained these, all Buddhas appeared before him and preached the Dharma of signlessness (*animitta*). In a mere moment, he attained the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*.

At that time, because that youth had received the three refuges and had paid a single prostration to the Buddha, he contemplated the marks of the Buddha with focused attention, his mind free from [distraction].

“[He was] weary and exhausted. By virtue of these causes and conditions, he encountered countless Buddhas; how much more so for one who fixes their mindfulness and fully contemplates, observing the Buddha’s form-body?
At that time, was that youth anyone else? It was none other than myself. The Buddha told Ānanda:
‘Hold the words of Mañjuśrī and proclaim them everywhere to the great assembly and to sentient beings of future ages: if there are those who can perform prostrations,’”
If one is able to recollect the Buddha or is able to contemplate the Buddha, it should be known that this person is no different from Mañjuśrī.
Furthermore, the *Mañjuśrī-praṇidhāna-sūtra* is largely identical to the final verse at the end of the "Universal Worthy’s Vows" (*Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*) chapter.
The conclusion says: "May I, at the time of my life's end, Have all obstacles extinguished; May I behold Amitābha face-to-face And be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Having been born in that Buddha-land, May I fulfill all great vows; May the Tathāgata Amitābha Appear before me and bestow upon me a prophecy.
May I purify the practices of Samantabhadra And fulfill the aspirations of Mañjuśrī. Throughout all kalpas until the end of the future, May I reach the ultimate state of Bodhi."

Regarding the practices of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, the two sages of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the conduct and vows they set forth, their preaching of the Dharma, and their saving of sentient beings are all invariably based upon the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) and take the Pure Land as their ultimate refuge.
In this world, there are those who cling to the *Avataṃsaka* while disparaging the Pure Land.
One should know what is reflected therein.
When the Venerable Āṭavaka was about to enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees at the birthplace of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara, the Buddha— [for him]— said:
The devas and humans spoke various Dharmas. They further addressed Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, in a future age, in the land of Northern India, there shall appear in the world a bhikṣu named Gopaka.

He will have planted roots of goodness under immeasurable hundreds of Buddhas in the past; he will possess profound faith, having made offerings and paid respect, and will dwell securely in the Mahāyāna."
Out of a desire to have compassion for, benefit, and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, he gave rise to such a mind:
to be widely learned and uphold the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; to praise the Mahāyāna and manifest the Mahāyāna;

and to fashion immeasurable images of the Tathāgata as well as various stūpas and temples, thereby enabling the multitudes of devas and humans to give rise to faith and joy in their hearts. That bhikṣu Gopaka cultivated...

Having measured these various most excellent roots of merit for awakening, he passed away and was reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Life, located to the west beyond hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-worlds.
There, in the presence of that Buddha, he planted various roots of merit.
Furthermore, he practiced the holy life under eighty billion Tathāgatas. By virtue of these roots of merit, in a future age, beyond...

After ninety-nine billion kalpas, he attained perfect enlightenment; the Buddha was named Vimalaprabha (Stainless Light), and the world was named Sarvaguṇavyūha (Adorned with All Merits) (*Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*).
Venerable Aśvaghoṣa:
"Aśvaghoṣa" is the Sanskrit term. He was a Brahmin from the kingdom of Saṃkīrti in Eastern India.

He received the Dharma from Venerable Yaśas and once composed the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in Mahāyāna). In his final years, he exhorted people to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.

The Earth Deity said: "Sentient beings dwelling in this Sahā world may fear that they will not always be able to encounter the Buddhas to personally receive their teachings and make offerings to them;
they may dread that their faith will be difficult to perfect and thus intend to retreat. You should know that the Tathāgata possesses a supreme skillful means to protect and sustain such faith:
namely, through the causal conditions of single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha, one shall be born in the Pure Land according to one's vow."
In that buddha-field, one shall constantly behold the Buddha and forever leave the evil realms behind. As it is said in the Sūtra:

"If a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and dedicates their cultivated roots of goodness with the vow to be born in that world, they will immediately attain rebirth there.
Because they constantly behold the Buddha, they shall never fall back. If one contemplates the True Suchness (Tathatā) of that Buddha..."
He constantly and diligently cultivated the Dharma-body until it was ultimately realized;

because he abided in right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), after entrusting the Dharma to the Venerable Kāpimāra, he immediately entered the Dragon’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi (*nāga-vikrīḍita-samādhi*) and rose up into the void like the orb of the sun.
Returning to his original station, he entered nirvāṇa (*Chuan deng lu* and *Dacheng qixin lun*).
Venerable Nāgārjuna—Nāgārjuna in Sanskrit—is of Brahmin descent from the Southern Land of India. He received the Dharma from...

When the Venerable Kāpimāla intended to extensively expound the scriptural teachings, the Bodhisattva Mahānāga immediately used his supernatural powers to escort him into the palace of the ocean dragon king.
There, he opened a casket of the seven precious gems and was granted various Vaipulya sūtras. Within ninety days, he attained a profound and extensive understanding of them.
The dragon king then sent him out from the palace, and he returned to the kingdom of India, where he widely propagated the gift of the Dharma. He once composed the *Vibhāṣā*...
In the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there is a verse praising Amitābha, which states in brief:
"If a person aspires to become a Buddha and mindfully recollects Amitābha, he shall manifest his body at that very moment; therefore, I take refuge in him.

By the power of that Buddha’s original vow, bodhisattvas from the ten directions come to make offerings and listen to the Dharma; therefore, I bow my head in prostration. The bodhisattvas of that land are complete..."
Adorned with all the marks and signs, you have graced your own bodies; I now take refuge in and pay homage to those great Bodhisattvas.

Day after day, at the three times, they make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions; therefore, I bow my head in reverence. If a person plants roots of goodness, yet harbors doubt, the flower will not open.
For one whose mind of faith is pure, the flower opens and they behold the Buddha. By the Buddhas currently present in the ten directions...
Through various causes and conditions, I praise the merits of that Buddha; I now take refuge in and pay homage to him. His land is fully adorned, surpassing the palaces of all the devas;

his merits are exceedingly profound and vast, and for this reason I prostrate at the Buddha’s feet. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* establishes the method for practicing the Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*) samādhi, stating:
"The Buddha-recollection samādhi can eliminate various afflictions as well as [the karmic obstacles of] previous lives."
As for the remaining samādhis: some are able to eliminate lust but cannot eliminate anger; some are able to eliminate anger but cannot eliminate lust;
some are able to eliminate delusion but cannot eliminate lust and anger; some are able to eliminate the three poisons but cannot eliminate the karmic offenses of previous lives.
This *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, however, is able to eliminate all manner of afflictions and all manner of offenses. Furthermore, as for the *buddhānusmṛti*...
It is profound. It possesses great merit and is able to deliver sentient beings.

Among all the various samādhis through which these bodhisattvas wish to deliver sentient beings, none possess such merit as this Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) for swiftly extinguishing all transgressions.

Furthermore, the Buddha is the Dharma King and the bodhisattvas are the Dharma Generals; he who is most honored and revered is solely the World-Honored One, the Buddha. Therefore, one should constantly practice the remembrance of the Buddha.
For example, it is like a high minister who, having received exceptional favor, constantly thinks of his sovereign. The Bodhisattva is also like this:

knowing that all various merits and immeasurable wisdom are obtained from the Buddha, he constantly recollects the Buddha because he recognizes the gravity of this debt of gratitude. Furthermore, it is said:
"One who desires not to be separated from the Buddhas" refers to a Bodhisattva who, in every lifetime they are born, always encounters the Buddhas. Question: Regarding the Bodhisattva...
"When one transforms sentient beings, why is it that one always desires to encounter a Buddha? Answer:

"Because there are those who have not yet entered the stage of a bodhisattva, have not attained *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), and have not received a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). If they distance themselves from the Buddhas, they will destroy their roots of goodness and sink into afflictions;
being unable to save themselves, how could they possibly save others? It is like a person traveling by boat who, having been wrecked in midstream, wishes to cross [to the other shore]..."

It is like another person who, instead of helping themselves, sinks into the water. Or it is like a small amount of hot water poured into a great pool of ice: although it melts a small portion, it instead causes that very spot to freeze over again.

A Bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stage of the Dharma-position (*dharmatā*), if they distance themselves from the Buddhas and, with only slight merit and a lack of skillful means (*upāya-bala*), attempts to transform sentient beings, may provide some slight benefit, but will instead fall back into ruin. Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess *nirvāṇa*...
...benefit others. Because they lack omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they cannot instruct bodhisattvas;
because the Buddhas possess the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are able to instruct bodhisattvas. It is like an elephant sinking in the mud: no other elephant can pull it out.
If a bodhisattva enters a non-path, only a Buddha can rescue them, for they share the same Great Path. Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects: "I have not yet attained..."
The Buddha-eye is no different from being blind. If one is not guided by the Buddha, there is no direction to follow; one may mistakenly enter other paths.
Even if one hears the Buddha-dharma, if one practices in a different manner, one will not know the proper timing for conversion or the extent of the methods of practice.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees the Buddha—whether seeing him with the eyes or through mental purity—and hears what he teaches, the mind then delights in the Dharma and attains it.
With great wisdom, one attains liberation by practicing in accordance with the Dharma. Such benefits, equal to those of the Buddha, are immeasurable;
how could one not single-mindedly seek to behold the Buddha?

Just as an infant should not be separated from its mother, a traveler from his provisions, one suffering great heat from cool breezes and cold water, one suffering great cold from fire, or one crossing deep waters from a boat.
A patient does not part from a skilled physician; likewise, a bodhisattva does not part from the Buddhas. This surpasses all other matters;
neither parents, relatives, friends, nor kings and deities can benefit one as much as the Buddha.

The Buddha benefits all bodhisattvas, leading them away from places of suffering and establishing them on the ground of the World-Honored One. Question: How is it that they do not part from the Buddhas? Answer: Sentient beings possess...

Regarding the causes and conditions for offenses committed over immeasurable kalpas: although one may practice merit, if wisdom is meager, [the result is limited]; although one may practice wisdom, if merit is meager, [the result is limited].
A Bodhisattva seeking the Buddha-way must practice both the patience toward beings (*sattvakṣānti*) and the patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*).

Because they practice patience toward beings, they give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings; thereby they extinguish the offenses of immeasurable kalpas and attain immeasurable merit. Because they practice patience toward phenomena...
He destroys the ignorance regarding all phenomena and attains immeasurable wisdom. Through the union of these two practices, he is never separated from the Buddhas in life after life.
Furthermore, because the bodhisattva constantly delights in mindfulness of the Buddha, whenever he casts off one body and receives another, he always encounters a Buddha.

Just as sentient beings who habitually indulge in desire with heavy intent receive the bodies of lustful birds, and those with an excess of hatred are born among poisonous insects, the bodhisattva does not [fall into such states].
One values the noble wheel-turning sage-kings and the blissful fortune of humans and devas; yet, because one contemplates the Buddhas, one receives a physical form according to what the mind esteems.

Furthermore, because a bodhisattva constantly and skillfully cultivates the causal conditions of the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, they always encounter the Buddhas in their births, as described in the *Pratyutpanna-buddha-saṃmukhāvasthita-samādhi-sūtra*:
when a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, they immediately see [the Buddhas] being born in the Pure Land.
In the Land of Amitābha, after entrusting the Dharma to the Venerable Gaṇadeva, he entered samādhi and departed like a cicada shedding its shell.
According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Mahāmati, you should know that after the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata, there will be in a future age one who upholds my Dharma, in the land of South India, of great fame and virtue."
There was a bhikṣu named Nāgārjuna, who was able to refute the tenets of existence and non-existence.

In this world, he manifested my Unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma and attained the first stage, the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), whereupon he was reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Seven hundred years after the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, [he appeared].
Then Nāgārjuna appeared in the world, precisely fulfilling the Buddha’s prophecy (*Record of the Transmission of the Lamp*, *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*).
The Master Vasubandhu—Vasubandhu in Sanskrit—was a native of Puḷukṣa in India. Having left the household life, he delighted in hearing the Dharma.
The Śrāvaka school [of Vasubandhu] had habitually disparaged the Mahāyāna sūtras. Later, upon hearing his elder brother Asaṅga reciting the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, he was moved to realization.
He repented his former transgressions and intended to cut out his own tongue. Asaṅga stopped him, saying: "In the past you used this tongue to disparage the Mahāyāna;
now use this tongue to praise the Mahāyāna. To rectify past errors and renew yourself in this way is still a virtuous thing. To cut out your tongue and silence yourself..."
Lì'ān was present there. Vasubandhu then applied himself with refined precision and profound contemplation, composing over a hundred Mahāyāna treatises, all of which have circulated in the world.
Among these, he composed the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra-śāstra*, which elucidates the Pure Land by establishing the five gates of mindfulness:
first, prostration; second, praise; third, making vows; fourth, observation; and fifth, dedication. He prefaced it with a verse, saying: "O World-Honored One, I..."
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in the Tathāgata Unobstructed Light throughout the ten directions. May I be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.

Relying upon the sūtras and the characteristics of true merit, I shall now recite this dhāraṇī of aspiration verses, which accords with the Buddha’s teaching. Contemplate the appearance of that world:
it surpasses the paths of the triple realm; it is ultimately like empty space, vast and without limit. It is the Great Path...
Compassion gives rise to supramundane roots of goodness. Pure radiance is fully perfected, like the orbs of the sun and moon in a mirror.
Endowed with the nature of all precious gems, it is replete with wondrous adornments. Stainless light blazes intensely, shining brightly and purely upon the world.

Grasses of the nature of jewels and merit are soft and curl to the left and right; those who touch them experience supreme bliss, surpassing even the kāñcana and tinduka trees. A thousand jewel flowers...
Ten thousand varieties cover the ponds, streams, and springs. A gentle breeze stirs the flowers and leaves; their interlacing radiance swirls in confusion.
The palaces and various towers allow unobstructed views in the ten directions. Trees of diverse forms emit varied lusters, while jeweled railings encircle them everywhere.
Immeasurable jewels are interwoven, and nets spread throughout the void. Various bells produce resonant sounds, proclaiming the sublime Dharma. Flowers and garments rain down.
Adorned and magnificent, immeasurable fragrances are universally diffused. The Buddha’s wisdom is a bright and pure sun that dispels the darkness of worldly delusion.

With a Brahma-voice deep and far-reaching, its subtle and wondrous resonance is heard throughout the ten directions. Amitābha, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Dharma King who skillfully sustains all, is surrounded by a host of Tathāgatas’ pure lotuses.

These beings are born through transformation from the flowers of the Perfectly Awakened One; they delight in the flavor of the Buddha-Dharma and take dhyāna and samādhi as their food, forever free from the body.
With a mind of longing, I constantly and without interruption take delight in the realm of the Mahāyāna roots of goodness, which is free from even the name of reproach.
There, women and those with impaired faculties, as well as those of the two vehicles, are not born. It can fully satisfy all the aspirations and desires of sentient beings;
therefore, I vow to be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, upon a subtle, pure lotus pedestal of immeasurable great jewel-kings, radiant with the marks and signs of perfection.
One fathom in height, his physical form transcends all living beings. The Tathāgata’s subtle and wondrous voice, like the resonance of Brahmā, is heard throughout the ten directions.

Like earth, water, fire, wind, and space, it is free from discrimination. From the ocean of pure wisdom, the assembly of devas and humans—the immovable multitude—arises. Like Sumeru, the King of Mountains, he is supreme and unsurpassed.
The host of devas, humans, and great men circumambulate him with reverence and gaze upon him in adoration. Thus they contemplate the Buddha’s original...
Through the power of his vows, no encounter with him is ever in vain; he is able to swiftly fulfill the great ocean of jewels of merit.
In the pure Land of Peace and Bliss, he constantly turns the stainless wheel, appearing as the sun of the transformation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Like Mount Sumeru, he abides and sustains all;

with the light of stainless adornment, in a single thought-moment and at every instant, he shines universally upon the assemblies of all Buddhas, benefiting all living beings by raining down celestial music.
With offerings of fine robes, exquisite incense, and the like, I praise the Buddha’s manifold virtues with a mind free from discrimination.
In whichever world the jewels of the Buddha’s Dharma and merit do not exist, I vow to be reborn there all, manifesting the Buddha’s Dharma just as the Buddha does.

Having composed this treatise and these verses, I pray to behold Amitābha Buddha; together with all sentient beings, may we be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. [This concludes] the daily practice.
He practiced the visualization of Tuṣita Heaven, vowing to behold Maitreya. Six months after he passed away, he manifested his form and told Asaṅga:
"I have already been born before Maitreya" (*Wǔliàngshòujīnglùn Fānyìmìngyì*).
The Bodhisattva Jue-ming-miao-xing descended upon Wumen in the sixteenth year of the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty, continuing until the fourth year of the Shunzhi era of our present dynasty.
Due to past karmic conditions, he responded to the capacities of sentient beings to preach the Dharma, opening and elucidating the Pure Land teaching. First...
He spoke in verse: "The essential Dharma of all Buddhas is subtle, secret, and inconceivable. Because it is beyond thought, no one can fully proclaim it.
Yet the Great Compassionate Father, the Muni who pities sentient beings, speaks that which cannot be spoken, guiding them through this life and into the next.
Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful expedients, he reveals the Land of Peace and Bliss, causing them to resolve to be reborn there and thus cross over [samsara] horizontally."

Regarding all evil destinies: through the great vows of the Buddha Amitābha, which gather in all beings, those who hear his name and are able to uphold it will certainly be born [in the Pure Land] without doubt.
If there are those with great power who focus their minds with constant one-pointedness and achieve profound samādhi, they shall see the Buddha manifest before them.
Now, following the Buddha’s teaching, I shall open the gate of conversion and guidance; mindful of your delusions and inversions, I point clearly toward [the path].

This is the path of right cultivation. It is no small or insignificant cause; one should conceive the thought that it is difficult to encounter. Though the Western Land is ten thousand *billion* leagues away, a single moment of faith reaches it immediately.
Furthermore, it is said: "The single gate of the Pure Land shown here is truly the heart-essence of all Buddhas and the direct path for humans and devas."
Now, although you all seek rebirth in that land, if your aspiration is not earnest, it will be like entering the sea without obtaining a precious jewel;
your toil will be in vain and of no benefit. In the past, during the time of Emperor Ming of the Jin dynasty, I received the body of a poor man. Because of my poverty and suffering, I...
He then made a great vow, saying: "Because of my past karma, I have received this bitter retribution.
If today I do not behold Amitābha Buddha, be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and accomplish all merits and virtues, I shall lose my life rather than ever withdraw from this resolve.
Having sworn this oath, he focused his mind with single-minded diligence for seven days and seven nights; thereupon, his mind was opened, and he beheld Amitābha.
The Tathāgata’s marks and signs and his radiance pervade the worlds of the ten directions.
Before the Buddha, I personally received the prediction that in the future, at the age of seventy-five, I would pass away by sitting in meditation and be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Later, because the vow to deliver sentient beings was weighty, I returned to this land to manifest transformations according to various circumstances—sometimes as a bhikṣu, sometimes as a layperson, sometimes as a king, or sometimes as a minister.

As a ruler, or as a woman, or as a butcher or a beggar—whether hidden or manifest, whether conforming or contrary—he always preached the Dharma in accordance with [the needs of beings] to guide all classes of creatures.
Now, he has once again appeared for you to clarify the heterodox and the orthodox, and to proclaim the glory of the Pure Land.

"You all should be single-minded and focused. Cultivate this gate with steadfastness, and you will certainly not err. If your resolve is unified and firm, you need not wait for a future life to be born;
you shall behold the Buddha even in the present life. As a verse says: 'Speak but a single word, recite the Buddha's name but once;
strike the thought-moment until it dies, and I grant that your Dharma-body lives. Someone asked about the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation):"
"If you cannot concentrate the mind, what expedient means should be employed? The Bodhisattva replied, "You need only cease deliberate contemplation and recite slowly.

Huiyuan.

Huiyuan’s secular surname was Jia; he was a native of Loufan in Yanmen. From his youth, he was fond of learning and extensively mastered the Six Classics, being particularly proficient in the *Zhuangzi*.
In his old age, Shi Dao’an established a monastery on Mount Heng in the Taihang range. Huiyuan traveled there from afar to take refuge with him.

Upon hearing Dao’an lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained sudden and profound enlightenment. He subsequently cast aside his hairpin (to renounce secular life) and received formal instruction, engaging in diligent contemplation and recitation day and night.

Dao’an sighed in admiration, saying, "He who shall cause the Way to flow to the eastern lands is surely this Huiyuan. In the sixth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he passed through Xunyang.
Seeing that Mount Lu was secluded and spacious, providing a suitable place for him to dwell, he established a vihāra which he named Longquan Temple.

At that time, Huiyong, a fellow disciple of Huiyuan, was already residing at Xilin on the western side of Mount Lu; he wished to invite Huiyuan to live with him there. However, as Huiyuan’s circle of disciples gradually increased, Xilin became cramped and could no longer accommodate them.
Consequently, the Regional Inspector Huan Yi established another temple for Huiyuan on the eastern side of the mountain, which was subsequently named Donglin (East Forest).
Huiyuan thereupon led the assembly in the practice of the Way. He excavated a pond and planted lotuses, upon which he erected a twelve-petaled lotus flower that rotated with the waves;
by this means, he measured the divisions of day and night to establish the intervals for their practice.
Subsequently, one hundred and twenty-three men of pure faith from the four quarters arrived, having heard of his reputation. Huiyuan said, "As for your coming here, you have been able to..."

Was he not intent upon the Pure Land? He therefore fashioned images of the Three Sages of the West, established a vegetarian fast and a religious society, and commissioned Liu Yimin to compose a "Text of Vows," which was engraved upon stone.
At that time, Wang Qiao and several others further composed poems on the *Nianfo Sanmei* (Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection) to manifest their aspirations.
Huiyuan wrote a preface for them, stating: "Now, what is meant by 'samādhi'? It is the single-minded contemplation and silent visualization."
This is what is meant by that. When thought is concentrated, the will becomes one and undivided. When contemplation is still, the vital energy (*prāṇa*) becomes empty and the spirit becomes clear.

When the vital energy is empty, wisdom awakens and its illumination shines forth; when the spirit is clear, there is no obscurity it does not penetrate. These two are the primordial seals of nature; they converge into one to bring about their function.
Furthermore, among the various *samādhis*, there are many names; yet for those whose merit is high and who advance easily, the practice of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*) is [the best].

First, what is this? It is the ultimate quiescence that exhausts the source; the Honored One is titled the Tathāgata. His essence is divine and harmonizes with transformation, responding without fixed direction.
Therefore, those who enter this samādhi become dark and oblivious, forgetting all cognition. Yet, by means of the very object of perception, they achieve discernment.
When this discernment is clear, internal illumination reflects back and forth, and the myriad phenomena arise. Though beyond the reach of ears and eyes, hearing and seeing proceed. Thus it is said:
The numinous aspect is profoundly unified; its clarity and purity are spontaneous. When the primordial resonance strikes the heart, obstructed emotions melt into lucidity.
Were it not for the ultimate subtlety of all under heaven, who could participate in this? Therefore, the worthies who uphold the Dharma all contemplate the accord of a single principle.
