Huishong was a native of Liangzhou. During the time of Emperor Wu of the Tuoba Wei, he served as the gate-teacher (men-shi) to the Minister of State Han Wande;
together with Shi Shigao, they were both held in high esteem by their contemporaries. It so happened that Crown Prince Huang committed an offense, and the matter implicated both Shigao and Huishong.
Thereupon, he simultaneously beheld both the Dharma and the Sangha. Fada, who had long admired Gao’s lofty virtue and conduct, wept with grief and longing, fasting for several days.
Suddenly, Gao appeared, flying through the air. After Fada had prostrated himself in worship, he asked where both the Master and Master Chong were currently reborn.
Tangao said, "I vowed to be born in an evil age to rescue and protect sentient beings; thus I have returned to be born here in this Jambudvīpa.

Master Chong had always prayed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), and now his wish has indeed been fulfilled. Having finished speaking, he vanished. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*)

Tanjian (d. 540). His secular surname was Zhao, and he was a native of Jizhou. He left home to become a monk at an early age and served Zhu Daizu as his teacher. He maintained a vegetarian diet and wore simple cloth garments;

his observance of the Vinaya was rigorous and austere. Later, he traveled abroad to propagate the teachings, eventually reaching Jingzhou, where he resided at Xin Temple in Jiangling. He was sixty years old [at the time].
He was over ten years old. Whatever slight merit he had accumulated throughout his life, he invariably dedicated toward the Western Pure Land, vowing to behold the Buddha.
One day, while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he saw Amitābha Buddha, who sprinkled water upon his face and said, "I wash away your defilements and purify your thoughts;

both your body and speech are now entirely adorned and pure. Furthermore, the Buddha drew a single lotus flower from a vase and bestowed it upon him. Upon arising from his concentration, [he found the flower there].
He then entrusted his final affairs to others and conversed with the monastery monks on the theme of impermanence.

When night was deep and the other monks had retired to their rooms, he walked alone along the corridor, reciting the Buddha’s name until the fifth watch. His voice grew increasingly resonant. At dawn, when his disciples came as usual to inquire after him, they found him sitting cross-legged, motionless.
Upon approaching to look at him, they saw that he had passed away. He was seventy years old. At that time, there was also the monk Daohai of Jiangling.
Shi Huikan of Beizhou, Shi Huigong of Dongzhou, Shi Tanhong of Huainan, Shi Daoguang of Mount Dongyuan, and Shi Daoguang of Hongnong—
all vowed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), and at the time of their deaths, each manifested auspicious signs (from the *Gaoseng zhuan*, "Pure Land Texts").
Huītong (慧通), whose secular surname was Huītong, was a native of Guanzhong. In his youth, he resided at Tàihòu Temple in Cháng'ān, where he maintained a vegetarian diet and recited dharanis.

He chanted the *Ekottarika Āgama* and studied the practice of dhyāna under the Chan Master Huìshào of Liangzhou, receiving instruction in the contemplative methods of the Dharma-gate. He traveled extensively in many places.

Ren constantly prayed for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). One day, while suffering from a slight illness, he saw a person appear within his state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);

the figure was exceedingly dignified and noble. The person addressed him, saying, "The auspicious time has arrived. Shortly thereafter, he beheld Amitāyus Buddha, whose radiance was brilliantly resplendent.

He emerged from meditative concentration and informed his fellow students of all that had occurred. Having finished speaking, he passed away by transformation. A rare fragrance lingered for three days before fading.
He was fifty-nine years old (*Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Tanhong, Tanhong.
A native of Huanglong, he cultivated the practice of the precepts from his youth and specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka.
He traveled south to Jiaozhi, where he recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* countless times. During the Yongchu era, he traveled to Panyu and stayed at Taishi Temple; later, he went to Mount Xian in Jiaozhi.
At the temple, he recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).

In the second year of the Xiaojian era, he gathered firewood on the mountain and secretly went to the pile to immolate himself with fire. His disciples rushed to embrace him and brought him back; half of his body was already charred.
After a month, his condition slightly improved. He entered a valley once more to perform self-immolation. His disciples pursued him to rescue him, but his life had already ended.

Thereupon, they piled up firewood and set it ablaze; by the following morning, the body was entirely consumed. On that day, the villagers all saw Huihong’s body, golden in color, riding a golden deer and traveling westward with great haste.
Only then did the monastics and laypeople realize his divine and extraordinary nature, and they collected his remains for burial. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*)

Huijin, whose secular surname was Yao, was a native of Wuxing. In his youth, he followed his impulses as a wandering knight-errant. At the age of forty, he suddenly attained awakening through the spontaneous opening of his own mind and subsequently left the household life.
He resided at Gaozuo Temple in the capital, where he maintained a vegetarian diet and wore plain garments, vowing to recite the Lotus Sutra with diligent application of mind.

He suffered from illness; whenever he took up a volume [of scripture], his sickness would flare up. He then made a vow to produce one hundred copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to repent for his previous obstacles.

Thereupon, he gathered various offerings of faith and produced a full hundred copies of the sutra. His illness soon abated, and his rigorous resolve became even firmer. He constantly dedicated all his meritorious deeds, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).
Suddenly, he heard a voice from the air saying: "Your vows are already fulfilled; you shall certainly attain rebirth in the Western Land."
In the third year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, he passed away without illness at the age of eighty-five (*Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
As for Daozhen:
his origins are unknown. At the beginning of the Liang dynasty, he resided on Mount Lu and practiced the visualization of Amitābha; however, his mind still...
He was hesitant. One night he dreamed of a person on a boat in the great ocean who said they were going to the land of Amitābha Buddha and invited him to go along.
The boatman said, "You have not yet prepared a bathhouse, nor have you recited the Amitābha Sūtra; your pure karma is not yet perfected."
"You may not yet depart. Upon awakening, he then renovated his quarters and bathed the monks, reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra* without ceasing for many years.

Later, while entering into meditative contemplation in his room, he saw someone carrying a silver platform arrive. The person said, "The Dharma Master’s retribution is exhausted; you shall ascend this platform.
He further said, "The merit and practice of the Master should have been such that you would ride upon a golden platform; however, because your initial resolve was hesitant, it has stopped here."

This was it. Zhenxi silently recorded the event and concealed it within his scripture case. On the evening of his death, from halfway up the mountain upward, it appeared as if thousands of torches were arrayed.
Villagers nearby saw this and believed it was the various kings coming to pay their respects. When dawn broke, [they realized it was not so].

It was only after hearing of the death of [Master] Zhen that, upon later searching through his scriptural cases, one finally learned of the auspicious signs of his rebirth (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* and *Lebang wenlei*).
Tánluán:
Tánluán was a native of Yànmén. In his youth, he traveled to Mount Wǎitái, where he witnessed divine traces and spiritual wonders; consequently, he conceived faith and departed [from secular life].
At home, he read the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra. Because its words and meanings were profound and subtle, he began to provide annotations for it.

When more than half of the text had been transcribed, he suddenly suffered from a severe illness. He traveled everywhere seeking medical treatment. Eventually, he sighed and said: "Human life is precarious and fragile; morning and evening one may face impermanence.
I have heard that immortals who attain longevity appear from time to time. Once I have mastered this Dharma, I shall then honor the Buddha's teachings—is this not fitting?"
He then went to the residence of Tao Yinyu in Jiangnan and earnestly requested instruction in the arts of the immortals.
Yinyu bestowed upon him ten scrolls of the *Xiánjīng* (Scripture of the Immortals), and he returned with great joy. Upon arriving in Luoyang, he met the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci.
Sengluan asked, "Within the Buddha-dharma, are there perhaps methods for longevity and immortality that surpass this *Xiánjīng*? Bodhiruci replied, "In this land..."

In this world, there exists a method for long life and immortality; yet even if one attains a long lifespan, it is but a brief duration before death, and one ultimately returns to the cycle of rebirth—how can such a thing be deemed noble?
True longevity and immortality are the Way of our Buddha. Thereupon, he bestowed upon him the *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations*, saying:

"If you study this, you shall no longer be born within the three realms, nor shall you again travel through the six paths. You will understand the waxing and waning of all things, and the nature of calamity and fortune."
Success or failure cannot be reached through such means. As for his longevity, even the measure of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges cannot compare to it;

this is the "long life" of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha). Luan was greatly delighted and subsequently burned the immortal scriptures to devote himself exclusively to the cultivation of pure contemplation (*śubha-bhāvanā*).

He practiced it himself and transformed others, spreading it ever more widely. He composed twelve stanzas on the worship of the Pure Land (*Sukhāvatī*) to continue the verses of Nāgārjuna, and further composed...

The two-fascicle *Anle ji* (Collection on Peace and Bliss) was transmitted to the world. The Wei ruler held him in high esteem and bestowed upon him the title Shenluan. By imperial decree, he was stationed at the Great Monastery in Bingzhou;
later, he moved to Yuanchong Monastery in Fenzhou. In the fourth year of the Xinghe era, one night, he saw a foreign monk within his chamber who said to him, "I am Nāgārjuna.
I have long resided in the Pure Land; because you share my same aspirations, I have come to meet you. Luan himself—
Knowing that the time had come, he gathered the assembly and instructed them, saying: "Life is weary toil, with no day of rest. The various sufferings of hell must not be feared;
the nine grades of pure karma must be cultivated. Therefore, have my disciples chant the name of the Buddha aloud."

Facing west, he performed the kṣamā-praṇipāta (prostration with the forehead touching the ground) and passed away. Those in the monastery all saw banners, flowers, victory standards, and parasols coming from the west, while celestial music filled the sky;
after a long while, these things ceased. When the matter was reported to the court, an imperial edict ordered his burial at Wengou in Fenxi, where a stupa was erected and a stele inscribed.
(*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, *Lebang Wenlei*).

Falin, Falin—whose secular surname was Yue and who was a native of Linqiong—left home to become a monk in his youth and resided at Pei Temple in Shu Commandery. He specialized in the study of the precepts and devoted his mind to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong).
At that time, Master Yin arrived in Shu, and Falin followed him to study. He disciplined himself and sharpened his resolve, practicing day and night without ceasing.
When Huiyin returned to Shaanxi, [Huiyuan] again followed him for several years. He thoroughly mastered the details of all the Vinaya texts.
Later, he returned to Shu and stayed at Lingjian Temple, where he cultivated the practice of purity. He constantly recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.
While he was turning and reciting them, he would invariably see a majestic śramaṇa of exceptionally large stature standing resolutely before him. (The Qi Jianwu era, year 2...)
In his later years, he fell ill and lay in bed. He focused his mind on the Western Pure Land and performed rites of repentance without ceasing.

He saw various worthies and sages all gathering before him, whereupon he described what he had seen to his disciples and instructed them to cremate his body after his death. Having finished speaking, he joined his palms and passed away (*Biographies of Eminent Monks*).

Huiguang resided in Luoyang. He composed commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Daśabhūmika* sūtras, which perfectly exhausted the profound meaning of the provisional and the ultimate.
One day, he fell ill and saw a host of celestial beings coming to welcome him. Huiguang said, "My vow is to return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). Shortly thereafter...
Buddhas manifested from the Pure Land filled the void. Guang said, "I only pray that our Buddha will accept me and fulfill my original vow.
He then snapped his fingers and passed into stillness (*Fozu Tongji*).
Sengrou, whose secular surname was Tao, was a native of Danyang. From his youth, he harbored aspirations to transcend the mundane world.

He left the household life as a disciple of the Dharma Master Hongcheng and applied himself with diligence to the precepts while extensively studying the various sections of the sūtras. Later, he entered Lingjiu Temple on Mount Bai in Shan; however, before he had yet arrived...
On the night before [his arrival], the śramaṇa Sengxu dreamed that divine beings with colorful banners and white armor emerged from the mountains, saying, "The Dharma Master is about to arrive.

The following morning, Fayou indeed arrived. During the Qi dynasty of the Xiao family, at the invitation of various princes, he went to reside at Dinglin Temple in the capital, where he served as the preeminent master;
those from all quarters revered him. Fayou vowed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), and whenever the sun was about to set, he would...
In the west, he would repeatedly knit his brows and join his palms in reverence. On the day of his passing, his body was free from ailment. He said to his disciples, "It is time for me to depart.

He spread a mat upon the ground, faced west, and passed away while performing a devout prostration. Both inside and outside the room, a wondrous fragrance was perceived. This was the first year of the Yanxing era;
he was sixty-four years old (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Daoping’s secular surname was Han. A native of Píng’ēn, he entered the monastic order at the age of twelve. He mastered the sūtras and śāstras, visiting every lecture hall to study;

daily he attained the profound and subtle mysteries. He propagated the Dharma between the regions of Wèi and Zhào, lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and various vinaya-śāstras. His eyes never... [text truncated]
Examining the text, one finds the essential points within it. In his daily life, he practiced both merit and wisdom; he bared his shoulders and went barefoot, supporting himself by begging for food.

He made vows and dedicated his merits, aspiring to be reborn in the Western Land. On the seventeenth day of the third month in the tenth year of the Tianbao era of the Qi dynasty, he passed away at Baoshan Temple to the southwest of Ye City at the age of seventy-two.
At the time of his death, a Buddha-light filled the room and a wondrous fragrance [pervaded the air].
Chongting (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks):

Huiming, whose secular surname was Guo, was a native of Jinyang in Taiyuan. After entering the monastic order, he specialized in performing the repentance rites of the Vaipulya sutras and Samantabhadra.
Tou En-guang was preceded on his journey by the two Chan masters. Later, he traveled to Mount Xiancheng.
Previously, there had been a Daoist named Meng Shou who, having resolved his heart toward the orthodox [Buddhist] path, had relinquished his residence and converted it into a temple and pagoda.

When the Master’s arrival at the mountain was imminent, Meng Shou suddenly experienced a dream-like vision in which he saw deities providing a solemn guard beside his residence. Upon waking, he summoned them; they immediately abandoned their dwelling for [the new monastery].
He served at Shanguang Temple, where the assembly of fellow practitioners gathered in full. Before long, he took his leave and returned to his former forest retreat.

At that time, there was a Chan Master named Fayin, who was close friends with Huiming; together they went to Chan Master Neng at Guoyuan Temple in Changsha to study meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Later, they both returned to Xiancheng, where they resided for five years. Huiming and Fayin knew the day of their own deaths beforehand; they walked hand-in-hand among the pines.
Beneath the forest trees, they looked at one another and smiled, saying, "We may well spend our final days right here. When the attendants first heard this, they did not yet understand its meaning.

Before ten days had passed, both men simultaneously fell ill. On the fifth day of the eleventh month in the third year of the Tianhe era of the Northern Zhou dynasty, they instructed their disciples to sit upright in the lotus posture, facing west to recite the Buddha's name. The assembly all saw the Buddha approaching; with palms joined, they passed away. The assembly—
There were dreams of heavenly beings descending to visit them, with banners and streamers shining like the sun. Furthermore, they heard the cry of "Excellent!

from within their rooms, along with extraordinary fragrances and marvelous music; the sounds that permeated them were manifold. On the seventeenth day of that month, they sat in their original positions, recollecting the Buddha, and passed away.
The auspicious signs manifested were identical for both. They were both thirty-eight years of age. Immediately beneath the trees, they constructed brick tombs.
(*Xu gaoseng zhuan*). Jing’ai’s secular surname was Zheng;
he was a native of Yingyang. In his youth, he frequented temples and monasteries. Upon seeing the transformed images of the hells, he was struck with awe and sought to leave the world.
He went to Waguan Monastery and relied upon Master He. At the age of seventeen, he received full ordination. He strictly observed the Vinaya precepts and mastered the sutras and śāstras.
He practiced the gate of great compassion; he never stepped upon or wore silk, cotton, or leather, but throughout his life, he wore only coarse wool and cloth.

When Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou was about to suppress the Dharma, Fayai went to the palace gate to submit a memorial pleading for its preservation, and he personally presented his petition to the Emperor.
Finding that his teachings were not being put into practice, he took his disciples and entered Mount Zhongnan to dwell there. Later, he again went into hiding in the Xigu Valley of Mount Taiyi.
Wearing the *zhanshui* (hempen sackcloth) mourning dress, he secretly propagated the Mahāyāna and composed many works, which he stored within mountain caves.

Lamenting that the Great Dharma was falling into decline and being abandoned, he said to his disciples: "I shall have no further benefit for the world; I will now perform the practice of *kāyotsarga* (casting off the body). One—
On that day, Daoji occupied a separate rock by himself and ordered his attendant to go down the mountain, telling him to return early the following morning.

Da’ai then sat cross-legged upon a flat stone, cutting flesh from his own body and arranging the pieces one by one upon the rock. He drew out his intestines and hung them from the branches of a pine tree;
his five viscera were all exposed, and his muscles, sinews, hands, feet, head, and face were entirely sliced into morsels. Finally, he cut out his heart with a knife, held it up, and passed away.
This was the sixteenth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Xuandeng era. He was forty-five years of age.
When his attendant Mingchen arrived, he still saw him sitting cross-legged facing west with palms joined at his heart, just as before. There was no blood remaining on the remains;
instead, white milk flowed profusely and congealed upon the rocks. Furthermore, he saw the hand-written testamentary verse left upon the stone wall, which read: "All..."
Those who have the karmic affinity—whether householders or renunciants, men or women—should all dwell happily within the Buddha-dharma and never give rise to regression.
Should you regress, you will lose the benefit of the wholesome. For three reasons, I shall relinquish this body and life.
First, seeing that one’s own body has many faults; second, being unable to protect the Dharma; third, desiring to see the Buddha quickly. A verse says:
"This useless body is a source of vexation to others' efforts; let it dissolve into stone and scatter among the pines of the crags.

Whether devas, humans, asuras, mountain deities, or tree spirits—may those seeking the Way observe my relinquishing of this body, and vow that all sentient beings may behold my skeletal remains, so that their afflictions shall be extinguished."
The ships were all capsized and submerged. May all sentient beings, upon hearing of my passing, achieve the divine ear and reach the ultimate state of Bodhi.
May all sentient beings, when they call me to mind, be endowed with the power of mindfulness, vast learning, and dhāraṇī.

When this retribution ceases and the four elements decay, may the springs and groves fall silent and the mountain caves be still, while I continue to bestow [benefits] universally upon birds and beasts, even down to the smallest insects.

Worms that eat flesh and drink blood; may my roots of goodness be fully developed within, so that in the future I may swiftly become a Sugata, with mastery over body and mind, and surely deliver others.
This body is impure, a base sack of excrement from which nine orifices constantly flow like a leaking embankment.
This body is loathsome, unfit to be gazed upon; it is wrapped in thin skin, smeared with blood and filth. This body is foul-smelling.
Foul, it is like a dead dog. Composed of the six elements joined together, it does not come from another. Contemplate this stinking body, imprisoned by impermanence;
whether advancing or retreating, there is no escape. It will inevitably encounter ants and termites; this body is difficult to preserve. Where there is life, there must be death;

it will be devoured by foxes and wolves, finally becoming maggots and worms. Whether they be gods or humans, men or women, beautiful or ugly, noble or base—all are consumed by the fire of death, appearing for but a brief moment.
[The Buddha] said: "Death’s law invades all people; it is the enemy of enemies. I regard it as my foe and vow to sever its very root. This body knows no joy; it is a basket for venomous snakes.
Encompassed by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is beset by a hundred maladies. It is called a 'mass of suffering' (*duḥkha-skandha*) and a thicket of old age, sickness, and death.
Body and mind are tormented with feverish affliction, fraught with many faults and transgressions. This body is without self (*anātman*), for it lacks autonomy and is devoid of reality."
Consider this: ordinary beings are governed by delusion; long lost in confusion, they are driven by false inversions. They lose their roots of goodness and die the same death as animals.
Having cast aside hundreds of thousands [of lives], oceans of blood and milk have been formed, and mountains of bones have accumulated.

In the future, these shall double; yet never for the sake of benefit have they endured such toil and suffering. It profits no sentient being and contributes nothing to the Dharma. To endure pain and practice giving—such effort is without [ultimate] fruit.
At the boundary, I vow never to regress. Having emerged from the four abysses and cast off this defiled form, may I be born in the Pure Land.
At the blooming of a single thought-flower, may I swiftly behold the Buddhas and sages of the ten directions at the abode of Amitābha Buddha. May I forever part from the three miserable realms;

with the right path determined, may I obtain the five supernormal powers as a karmic reward, flying freely through the air. Feasting on the Dharma beneath jeweled trees, may I realize the Great Non-arising, and the Dharmakāya shall manifest of itself.

Abiding therein, they ceaselessly transcend the three realms of existence and utterly eliminate the paths of Māra. With the protection of the Dharma as their primary concern, they fulfill the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Their spiritual transformations are boundless, and their virtues are complete in the four excellences; thus they are titled "Dharma Kings. I vow that after casting off this body, may I soon attain mastery over my own form.

Once mastery over the Dharma-body is attained, wherever there are various realms of existence, in every place where there is benefit to be found, I shall protect the Dharma and save sentient beings. Furthermore...
Karmic retribution must inevitably be exhausted; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are thus. The three realms are all impermanent; when their time comes, one has no autonomy.
Whether killed by another or dying of natural causes, one ultimately returns to such a state—a place not desired by the wise. One should reflect in this way:
"Since the various conditions have converged, my karma shall be exhausted this very day. (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks)

Huìjìng (慧敬). A native of Nánhǎi (South Sea). In his youth, he traveled to study in the regions of Jīng and Chǔ, where he became widely versed in the sūtras and śāstras. He constantly devoted himself to meritorious deeds;
wherever he went, he invariably established stūpas and images. Later, upon returning to his hometown, he further renovated the Yúnchēn and Yǒng'ān monasteries. His resolve...

Cao was stern and upright, and he was highly proficient in the precepts and regulations. He was appointed by imperial decree as the Head of the Monastic Community (*Sengzhu*), and his leadership and instruction were meritorious.

Whenever he undertook acts of merit, he dedicated them all toward rebirth in the Western Paradise. On the day of his death, a wondrous fragrance filled his chamber, which only subsided after a long time (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).

Tanyan, whose secular surname was Wang, was a native of Sangquan in Puzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of sixteen and traveled to various lecture halls, where he attained a profound realization of the essential teachings of the Dharma.
He composed a great commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; once it was completed, the scrolls emitted light throughout the entire night. Furthermore, śarīra relics appeared within his stupa.

He emitted extraordinary light. Wei Xiang Yuwentai established a monastery for him to the west of the capital, naming it Yunju. During the Jiande era of the Northern Zhou, he was appointed as the Sanghasthavira.
At the beginning of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he was decreed to preside over Yanxing Monastery.

On the thirteenth day of the eighth month in the eighth year, he passed away at the age of seventy-three. He took the Western Paradise as his primary object of contemplation; whether speaking or remaining silent, his thoughts were focused upon it.
He did not move. While he was in deep meditative concentration, he left instructions that his body and bones should be given to various birds and beasts.
At the time of his passing into nirvana, a man named Ren Jinbao claimed to see canopies and banners in the air, arranged in two rows before him as they were drawn forward.
From Yanxing Temple he traveled to Shanxi (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks). Daoyu:
Daoyu’s origins are unknown. He resided at Kaijue Temple, where he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha and fashioned a sandalwood image.
It was only three inches tall. Later, while in meditative concentration, he saw the Buddha, who said to him, "Why have you made my image so small?
He replied, "If the mind is great, it is great; if the mind is small, it is small. Having spoken, the Buddha's body suddenly appeared, filling the entirety of space.
The Buddha told him, "You should bathe yourself; when the morning star appears, I will come to welcome you. When the time arrived, he saw the Buddha coming to welcome him.
A light filled the room, and then he passed away. This was in the eighth year of the Kaihuang era (*Jingtu wen*).

As for Zhishun, Zhishun—his origins are not clearly known—he entered Mount Lu and followed Master Huiyuan’s practice of pure karma. At the beginning of the Daye era, he lectured on the *Guan* [Sutra].
When the sutra was finished, he manifested illness. Seeing the parrots and peacocks, he called upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and they emitted subtle and wondrous sounds.
He told his disciples, "I shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land this very day," and then passed away (Fozu Tongji).
Deng Fashi.

His origins are unknown. He lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Xingguo Monastery in Bingzhou. To all who came to hear his sermons, he universally exhorted them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land.
He passed away in the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era. At the time of his death, a rare fragrance filled the room.
At his enshrinement, fragrant clouds pervaded all the villages (*Wangsheng ji*).
Zhiyi, whose courtesy name was De’an, was surnamed Chen and was a native of Yingchuan. When his mother was pregnant with him, she dreamed of five-colored smoke swirling around her womb.

When she was pregnant and gave birth, the interior of the room was filled with a brilliant light. He had double pupils in his eyes; he would always join his palms when lying down and face west when sitting.

As he grew older, he would prostrate before any image he saw and show reverence to every monk he encountered. At the age of eighteen, he entered the monastic order under Fǎxù at Guòyuàn Monastery in Xiāngzhōu.
He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and was also thoroughly versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka. By nature, he delighted in the joy of meditation (*dhyāna*). He then traveled to Dà... in Guāngzhōu.
Sushan paid homage to Meditation Master Huisi. Upon seeing him, Huisi said, "In the past at Vulture Peak, we heard the Lotus Sutra together.

Pursued by our karmic affinities from that former life, you have come here once again. He then showed him the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s place of practice and expounded for him the four modes of peaceful conduct.
Zhiyi then practiced the Lotus Samādhi on this mountain. After only three nights had passed, as he recited to the "Chapter on the Medicine King," where it says, "This is true diligence;
this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata," his body and mind became suddenly clear and expansive.

He entered a state of tranquil meditative absorption, clearly illuminating the *Lotus Sūtra* and penetrating the characteristics of all dharmas. In the first year of the Guangda era of the Chen dynasty, he first arrived in Jinling and resided at Waguan Monastery.
He founded the Hongchan school of Chan. In the seventh year of the Taian era, he traveled to Mount Tiantai in Linhai and established a hermitage on its northern peak, where he resided.

Not long after, he received an imperial decree to enter Jinling. Following the fall of the Chen dynasty, he went to Mount Lu and subsequently traveled extensively through the regions of Jing and Yang.
In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he returned to Tiantai.

Throughout his career, he established thirty-six monasteries, cast eight hundred thousand Buddha statues, personally ordained fourteen thousand monks, and redeemed more than sixty fishponds by constructing bridges over them.

He established a pond for the release of living beings and reported this to the imperial court, strictly prohibiting all hunting and fishing. Dragons and deities paid him their respects, and both monastics and laypeople were transformed by his influence;
thus, the Dharma teachings flourished greatly there. Prince Yang of Jin received the Bodhisattva precepts from him and honored him with the title "Zhizhe" (the Wise One).
He once composed the *Ten Doubts Regarding the Pure Land*. In its final chapter, he sets forth the two principles of "aversion" (*yǎn*) and "aspiration" (*xīn*), stating:

"Those who wish to be definitively reborn in the Western Land must possess two types of practice to ensure they attain birth there: first, the practice of aversion and detachment; second, the practice of aspiration and longing.

As for the practice of aversion and detachment: since beginningless time, ordinary beings have been bound by the five desires and transmigrated through the six realms, undergoing all manner of suffering."
Amidst these manifold sufferings, they do not give rise to a mind of weary detachment from the five desires, and thus there is no prospect of escape.

For this reason, one should constantly contemplate this body as being full of pus, blood, excrement, urine, and all manner of foul secretions—impure, stinking, and loathsome. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"In this city of a body, the rākṣasa of ignorance dwells; what wise person would take pleasure in such a body? Furthermore, another sūtra says: "This body..."
This is a collection of manifold sufferings; everything is utterly impure. Like shackles, bonds, abscesses, and sores, it is fundamentally devoid of benefit.

This remains true even up to the bodies of the gods. Whether walking or sitting, sleeping or waking, the practitioner should constantly contemplate this body as being solely suffering and devoid of pleasure, thereby giving rise to a profound sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*).
Even if one cannot suddenly sever attachment to one’s wife and household, one will gradually develop such disenchantment.
One performs seven kinds of contemplations on impurity: First, one contemplates that this body of lustful desire arises from the affliction of craving;
this is impurity of the seed. Second, it is the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood; this is impurity of conception. Third, it dwells within the mother’s womb.
1. This dwelling place is impure. 2. While in the womb for four months, one consumes only the mother’s blood; this is the impurity of consumption. 3.
When the ten months are complete, one emerges through the birth canal; this is the impurity of birth. 4. Covered by a thin skin, its interior—pus and blood—is present everywhere;
this is the impurity of the entire body. 5. After death, it swells, festered, and decays; this is ultimate impurity.

Purity. Just as one contemplates the body in this way, so too does one contemplate others. One should develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward beloved objects, such as the bodies of men and women, and constantly contemplate their impurity.
For one who can contemplate in this manner, the afflictions of lust will gradually diminish. Furthermore, one should make this vow:
"May I forever leave behind the three realms, with their various foods, foul odors, pus, blood, and impurities; may I abandon my addiction to the five desires and [the company of] men."
The bodies of women and so forth—may I obtain the Dharma-nature birth-body of the Pure Land. This constitutes the practice of renunciation. The practice of joyful aspiration is further twofold:
first, clarifying the intent for seeking rebirth; second, contemplating the adornments and other matters of that Pure Land with a joyful mind and aspiring for them.
Regarding the clarification of the intent for rebirth: the reason for seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is the desire to rescue and deliver all [sentient beings].
"Sentient beings suffer. Thus he reflects: "I am currently powerless. If I remain in this evil age, the objects of affliction will be powerful;
bound by my own karma, I shall sink into the three miserable realms and pass through kalpas. Such cycles have continued without respite since beginningless time.
When can I rescue these suffering sentient beings? For this reason, I seek birth in the Pure Land to draw near to the Buddhas. If...
Only by realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) can one rescue suffering sentient beings in an evil age.

Therefore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-upadeśa* states that for one who has resolved upon bodhicitta, this is precisely the mind that vows to become a Buddha. The mind that vows to become a Buddha is the mind that seeks to deliver sentient beings.

The mind that seeks to deliver sentient beings is the mind that gathers sentient beings into the Buddha-land. Furthermore, to vow to be born in the Pure Land, one must possess two practices. First, [the practice of the six perfections]. Second, [the practice of the three minds]. First...
One must distance oneself from three factors that obstruct the gateway to enlightenment, and one must attain three factors that accord with the gateway to enlightenment.

What are the three factors to be distanced that obstruct the dharma of enlightenment? First, relying on the gate of wisdom, one does not seek personal pleasure, because one distances oneself from the egoistic mind and its attachment to the self.
Second, relying on the gate of compassion, one uproots the suffering of all sentient beings... [and distances oneself from...]

Because he is free from the mind that finds no peace in sentient beings; third, by relying on the gateway of skillful means, he feels compassion for all sentient beings and desires to grant them happiness, remaining far removed from the mind that seeks honor and offerings for himself.

If one can distance oneself from these three obstacles to enlightenment, one will attain the three factors conducive to enlightenment: first, an unstained and pure mind that does not seek [benefit] for oneself.
Because it is the source of all bliss, bodhi is the place of stainless purity. If one seeks happiness for oneself alone, one defiles the body and mind, thereby obstructing the gateway to bodhi;
therefore, a mind that is stainless and pure accords with the gateway to bodhi.
Second, the mind of peaceful purity is for the sake of uprooting the suffering of sentient beings. Bodhi is the place of purity where all sentient beings find peace and security. If...
If one does not resolve to uproot all sentient beings and cause them to leave behind the suffering of birth and death, one violates the gateway to Bodhi;
therefore, establishing a pure mind is to follow the gateway to Bodhi. Third is the pure mind of joy, which desires to cause all sentient beings to realize Great Bodhi and Nirvana.
Since Bodhi and Nirvana are the ultimate state of eternal bliss, if one does not resolve [to this], [one fails in this third purity].
To cause all sentient beings to attain ultimate and eternal bliss would obstruct the gateway to Bodhi; therefore, delighting in a pure mind is that which accords with the gateway to Bodhi.
From what cause is this Bodhi attained? It must depend upon being born in a Pure Land and never being separated from the Buddha.

Once one has attained the Patience of Non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), one rescues suffering sentient beings within the realm of birth and death, with compassion and wisdom internally fused in meditative concentration.
To be constantly employed with sovereign non-obstruction is the bodhicitta; this is the meaning of the aspiration for rebirth. Second, regarding the longing mind that seeks:

it is the arising of thoughts through a yearning heart, taking Amitābha Buddha as its object—whether as the *dharmakāya* or the *saṃbhogakāya*, his golden radiance, the eighty-four thousand marks (*lakṣaṇa*), each mark possessing eighty-four thousand secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), and each secondary sign emitting eighty... [thousand rays of light].
Fourteen thousand rays of light constantly illuminate the Dharma-realm, gathering in those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Furthermore, one should contemplate the wondrous bliss and adornments of the seven treasures in that land, as fully described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra*, and other texts.

Constantly practicing the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, as well as all virtuous deeds such as giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation, one should dedicate them all to sentient beings so that they may be born together [in that land].

"One will certainly be reborn in that land"—this is the gate of joyful aspiration. When Zhiyi’s work of transformation was complete, he went to Shicheng Temple east of Shan County and said to his disciples, "I shall pass away here.
He ordered a bed to be placed against the eastern wall, facing west, and focused exclusively on reciting the names of Amitābha Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā, and Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, he lit many incense offerings and chanted the name of the Immeasurable [Life].

Having finished the titles of the *Sūtra on the Buddha of Longevity* and the *Contemplation Sūtra*, he praised them, saying: "The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land with lotus ponds and jeweled trees;
yet, though it is easy to go there, no one does so. Even those who, when the signs of the fiery chariot appear, repent for a single thought, still attain rebirth there.
How much more so for those who cultivate precepts and wisdom through the power of the holy path—how could their merit be in vain? The disciple then asked: "I do not yet know, Great..."

"Master, what stage of realization have you entered? Where will you be reborn after passing away here? Zhiyi replied, "I did not lead a large assembly, so I shall surely purify my six sense faculties.

Because I sacrificed myself to benefit others, I have merely attained the fifth stage. My teachers and friends are now all coming to welcome me from the presence of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Having finished speaking, he sat upright as if entering samādhi. He was sixty-seven years old at the time, in the tenth month of the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era.
On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, Shi Huiyan of Tianxiang Temple heard that Zhiyi had passed away.

Overcome with incessant grief, he wished to know the place of Zhiyi’s rebirth; consequently, he transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra* to seek a divine sign. That night, he dreamed that Zhiyi was coming from the west accompanied by Avalokiteśvara.
Turning to look at him, Zhiyi said, "Has your doubt been dispelled? His other supernatural manifestations were similarly frequent, as recorded in the *Xu Gaoseng Zhuan*.
*Biographies of Eminent Monks*, *The Comprehensive Record of the Buddha and Patriarchs*, and *The Treatise on the Ten Doubts*.
Huicheng, whose secular surname was Duan, was a native of Liyang. Initially, he received his training at Shizhu Temple; later, he heard of the Chan Master Sengzhi of Mount Nanyue.
When the Master’s flourishing propagation of the Dharma reached that region, [Huiyuan] went there to rely upon him. He sat in meditation with eyes open, continuing from night until dawn.
Nanyue ordered him to enter the Vaipulya, Avalokiteśvara, Lotus, and Pratyutpanna Samādhis in order to eliminate his past karmic obstructions.

After practicing these for three years, he attained the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of Sentient Beings. Later, at Zhiyang in Jingzhou, he founded a monastery where he resided; there he recited the name of Amitābha.

He practiced the contemplation of the Western Paradise for thirty years, remaining constantly seated without lying down. Whenever he entered meditative absorption, he would invariably see the lotus pedestals and jeweled trees of the Pure Land.
One day, he told his disciples, "Quickly pave the steps of the hall; I am about to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

When the preparations were complete and the lecture was being held, Master Zhiyi arrived from Yuyuan. They discussed the fundamental principles of reality at length, after which [the master] entered nirvana. This is...
In a dream at dusk, he saw himself sitting upon a series of platforms that receded westward into the distance (from the *Fozu tongji*). "O life of wisdom!
O life of wisdom!

[Thus spoke] Huiming of Xiancheng in Tiantai, who studied under Chan Master Huisi of Nanyue; upon hearing the exposition of the Three Contemplations, he attained a profound realization of the fundamental source.
He attained unhindered eloquence and preached the Dharma as freely as pouring water. As he was about to pass away, he exhorted his disciples to cultivate pure conduct with diligence.
Suddenly, the assembly saw Amitābha Buddha and the Great Beings coming to welcome him; he then commanded them to follow the Buddha toward the west (Fozu Tongji).
Huǐhǎi, Huǐhǎi, whose secular surname was Zhāng, was a native of Qīnghé Wǔchéng. He entered the path in his youth and served as a disciple of Dharma Master Jiǒng of Guǎngguó Temple in Yèdū.
Having heard the *Nirvāṇa* and *Laṅkāvatāra* Sūtras twice, he was able to recite them from memory immediately; his wisdom and eloquence surpassed those of others, and his learning...
All his disciples admired and submitted to him. In the second year of the Daxiang era of the Northern Zhou dynasty, he came to Taopu, where he renovated the monastery and adorned the Buddhist rites.
He had long set his aspirations upon the Pure Land; through the power of his sincerity, a monk named Daoquan from Qizhou suddenly appeared.
He brought a painted image of Amitābha Buddha that was so subtle and exquisitely crafted it was unprecedented in this world.

It was said that a Bodhisattva possessing the five supernatural powers from the Kukkuṭārāma Monastery in India had traveled through the air to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and brought back this depiction.

Haiming, whose long-held aspirations were now fulfilled, paid him reverent homage with utmost sincerity. He beheld divine light shining brilliantly, whereupon he copied the image with great earnestness, making a vow.

He was born in that land and held this thought until the end of his days. On the morning of the fifth day of the fifth month in the fifth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he fell ill and said to his disciples, "I am about to pass away.
He extended his five fingers to signify the time of his final departure. Then, on the night of the fifth day, he suddenly rose up.

Having finished his prostrations facing west, he sat in the full lotus posture until dawn, when he passed away at the age of sixty-nine. From his youth, Hai had been diligent and austere, becoming even more earnest in his old age;

he further engaged with others through benevolence and compassion, encouraging and exhorting those who followed him. At his death, both the monastic community and the laity were filled with profound sorrow.
He scattered incense and flowers and bestowed gold and jewels beyond measure (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
Zhìtōng, whose secular surname was Chéng, was a native of Yǐzhī in Hédōng. From birth, he delighted in the Way and resolved to seek ordination as a monk; his parents were astonished.

He granted his permission. At the age of ten, he shaved his head and entered the monastic order. He attended to his teachers and elders with devotion, maintaining a humble and modest demeanor and strictly observing the precepts.
Day and night, he recited the words of the Dharma without ceasing, memorizing more than three thousand essential verses in praise of the Buddha from various sutras.

Subsequently, he studied under Master Jun and Master Yan, establishing Guilao Temple where he impartially provided relief and support to the needy. In the intervals between these duties, he further bestowed [instruction].
He preached the Dharma on the precepts and extensively cultivated all manner of wholesome deeds. In the tenth month of the seventh year of the Daye era, he fell ill.

He instructed his attendant to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and dedicated his merit toward the vow to be reborn in that land. Thereupon, he opened his eyes and gazed straight ahead; for a long time, he did not blink.

As he saw something, he said, "It is inconceivable. An attendant monk asked for the reason, and [Huiyuan] replied, "I see jeweled banners, flowered canopies, and the magnificent adornments of stupas and temples.
At the beginning of the night, he spoke again, asking, "For what reason are so many lamps and candles burning brightly? He then extinguished the lamps to make it dark.
A moment later, he spoke again, saying, "Why has the radiance become even more intense? The attendant said, "This is the Master’s pure manifestation; it is not to be wondered at."
He then joined his palms and remained in prayer until dawn, saying, "I shall be born in the Pure Land," whereupon he passed away. The mountain shook and the earth trembled;
all the windows rattled and cracked open. At that time, the temple monk Daohui happened to be dozing off and dreamed of multi-storied pavilions and halls atop the western ridge.
He ascended into the air and departed (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Zhenhui’s secular surname was Chen; he was a native of Hebei in Shan Prefecture. Disgusted with his worldly existence due to a drought, he went to Dàtōng Temple at the age of twenty.
He went to the abode of Chan Master Qing to leave the household life and receive full ordination. He traveled to study in the four directions, and his spiritual practice progressed daily.
Later, he built a dwelling on Mount Mashu at Puban Shou and resided there for eighteen years. He erected a four-pillar jeweled banner to enshrine the Three Sages.

Every day, he would rouse his body and maintain right mindfulness, relying upon the images to cultivate contemplation. In the fourth year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, he was summoned to reside at Qiyuan Temple. As for his character...
He was pure, frugal, and humble, delighting in solitude and tranquility. He sat in meditation and performed repentance rites, exerting himself diligently day and night.

In the tenth month of the eleventh year of the Daye era, he fell ill while resting; his countenance remained as usual, and he said, "I shall be born in the Pure Land; I see lotus flowers waiting for me."

Furthermore, he heard the sound of an extraordinary bell, its resonance deep and far-reaching, accompanied by a pervasive and luxuriant fragrance that suddenly ceased. "Fa-zhi! Fa-zhi! [he cried], though he did not know from whence it issued.
Having entered the monastic life at the age of seven, he applied his mind with undivided attention to every lecture hall he attended. In his later years...
In this age, when hearing of direct paths to liberation, none is like the recitation of the Buddha's name. He then said to others:

"I have heard it stated in the sutras that for committing a single *duṣkṛta* offense, one must undergo suffering in hell for an entire intermediate kalpa; this is credible. Yet I have also heard it stated in the sutras that by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha even once,"
He did not yet believe that the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eight billion kalpas could be extinguished. A wise person pointed out to him, "This is a great false view of yours;

both [teachings] are the words of the Buddha. How can you fail to believe? Thereupon, at the Tushita Terrace in Guoqing Monastery, he practiced the mindfulness of the Buddha with diligent devotion day and night.
He was moved by the manifestation of the two Bodhisattvas, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta. On another day, he further experienced the appearance of a celestial crown.
He possessed a precious vase that radiated light across his body. One day, he took leave of the monastics and the laity, saying, "The day will come when I am born in the Western Land.
How shall you see me off? He then fixed the date for a farewell meal three days later. After the meal, some stayed in his room to await him.
At midnight, Zhi was reciting the Buddha’s name upon his rope bed; sitting peacefully, he passed away. At that moment, a golden light came from the west.

It illuminated several hundred *li*. Fishermen on the river thought it was already dawn; only after a long while did it truly brighten, at which point they realized that Hui-zhi had been reborn in the Pure Land (*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*, "Classified Texts on the Land of Bliss").
Shanzhou, whose secular surname was Huai, was a native of Yingzhou. He left home to become a monk in his youth; he was quick-witted and easily enlightened, attending numerous lecture assemblies.

He was particularly proficient in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and frequently humbled and converted his masters. At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, he traveled north and followed Master Huiyuan, residing at Jingying Monastery in the capital.

After Sengyuan passed away, an imperial edict appointed Sengzhou as the presiding master for the *Nirvāṇa* assembly at Jingying Monastery. During the Daye era, monks of extensive virtue were widely selected;
Sengzhou was chosen repeatedly and frequently opened Dharma assemblies. Nevertheless, he constantly practiced the Pure Land path in secret, such that no one knew of it.

Consequently, he suffered from a wind-related ailment, causing his lips and mouth to slant. Later, the affliction suddenly subsided, returning to normal. Sengzhou said, "My illness has now been cured."

"His life must surely come to an end. In the third month of the third year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, his illness became critical. He said to his disciples, "Throughout my life, I have maintained right faith;

moment by moment, my mind has been fixed upon the Buddha. I have no concern that I shall not be reborn in the Pure Land. He immediately ordered his quarters to be swept and cleaned, incense to be burned, and himself to wait with solemnity.
Rising and sitting up, he joined his palms and said to his attendants, "Prepare a high seat; the World-Honored One is coming! [Zhou] Jin—
He repented and felt deep shame. After this had continued for a long while, he turned toward his bed and said, "Just now Amitābha Buddha came;
did you all see him? I am about to depart. Having finished speaking, he passed away (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Daojie, whose secular surname was Yang, was a native of An-yi in Hedong. From his youth, he possessed the aspiration for the transcendent life.

In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, when he was nearly twenty years of age, he went to Dharma Master Ying to receive the tonsure and the full precepts. He subsequently traveled to Qingzhou to study under the master of śāstras, He Ji.

Having completed his studies under Chengshih, he learned that his teacher had passed away. He then traveled throughout the territory of Qi to seek out masters of the Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra and frequently established lecture halls.
After some time, he suddenly reflected to himself: "I have merely occupied myself with verbal explanations while the path of the mind remains obscured.

As for the arising of wisdom, it will not manifest without meditative concentration. He consequently suspended his lectures and went to Magu to study seated meditation under Chan Master Zhenhui, whereupon he gained profound insight into dependent origination.
Huìtàn was of sharp faculties. Jié was a man of few desires and sparse speech; he was indifferent toward wealth and meager in his food. He did not allow pleasure or pain to burden his mind.

In his later years, he served as the abbot of the monks dwelling on the cliffs. On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away on the mountain at the age of fifty-five.
Previously, there had been one Fan Chuo of Sangquan, a monk from the period when the teachings were suppressed during the Northern Zhou dynasty. Although he...
The layman Baiyi (Cai Yong) frequently attended the Dharma hall, and Sengjie held him in high esteem.

After Sengchuo had already passed away, his two daughters both dreamed that their father arrived through the air, saying, "I have been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Knowing that Master Sengjie was about to pass away, I have come to welcome him.
Having spoken thus, he vanished toward Qiyuan. On that day, Sengjie happened to be ill and had suspended his lectures; as he approached the end of his life, he saw [his father].
He stood poised in mid-air. The entire monastery smelled a wondrous fragrance and heard the sound of celestial music (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).
Guanding’s secular surname was Wu; he was a native of Zhang’an in Linhai. When he was only three months old, he could recite the names of the Triple Gem. At the age of seven...

He entered Shoujing Monastery to become a monk. At the beginning of the Zhide era of the Chen dynasty, he visited Zhiyi at Xuchan Monastery and received instruction in the method of contemplation (*guanfa*).

After a long period of diligent study and reflection, he suddenly received his teacher’s seal of approval. He subsequently served as an attendant; whatever teachings he heard, he was able to fully comprehend and internalize.

During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, after Zhiyi entered *parinirvāṇa*, Huiding propagated his legacy, diligently cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and frequently engaged in [meditative] retreats.

While sitting and reciting the sutras, heavenly flowers would often drift down and fall by his side. Once, while he was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Shejing Temple, a band of robbers suddenly arrived.
Upon seeing the temple gates filled with banners that obscured the sun, and divine soldiers all over ten feet tall, the robbers were terrified and scattered.
On the seventh day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at Guoqing Temple. When he first manifested his illness, there were wonders within his chamber.
Xiang, at the time of his death, instructed his disciples, saying, "You may burn many varieties of incense; I am about to depart.
Suddenly he rose and joined his palms as if paying homage to something, reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha three times. His countenance was serene as he lay down and passed away.
The crown of his head remained warm for several days. He was seventy-two years old (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, *Fozu Tongji*).
Sengzang, a native of Xihe, entered the monastic order in his youth. He humbled himself to serve others, showing all forms of reverence and never declining labor or hardship.
Whenever he saw the robes of other monks in need, he would secretly wash and sew them for them. During the heat of summer, he would strip off his clothes and sit upon the grass.
In the midst of this, she offered her own flesh and blood as alms to the mosquitoes and gnats. Day after day she recited the Buddha’s name without keeping count;

her resolve was firm and her mind tranquil, never for a moment neglecting her practice. When her life came to an end, she saw various devas coming one after another to welcome her, yet she did not go with them.

Suddenly, she said to those around her: "I have just gone to the Pure Land and seen many noble and virtuous beings scattering flowers through the air. Thereupon, she joined her palms and recited the Buddha’s name.
[He was] transformed by [the teachings of] the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*.

As for "Dharma-joy, Dharma-joy," its origin is not clearly known. He traveled extensively to consult various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and studied with diligence without weariness. At the age of sixty, he finally...
On Mount Dasu, he encountered the Great Master Zhiyi; upon hearing his Dharma voice but once, he attained profound realization instantaneously.
Thereupon, he devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of dhyāna and wisdom. While once practicing the Vaipulya Samādhi, a pheasant suddenly appeared and sought its life.
A divine being rebuked it, saying, "The Dharma Master is destined to be born in the Pure Land; how could he repay your life with yours? Later, while ill, he made a vow based on his lifelong practice.

He dedicated his karma toward the Pure Land and recited the Buddha’s name with a sincere heart; immediately, he saw the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas come to welcome him, and he passed away while sitting upright (Fozu Tongji).

Daowang of Wei Commandery possessed a spirit that was clear and penetrating, and his intellectual understanding was formed at an early age. He entered the monastic life under Dharma Master Lingyu and delved deeply into the Great Teachings.
Once, while lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* at Hangling Mountain Monastery during the night, there was no lamp; Daowang—

He raised his palm high to show it, whereupon an extraordinary light was emitted that illuminated the hall and its contents. The assembly was struck with wonder and astonishment. Daowang said, "This light is always present in my hand; why should it be considered strange?
Having long since set his will upon the West, he vowed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

Later, while at Baoying Temple, he knew for himself that the time had arrived. He announced this in advance to those with whom he shared a karmic connection, saying, "On the eighth day of the eighth month, I shall come to take my leave. When the appointed time arrived—

He was free from any distress or suffering. When asked whether the time for the fast had arrived, he immediately ascended the high seat. A wondrous fragrance issued from the incense burner as he led the fourfold assembly to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

His words and principles were essential and profound; those who listened felt their spirits uplifted. Raising his head and gazing upward, he saw a multitude of celestial beings appearing in profusion.
Amidst the clamor of pipes and strings, a clear and far-reaching melody emerged, announcing to the assembly: "The Tuṣita Heaven is coming to welcome you."
"I replied, 'Indeed, the heavenly realms are the very root of birth and death; they are not what I desire. I constantly pray for the Pure Land.
Why, then, has this vow not been fulfilled? As soon as he finished speaking, celestial music soared upward and vanished in an instant.
Immediately, fragrant flowers and musical instruments appeared in the west, filling the sky like clouds, surging forward and circling above his head. This was seen by the entire assembly."
Fawang said, "May the great assembly dwell in peace. Now the spiritual manifestations of the West come to welcome me; I am going.

Having spoken these words, he was seen to let go of his incense burner from his hand and passed away while seated upon the high throne. He was sixty-nine years old; it was the seventh year of the Zhenguan era (as recorded in the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).

Zhìyǎn, whose courtesy name was Míngcàn, was surnamed Zhū and was a native of Wújùn. He was the grandson of Zhū Xiàn, a Gentleman Attendant at the Court of Imperial Entertainments during the Liáng dynasty.

From birth he possessed extraordinary qualities; at the age of eight, he left the household life and became a disciple of Dharma Master Qú of Tōngyuán Temple. He traveled extensively across renowned [monasteries].

He propagated the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras. After the fall of the Chen dynasty, he returned to Mount Huqiu, where he lived facing the cliffs and ravines for thirty years. Later, fleeing from the chaos of war, he moved elsewhere.
In the seventh year of the Wude era, Li Shijia, the Governor-General of Suzhou, welcomed him back to the mountain temple.

There, he practiced the three kinds of pure karma and cultivated the sixteen subtle contemplations. He gathered over five hundred virtuous companions who would recite the Buddha’s name at the temple every month.

One compilation was completed. It had been more than ten years since its inception. In the tenth month of the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, he saw a foreign monk holding a precious vase who came forward and said to him, "I am Amitābha.
That which is later called the King of Merit-Jewels in the Pure Land is none other than I.
Yan then said to the assembly of the monastery, "Amitābha is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara; the King of Merit-Jewels is his [Avalokiteśvara’s] accomplishment."
"This is the title of the Buddha. Shall I not return to the West? That evening he passed away at the age of seventy-one (*Fozu Tongji*, *Wuqiu Zhi*).

Dingguan, whose secular surname was Sun, was a native of Fuyang. He received the practice of *citta-vipaśyanā* (contemplation of the mind) from Master Zhizhe and resided at Tiantai. He constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.
In the winter of the ninth year of the Zhenguan era, he was invited by Fayin Temple in Yuhang to deliver lectures. In the first month of the following year...
At dawn, someone dressed in royal attire arrived and said to Guān, "I am the deity of the Gaotíng Temple.

Yesterday, when you, Master, passed by the temple grounds, I was just then out on patrol and did not have the opportunity to welcome you. I have now come from afar specifically to seek the dharma of the precepts.

Guān then burned incense and conferred upon him the Bodhisattva Great Precepts. He paid his respects with gratitude and withdrew. The following day at midnight, he bathed, changed his clothes, and prepared himself.
Facing west, he sat in the full lotus posture. He recited the names of the Three Holy Ones of the Western Quarter and the title of the Master Zhizhe more than one hundred times each.
He then preached the Dharma-gate of the Three Contemplations to his disciples; having finished speaking, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).

Shouhong, whose secular surname was Shou, was a native of Fenyang. He constantly and diligently recited [the Buddha’s name], aspiring to be reborn in the Western Pure Land. As he was about to pass away, a youth from Tuṣita Heaven came to welcome him.
Shouhong said, "My heart aspires to go to the West; I shall not be born in the heavens. He then immediately ordered the assembly to chant the Buddha’s name, and suddenly declared:
"The Buddha has come from the West. Having finished speaking, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*). Daocuo’s secular surname was Wei;
he was a native of Wenshui in Bingzhou. At the age of fourteen, he left the household life to study the sūtras and śāstras, and later served Master Zàn.
The Chan Master studied Chan meditation. Later, he resided at Yuanzhong Temple in Shibigou on the Wen River, a site established by Dharma Master Tanyuan.

Because Tancho admired Dharma Master Tanyuan’s practice of the Pure Land, he devoted himself to contemplation and visualization. He sat facing west at all times, never failing in his six-period daily prostrations and veneration.
His recitation of the Buddha’s name averaged seventy thousand times per day. A monk beheld him in the West during a state of meditative concentration.
At that time, Lingxiang saw that Tan-chuo held a rosary in his hand, which blazed like a mountain of the seven treasures. Other auspicious omens were too numerous to describe in full.
Tan-chuo lectured on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* nearly twenty times for the assembly.

Those listening each held a rosary and recited the Buddha’s name with a sound like the tide. Occasionally, when he dispersed the gathering, the resonance filled the forests and valleys, continuing to stir even in ordinary times.
He exhorted others to purify their karma; his reasoning flowed forth like a spring. He urged people to collect their thoughts, quiet external conditions, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.

He authored the *Treatise on the Pure Land* in two fascicles, which comprehensively integrated the works of Nāgārjuna and Vasubandhu, as well as those of Huiyuan and Tanluan. Its phrasing was concise and its essential meaning profound, earning it great esteem in his time.
In the second year of the Zhenguan era, the assembly all saw Dharma Master Tanluan seated upon a boat made of the seven precious gems.

He said to Chao, "Your Pure Land hall is completed; it is only that your remaining karmic retribution has not yet been exhausted. He further saw transformation-buddhas dwelling in the void as celestial flowers fell and scattered.
The assembly all looked up with joy and marveled at the wonder. From this point on, Chao’s power of retribution grew ever stronger and his complexion became radiant.
Those among both the clergy and the laity who were drawn to his influence increased day by day. At over eighty years of age, he passed away. At that time, there was a monk named Shi Daofu who...

Daocuo shared the same aspiration. Whenever they met, they invariably took the Pure Land as their goal. Three days after Daocuo passed away, Sengfu heard of it and said, "I have always expected to go first, yet now I am behind.
If I apply myself with one more breath of effort, I shall be able to catch up and reach him."

Before the Buddha image, he prostrated himself with his forehead touching the ground and offered prayers; then, withdrawing to his seat, he passed away (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*, *Fozu Tongji*).
Sengxuan:
a native of Bingzhou, whose learning was comprehensive and whose understanding matched his practice. At the age of ninety-six, he met Daochuo.

The Zen Master composed the *Anleji* (Collection on Peace and Bliss) and lectured on the *Amitābha Sūtra*. He had first turned his mind toward the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha’s name), fearing that his life was nearing its end;

thus, day and night he performed one thousand prostrations to the Buddha and recited the Buddha’s name eighty- to ninety-thousand times. For five years, he remained single-minded and untiring. Later, when he fell ill, he told his disciples:
"Amitābha Buddha has come to bestow upon me fragrant robes; Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are walking [before me]."
They stood in a row before him. Transformation-buddhas filled the void of space. "I shall now depart," he said, and having finished speaking, he passed away.
For seven days, a wondrous fragrance did not dissipate. At that time, there were two Dharma Masters, Qifang and Yuanyou, who personally witnessed this event.
They subsequently spent an entire summer retreat at Wuzhen Temple in Lantian County, reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha. Together they broke off a single willow branch and placed it in the pond.
He placed it in his hands and made this vow: "If I am to be born in the Pure Land, may it not wither for seven days.

When the time arrived, it became even more fresh and verdant, its fragrant fruit swelling in celebration. Day and night he practiced *nien-fo* (recollection) without ceasing. After five months, within his visualization, he felt his body standing by a jeweled pond;
he beheld Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta seated upon two great precious lotus flowers, surrounded by ten million lotuses.
It was filled to capacity. Amitābha Buddha came from the west and sat upon a most magnificent lotus flower, its radiance shining brilliantly.
Fragrant fruits bowed in homage and asked: "Can the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, by recollecting the Buddha in accordance with the sutras, attain birth here?
The Buddha said: "Do not doubt; they will certainly be born in my land. Furthermore, he heard Śākyamuni World-Honored One and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva offering praise.
Before the Lotus Sutra [Hall], there were three jeweled stairways. The first was for laypeople; the second was for a mixture of monastics and laity;

and the third was for monastics alone. It was said that these were all those who had practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name and had been reborn here. Once Fangguo had emerged from meditative concentration, he...
Li recounted this to his disciples as follows (*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*). Puming’s secular surname was Wei;
he was a native of Anyi in Puzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of thirteen and traveled extensively among various lecture halls during the Daye era.
In the fourth year [of the Sui dynasty], he was summoned to enter the Great Chan Meditation Hall. In the first year of the Wude era, he resided at Renshou Temple in Puzhou.
Every day he would recite the *Prātimokṣa* once and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* twenty times.

He performed prostrations and repentance during the six periods of the day, dedicating all his roots of goodness toward rebirth in the Pure Land. He continued in this manner until the end of his life, having fashioned several dozen niches for sandalwood Buddha images and transcribed [the scriptures].
He lectured on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* more than a thousand times and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* over eighty times.

As for the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, and various other sūtras and śāstras, their number cannot be recorded. At the age of eighty-six, he passed away at his resident monastery (*Xu gaoseng zhuan*).

Two śrāmaṇeras from Wenzhou were śrāmaṇeras of unknown origin. They shared the same aspiration for the practice of Buddha-recitation (*buddhānusmṛti*). After five years had passed, the elder one died first and was reborn in the Pure Land.
Seeing the Buddha, he addressed him, saying: "There is a junior śrāmaṇera who practiced together with me; may he also be able to attain birth [in this land]?"
The Buddha said, "It was because of his exhortation that you first resolved to seek enlightenment. You may now return home and further cultivate pure deeds.
Three years hence, you shall come here together with him. When the appointed time arrived, the two men saw the Buddha and the assembly of sages coming from the west;
the great earth shook, celestial flowers fluttered down, and they were all simultaneously transformed [into Buddhas] (Fozu Tongji).
Deimei’s courtesy name was Wang; she was a native of Linqing in Qinghe. She entered the monastic life at the age of sixteen and received the full precepts at nineteen.

During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, she traveled to the capital to observe and transform others there. She upheld the Vinaya and made daily ritual repentance her primary practice, constantly reciting fifteen thousand [verses].
The *Names of the Thousand Buddhas*. During the Daye era, he resided at Huiling Temple in the capital, where he extensively promoted meritorious deeds and experienced many spiritual responses.
At the beginning of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, he lived at Huichang Temple, where he constructed a hall for repentance to the west of the monastery and practiced the Pratyutpanna Samādhi.
Throughout the summer, he did not sit; at times, he ceased verbal transgressions. For three years, he did not speak; at other times, his conduct was never frivolous.

He extended his courtesy to all seven classes of practitioners, severed worldly thoughts, and focused his mindfulness exclusively on the Western Paradise. He maintained the recitation of the Buddha’s name throughout his life without ceasing.
In the twelfth month of the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, he suddenly joined his palms in prayer while reciting the Buddha’s name and passed away at the age of sixty-three (*Xu Gaoseng Zhuan*).

Huiman (Hui-man), whose secular surname was Liang, was a native of Chang’an in Yongzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and was meticulous in observing the rules of decorum. He traveled to various regions to lecture on the scriptures.

During the Zhenguan era, he received an imperial decree to reside at Hongji Temple, where he devoted himself to propagating the Vinaya teachings and exhorting the monastic community. He once made a vow...

He was reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). His lifelong vocation was bathing the monastic community. On the twentieth day of the fourth month in the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he suffered from a slight illness and knew that his end was near.
He brought forth all his personal belongings and donated them entirely to the permanent property of the monastery (*sangha*).
Sitting upright upon a rope bed, he summoned the assembly of the temple for a final farewell and passed away at the age of seventy-five (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Shensu’s secular surname was Wang. He was a native of Mingtiao in Anyi. In his youth, he rose as a preeminent figure in the Way, sharing equal renown with Sengjie.

They frequently accompanied one another to inquire about the Dharma and traveled together between lecture halls and study centers. In the fourth year of the Daye era, when Master Sengjie ceased his lectures, Shensu succeeded him; he completed the exposition of the *Abhidharma*.
The *Shilun* (Treatise on Reality) comprises more than sixty fascicles. In the second year of the Zhenguan era, he resided at Qiyuan.

On the twenty-third day of the second month in the seventeenth year, he passed away on the mountain at the age of seventy-two. Throughout his life, his practice had been focused on the Western Pure Land.

On the day of his death, he summoned the assembly to bid them farewell; sitting upright in the full lotus posture, he ordered that the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* be recited twice, and he concentrated his mind with single-minded devotion.
Listen attentively. He himself recited "Namu Amida Butsu" five or six times. Then he had one person chant while the others joined in harmony until nightfall.

Sitting upright and solemnly, he passed away before their eyes. That evening, Dharma Master Zhikuan of Renshou Temple was sitting in meditation when [the deceased] appeared as usual to bid him farewell, entrusting him with the protection of the True Dharma and the repayment of the Tathāgata’s kindness.
When dawn arrived, it was first discovered that Sù had entered nirvana (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks).

Míngzhān, whose secular surname was Dù, was a native of Shíyì County in Héngzhōu. From his youth, he possessed a resolve to transcend the mundane world. At the age of seventeen, the local prefectures and counties...

He was nominated as a jinshi candidate but did not take office. He entered the monastic order at Yingjue Temple on Mount Feilong. At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, he resided in the capital and frequently presided over the Dharma seat.
