In the early years of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, an imperial decree summoned him to the inner palace. He ascended the imperial throne;

after the meal was finished, he expounded extensively upon the arts of a wise ruler governing the world, taking compassion and protection as his primary tenet. The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued a decree on the sixth day of the third month to [proclaim it] universally.

He abolished slaughter and, at every military encampment, established Buddhist temples on a large scale. He personally provided offerings and distributed goods, providing meals for a thousand monks annually and transcribing Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras.
Later, he entered Zhiju Temple on Mount Taiyi to live in seclusion. In his later years, he set his mind upon rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
When others mocked him for doing so late in life, Zhān said, "If the merit of ten recitations is accomplished, one may still behold the Buddha."

"What need have I for anxiety? In the winter of the second year of the Zhenguan era, he fell ill. Knowing that his time had come, he went to Xingshan Temple in the capital to prepare a vegetarian feast and bid farewell to the assembly.
At that time, the Chief Executives (Puye) Fang Yuanling and Du Ruhui were both present.

That very day, he returned to Zhiju Temple to contemplate the Western Paradise, exhausting his sincerity without ceasing. On the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month, he suddenly addressed his attendants:
He said, "The Buddha has come. A moment later, he added, "The two great Bodhisattvas have also arrived.
Regarding the *Sūtra of Contemplation*, I have accomplished the twelfth contemplation, though I have not yet mastered the others. Now that I see these auspicious signs, I shall depart.
With a serene expression, he joined his palms and passed away at the age of seventy (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*; *Fozu Tongji*).
Yuánhuì (元會), courtesy name Huìmò (懷默), surnamed Xí (席), was a native of Fánchuān in Jīngzhào. At the age of twelve, his aspirations were set upon renouncing the secular world;

he entered the monastic order at Hǎijué Temple as a disciple of Dharma Master Zǒng. After his tonsure, he immediately joined the lecture halls, dedicating himself exclusively to the study of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

He composed the *Niepan yi zhang* (Treatise on the Meaning of Nirvāṇa) in four fascicles, providing comprehensive explanations of its doctrinal significance. At that time, as Ciwei Temple was newly established, he was invited to serve as its abbot;
there he expounded the scriptures and teachings, guiding and introducing later students. In the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, by imperial decree, he resided at Hongfu Temple.
He immediately suspended his lecture activities and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). In a dream, Amitāyus Buddha received him with his hand.
He subsequently fashioned an image of Amitābha and focused his mind upon it through visualization (*vipaśyanā*), remaining constantly seated without lying down.

In the fifth month of the fourteenth year, he fell ill and returned to Cíbēi Temple, where he saw the Buddha coming to welcome him; he then passed away at the age of fifty-nine (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).

Huixuan, whose secular surname was Dong, left home to become a monk at a young age in Xiangzhou. After the Northern Zhou suppression of the Dharma, he traveled south to Maoshan and subsequently stayed at Qixia.

He went to Anzhou to listen to lectures on various sutras and śāstras, attaining a profound realization of their deepest mysteries in all cases. In his later years, he returned to Xiangzhou and resided at Guangfu Temple.

The monastery was situated on a mountain peak; drawing water for irrigation was a laborious task. As he was about to move to another temple, he saw a divine being at night wearing a purple robe and standing one zhang tall.
The deity prostrated before Huixuan and said, "I request that you dwell here and constantly preach the Mahāyāna.
Do not set your mind upon the Hīnayāna. That Hīnayāna is like a high mountain without water—it cannot benefit others. The Mahāyāna sūtras, however, are like..."

It is like the great ocean: if one person preaches [the Dharma], it can cause the land where they dwell to abound in precious jewels and radiant light, their retinue to flourish and excel, and food and drink to be plentiful.
If one thinks of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), all these former benefits will be lost. I only pray that you will uphold this grandly and not frustrate my hopes.
If the Dharma Master requires water, it is easy to obtain; on the eighth day of next month, you shall certainly receive it. Go yourself.
At the Great Spring of the Compassionate Mother in Jiannan, she requested that a dragon king depart. As soon as she had spoken, he was no longer seen.

On the seventh day of the following month, at the beginning of the night, a great wind suddenly arose from the southwest; thunder shook the earth and rain poured down, continuing throughout the entire night until it finally ceased at dawn.
Only then was it seen that a clear, fragrant, and delicious spring had appeared in the hollow north of the temple. The entire monastery rejoiced, and Xuan raised them with maternal compassion.
He harbored these thoughts. He always maintained a smiling countenance. Having resided in the mountains for a long time, both monastics and laypeople held him in high esteem.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, he saw a mountain deity at night who told him: "Dharma Master, before long you shall be reborn in the Western Land.

On the fourteenth day of the seventh month, having finished preaching the *Ullambana Sūtra*, he folded his hands and said: "Throughout my life I have accepted offerings from the faithful; now I must repay them."

He distributed everything from a single hair’s breadth upward, bestowing it upon the monastic community of the ten directions, the destitute and solitary beggars, and followers of various non-Buddhist paths.
Having spoken thus, he passed away at his Dharma seat at the age of seventy-nine (*Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*).
Mingjun, surnamed Sun, was a native of Qi. He made it his constant practice to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

On the night of the twelfth day of the second month in the first year of the Yonghui era, he died suddenly; however, his heart remained warm. After a period of time, he revived and said that he had first seen two youths dressed in green.
As the disciple was about to arrive at the King’s residence, he asked what deeds he had performed during his lifetime. He replied, "I have merely recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The King said, "The merit is beyond words; you may recite it another hundred thousand times, and next year you will surely be born in the Pure Land.
I shall not see you again. He then ordered two green-clad attendants to escort him back to the monastery. From that time on, Daojun applied himself with diligent effort.
It increased twofold. He passed away in the third month of the second year [of the Zhenguan era]. The monastics of the temple all smelled a wondrous fragrance (from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*).
As for Shan Dao, "Shan Dao" is not clearly known as his original name. During the Zhenguan period, he encountered Master Chao of Xihe, who [expounded] the nine grades of the Pure Land.

At the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), Xi said, "This is truly the essential ford for entering the Buddha-way. Cultivating other practices is circuitous and difficult to accomplish; only this Dharma-gate allows for swift transcendence of birth and death.
Thereupon, he applied himself with diligent and arduous effort, chanting and prostrating day and night. Eventually, he reached the capital, where he inspired the fourfold assembly.
Whenever he entered his room, he would kneel upright and chant the name of the Buddha, never ceasing until his strength was exhausted. Upon leaving, he would expound the teaching.
For over thirty years, he preached the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land without ever sleeping. He guarded his precepts so strictly that he did not transgress even the slightest detail.
He delighted in providing fine food for the assembly while consuming coarse and simple fare himself.

All offerings and donations he received were used to copy more than one hundred thousand scrolls of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Amitābha Sūtra), to paint three hundred wall murals depicting the transformations of the Pure Land, to construct pagodas and temples, and to light lamps to maintain constant illumination. Thus he propagated the Way.
Those who followed his transformation were very numerous. There were those who recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* one hundred thousand to five hundred thousand times;
there were those who daily chanted the Buddha’s name from ten thousand to one hundred thousand times. Among them, those who attained samādhi and were reborn in the Pure Land cannot be fully recorded.
Someone asked, "Is it through mindfulness of the Buddha that one is born in the Pure Land? Tanyou replied, "It is according to how you practice mindfulness. Thus...

As you made this vow, you thought of it once; a single ray of light issued from your mouth. When you thought of it ten times, it reached a hundred, and the light was likewise. The verse for exhorting the world says:
"Gradually the skin becomes like that of a chicken and the hair like that of a crane; look at the gait, growing increasingly faltering.
Even if gold and jade fill the hall, how can one escape decay, aging, and the suffering of illness? No matter how many kinds of pleasures you may have..."
This is the constant conclusion that has arrived. There is only the path of practice: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Someone may ask:

"For what reason do you not cause people to perform meditative visualization (*vipaśyanā*), but instead directly command them to single-mindedly recite the name? The answer is: "Sentient beings have heavy afflictions; their objects of perception are subtle while their minds are coarse;

their consciousnesses are fluttering and their spirits are scattered, making visualization difficult to accomplish. Therefore, out of great compassion, the Great Sage directly exhorts them to focus [on the Name]."
Reciting the Name: It is precisely because reciting the name is easy that the continuity [of mindfulness] arises immediately.

If one can maintain this continuity from moment to moment, making it the end of one's life, then ten will be reborn for every ten recitations, and a hundred for every hundred. Why is this? Because there are no external distracting conditions and one attains right mindfulness;
because it accords with the Buddha’s original vow; because it does not contradict the teachings; and because it follows the Buddha’s words. If one should abandon...
Among those who practice while focusing their thoughts on various matters, one or two out of a hundred may succeed; three or four out of a thousand may succeed. Why is this?
Because their various conditions cause distraction and agitation, leading them to lose right mindfulness; because it does not accord with the Buddha’s original vow;

because it contradicts the teachings; because it does not follow the Buddha’s words; and because their focused recollection lacks continuity, such that their minds do not maintain a continuous flow of mindfulness as they repay the Buddha’s kindness.

Therefore, although they perform the practices, they are constantly associated with fame and profit; thus, they delight in frequenting distracting conditions, which obstructs both themselves and others from attaining the right practice for rebirth.
Observing those among the clergy and laity in various regions today, their understanding and practice differ, and their focus is either single-minded or distracted.

Among those who practice with single-minded intent, ten out of ten will be reborn [in the Pure Land]. Among those who cultivate in a distracted manner without sincerity, not even one in a thousand will succeed. I pray that...

All people, reflect well upon yourselves. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must strenuously discipline your minds and subdue yourselves, never ceasing day or night, making it your lifelong vow until the end of your lives.
When the preceding thought ends, the succeeding thought immediately arises;

for long ages and eternal kalpas, you shall enjoy the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma until the attainment of Buddhahood—how joyful this would be! Furthermore, he composed the "Text for Right Mindfulness at the Hour of Death," stating: In general...
When a person is approaching the end of life and desires to be reborn in the Pure Land, they must not fear death.
They should constantly reflect that this body is full of suffering, impurity, and various evil conditions that entangle it.

To be able to cast off this defiled body, transcend to the Pure Land, and experience immeasurable bliss while attaining liberation from the miserable realms of birth and death—this is truly a matter to be desired, like casting off tattered clothes to obtain new ones.
Change into fine robes. Relax the body and mind; do not give rise to attachment or craving. As soon as you encounter illness, contemplate impermanence and wait for death with single-minded resolve.

You must instruct your family members and those who come to inquire after you that they should recite the Buddha’s name for you, and that they must not speak of trivial, mundane matters of the moment or domestic affairs, nor need they offer words of consolation.
To offer words of consolation and prayers for peace and happiness is entirely empty and of no benefit.

If the illness is grave and death is imminent, relatives must not shed tears or wail, nor should they utter sounds of lamentation and resentment, which will disturb the mind and cause one to lose right mindfulness.
One should simply instruct them to keep Amitābha Buddha in mind until the last breath is drawn. If there is someone who clearly understands the Pure Land, they should [instruct them] frequently...
Come, exert yourselves! This is a most great fortune. Those who employ this Dharma will certainly attain rebirth; of this there is no doubt. The gateway of death is vast;
one must apply effort from within oneself before success can be achieved. If there is a single moment of error, one will suffer for kalpas;
who can take one’s place? Reflect on this, reflect on it! One day, Dao suddenly said to others: "This body is loathsome; I shall go to the West."
He returned and climbed a willow tree in front of the temple, facing west, and prayed, saying: "May the Buddha receive me;
may the Bodhisattvas assist me, so that I shall not lose right mindfulness and attain rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. Having spoken these words, he threw himself down and passed away.
Emperor Gaozong, recognizing his spiritual extraordinariness, bestowed upon the temple the plaque name "Guangming" (Radiance). (From the *Fozu Tongji* and *Lebang Wenlei*).
Huai-gan, Huai-gan—his origins are not clearly known. He was steadfast and resolute, studying with arduous diligence.

Upon hearing the scriptural teaching that one could attain rebirth in An-yang through a brief period of mindfulness of the Buddha, his doubts remained unresolved. He returned to consult Shan-dao, who said: "Mindfulness of the Buddha leads to rebirth."
"The true words of all Buddhas state: 'If you, my son, can believe and enter [this path], and mindfully recollect the Buddha with utmost sincerity, there shall surely be verification.

He then entered the *maṇḍala* for twenty-one days. Seeing no spiritual omens, he lamented his own deep karmic obstructions and intended to end his life by fasting. His teacher did not permit this, but exhorted him to increase his diligent practice even further.
After three years, he was moved by the Buddha’s manifestation of golden light and beheld the tuft of white hair between the Buddha's eyebrows, thereby attesting to his mindfulness."

He composed the *Foshanmei zhu jueyi lun* (Treatise on Adhering to the Buddha’s Samādhi and Resolving Doubts) in seven fascicles. At the time of his death, he saw a transformed Buddha coming to welcome him;
he passed away facing west (*Song Gaoseng zhuan*).

Faxiang, Faxiang, was a native of Tongzhou. He left home to become a monk in his youth and traveled extensively to seek the Way. Pure, poor, and possessing few desires, he had no fixed place of residence.
Later, he lived at Daxingguo Monastery in Yangzhou for over thirty years. His conduct was solemn and austere; he constantly maintained a seated or reclining posture.
He occupied a single large room, opening both to the front and the rear, situated directly facing the wind. He made the recitation of sutras his primary occupation.

When members of the clergy or laity came to inquire after him, he would not exchange a single word until they had finished reading the entire scroll. He took rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) as his ultimate goal; whatever meritorious deeds he performed, he invariably dedicated toward that pure land.
Later, when his illness became severe, his attendant stood by his side and heard him repeatedly call out the name of the Buddha-image. The attendant turned [to listen].
Looking up, he caught a fleeting glimpse of the Buddha manifesting his form, standing poised against the western wall; his radiance was like a mirror. In a moment, the light gradually faded.

Without resistance or solicitation, once the temple buildings were completed, it was named Mida Temple (Amitābha Monastery). What remained after the construction was distributed to the hungry and the sick. (Zhenyuan...)
On the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the eighteenth year, he passed away at the temple at the age of ninety-one.

Previously, there was a monk named Fashao who resided on Mount Lu; while in a state of right concentration, he traveled to the Land of Bliss and saw a person clad in coarse garments attending upon the Buddha.
The Buddha [the Emperor] said: "This is Chengyuan of Mount Heng. Go forth and seek him out; he is the one. He then followed him to study and spread the teachings throughout the world.
When Zhao served as State Preceptor during the reign of Emperor Daizong, he spoke of his teacher’s supreme virtue, and the Son of Heaven turned toward the south to pay him homage.
As his virtue could not be fully encompassed by worldly measures, the Emperor named his residence the "Pratyutpanna Samādhi Dharma Hall" (Banzhou Daochang). Liu...
Zongyuan composed an inscription for him. A stone was erected to the right of the temple gate (from the *Collected Works of Liu Zhitou*).
Fazhao—Fazhao—was a man of unknown origins. In the second year of the Dali era, he resided at Yunfeng Temple in Hengzhou and applied himself diligently to his practice.
Without slackening his efforts, one day in the monastic hall, while looking into his porridge bowl, he beheld auspicious clouds of five colors. Within the clouds appeared a mountain temple.
To the northeast of the temple was a mountain; at the foot of the mountain was a stream; to the north of the stream was a stone gate; and within the gate was yet another temple.
The inscription read: "The Great Sage’s Zhulin Monastery. On another day, he again saw several monasteries within the clouds inside his alms bowl;
ponds, terraces, and towers were there, with tens of thousands of bodhisattvas dwelling amidst them. He questioned those he knew about what he had seen, and one monk said:
The transformations of the Holy Spirit are unfathomable to the emotions. As for the topography of the mountains and rivers, it is Mount Wutai.
In the fourth year, at Hudeongsa Temple in Jun, he established a five-assembly *nienfo* (Buddha-recitation) practice hall.

He was moved by auspicious clouds that covered everything, and within the clouds appeared pavilions, with Amitābha Buddha and two Bodhisattvas filling the void of space. This was witnessed by the entire population of Hengzhou.

Everyone burned incense and gazed upon it in worship; after a long while, it finally extinguished. Daoyao then encountered an old man who said to him, "You once made a vow to go to the Golden World to pay homage to the Great Sage.
Why have you now stopped so abruptly? Having spoken, he vanished.
Daoyao subsequently traveled far with several companions to Mount Wutai. On the sixth day of the fourth month in the fifth year, they arrived at the Buddha [Temple] in Wutai County.
At Guang Temple, during the fourth watch of that evening, he saw from afar a strange light illuminating his body. He followed it for fifty *li* until he reached a mountain.
At the foot of the mountain was a stream, and to the north of the stream stood a stone gate. There he saw two youths who called themselves Sudhana and Nanda.
They led him to a temple with a signboard reading "The Great Sage’s Bamboo Grove Temple," which was exactly as he had seen within the alms bowl—the golden ground and the jewels.

The trees served as a magnificent adornment. Upon entering the monastery and ascending the lecture hall, he saw Mañjuśrī to the west and Samantabhadra to the east, each occupying a lion throne and preaching the Dharma while surrounded by a multitude of ten thousand beings. Daoyao prostrated himself and asked:

"In this final age, ordinary people are far removed from the time of the Sage; their understanding is narrow and inferior, and their afflictions and defilements are particularly deep. There is no way for their Buddha-nature to manifest. The Buddha—

The Dharma is vast and expansive; I do not yet know which dharma-gate one should practice as being most essential. Mañjuśrī replied: "Now is the very time for you to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Among all gates of cultivation, none surpasses mindfulness of the Buddha. To make offerings to the Triple Gem is to cultivate both merit and wisdom together;
these two gates are the most excellent and essential. In past kalpas, it was because I contemplated the Buddha that [I attained realization]."
Because of mindfulness of the Buddha and because of making offerings, one attains the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, all dharmas, the *prajñāpāramitā*, the arising of profound dhyāna, and even all Buddhas, are born from mindfulness of the Buddha.

Thus, one knows that mindfulness of the Buddha is the king of all dharmas. [The interlocutor] asked: "How should one practice this mindfulness? Mañjuśrī replied: "To the west of this world, there is the [Buddha] Akṣobhya..."
"Amitābha Buddha! The vow-power of that Buddha is inconceivable. You should maintain mindfulness of him without interruption;

then, at the end of your life, you will certainly attain rebirth there and never fall back. Having spoken thus, the two Great Sages simultaneously extended their golden arms and stroked Śāriputra’s head, saying:
"Because you have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, you shall before long realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. If any man or woman of good family..."
"Those who wish to swiftly attain Buddhahood have no practice superior to the recollection of the Buddha; thus they can quickly realize unsurpassed Bodhi.
Having said this, Zhào paid his respects and took his leave. The two youths escorted him out of the temple gate, but when he looked up, they had suddenly vanished.
He then erected a stone monument to mark the spot. On the thirteenth day of the fourth month, Zhào went there together with more than fifty monks.
At Vajra Cave, he prostrated with a devout heart before the names of the Thirty-five Buddhas.
After reciting them only ten times, he suddenly beheld that place as a vast, magnificent, and pure palace of lapis lazuli, where Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra were together in one location.
He then went alone back to Vajra Cave, vowing to see the Great Sage; as he threw himself to the ground, he saw the Indian monk Buddhāpālita, who led him inside.

There was one hall with a plaque inscribed "Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Temple. It was adorned with rare treasures, its radiance flashing and shimmering. Although [the author] had personally witnessed these spiritual wonders over time, he had not spoken of them to others.
In the twelfth month of that year, at Huayan Temple, he entered a Buddha-recitation retreat (*nienfo daochang*), abstaining from grain for a fixed period and vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land.
On the first watch of the seventh day, while he was engaged in the formal practice of Buddha-recitation, he saw—
A Brahmin monk entered and said to him, "Why do you not transmit to the people of the world the realm of Mount Tai that you have seen?

Having finished speaking, he vanished. Zhaoxin marveled at this. On the following day, he saw the Brahmin monk again, who spoke as before. Zhaoxin said, "It is not that I dare keep the holy Way secret;
I fear only that it might give rise to doubt and slander. The monk said, "The Great Sage Mañjuśrī is currently manifest on this mountain. Still...

"You will incur public reproach; why do you begrudge it? Simply use the realms you have seen to announce them universally to sentient beings, so that those who see or hear of them may resolve their minds toward Bodhi, serving as the conditions for a 'poison drum' (to awaken the world). Zhao then recalled what he had seen and recorded it for posterity.
The following year, the monk Huìcóng of Jiangdong, together with various monks from Huayan Monastery, accompanied Zhao to the Vajra Cave (*Kongōkutsu*). Upon arriving, they...
At the site marked by stones, as the great assembly gazed upon the ancient traces with unceasing sorrow and joy, they suddenly heard the sound of a bell.
Its tone was elegant and resonant, with distinct rhythmic intervals. The crowd was further struck with wonder, realizing that what they had witnessed was not in vain.

Consequently, they inscribed this account upon the walls of their dwellings, vowing that all who see or hear it would together give rise to the supreme resolve (*viśiṣṭa-citta*). Later, at the place where the temple plaque for Huazhu Lin Monastery was inscribed, a monastery was established.

He established one precinct, which he continued to call "Bamboo Grove. Thereupon, Daozhao devoted himself earnestly to the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name), never neglecting it day or night.
Suddenly, he saw Fotuo Bolu, who said to him, "Your flower has already formed; three years from now, it will bloom.

When the appointed time arrived, he said to the assembly, "I am going," and passed away while sitting upright. Some say that Daozhao once practiced *nianfo* at the Five Assemblies in Bingzhou, and his virtue...
During the Zong era, he was summoned to the capital to instruct the palace ladies in the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), extending even to the Five Assemblies (*wuhui*).
He was thus titled the Dharma Master of the Five Assemblies (*Wuhui Fashi*) (as recorded in the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* and the *Lebang Wenlei*).
Shaokang, Shaokang: his surname was Zhou. He was a native of Shandu Mountain in Jingyun. From birth he did not speak. At the age of seven, he entered Lingshan Temple to pay homage to the Buddha.
When his mother asked if he recognized him, he suddenly spoke, saying, "Śākyamuni Buddha. His parents then abandoned [their worldly life] to follow him.
He left the household life at the age of fifteen and was able to master the five divisions of the sutras.

At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he went to Baima Monastery in Luoyang and saw that the texts within the hall were emitting light. Upon examining them, he found they were the "Text on the Western Paradise for Guiding Transformation" by Master Shandao.
He made a vow, saying: "If I have a karmic affinity with the Pure Land, may these texts once again manifest radiance. Having spoken these words, the light returned.
It flashed with light, and within the radiance there were faintly visible transformed bodhisattvas. Kang said, "Though the kalpa-stones may be worn away, my vow shall never change.
He then went to the Shadow Hall of Master Shandao at Guangming Temple in Chang'an to pay his respects.

Suddenly, he saw the true image of Shandao ascend into the air and say to him, "If you follow my teachings and extensively transform sentient beings, when your merit is perfected in a future day, you will surely be reborn in peace."
Yang traveled south to Jiangling, where he encountered a Dharma Master who said to him, "If you wish to transform people, you should go to Xinding;

your karmic affinity lies there. Having spoken, the Master vanished. Yang then proceeded to Xinding, where he begged for money to entice small children to recite the Buddha's name, giving them one coin for every single recitation.
After doing this for over a year, whenever men or women, young or old, saw Kang, they would all say:
The name of Amitābha Buddha and the sound of his recitation filled the roads. He subsequently established a Pure Land practice hall on Mount Oryong, constructing a three-tiered altar.
Whenever a day for ritual offerings arrived, faithful believers would gather in full; he converted approximately three thousand people.
Every time he ascended the seat, he would chant "Buddha" in a loud voice, and the assembly would join him in unison. When Kang chanted "Buddha" once, the assembly saw a Buddha emerge from his mouth;
when he chanted ten times, there were ten Buddhas, appearing like a string of pearls. Kang said to the assembly, "Those of you who have seen the Buddha will surely attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
The assembly was all filled with joy and comfort. In the tenth month of the twenty-first year, he addressed the monastics and laypeople, saying: "You should..."
He gave rise to a mind of aspiration for the Pure Land and a mind of weary detachment toward Jambudvīpa. At that time, you all beheld my radiance;
truly, you are my disciples. Thereupon, he emitted several rays of extraordinary light and passed away in silence.
His stupa was enshrined on Mount Tairan, and he was known as the Dharma Master of Tairan (as recorded in the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* and the *Lebang Wenlei*).
Biàn Tài (Biàn-cái). Her surname was Li; she was a native of Xiangyang. At her birth, a wondrous fragrance issued from her chamber.

At the age of seven, she entered the monastic order under Chan Master Jì of Mount Xián. She traveled through various prefectures and served as a disciple to Vinaya Master Huáiwēi of Ān Guó Temple in Cháng'ān.
Master Yiban of Baonensi was a master of exegesis who attained comprehensive mastery of the meanings of the sutras. Later, he served as the *sanghādhipati* (monastic head) of Zhangxinsi.
For twenty years, he practiced the Pure Land path in secret, never disclosing it to others; he was on intimate terms only with Ren Gong of Huerong.

He said, "Tài will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land; my expectation is within ten years. When the time arrived, he sent his disciple to inform Ren Gong, saying, "The period previously expected has now come.
When Ren Gong arrived, Tài said, "I am departing. He sat upright upon his rope-cot and, in silence, returned to quiescence.
The assembly heard celestial music coming from the west, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room. He was fifty-six years old. (From the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* and *Fozu Tongji*)
Shandao, a native of Linzi, once entered the Great Canon and, reaching into it at random, drew out a scroll of the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*.

Thereupon, he concentrated his mind on the recitation of the Buddha’s name and practiced the sixteen sublime contemplations. Later, he traveled to Mount Lu to visit the remains of Master Huiyuan, sighing with emotion.

However, his resolve increased further. Later, he withdrew to Mount Zhongnan, where he practiced the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* for several years. He beheld jeweled pavilions and jade ponds as clearly as if they were before his eyes.
He then traveled to Jinyang, where he received the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* from Master Chao.

After entering meditative absorption for seven days, Chao requested that he observe the place of his future rebirth. Daobao replied, "Master, you must repent for three offenses; only then will you be able to attain rebirth there."
The Master once placed Buddhist images beneath the eaves and windows while residing himself in a secluded room; this is the first offense. One should repent before the Buddha.
Furthermore, he once conscripted ordained monks for labor; this is the second offense. One should repent before the Sangha of the four quarters.

Furthermore, because of constructing houses, many insect lives were sacrificed; these constitute the three sins. One should repent before all sentient beings, contemplating past transgressions with profound stillness and washing the mind to express remorse.
After doing this for a long time, the Way will emerge through meditative concentration. [The deity] said to Cuo: "Your teacher’s sins have been extinguished.
When white light comes to illuminate you hereafter, that is the sign of rebirth in the Pure Land. Daoxuan traveled to convert the capital and returned.
He was like a person in a marketplace. Suddenly, he fell slightly ill; he then closed his room and passed away while joyfully reciting the Buddha’s name.
A wondrous fragrance and celestial music emerged as he vanished toward the west (Fozu Tongji).
Zhiquin (智欽).

Nothing is known of this person’s background; he specialized exclusively in the practice of dhyāna. Furthermore, he performed the ritual of bowing and reciting the names of fifteen thousand Buddhas up to ten thousand times.
Later, before the Aśoka Stūpa in Liuzhou, he set fire to one of his arms, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. His disciple was the monk... [text ends].
Dharma Master Hu was at his residence when he saw an extraordinary light illuminating the courtyard at midnight. He asked, "Who is carrying this torch?
He asked this three times, and a voice from the air replied, "It is to come and welcome Dharma Master Qin. Hu hurriedly opened the door and beheld the Buddha’s body emitting a great radiance.
Banners, flowers, and jeweled canopies soared through the air and descended. Qín immediately passed away (Fó-zǔ Tǒng-jì).
Zhīyuán, whose courtesy name was Hòujié, was surnamed Chén and was a native of Hóngyā in Méizhōu. At the age of seven, he listened to lectures at Níngyísì.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was as if a long-standing habit from his past lives. That evening, he dreamed that the Buddha stroked the crown of his head with his hand. At the age of eleven, he left the household life;

he was granted the commentaries on the sutras and attained mastery over their profound depths. At thirteen, he ascended the lecture hall to discourse, and both monastics and laypeople listened with rapt attention.
During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, he was summoned to the capital and granted a purple *kāṣāya*. He petitioned to restore the abandoned temples throughout the empire.

Shortly thereafter, he requested to return to his native mountain. During the reign of Emperor Xizong, he was conferred the title National Teacher Wudao and granted a sandalwood seat. Suddenly, a human-faced ulcer grew upon his knee.
At that time, the Sichuanese monk Karuma instructed Yuan to wash it with spring water. The ulcer suddenly spoke, saying: "Do you know?"
"Did Yuan Ang kill Chao Cuo? You are indeed Ang, and I am Cuo.

For generations we have sought revenge, yet you have been a high monk for ten lifetimes with your precepts so strictly observed that I could find no opportunity to harm you. Now, because you received a gift that was excessively lavish, I was able to injure you.
But since the Venerable Kanaka washed me with the water of samādhi, I shall leave you; I will no longer be your enemy."

The ulcer subsequently healed. Yuan was one of few desires; he did not eat after midday and practiced the Way throughout the six periods of the day, repeatedly bringing about manifest spiritual responses.
One day, he suddenly heard a voice from the air saying, "You shall certainly be reborn in the Pure Land. He then asked, "Whose words are these? The void again replied, "It is the Buddha.
Furthermore, he saw a Bodhisattva descend into his courtyard, who earnestly praised and exhorted him before suddenly vanishing. At the time of his death—
At that time, he instructed that his corpse be discarded to feed the fish and birds, saying, "I have long had an appointment with the Pure Land of the West; now the time has come.
Having spoken these words, he passed away facing west on his right side at the age of seventy-three (*Song Gaoseng zhuan*, *Shenseng zhuan*).
Duanfu, Duanfu:
his secular surname was Zhao, and he was a native of Tianshui. His mother dreamed that a Buddhist monk gave her a *śarīra* relic and commanded her to swallow it; she subsequently gave birth to him.
At the age of ten, he entered the monastic life under Chan Master Daowu at Chongfu Temple. At seventeen, he received the tonsure and was registered at Anguo Temple.
He traveled extensively to attend various lecture halls and became proficient in both the Sūtras and the Vinaya.

He dreamed of a Brahman monk who presented him with a lapis lazuli vessel filled to the brim with *śarīra* relics, commanding him to swallow them, saying, "The great teachings of the Tripiṭaka are now entirely stored within your belly. From that time on, his eloquence and discernment were unimpeded.

When he preached the Sūtras in Taiyuan, the entire capital flocked to attend. Emperor Dezong summoned him to court and bestowed upon him a purple cassock; this continued through the reigns of both the Shunzong and Xianzong emperors.
He was seen by all as one worthy of honor and respect. He lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Yogācāra) on one hundred and sixty occasions.

Daily, he maintained the recitation of various sections of the scriptures, regarding the Pure Land as his place of rest. Of the tens of millions of offerings and donations he received, he used them all to adorn and embellish the temple halls.

In his quarters, he sat alone upon a single bed, dwelling in a state of serene self-realization. On the first day of the sixth month in the first year of the Kaicheng era (836 CE), he passed away reclining on his right side facing west.
A wondrous fragrance filled the air. Upon cremation, more than three hundred śarīra relics were recovered. (From the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*)

Xiongjun, Xiongjun. His secular surname was Zhou; he was a native of Chengdu. He was skilled at lecturing and preaching, yet lacked any observance of the precepts. He once left the monastic life to join the military, but soon returned to being a monk, for which he felt considerable shame and regret.
He constantly recited the names of the Buddhas. During the Dali era, he died suddenly and entered the underworld. There, the presiding official...

He was rebuked and sentenced to hell. Xiongjun cried out loudly, saying, "The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that even those who have committed the five heinous crimes can attain rebirth in the Pure Land through ten recitations at the moment of death.
Although I, Xiongjun, have committed sins, I have not perpetrated the five heinous crimes. If one follows the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name..."

He was reborn in the Pure Land. Otherwise, the Buddhas of the three periods would be guilty of falsehood. Thereupon, he joined his palms and meditated with focused mindfulness; suddenly, a jeweled platform appeared, and he ascended into the air and departed toward the west.
At the same time, there were those who returned from the underworld and recounted the event, saying: (From the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*;

the *Fozu Tongji* records that Xiongjun entered the underworld and personally testified to the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name, whereupon his presiding official released him to return. He then entered the western mountains to devote himself exclusively to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. After four years, he took leave of the assembly and passed away while seated. This account differs from the former.)
Weiyong was from Jingzhou. He frequently indulged in wine and gambling, yet in his leisure time he would recite the sutras, praying to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
There was another in the same monastery named Lingkui whose conduct was quite similar to his; the villagers had a proverb about them that went: "Lingkui commits the karma; Weiyong prays for it."
Following in his footsteps, there are tens of millions of layers of hells; do not disdain being pushed at the head to enter them.
Gongwen said, "Although my sins leave me no place to escape, I rely upon the power of the Buddha to attain rebirth through ten recitations. How could I fall again into the evil realms?

One day, while Gong was ill, Kui went out of the temple and saw a youth holding a musical instrument. When he asked where the youth had come from, the youth replied, "I have come from the West to welcome Gong."

He was indeed a man of superior character. One day, a person took a lotus flower from his bosom; the flower was closed like a fist, and its petals emitted a strange light as it sped toward the temple.

When he arrived at the temple the following day, Sengcong had already passed away. Thereupon, Xue Kui was moved to realization and changed his ways, becoming renowned for his eminent virtue (from the *Fozu Tongji*).

"Great practitioner, great practitioner! A man from Qizhou first studied the Tiantai teachings, later entering Mount Tai to dwell there. He fashioned clothing from grass and gathered wild fruits for food.
While practicing the Lotus Samādhi, he was moved by the manifestation of the Great Being Samantabhadra. One day, he sighed and said:"
Human life is impermanent; before long it will be worn away and extinguished. Not knowing where one will be reborn in the next world, he entered the great storehouse and prayed with fervent devotion.
Reaching out his hand at random, he drew forth the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Amitābha Sūtra). Thereupon, he focused his mind single-mindedly on recollecting Amitābha Buddha.
After three weeks of reading and contemplation, at midnight, he suddenly beheld the lapis lazuli ground; his mental eye became clear and penetrating, and he further saw the Buddha and...

The two great beings emerged and stood in mid-air. When Emperor Xizong heard of Daoxing’s reputation, he issued an edict for him to enter the palace and bestowed upon him the title "Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent.
One year later, the lapis lazuli ground appeared once more. He said to his attendants, "The precious ground has appeared again;
the time for rebirth in An-yang (Sukhāvatī) has arrived. That very day, he passed away lying on his right side (*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*, *Fozu Tongji*).
Zhītōng, whose secular surname was Zhāng, was a native of Fēngxiáng. Having left the household life, he traveled to Luòxià, where he encountered the Tripiṭaka Master Vajra.
He practiced the teachings of Yoga-tantra and thoroughly mastered its ritual protocols. During the reign of Emperor Wénmù of the Qián dynasty, he traveled east to Wúyuè and entered Tiāntái Mountain.
At the site of the Sage’s Enlightenment, he perused the *Record of the Auspicious Omens of the Pure Land* and resolved to be reborn in that realm.
From then on, he never spat toward the west nor sat with his back to the west. One day, while climbing Mount Zhong, he reached Shouzhao Rock and recited the Forty-Eight Vows.
"May I be swiftly reborn in the Pure Land. He threw himself down and fell into the midst of a great tree; its branches were supple and yielding, so that he suffered not the slightest injury.
He then straightened his body and climbed back onto the cliff, vowing: "The Great Vow has already been made, and this remaining life is to be loathed.

I only hope that the Holy Assembly will come together to welcome and guide me. He threw himself down once more, landing upon some grass, where he remained for a long time before regaining consciousness. The assembly of monks...
He soon returned to Yexi and went to Mount Fahu in Yuezhou, where he silently cultivated the Pure Land practices.

Later, he saw white cranes and peacocks descend in formation, and he also saw lotus flowers opening and closing before him. He declared, "The white cranes and peacocks are the scenery of the Pure Land;
the radiant appearance of the lotuses is the place of rebirth. I have seen the signs of purity. Thereupon, he rose to prostrate to the Buddha and passed away.
Upon the cremation, auspicious clouds of five colors encircled and covered the flames. The *śarīra* relics were arranged in scales upon the body (*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*, *Fozu Tongji*).
He may stop; he may stop.
His surname was Ma. He was a native of Dafangshan in Fanyang. At the age of twelve, he left the household life.

At nineteen, he traveled to Mount Wutai to seek the precepts, where he was moved by the spiritual light of Mañjuśrī illuminating his body. At twenty-three, he went to the Bingzhou region to study the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Regarding the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas): later, while expounding it in Chang’an, he converted and guided the masses daily. Before long, he returned to his hometown, where his mother was still living at home.

He sustained his mother by begging for alms with a bowl and constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. In his later years, he resided at the Jingtu-yuan (Pure Land Monastery) in Changshou.
On the twenty-second day of the first month in the first year of the Guangshun era of the Later Zhou dynasty, he fell slightly ill and summoned his disciples to recite the name of Amitābha.
"Amitābha Buddha, assist me in being reborn in the Pure Land. Having spoken thus, he suddenly passed away at the age of seventy-five (*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*).

Shao Yan’s secular surname was Liu; he was a native of Yongzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and relied upon Master Ga’an, under whom he extensively studied the scriptures and treatises.
Possessing such karmic predispositions from past lives, he later resided at Huixin Temple on the heart of Qiantang Lake.

He constantly recited and upheld the *Lotus Sūtra* day and night without interruption, vowing that upon completing ten thousand recitations, he would be reborn in the Pure Land. Suddenly, he experienced a spiritual response as lotus flowers sprouted upon the dry land.

He then vowed to perform self-immolation as an offering to the Three Holy Ones of the Western Paradise. King Qian Chu of Wuyue earnestly exhorted him to desist, but he nevertheless cast himself into the Cao'e River.
[He was] inside [the coffin]. It was as if something had been placed beneath his feet so that he did not die. The King of Wuyue established a Pure Land Cloister at Baota Temple to house him.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of the Kaibao era of the Song dynasty, he fell ill; he sought no medicine but composed several gāthās to instruct his disciples, saying:
"I have recited twenty thousand sections of the sutras; I shall certainly be reborn in An-yang (Sukhāvatī). He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. [His remains were then] cremated.
Vishakha. His *śarīra* relics were beyond counting; he was seventy-three years old (*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*, *Fozu Tongji*).
Shouzhen, whose secular surname was Ji and courtesy name Fading, was a native of Wanan in Yongxing. He entered the monastic order at Shengshou Temple and went to visit Conglang.
The Master studied the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*. Next, he followed the lineage of Master Xingguang to receive the transmission of the Huayan *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*.
Later, he paid homage to Ācārya Yanmi to be granted the *Yogācāra* teachings. In all these matters, he attained the essential points and became profoundly enlightened regarding all phenomena.

He propagated the sublime scriptures with vigor for forty years without the slightest negligence. He was bestowed the honorary title "Zhaoxin" (Luminous Faith). He regularly practiced the visualization of Amitābha Buddha of the Western Paradise during the middle of the night.

He cultivated the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection and vowed to be reborn in a Pure Land. On the ninth day of the eighth month in the autumn of the fourth year of the Kaibao era, he commanded the assembly to chant the Buddha’s name together.
After a long while, he ordered them to cease; suddenly, he passed away into stillness at the age of seventy-eight.
Upon cremation, śarīra relics were obtained (from the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan*).

Yanshou, whose courtesy name was Chongyuan, was the son of the Wang family of Qiantang. In his youth, he recited the Lotus Sūtra. During the reign of Prince Wenmu of the Qian family, Yanshou served as a tax collector;
because he frequently used official funds to purchase and release living beings, he was sentenced to death. As he was being led to the marketplace for execution, the Prince...
A person peered at him; his facial expression did not change. [The person] ordered him to be released. He went to Master Cuiyan of Siming to leave the household life.
He further studied under National Teacher Shaokang of Tiantai, where he realized the essential point of the mind.

Once, while performing the Lotus Repentance at Guoqing Temple, he saw Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva pouring nectar into his mouth during meditative contemplation. Because of this, he attained great eloquence. Due to his past...

His resolve remained undecided, so he ascended the Chan Hall of Zhizhe and fashioned two lots: one read "Single-minded Chan Samādhi," and the other read "Adorning the Pure Land through Myriad Practices.
With a focused mind and fervent prayer, he drew the lots seven times and each time obtained the lot for the Pure Land. Thereupon, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the cultivation of pure karma.
In the second year of the Jianlong era, King Zhongyi invited him to reside at Yongming Temple and bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Zhijue.
The Master performed one hundred and eight daily recitations. At night, he went to a separate peak to practice the Way and chant the Buddha’s name;
bystanders occasionally heard the sounds of conch shells and celestial music. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* until he had accumulated thirteen thousand fascicles.

He resided at Yongming for fifteen years, with one thousand seven hundred disciples, constantly bestowing the Bodhisattva precepts upon the assembly and providing food for spirits and ghosts. He purchased...

He ransomed lives and dedicated them all toward the Pure Land. He authored the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in one hundred fascicles, which harmonized the differing tenets of the Tiantai, Xianshou, and Cien schools.
He also authored the *Wanshan tonggui ji* (Collection on the Common Return of Myriad Good Deeds).

Within this collection, the sections pointing toward the Pure Land are the most essential. A brief excerpt states: Question: If the Pure Land of the Mind alone pervades the ten directions, why must one rely upon [a specific place]?

To offer one's body at the lotus pedestal and take refuge in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*) while still harboring thoughts of acceptance and rejection—how could this reach the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*)?
If feelings of longing and aversion arise, how can equanimity be achieved? Answer: As for the Pure Land of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*), it arises only when the mind is fully realized.
The *Tathāgata-acintya-viṣaya-sūtra* states: "All Buddhas of the three periods of time are solely the measure of the mind; they have attained the Patience of Accordance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*)."

Alternatively, one may enter the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) and, upon casting off the body, be swiftly reborn in the Buddha-land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). Thus, one knows that it is only through the awakening of the mind that the Pure Land of Mind-Only arises;

to be attached to objects is merely to fall into the realm of objective conditions (*ālambana-viṣaya*). Having clarified that cause and effect are without discrepancy, one realizes that there are no phenomena outside of the mind.
Furthermore, regarding the gate of equality and the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*), although one may develop faith by looking up to the teachings, what can be done about one’s own capacity?
One’s capacity is not yet sufficient; one’s contemplation is shallow, the mind is flighty, and the objects of perception are powerful while habitual tendencies are heavy.

One must therefore be born in a Buddha-land to rely upon superior conditions, so that the power of patience may be easily perfected and the Bodhisattva path swiftly traversed. The *Ten Doubts Treatise* states: "The Wise One ardently seeks birth in the Pure Land."
To realize that the nature of birth is unobtainable is itself true non-arising. This is what is meant by: "Because the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.
The foolish are bound by birth; when they hear of birth, they conceive the notion of birth, and when they hear of non-arising, they conceive the notion of non-arising.
One does not know that birth is itself non-birth, and non-birth is itself birth. Failing to realize this principle, one recklessly disputes right and wrong;

such a person is one who slanders the Dharma with false views. Question: If there are no phenomena outside the mind and the Buddha neither comes nor goes, how can there be the seeing of the Buddha or the event of his coming to welcome one?

Answer: It is through mindfulness of the Buddha as "mind-only. By means of the contemplation of mind-only, all phenomena are universally encompassed. Once one has realized that objects [are but the mind],...
It is mind-only. To realize that the mind is itself the Buddha, then whatever one contemplates is none other than the Buddha.
The *Pratyutpanna Sūtra* says: "It is like a person who dreams of seven treasures and their kinsmen, and awakens with joy; having awakened, they long for them but do not know where they are.
Such recollection of the Buddha is a metaphor for what is produced by mind-only: it exists yet is empty, and therefore has no coming or going. Furthermore, it is like an illusion, which is not real.
Thus, both mind and Buddha are forgotten, yet illusory appearances are not absent. In this way, one does not destroy the mind-Buddha;

emptiness and existence are unimpeded, and there is neither coming nor going, while universal manifestation remains unobstructed. To see is to have no seeing; one is thus constantly in accord with the Middle Way.

Therefore, the Buddha truly does not come, and the mind likewise does not go. When the path of resonance and response intersects, it is seen by the mind alone. It is like sentient beings who commit offenses and thereby evoke the earth.
Regarding the characteristics of the hells, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "All [hells] are like the hell-realms; people alike perceive wardens and others who can inflict harm and torment.
Therefore, these are all manifestations of the minds of sinful beings due to their evil karma. There are no real copper dogs, iron snakes, or other such things existing externally to the mind.
All phenomena and events in the world are likewise so. However, that realm of Śākyamuni Buddha is not restricted to the East.
West. If one’s correct understanding is clear and vivid, habitual afflictions are entirely extinguished; principle and cognition are both embraced. Question:

The *Contemplation Sūtra* elucidates the sixteen gates of contemplation, all of which involve gathering the mind to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*). One must contemplate the Buddha’s marks and signs until they are clearly realized as perfectly luminous before one can ascend to the Pure Land.
Question: How can one who possesses a distracted mind achieve rebirth through transformation? Answer: The scriptural texts of the nine grades naturally encompass varying levels of ascent and descent;

they are subsumed within two types of mind. First is the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), such as when practicing meditative cultivation, which results in rebirth in the highest grade. Second is the single-minded (*ekāgra*) mind.
Merely by reciting the Name, one is perfumed by a multitude of virtues; through dedication and the making of vows, one attains the lowest grade [of rebirth].
Nevertheless, one must take refuge for the duration of one’s life and practice with diligence until the end of one’s natural term. Whether sitting or lying down, one should always face west.

During the time of walking the path, prostrating, recollecting the Buddha, or making vows, one should be earnest and sincere, free from all distracting thoughts, as if facing execution in a prison. If...

Whether confined in a prison, pursued by vengeful bandits, or beset by water or fire, if one seeks refuge with single-minded devotion, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, swiftly realize non-arising (*anutpāda*),

extensively deliver all sentient beings, perpetuate and honor the Triple Gem, and vow to repay the four debts of gratitude— if such sincerity of will exists, it shall certainly not be in vain. However,
if one’s words do not accord with one’s deeds, if the power of faith is feeble, and if there is no mind of continuous mindfulness from moment to moment, [the merit shall not be attained].
There is a sense of frequent interruption. Relying on this indolence, one hopes for rebirth at the moment of death;

yet, being dragged by karmic obstructions, it is feared that one will find it difficult to encounter a virtuous friend. Pressed by the winds and fires [of dissolution], right mindfulness will not be achieved.

Why is this? The present is the cause, and the moment of death is the effect. The cause must be real so that the effect is not in vain. When the sound is harmonious, the resonance follows suit; when the form...

If the source is straight, the shadow will be upright. If you wish to achieve the "ten recitations" at the moment of death, you should simply prepare the ferry and bridge in advance by gathering and combining meritorious deeds and dedicating them toward that time; if each thought remains unimpaired, you need have no anxiety.

Indeed, the two wheels of good and evil and the two retributions of suffering and joy are all created by the three karmas, produced by the four conditions, accomplished by the six causes, and encompassed by the five fruits.

If, for even a single thought-moment, one harbors anger or engages in sexual misconduct, that is the karma of hell. If one is stingy, greedy, and refuses to relinquish [possessions], that is the karma of a hungry ghost.
If one is deluded and shrouded in darkness, that is the karma of an animal. If one is arrogant and conceited, that is the karma of an asura. To firmly uphold the five precepts—

The diligent cultivation of the ten wholesome actions is the karma of humans. The realization of the emptiness of persons is the karma of śrāvakas. Knowing that the nature of conditions is detached is the karma of pratyekabuddhas.
The simultaneous cultivation of the six pāramitās is the karma of bodhisattvas. True compassion that is impartial is the karma of Buddhas.
If the mind is pure, one is born through transformation in a pure land of fragrant terraces and jeweled trees; if the mind is defiled, there are hills, mounds, pits, and hollows.
Those born with physical forms in this defiled land are all the fruits of their own common karma, yet they are able to evoke superior conditions.
Therefore, apart from the source of one’s own mind, there is no separate essence. If one wishes to attain pure fruits, one need only practice pure causes.

Just as the nature of water is to flow downward and the nature of fire is to rise upward, such is the principle of causal necessity; what cause for doubt is there? Furthermore, I once composed the "Fourfold Logical Analysis" (*catuṣkoṭi*), which states: "There is Chan..."
Without Pure Land, nine out of ten people go astray; when the realm of the skandhas appears before them, they are instantly carried away by it.
With no Chan but Pure Land, ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go; once you have seen Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment?
With both Chan and Pure Land, one is like a tiger with horns; in this life one becomes a teacher of men, and in the future one becomes a Buddha or Patriarch. Without Chan...
There is no Pure Land; there are only iron beds and copper pillars. Through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, not a single person has anyone to rely upon.
On the twenty-sixth day of the second month in the eighth year of the Kaibao era, he rose at dawn, burned incense, addressed the assembly, sat in the lotus position, and passed away.
He was seventy-two years old. Later, a monk came from Linchuan who circumambulated his stupa for a year. When people asked the reason, he said, "I am ill."
He entered the underworld and saw a statue of a monk enshrined to the left of the hall. The King reverently performed prostrations and inquired about the person;
it was said to be Chan Master Yongming Shou of Hangzhou, who had already attained rebirth in the Western Paradise at the highest level of the superior grade. The King held his virtue in high esteem.
Therefore, he paid his respects (from *Wan shan tong gui* in the *Lebang wenlei*).
Wumen Wumen, whose courtesy name was Xiujǐ, was surnamed Lù and was a native of Chángshū. At the age of thirteen, he heard someone reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*, and his heart...

Moved by these circumstances, he subsequently entered the monastic order at Xingfu Temple. During the Changxing era of the Later Tang dynasty, he traveled to Huipuji Temple in Kunshan to study the Nanshan Vinaya.
Thereafter, he audited and practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, and other scriptures, as well as the *Mohe zhiguan* and various treatises, mastering their subtlest nuances.

He maintained the practice of eating only once a day, never being parted from his robes and alms bowl, and refrained from accumulating wealth or goods. When sleeping, he always lay on his right side. When sitting, he remained upright.

He invariably sat in the full lotus posture. At every *poṣadha* ceremony, he would invariably shed tears of deep emotion. He extensively instructed others in the practices for the Pure Land of the West and the perfect meaning of the One Vehicle.
He lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* more than twenty times. On the first day of the eighth month in the third year of the Yongxi era of the Song dynasty, he passed away.
One night, he saw white light emerging from the well and said to his disciples, "My allotted lifespan has reached its end here.

He then ceased eating grain and refrained from speech, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name. He dreamed of a śramaṇa holding a golden incense burner and burning incense, who circumambulated his room three times and said, "This is Guanding;
I have already been born in the Pure Land. I admire what you have cultivated, and thus I have come to welcome you. Upon waking from the dream, [he passed away].

He summoned his disciples; even then, a wondrous fragrance was still perceived. On the twenty-fifth day, he preached for the assembly on the ultimate aim of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as the great meaning of contemplating the mind (*cittānupaśyanā*).
Sitting upright facing west, he passed away at the age of seventy-five. The monks of the monastery heard the sounds of pipes, strings, bells, and chimes resonating brightly in the air;
after a long while, they gradually faded into the distance. Upon cremation, incalculable *śarīra* relics were obtained. (En Di)

Ziwen was fully prepared. He possessed profound clarity regarding contemplative methods and sat in *zuowang* (forgetting through sitting) within a single room for thirty years. In the second year of the Yongxi era, he suffered a slight illness;
the Pure Land appeared before him, and he passed away with his feet placed one upon the other (*liuzu*). (From the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* and the *Fozu Tongji*)
Wenluan, Wenluan:
a native of Pingyang in Yongjia. Having received the precepts, he studied the Three Vehicles extensively.

Relying on the Dharma assembly of Chan Master Mingzhao of Jin’yun, his doubts were suddenly resolved. Later, he again relied on Chan Master Deshao of Tiantai, through whom he attained further realization.
Having read through the Tripitaka three times, he was thoroughly versed in both the philosophical tenets and the scriptural expositions, moving with unhindered ease.
In the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he had sandalwood carved to construct a niche; sitting cross-legged within it, he held a torch himself and made a vow, saying:

"I wish to offer this remaining body as a supreme offering to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions. He then requested the assembly to chant the Buddha’s name to assist him in his rebirth. In a brief moment, the flames—
The smoke rose, five-colored and swirling through the void; one could still hear the voice of the Buddha. After a short while, it became still and the fire was extinguished.
They collected the śarīra relics in incalculable numbers. He was eighty-four years old (*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*).

Yitong (義通), whose courtesy name was Yuan (遠) and whose family name was Yin (尹), was a native of Goryeo. He possessed a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) on his crown, and his eyebrows were five or six inches long.
After receiving full ordination, he studied the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Awakening of Faith*. During the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to China and arrived at Tiantai Yunmen.
While residing at the temple, he encountered National Teacher Shao and suddenly attained a profound realization.

Later, upon visiting Dharma Master Jik of Luoxi, he heard the principles of the "Three Contemplations in One Mind" and subsequently remained there to receive formal instruction, becoming renowned for his embodiment of the master's teachings.

In the first year of the Kaibao era, the Canal Commissioner Gu Chenghui donated his residence to establish a temple and invited Tong to reside there. In the seventh year of the Taiping Xingguo era, the imperial plaque was bestowed, naming the temple Bao.
Yun spent nearly twenty years propagating the teachings and practices of the school. He habitually addressed others as "villagers" (*xiāng-rén*).
When asked the reason for this, he said: "I regard the Pure Land as my native village; all of you shall surely be reborn there, and thus you are all people of my own village.
On the twenty-first day of the tenth month in the first year of the Duāngǒng era, he passed away while lying on his right side. Upon cremation, *śarīra* relics were found in abundance.
[He] completed [his years]. At sixty-two (according to the *Fozu Tongji*).
Yujī, courtesy name Jixian, was surnamed Wang and a native of Qiantang. He left home at the age of five and followed Shouchang of Tiantai.
Chao served as his teacher. At the age of ten, he received full ordination. Having heard that Baoyun of Siming transmitted the teachings of Zhiyi, he went to serve him.

He received the *Fahua zhiguan* (Lotus Sūtra Meditation and Insight) and understood its meaning according to the words, exhausting every subtlety of its profound essence. In the first year of the Duan-gong era, he lectured on the teachings at Taiping Xingguo Temple for the local people;
several hundred students attended. Every fortnight, during both the waxing and waning phases of the moon, he invariably gathered the assembly to recite [the scriptures].
Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, he exhorted both monastics and laypeople to practice mindfulness of the Buddha for forty years, with the number of followers reaching ten thousand.

Whenever the harvest failed, he would carry his alms bowl to provide for his listeners. In the sixth month of the eighth year of the Xiangfu era, he manifested illness. His disciple Lingxiang requested of him, saying:
When the Upādhyāya was about to pass away, he offered no final instructions. Daoki then expounded extensively upon the perfect meaning (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

After some time, the assembly suddenly saw light manifest in the west and music resound from the sky. Daoki said, "The Three Holy Ones of the West are coming. He then passed away while reclining on his right side facing west.
Some dreamed that Daoki, arrayed in full ceremonial regalia, departed for the West; others dreamed that Daoki sat upon a blue lotus flower.
Regarding those who preached the Dharma for the Buddha, there was one who dreamed that Amitābha Buddha conferred upon him the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
When Fazhi heard of this, he sighed in admiration, saying: "To discuss Chan while lying ill, and to see the Buddha at the moment of death—how rare and wondrous a thing this is!
After his cremation, countless *śarīra* relics were recovered (from the *Fozu tongji*).
Shengchang, whose courtesy name was Zaowei and whose secular surname was Yan, was a native of Qiantang. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and received full ordination at seventeen.
During the Chunhua era of the Song dynasty, he resided at Nan-Zhaoqing Temple. Admiring the tradition of Mount Lu, he planned to establish a Lotus Society and carved an image of Amitābha Buddha.

He drew blood from his own body to transcribe the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Vimalacaryā*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Thereupon, he changed the name of the Lotus Society to the Society for Pure Conduct.
One hundred and twenty men joined the assembly, all of whom were styled "Disciples of Pure Conduct," with the Duke Wen Zheng Gong Dan at their head.
There were also one thousand bhikṣus. On the twelfth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Tianxi era, Chang Duan...
He sat in mindfulness of the Buddha. After a short while, he cried out in a forceful voice, "The Buddha has come! and passed away peacefully.
The assembly saw that the color of the ground had become entirely gold, which only faded after some time. He was sixty-two years old (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Zhili, Zhili—whose courtesy name was Yueyan—was the son of the Jin family of Mingzhou. His parents prayed to the Buddha for an heir;
in a dream, they saw a divine monk leading a young boy and saying, "This is the Buddha’s son, Rāhula. Not long after, Li was born at the age of seven.

Upon the death of his mother, he wailed incessantly and petitioned his father to allow him to leave the household life. He subsequently went to Taiping Xingguo Temple, where he received the full precepts under Master Hongxuan.
As he grew older, he relied on Dharma Master Yitong of Baoyun Temple to study the teachings and contemplation;

having received the essentials of the Perfect and Sudden (Yuantun) doctrine, he understood them completely upon first hearing them. During the Chunhua era, after Yitong had passed away, he was invited to preside over Qianfu Temple, from which he later moved.
At Ba'en Temple, he propagated the teachings and contemplations, and disciples arrived one after another. During a drought in Mingzhou, Rili and Master Ciyun Shi performed the *Guangming* Repentance;
they vowed that if it did not rain within three days, they would burn off one of their own hands. When the time came, a great rain fell as expected.
In the third year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, Ba'en was rebuilt and granted the name Yanqing. In the sixth year, the Nianfo Si (Recitation of the Buddha) was established.

Regarding the Precept Assembly, he personally composed a prose text to exhort [the practitioners], saying: "To trace its origin, a single thought is fundamentally harmonious, and all phenomena are unimpeded.
Yet, as the conditions of perfuming differ, the resulting retributions vary accordingly. Therefore, if one cultivates in accordance with the true nature, the pure lands of all Buddhas are revealed;

if one acts according to deluded emotions, one follows the cycle of suffering within the five destinies. Thus, for those dwelling in this Sahā world, ascending and escaping [samsara] is especially difficult. He fell [into illness].
Those who fall are many. As the Sūtra says: "Those who obtain a human body are like the soil on a fingernail; those who lose a human body are like the soil of the great earth.

Only when the practices of the Three Vehicles are fully prepared can one avoid rebirth in the four realms of existence. This is because external conditions are coarse and powerful, and afflictions are fiercely blazing;

truly, it is difficult to find anyone capable of seeking liberation through their own efforts. As for those born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), the adornments of that land are magnificent.

Their body and mind will be pure until they attain Buddhahood, never falling into the three miserable realms. As the Sūtra says: "There is not even the name of the evil paths, let alone their actual existence.
It further states: "All beings who are born there are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive). If one wishes to be born there, [one should practice accordingly].

One should simply recite the name of that Buddha and cultivate his compassion; one will surely be gathered by that Buddha’s original vow and, upon casting off this retribution body, will certainly be born in his land, exactly as described in the sutras.
This is not mere conjecture. Now, ten thousand people have formed a single society, binding their hearts together in mindfulness and pledging daily.
Every year in the middle month of spring, they shall assemble at one place and practice together.

Make offerings together and listen to the sound of the Dharma, unifying the myriad minds of all present into a single resolve so that pure karma may be accomplished and the vow to attain rebirth in the Pure Land be fulfilled.
Furthermore, in this age of corruption, the light of life is like a candle in the wind; if but one breath fails to reach its end, the three miserable realms will appear before you.

How can you afford to be complacent? Do not fail to contemplate the retribution of future lives. You must rely upon the Buddha’s words and not follow worldly sentiments; immediately cease all攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to external conditions) and focus solely on...
He diligently recited the Buddha’s name. From the full moon of the second month of that year, he established an annual assembly as his regular practice.

He once gathered ten monks to perform the *Lotus Sūtra* repentance ritual for three years, vowing that upon its completion, he would cremate his body as an offering to the *Wonderful Dharma Lotus Sūtra* in order to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.

Later, however, he was dissuaded by the assembly and did not succeed. Subsequently, he again gathered ten monks to perform the *Great Compassion* repentance ritual for three years, burning off three fingers as an offering to the Buddhas.
In the fourth year of the Tianxi era, the Prince Consort Li Zunxu memorialized the throne regarding his refined conduct; he was granted the title of Dharma-Wisdom (Fazhi) Great Master.

By imperial decree, he was ordered to remain in the world to propagate the teachings. Li [observed that] among the various patriarchs of antiquity who expounded upon the Pure Land, many discussed the phenomena of ritual practice (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*).
The *Guānmén* (Gates of Contemplation) was rarely revealed, being suited only to temporary circumstances and failing to exhaust the fullness of the Perfect and Sudden teaching.

Consequently, [the author] took up Zhiyi’s *Commentary on the Infinite Life Sutra*, investigated its profound principles to the utmost, and fully expounded the original spirit [of the Tiantai school], composing the *Miaozōngchão* in several tens of thousands of words. Its brief explanation of the title states:
"Contemplation" (*guān*) generally refers to the subject who contemplates, namely the sixteen contemplations; "Infinite Life Buddha" (*Wúliàngshòu fó*) refers to the object [of contemplation].
The Essentials of Contemplation. This comprises fifteen objects of contemplation. The contemplating subject is always the single mind’s threefold contemplation;
the contemplated object is always the single realm of the three truths. Vairocana pervades all places; all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma—namely, the Buddha of the inherent virtue of sentient beings.
It is neither self nor other, neither cause nor fruit; it is precisely the perfect and eternal Great [Buddha-nature].
This is the essence of awakening. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "As for the meaning of 'awakening,' it refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought.

This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception; it is the single mark of the Dharma-realm, which is the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharmakāya.
Based on this Dharmakāya, it is called 'original awakening' (*mūla-awakening*). Therefore, one should know that the perfectly luminous essence of the Buddha of fruition is my own."

Ordinary beings inherently possess the nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*). Therefore, among all the practices taught in the various teachings, there is not one that does not aim to reveal this awakened essence (*bodhi-tattva*).

Thus, the four samādhis are collectively termed "Buddha-remembrance" (*nien-fo*): (1) constant sitting, which is the *ekavyūha-samādhi*; (2) constant walking, which is the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*; (3) half-walking and half-sitting, which is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*;

and (4) neither walking nor sitting, also called the *svacittānuvartana-samādhi* (as detailed in the *Mohe zhiguan*). Although all of these involve Buddha-remembrance, they represent the general approach.

This reveals the essence of all Buddhas. If one relies upon the environment and inhabitants of that Land of Peaceful Nurturing through this contemplative gate and the Pratyutpanna Samādhi, employing subtle and wondrous observation, one focuses exclusively on Amitābha to reveal the true essence of the Buddha.
Although one relies upon that realm, it must be understood that the environment and inhabitants coexist within a single mind;
the nature of the mind is all-pervasive, such that there is no phenomenon not created by it and no phenomenon not possessed by it. Even a single hair’s breadth...
If phenomena were to arise from outside the mind, it could not be called the Mahāyāna contemplation.

As for the statement that the nature of the mind possesses all phenomena and creates all phenomena, in reality there is neither a possessor nor a possessed, neither a creator nor a created; the mind itself is the phenomena.
That which is the dharma is itself the mind. Both the causes and conditions that create, as well as the dharmas created, are entirely the nature of the mind within their respective locations.
