Therefore, when one now contemplates the environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one is contemplating the realm of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-citta*) by means of the dharma-realm, giving rise to the environmental and inhabited form and mind of the dharma-realm.
This is what is called "only the environment and only the inhabitants," "only form and only mind," and "only contemplation and only the object."

Therefore, the character "contemplation" (guan) is explained through the three contemplations of one mind; the term "Immeasurable Life" (Wuliangshou) is explained through the three bodies of one essence.

As for essence, doctrine, power, and function, these meanings all follow the Perfect [Teaching]. In terms of doctrinal classification, they belong to the Sudden [Teaching]. I address practitioners with this:

although the contemplation is profound and subtle, it is fundamentally intended for those at the beginning stage. If you can advance in your practice, why worry that you will not succeed? Even if you have not yet entered the stages of realization, your causal roots will be powerful. [This leads to] birth...

In that land, one is permitted to participate in the great assembly; what is seen of both the primary and secondary realms is subtle and inconceivable. One swiftly ascends the stages of sagehood, and the salvation of sentient beings is likewise vast.

How much more so, then, must one apply external ritual repentance and internal diligent contemplation of principle when confronted with the coarse and powerful conditions of this dusty world, which is truly a perilous place?

Thus, by practicing the primary and auxiliary methods together, and by adding vows and essential restraints, one will surely realize the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in that precious land. Now, I shall explain the contemplation.
The meaning lies herein. Among the works composed by Yili, most point toward the Pure Land; this is the most urgent among them.

At that time, an imperial decree was issued for the establishment of "fish-release ponds" throughout the realm. On the anniversary of the Buddha’s birthday each year, Yili convened a fish-release assembly, gathering the multitude to perform the rites and releasing various fish and birds.
The officials reported this to the throne, and an edict was issued for Liu Yun, the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, to compose a text for an inscription on a stele.

In the monastery, on the first day of the first month in the sixth year of the Tiānshèng era, he was about to manifest his passing. He established a seven-day *Guānmíng* (Light-Emanation) repentance ritual.

On the fifth day, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), summoned the assembly, and after finishing his preaching of the Dharma, suddenly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha several hundred times before passing away abruptly.
He was sixty-nine years old. His shrine remained exposed for fourteen days, during which his fingernails and hair grew longer. He was then cremated.

At that time, his tongue-organ was not destroyed, appearing like a lotus flower (from the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha* Commentary, the *Record of the Teachings and Practices of Zongxian*, and the *Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs*).
Zongshi, whose courtesy name was Zhibai, was the son of the Ye family of Ninghai, Taizhou. His mother dreamed of swallowing a bright pearl before giving birth to him.
Shi, who was somewhat older, went to Dongye Mountain to receive the precepts under Master Yiquan. He applied himself with diligent self-exertion and initially studied the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Subsequently, he entered Guoqing Temple, where he burned one finger before an image of Samantabhadra, vowing to transmit the teachings of Tiantai.

At the beginning of the Yongxi era, he went to Baoyun Temple in Siming to serve under Dharma Master Yitong, where he constantly practiced the Vaipulya Samādhi and accumulated great merit through his labors.
He vomited blood, and the skin on both his feet cracked. Vowing to die, he suddenly saw Avalokiteśvara lowering a finger to his mouth and drawing out several worms.
Then, from the tip of that finger, nectar issued forth and was poured over him; he felt his body and mind become cool and refreshed, and his ailment vanished instantly.

Shortly thereafter, his crown rose about one cun; his voice was like a great bell, and his wisdom and eloquence were unimpeded. Upon learning of Tong’s passing into *nirvāṇa*, Shi returned to Tiantai.

In the first year of the Chunhua era, he resided at Baoyun Monastery. In the second year of the Zhidao era, he gathered both monastics and laypeople to cultivate the Pure Land practices exclusively, composing the *Record of the Vow for Rebirth in the Western Paradise*.
During the Xianping era, he returned to Dongye, where he built a vihāra and led the assembly in the cultivation of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*nienfo sanmei*).

[Daoyi] Mei. In the seventh year of the Shengfu era, at the request of the people of Hangzhou, he presided over Zhaoqing Temple. Shortly thereafter, he traveled to Suzhou to lecture on the sutras at Kaiyuan Temple, after which he returned to Hangzhou to preside over Ling Shan.
When Wang Qinruo was the Governor of Hangzhou, he petitioned the throne to restore the former name of Tianzhu Temple and bestowed upon [Daoyi] the honorary title "Ciyun" (Cloud of Compassion).
Ciyun once recounted to Qinruo the story of Tiantai Zhiyi’s practice of releasing living beings.
If Qinruo subsequently petitioned that West Lake be designated as a *fangsheng chi* (refuge for living beings), he was granted permission.
Throughout his life, he compiled various methods of repentance (*chanfa*) based on the sutras, harmonizing the three contemplations (*sanguan*) and taking the Pure Land as his ultimate refuge.

Furthermore, in response to inquiries from the Prefectural Governor Ma Liang, he composed the *Wangsheng jingtu jueyi xingyuan ermen* (Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and Cultivating Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land). In the "Resolving Doubts" section, it states briefly: "The Buddha-dharma..."
There are two [types of teachings]: first, the *neyārtha* (provisional) teachings of the Hīnayāna; second, the *nītārtha* (definitive) teachings of the Mahāyāna.

Within the Mahāyāna, there are further both *nītārtha* and *neyārtha* teachings. What is now discussed regarding the Pure Land is exclusively the most definitive among the definitive teachings of the Mahāyāna.
The essential purport of this teaching is the perfect fusion of cause and effect, fully embodying the wondrousness of the Buddha-dharma. As the Sūtra says: "Ten..."
When one seeks with true discernment, there is no other vehicle; there is only the Single Buddha Vehicle—this is what is meant by that.

Thus, the pure and impure lands of the ten directions are all gathered and contained within a single kṣaṇa; the form and mind of a single thought-moment are arrayed and pervade the entire Dharma-realm.

Both are inherently present in their original, celestial nature and are not newly produced through dependent origination. If this is so for a single thought-moment, it is likewise so for a single atom. Therefore, one can [attain] the one...
Within a single atom are all lands; within each and every mind are all minds. Each mind and each atom mutually pervade one another, layer upon layer, inexhaustible and without obstruction.
They manifest instantaneously and all at once, neither hidden nor apparent. All things are perfectly accomplished, without superiority or inferiority.
Since my own mind is thus, the essence of sentient beings and Buddhas is equal. This is to turn the spirit toward billions of lands, truly giving birth [to them] within oneself.

Within the mind, the essence of the nine lotuses is already conceived; how could it escape the limits of a single *kṣaṇa*? If one believes in this perfect teaching, then there is no phenomenon that cannot be realized.
If one is ignorant of this ultimate principle, then one will be deluded in every encounter with phenomena. Therefore, it is said: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the body of the Dharma-realm;
they enter into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings," and so forth, up to: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. Now...

Simply resolve your doubts so that you may know that the adornments of the hundred jewels in the Pure Land and the causes and effects of the nine grades are both fully present within the infinitesimal mind of every sentient being.
When the rational nature (*li-xing*) is complete, one attains rebirth; then the phenomenal function (*shi-yong*) will spontaneously accord with one's vows.

Do not follow the common stream of belief by clinging to this while rejecting that. As for the details of the gate of practice and vows, they are not recorded here in full; there is a separate treatise on rebirth.

Regarding the practice of seated meditation to contemplate the Dharma: those who wish to cultivate the visualization for rebirth in the Pure Land should choose a single location and sit upon a rope-cot facing west.

This is because such a posture facilitates visualization and symbolizes the direction of the right path. One should sit upright in the full lotus position with the crown of the head and the spine aligned, neither leaning back nor hunching forward.

Having regulated the breath, one should settle the mind in concentration. Now, as for the various gates of visualization to be practiced, there are many such treatises and commentaries; however, for a beginner or ordinary person...

It would be impossible to practice them all exhaustively; therefore, for the sake of what is essential and easy, two types are briefly indicated. Within these two, one should still follow what is appropriate for oneself and need not employ both together.
Those who are already proficient in other forms of visualization may proceed as they wish;

provided that they do not depart from the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, all such practices should be cultivated. As for the two types mentioned: first, following the intent of the *Puguang* (Universal Radiance) visualization, having sat down, one visualizes for oneself:
At that time, according to the merit cultivated, one shall be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).

One should immediately arouse the thought of being born there and form the visualization of sitting cross-legged within a lotus flower. One should form the visualization of the flower closing and the visualization of the flower opening. At the moment the flower opens—
Visualize five hundred colored lights coming to illuminate the body. Form the visualization that the eyes are opening. Visualize seeing the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and their lands.
Then, sit before the Buddha and listen to the sublime Dharma, hearing all manner of sounds, each proclaiming the teachings one desires to hear.
Whatever is heard must accord with the twelve divisions of the scriptures. When forming these visualizations, one must be exceedingly firm and steadfast. Let...
The mind is undistracted and the mental image is clear, as if seen with the eyes; after a long time, one arises. Second:
visualize Amitābha Buddha directly, with a golden body sixteen feet tall, seated upon a lotus flower. Focus single-mindedly on the single mark of the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
This tuft is fifteen feet long, five inches in circumference, and has eight facets on its exterior. The interior of the tuft is hollow and curls to the right.
It is coiled and curled, situated between the eyebrows, brilliant, pure, and translucent beyond description. It reflects and illuminates the golden countenance with distinct clarity.
When forming this visualization, one should settle the mind and focus the attention, remaining firm and unwavering.

Furthermore, one should contemplate that whatever is seen through such mental recollection—whether fully realized or not—is entirely due to the causes and conditions of thought; it possesses no real nature or characteristics, for all things are empty. One.
Like the reflection of a face in a mirror, like the moon’s shadow appearing in water, like a dream, and like an illusion—it is emptiness, it is the provisional, and it is the Middle Way;
neither identical nor different, neither vertical nor horizontal, inconceivable. When mental conceptions are stilled, one can achieve the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection.
During the Tian-sheng era, he separately constructed the Riguān Hermitage to the east of the monastery to direct his thoughts toward the Western Pure Land. For...
Having completed his lecture on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*—which was intended as the karmic cause for his rebirth in the Pure Land—he took leave of the assembly.

He entrusted the lecture hall to his disciple Zu Shao and composed a poem of gratitude to his patrons, indicating that he was about to enter nirvana. The following year, the first year of the Mingdao era (502 CE), on the eighth day of the tenth month, he fell ill.
He declined medical treatment and, for the sake of the assembly, briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma, instructing them to invite an image of Amitābha. Or...
When Guanyin arrived, he prostrated, lit incense, and made this vow: "I observe that Avalokiteśvara does not come from the past nor go to the future;
the Buddhas of the ten directions dwell together in the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). I pray that you will accept this single offering of incense.

May the Buddhas bear witness as I am reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. When asked where he was returning to, he replied, "The Pure Land of Quiescent Light. That evening, he sat upright and passed away.
At the age of sixty-nine, people saw a great star fall upon Vulture Peak, its crimson light blazing brilliantly (from the *Lèbāng Wénlèi*,
*Fózǔ Tǒngjì*, and *Liánzōng Bǎojiàn*).
Yihuai (義懷), whose secular surname was Chen, was a native of Leqing in Yongjia. He traveled to the capital and entered Jingde Temple as a novice attendant (*śrāmaṇera*).

During the Tiansheng era, he passed the scriptural examination and received full ordination. He traveled extensively to consult various masters before taking up residence with Chan Master Mingjue at Cuifeng. Once, while drawing water...
While carrying his shoulder-pole across a stream, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse and presented it to Huichao, who praised it as excellent.

Subsequently, he occupied the seat of the Dharma five times, from Tiefo Temple to Tianyi Temple, where his transformative guidance was extremely extensive. Having already realized the fundamental source of the Dharma, he nonetheless practiced the Pure Land method in secret.

He once asked his students: "If one says that they abandon the defiled and take up the pure, or loathe this world while rejoicing in that, then the sentiments of grasping and rejecting are [still present]."
"This is the deluded conceptualization of sentient beings. If one were to say that there is no Pure Land, that would contradict the Buddha’s words.
What, then, is the ultimate truth? He answered himself: "To be born, one is certainly born; to go, one truly does not go.

Later, while residing at the Songshan Hermitage in Chiyang due to illness, his disciple Zhicai, who was staying at Furi Temple in Linping, welcomed him back to serve him. Zhicai then departed for Suzhou.
Carrying his departure in his heart, he took leave of the assembly and passed away at the age of seventy-two (*Sengbaozhuan* and *Lebang wenlei*).

Benru, whose name was Benru, was a native of Juchang in Mingzhou. In his youth, he studied under Dharma Master Faji; he was skilled in calligraphy and composition, and once requested instruction on the scriptures.
Yi served as the administrative manager for Fazhi for three years. When Fazhi said, "I shall tell you when the three years are up," Yi requested him again after the three years had passed.
Fazhi gave a sharp shout and called out, "Benru! At that moment, Benru attained sudden enlightenment and presented his realization in verse. Fazhi approved it.
In the fourth year of the Xiangfu era, he presided over Chengtian Temple on Mount Dongshan, where he greatly propagated the Way of the Dharma. He remained there for thirty years.

He lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, the *Amitāyus-sūtra*, and others, as well as the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school, up to sixty or seventy times.
He once assembled one hundred monks to perform the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Long Repentance for one year, during which auspicious responses were frequently observed.
In the second year of the Baoli era, he was granted the title Dharma Master Shenzhao. Together with Chancellor Zhang Dexiang and other worthies, he established the White Lotus Society. Ren—
The Emperor honored his Way and bestowed upon it the name Bailian Temple. On the eighteenth day of the fifth month in the third year of the Huangyou era, he suffered a slight illness;

he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, bid farewell to the assembly, and subsequently passed away at the age of seventy. At that time, fishermen on the river saw a monk in the clouds heading westward;
though the weather was in the height of summer, an extraordinary fragrance filled the air. The following year, his disciples opened the lock [of the tomb].
His appearance was as if he were alive. A great lotus flower grew before the stupa (Fozu Tongji).
Renyue, whose courtesy name was Qianfu, was surnamed Jiang and was a native of Xiachuan. Having heard of the transformative influence of Fazhi at Nanhu, he went there to study.

After a long time, he attained a sudden and profound realization. He then practiced the *Avalokiteśvara-samādhi* with ten like-minded companions; while sitting in meditation in a quiet chamber, he experienced a state as vivid as awakening from a dream.

Subsequently, he presided over various monastic centers (*saṃghārāma*) in Hangzhou, greatly propagating the Dharma. In his later years, he returned to his hometown to head Xiangfu Temple, where he was granted the honorary title "Jingjue" (Pure Enlightenment).
In his final years, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, burning three fingers as an offering to the Buddha while maintaining his recitations.
His discipline was most rigorous. On the twenty-fourth day of the third month in the first year of the Zhiping era, he said to his disciples, "I shall depart at noon tomorrow.
When the next day arrived, he remained seated in meditation, reciting a verse, and passed away.

He had previously composed two fascicles of a commentary on the *Amitābha Sūtra*, and further wrote two fascicles of the *Zhigui ji* (Record of the Pointing to the Goal) to explain it. Thirty years later, the monastic community of the temple dreamed of Mount [E].

It was therefore deemed appropriate to relocate the stupa and open the sarcophagus; the physical body remained undecayed and was filled with śarīra relics, whereupon he was interred with full ritual honors (from the *Fozu Tongji*).

Chuchuqian, surnamed Pan, was a native of Yongjia. His mother dreamed that auspicious clouds entered her bosom; after being pregnant for three years, he was born. He followed Qianeng of Changning Temple to leave the household life.
At the beginning of the Xiangfu era, he received full ordination and immediately went to study at Tiantong Mountain (Tianzhu). Ciyun [Zhiyuan] held him in high regard.
He was esteemed as a vessel of the Dharma. He further paid his respects to the Dharma Master Shenzhao Ru, through whom he greatly clarified the principles of the Sudden Teaching (*yuanton*).

Before long, he served as the Head Seat (*shouzuo*). Subsequently, he returned to preside over Changning, and later successively held positions at Ciyun, Miaoguo, Chicheng, Huelin, Jingzhu, Nanping, and Tiantong.

He occupied the site of enlightenment for ten years, spending forty years there preaching without weariness. Three thousand people came to his door. He was granted the title "Divine Enlightenment" (Shenwu).
On the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the eighth year of the Xining era, he rose at dawn, bathed, and changed his robes.

He gathered the assembly to chant the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* (Puxian xingfa) and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Amituo jing). After a short while, he ascended the seat and extolled the merits of the Pure Land. He then further addressed [the assembly]:
The assembly said, "I have attained non-arising (wu-sheng) long ago in my daily life; now, through non-arising, I am born into the Pure Land.
He then passed away in profound stillness (*Fozu Tongji*).

Huicai (慧才), whose secular surname was Wang, was a native of Leqing in Yongjia. He received the tonsure at the beginning of the Xiangfu era. At the age of thirteen, he received full ordination and went to study in Siming.
Depressed by his own dullness and lack of talent, he constantly recited the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī*. Suddenly, he dreamed of a tall Brahman monk...
[He was] several *zhang* [tall]. He took off his *kāṣāya* robe and donned it [over the other]. The following day, as he approached the lecture hall, he attained sudden and profound enlightenment;
everything he had heard previously, both before and after, was at once and completely understood. Later, he visited Ciyun, serving him with devotion from the north side, never flagging day or night.

At the beginning of the Tàipíng era, he resided at Fahui Baoge, where he was granted the title Guangci. Not long after, he retired to live beneath the Leifeng Pagoda. Every day, he would stand on one foot while reciting the Great... [Sūtra].

He took the *Bai-ba-zhou* (One Hundred and Eight Mantras of Compassion) as his daily recitation. Furthermore, for a full day and night, he stood on one foot while chanting the name of Amitābha Buddha.
One night, he dreamed that he had arrived at a palace of precious pavilions, where someone told him, "The middle grade of rebirth in the Pure Land is where you shall be born.

In the spring of the first year of the Yuanfeng era, he conferred the full precepts upon a thousand monastics and laypeople at Xuefeng; just as the *karmavācanā* was being performed, the image of Avalokiteśvara appeared above [the candidate's] head.
He emitted a brilliant light that eclipsed the radiance of lamps, torches, and the sun. Chan Master Shouyi of Jingci Temple composed the *Jiguang ji* (Record of the Light of Precepts) for him.
On the twenty-first day of the fifth month in the sixth year, he changed his robes, took his seat, and after finishing the writing of a verse in praise of the Buddha, said:
"I shall certainly be reborn in the Pure Land," she said, and she passed away with serene composure at the age of eighty-six (*Fozu Tongji*; *Shishi Jigu Lue*).

Lingzhao, whose secular surname was Lu, was a native of Lanxi. She entered the monastic order at Baohui Temple; within less than a month, she had mastered the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Prabhūtaratna Sūtra*.
For several years, he traveled to Qiantang to study the teachings and contemplation under Master Xiangyan Zhan. He subsequently went to Wuxing to rely on Master Jingjue Yue.
There was no door or window of the Tiantai school that he did not thoroughly understand. During the Yuanfeng era, he presided over Jiekong Temple on Mount Wu; later, he moved to Jingde Temple.
During the Xining era, he was transferred to Chaoguo Temple in Huating. Throughout these successive years, [he served in these positions].

Whenever the beginning of spring arrived, he would invariably establish a society for pure karma (*śukla-karma*), with as many as twenty thousand participants, who frequently obtained spiritual efficacy.

Once, in a dream, he beheld the majestic forms of the Three Holy Ones. He knelt and asked, "Lingzhao has spent her life reciting Mahāyāna sutras, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*);
will she fulfill this vow? Avalokiteśvara pointed and said, "The Pure Land is not far; if you have the vow, you shall be reborn there immediately. Furthermore, he [recited]:

Deep into the night, he suddenly dreamed that Samantabhadra manifested his form to him. He then resolved to create an image of Samantabhadra and recite ten thousand volumes of sutras to purify his karma.
In the winter of the fifth year of the Yuanyou era, while lying ill, he said to his attendant, "The time for my rebirth in Anāgata-sukhāvatī has arrived.
He then faced west, placed his feet together, and passed away. Upon cremation, a wondrous fragrance pervaded the air, and śarīra relics scattered forth. (From the *Buddha*)...
(Zutangji). Sanyi, courtesy name Hefu, surnamed Ling, was a native of Wukang in Huzhou. He received ordination after ranking first in the examination on the Lotus Sūtra.
He studied under the Dharma Master Miaoshao and attained an understanding that surpassed ordinary men. While practicing the four *samādhis*, a fleshy tumor grew on his neck.

One night, he dreamed that the Goddess of Merit (*Puṇyadevatā*) fed him a peach; immediately, the ailment vanished. In the fourth year of the Xīníng era, he was granted purple robes and the title Jinghuì (Pure Wisdom).
When Prime Minister Sū Sòng governed Hangzhou, he invited the Master to reside at Tiantzhi, where he greatly revitalized the Way and the Dharma.
On the eighteenth day of the second month in the third year of the Yuanyou era, at midnight, she suddenly sat cross-legged and passed away, departing from the assembly.
After the assembly had been chanting for a long time, she suddenly revived and said, "I have just followed the Great Being Avalokiteśvara and saw a golden person with a tall body and long arms.
He said to me, 'Your karmic conditions are not yet exhausted; seven days from now, I shall come to welcome you. On the twenty-fifth day," [she departed].

He again sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. On the day his stupa was enshrined, crimson clouds hung low and spread out as if in the manner of a guide, vanishing toward the west (Fozu Tongji).
Zongze, Zongze.

A native of Xiangyang, his father died early; his mother, née Chen, raised him with her maternal relatives. In his youth, he studied Confucian learning and became widely versed in the secular classics.
At the age of twenty-nine, he received the precepts from Chan Master Xiu of Changlu in Zhenzhou and attained a profound understanding [of the Dharma].

The Essential Summary: During the Yuanyou era, while residing at Changlu Temple, he invited his mother to the eastern chamber of the abbot’s quarters and exhorted her to shave her head and take the precepts, as well as to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
This continued for seven years from beginning to end. When his mother approached the end of her life, she passed away peacefully without illness, mindful of the Buddha.

Zhe said to himself that his filial duty toward his parent was now fulfilled; he then followed the regulations of Mount Lu to establish the "Superior Assembly of the Lotus" (Lianhua Shenghui) for the universal benefit of all.

I exhort both monastics and laypeople to practice the sublime contemplation of the Western Land. Failing that, they should single-mindedly uphold the Buddha’s name, dedicating their merit and making vows to aspire for rebirth in the Pure Land.
I have composed this text to proclaim [this teaching], saying: "To regard thought as thought and birth as birth is the error of common perception.
To regard non-thought as non-thought and non-birth as non-birth is a false view."
This is what causes delusion. To contemplate yet be without contemplation; to be born yet be without birth—this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Therefore, within the ground of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is received; thus, above, there are no Buddhas to be contemplated, and below, there is no Pure Land to be born into.

Yet, within the gateway of Buddha-activities (*buddhakārya*), not a single dharma is abandoned; thus, all faculties are comprehensively gathered, for there is indeed the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).
This is the essential method for returning to the source through samādhi. It reveals the single gate of rebirth in the Pure Land;
thus, one may recite the Buddha’s name all day long without deviating from non-thought, and fervently aspire for rebirth without deviating from non-arising.

Consequently, ordinary beings and sages each abide in their own stations while the path of resonance and response intermingles. Though there is no coming or going between east and west, the spirit transmigrates to the Pure Land. This is...
This can be subject to critical inquiry. Thus, the Sūtra says:

"If a person hears the name of Amitābha Buddha and upholds it, at the time of their death, their mind will not be inverted, and they shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.

Now, although the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, employs the two gates of *śamatha* (tranquility) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), and manifests his presence in both pure and impure lands, [the principle remains as stated].
However, the original intention of the Sage was not merely to regard the Sahā world—with its hills, mounds, pits, and ravines; its five realms of existence dwelling together;

its mountains of earth and stone; and its abundance of foul impurities—as something to be loathed, nor to regard the Land of Ultimate Bliss—with its ground of pure gold, its rows of trees reaching to the sky, its towers soaring with the seven treasures, and its flowers blooming in four colors—as something to be delighted in. Rather, it was because...
For one who has newly entered the Way, the power of patience (*kṣānti*) is not yet mature; one must rely upon pure conditions as a superior support (*adhipati*). Why is this?
In the Sahā world, Śākyamuni has already passed into extinction and Maitreya has not yet been born. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Amitābha Buddha currently dwells and preaches the Dharma.
In the Sahā world, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are merely objects of admiration for their noble names; in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, those two—
Venerable One, you are personally my supreme friend. In the Sahā world, various māras compete to create disturbances and vex practitioners;
however, within the great radiance of the Sukhāvatī world, there will certainly be no such demonic affairs. In the Sahā world, evil sounds cause turmoil and female forms are seductive and licentious;
in the Sukhāvatī world, the water-birds and forest trees all proclaim the sublime Dharma. As for the primary retribution, it is pure and truly free from [such defilements].

Women. Thus, for the cultivation of practice, the requisite conditions are not equalled by those in the Western Regions. Those of shallow faith have, moreover, given rise to biased doubts and slanders; I have ventured to discuss this:
among the people of this land, there are none who do not weary of the clamor and vexation of the secular home and long for the tranquility of an araṇya.
Therefore, when someone abandons their family to leave the household life, they praise them with earnest admiration. Yet, what are the manifold sufferings of the Sahā world but...
The clamor and vexation of the secular home contrast with the leisurely ease of Sukhāvatī; this is not merely a matter of the silence of a forest hermitage (*araṇya*).

To recognize the excellence of leaving the household life yet have no desire to be reborn there—this is the first delusion. Those who toil for ten thousand *li* to seek out a spiritual teacher do so truly to illuminate the Great Matter and to resolve the questions of birth and death;
yet they overlook that the World-Honored One Amitābha possesses supreme mastery over both form and mind, and wields the power of his vows.
How profound! A single utterance of the perfect sound brings clarity and accord to all. To wish to attend upon a spiritual teacher while having no desire to see the Buddha is the second delusion.
In monastic communities with vast assemblies, everyone delights in dwelling there; yet they do not wish to rely upon a small congregation’s place of practice.
Yet in the World of Ultimate Bliss, those who are in their final birth before Buddhahood are exceedingly numerous, and all these supreme virtuous people gather together in one place.
To wish to draw near to monastic groves while not aspiring for the pure assembly of the ocean-like Sangha—this is the third delusion.
The people of this land do not exceed a hundred years in their maximum lifespan; yet from childhood through senility, they are beset by illness, and they remain mired in dullness and sleep.

They constantly occupy the greater portion [of their time]. Yet, Bodhisattvas remain obscured by the "shrouding of the aggregates" (*guanyin*), and Śrāvakas are still dim-sighted regarding the emergence from the womb;

thus, of every inch of jade and every moment of time, nine-tenths are lost before one attains the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), which truly causes one’s heart to tremble with cold fear. As for the people of the Western [Land], their lifespan is immeasurable;
once entrusted to the lotus-womb, they suffer no further pain of death, continuing in uninterrupted succession until they reach Bodhi. Therefore...
One will then attain the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), and the rank of Buddhahood can be expected with certainty.
Yet, while the fleeting light of life flows through this Sahā world, one remains lost in the Pure Land for a long time; such is the fourth delusion.

Only when one’s rank is established in non-retrogression and the fruit of non-arising is realized—remaining free from desire while amidst desire, and remaining undefiled while dwelling in the dust—is one able to give rise to unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*) and exercise coessential pity (*sārūpya-karuṇā*), returning to enter the realm of dust.

Exhausting oneself in harmony with the five turbidities, those of shallow learning and meager wisdom—perhaps possessing a modicum of minor goodness—claim to have forever emerged from the four currents and transcended the ten stages.

They revile the Pure Land and cling to this Sahā world; closing their eyes, they return empty-handed, wandering aimlessly as if they were common oxen or horses, treading the same path as those in the hells.
Unaware of who they truly are, they dare to compare themselves to the Great [Buddha].
The power of the Bodhisattva is such that it overcomes the fifth delusion. Thus, the Sūtra says: "One should make a vow, vowing to be born in that land.
To fail to believe the sincere words of the Buddhas and not vow to be reborn in the Pure Land—is this not delusion?
If one believes the words of the Buddha and is born in the Pure Land, then one cannot be constrained by the bonds of the realms, nor can one be harmed by the passage of kalpas. Farewell.
The eight sufferings of humanity are absent; the five signs of decline in the heavens do not exist; even the name of the evil realms is unknown, let alone their actual presence.

Only the teaching of the One Vehicle is revealed, for there is definitively no third. Taking refuge in the Three Jewels of the One Essence, serving the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, the Buddha’s light illuminates the body and all delusions are secretly extinguished.
The flavor of the Dharma sustains the spirit, and the six supernormal powers are fully perfected. III.
The seventeen categories of factors that aid the Path should be brought to perfect completion through mindfulness.

The thirty-two manifestations of bodies according to the various classes of beings pervade all lands within the atoms of dust, circulating throughout the five realms of existence and universally benefiting all faculties. Without wavering from a single mind, one practices the universal samādhi, sprinkling the water of meditative concentration over the three thousandfold world-system and leading sentient beings out of the burning house.
Thus, both self-benefit and the benefit of others are entirely fulfilled. Now then, only...
The purity of the mind is the Buddha-land; the self-nature is Amitābha. This is indeed the essential gateway to liberation and the direct shortcut for cultivation.

Therefore, among the definitive teachings of the Mahāyāna, there are none that do not point toward the Pure Land. Sages of both past and present, as well as others and ourselves, all aspire to be reborn there.
For in all cases, those who would deliver others must first deliver themselves. Alas! If people lack far-reaching foresight, they will surely encounter immediate calamity.
Alas! Once one loses this human body, there will be deep regret for ten thousand kalpas.

Therefore, leading the great assembly of the ocean-like multitude, let each of you recite the name of Amitābha Buddha—hundred times, thousand times, even ten thousand times—and dedicate these merits with a common aspiration to be born in that land.

I secretly hope that in the sublime assembly at the Lotus Pond, where the Dharma-light shines upon the Golden Ground, we may mutually support one another so that this vow is surely fulfilled. It is like rowing a boat downstream; with the current already favorable, one need only add the strength of the oars.
By the power of the oar, even a distance of one hundred thousand *li* can be reached without toil.

One night, Zhe dreamed of a man wearing a black silk cap and white robes, whose appearance was refined and handsome, appearing to be about thirty years of age. He bowed and said to Zhe, "I wish to enter the Lotus Assembly and seek to have my name inscribed.
Zhe then took out the assembly register and asked, "What is your name? He replied, "Puhui. Having finished writing it, he said, "Farewell."

Yi also said, "My elder brother also requested that you write down one name. [The Master] asked, "What is your elder brother's name? He replied, "Puxian (Samantabhadra). As soon as he had finished speaking, he vanished.

Upon waking, [Yi] said to the senior monks, "In the 'Chapter on Leaving the World' (*Lokottara-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are the two Bodhisattvas Puxian and Puhui who assist in propagating the Buddha-dharma.
I shall now establish an assembly and look toward the Western Land together; I have been moved by these two Great Ones."
The Master [Yanshou] profoundly assisted [the cause], appointing two Great Beings as the presiding heads of the assembly; thereupon, both those far and near turned toward his transformation.
(From the *Lianzong baojian* and *Lebang wenlei*)

Yuánjìng, whose courtesy name was Wúxiàng and whose surname was Xú, was a native of Yúqián in Hángzhōu. He entered the monastic order at the age of ten. Upon reaching maturity, he pursued his studies under Cíyún;
after Cíyún passed away, he served Míngzhì. Having heard the lectures on *Zhíguān*, he attained realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). He was summoned by the Emperor...
At the request of Shou Lüzhen, he resided at Beigé (Great Compassion Pavilion) and was granted the title Biàn Cái (Eloquent Talent). He subsequently moved to serve as the abbot of Shang Tianzhu.

Shortly thereafter, he withdrew to seclusion at Longjing on South Mountain. At that time, the eminent figures Su Shi, Zhao Bian, and others admired his virtuous character and repeatedly composed verses in praise of him.

He subsequently presided over the lecture hall of Ciyun at Mount Ling, preaching the Dharma day and night without interruption. He constantly cultivated the Pure Land with diligent devotion, never ceasing for even a moment.
He burned three fingers on his left hand and two on his right as an offering to the Buddha. He once prayed to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) to request that he emit light.
Light would immediately manifest accordingly. One day, while eating together with the monk Xi Zhong, Zhong saw light like fireflies between [the Master’s] brows;
he reached out and obtained several grains of śarīra. Thereafter, śarīra were frequently found at his place of rest.
As he was about to pass away, he entered the Fangyuan Hermitage to sit in meditation, bid farewell to his guests, and ceased taking food and drink. He said to the monk Daoqian: "I..."

His pure karma was already perfected; for seven days he remained free from obstacles, and his aspirations were fulfilled. When the seven days had passed, he uttered a verse to the assembly and passed away while lying on his right side.
He was eighty-one years old. This was on the final day of the ninth month in the sixth year of the Yuanyou era (according to the *Fozu tongji* and *Lebang wenlei*).
Congya (從雅), a native of Qiantang, initially studied *śamatha-vipaśyanā* under Dharma Master Haoyue Bian. Later, he entered the Tianwangyuan of Nanshan,
where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* five times, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* four times, and the *Amitābha Sūtra* ten times.

He prostrated before the Śarīra stūpa one thousand times; he performed three hundred thousand prostrations to Śākyamuni and one million prostrations to Amitābha; he recited the name of the Buddha five million times;

and he performed three sets of three prostrations for each character of the *Ekākṣara-vidyā* from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. With his heart set upon the Pure Land, he sat facing west throughout his life.

Wuwei Yang Jie composed thirty verses in praise of the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Anle guo zan*) as a gift, desiring that [the recipient] would— (Note: The final phrase "desiring that" indicates the sentence is incomplete in the source text.)
He inspired great faith in the multitude and subsequently depicted the nine grades and three ranks at Jingzhu Temple, carving eulogies upon stone.
On one occasion, he performed refined music and was bestowed the title Fobao (Dharma-Treasure). One day, without illness, he passed away while sitting cross-legged facing west;
celestial music resounded in the sky, and a wondrous fragrance filled his chamber. (From the *Fozu Tongji*)
Kejiu (Can Long Live).
It is unclear where he originated from. He resided in Mingzhou and constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land; people called him "Jiu Fahua" (Jiu of the Lotus).
In the eighth year of the Yuanyou era, at the age of eighty-one, he passed away while sitting in meditation. Three days later, he returned and spoke to the people.
He said: "I have traveled through the Pure Land and beheld its various sublime realms; these accord perfectly with the scriptures.

Among those here who cultivate the practice of the Pure Land, their names have already been inscribed upon lotus pedestals. Those inscribed upon golden pedestals are: first, Master Xun of the Guangjiao Monastery in Chengdu;
second, Mr. Sun Shierlang of Mingzhou; and third, Kejiu. Those inscribed upon silver pedestals are: first, the Daoist nun Xu of Mingzhou. Thus he spoke.
After she had passed away, she was transformed again and departed five years later. When the Daoist nun Xu died, a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
In the twelfth year, when Sun Shierlang passed away, celestial music welcomed him into the void. All that Jingyan had said was verified. (From the *Jingtu wen*).
Zhaiying, Zhaiying:

surnamed Yu, a native of Tongjiang in Yanzhou. She entered the monastic order at Shouning Temple in Hangzhou. During the Xining era, she studied under Dharma Master Shenwu and attained a profound realization of the Way of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
She read the *Fenbie ermen lun* (Treatise on the Distinction of the Two Gates) and the *Jinbi lun* (The Golden Scalpel), remaining awake throughout the night.

After several months, the Lu family of Danghu established a monastery to welcome Ying, where he extensively opened up the practice of Dharma-giving. After a long time, he traveled among Hangzhou, Xiu, Suzhou, and Hu.
He once composed the "Ten Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land," which says: "I vow that I shall forever leave the three evil realms.
I vow that I shall swiftly sever greed, anger, and ignorance. I vow that I shall always hear the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. I vow that I shall diligently cultivate..."
Precepts, concentration, and wisdom—may I always follow and learn from all Buddhas. May I never retreat from the bodhicitta. May I swiftly behold Amitābha.
May I be certain to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. May my emanations pervade all lands as numerous as atoms. May I extensively deliver all sentient beings.
In the spring of the second year of the Yuánfú era, he manifested illness at Xiángfú Temple in Hángzhōu. Suddenly, he rose...
Leaning his body against a desk, he faced west and recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*. When the scroll reached its end, he passed away (*Lèbāng Wénlèi* and *Fózǔ Tǒngjì*).
Zōngběn, whose courtesy name was Wúzhé, was surnamed Guǎn and was a native of Wúxī in Chángzhōu. After leaving the household life, he studied under the Chan master Tiānyī Huái.
The Master attained a profound realization through the practice of *nianfo*. Later, while residing at Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou, a great drought occurred and the lakes and wells all ran dry.

Suddenly, from the western corner of the monastery, a sweet spring gushed forth, yielding golden eels. The monks dug this into a well, and the more than one thousand monks of the monastery relied upon it for their drinking water.
A daughter of the Zhang family died; her mother dreamed that the girl had become a snake. Upon waking, she found the snake beneath the coffin and took it to the Master.

He preached the Dharma for her. Suddenly, a black cicada flew over the coffin, and the snake vanished without a trace. Her mother made a vow, saying: "If she is truly my daughter, may she enter this cage;
I shall take her again to Jingci Monastery. It happened exactly as she had vowed. He then preached the Dharma for her once more.
That evening, the woman saw her in a dream, who said, "The two retributions have already been liberated. The mother then asked about the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*):
"I believe this truly exists; how can one escape it? The woman replied, "The six realms and four modes of birth are like a pulley on a well—there is not a single person who can escape them.
Only by practicing the world-transcending Dharma can one attain liberation. Why not ask the Master of the Law at Jingci? Thus it was.

His manifestations were of this nature. Originally, he had been summoned by imperial decree to enter Huilin Temple in the Eastern Capital; his audience with the Emperor was so well-received that he was granted the title Chan Master Yuanzhao.
During his lifetime, he secretly cultivated the Pure Land practices. At that time, Dharma Master Cairen of Leifeng Peak traveled in spirit to the Pure Land.
He saw a hall that was exceptionally magnificent. Someone said, "This is to await Master Ben of Jingci.

Furthermore, when Master Xi of Zifu arrived at Huilin, he prostrated at [Ben's] feet, offered gold, and departed. When people questioned him about his reason for doing so, he said, "In my meditative concentration, I saw a golden lotus flower;
people say it is to await Master Ben of Huilin. He added that there were countless other lotus flowers, saying they were to await those who would receive ordination.
Some who were withered were said to be people who had fallen back. Later, he resided at Lingyan Temple in Suzhou.
During the Yuánfú era, as he was about to pass away, he bathed and lay down. His disciples gathered around him and requested a verse of farewell. Fén gazed at them intently and said, "Fools!"
"Ordinarily I am too lazy even to compose verses; what kind of verse would I write today? Ordinarily I lie down whenever I wish to sleep;
why must I sit up specifically today? He then requested a brush and wrote his final instructions for Shou-rong, after which he threw down the brush and passed away, appearing as if in a deep sleep.
(From the *Fozu Tongji* and the *Suzhou Fu Zhi*)
Yuyan, whose secular surname was Hu, was a native of Linhai in Taizhou. At the age of six, he relied upon Master Lingjiu as his teacher; at fourteen, he received full ordination.
He went to Dongshan to study under Shenzhao, where he realized the principle of the three contemplations within one mind and practiced the Lotus Samādhi. As he turned [the beads of his rosary],...
He presided over Chijō-ji Temple. During the Shōshō era, he retired to the eastern peak of Mount Kōzan and built a hut beside a jujube tree (*zhā*), hence adopting the name Zhā’ān (Jujube Hut).

He strictly observed the precepts and monastic discipline, never keeping even a fraction of a measure beyond what was needed for his single alms bowl. The samādhis he cultivated frequently manifested auspicious responses.
He devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, and his writings were largely exhortations toward rebirth there. When someone asked about rebirth in the desire realm...
As for the heavens, the ten wholesome actions are their cause. As for being born in the heavens of form (*rūpadhātu*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the cause.

To be born in the Pure Land, one must necessarily cultivate the wondrous contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*); only then can it be attained. Those who study today are all ignorant of the essential teachings, claiming that birth in the heavens is difficult while birth in the Pure Land is easy;
who, then, would believe such a thing? The answer is: the Dharma has neither difficulty nor ease; difficulty and ease reside in the person.
What is difficult is the state of doubt; then even a distance of a few inches feels like ten thousand *li*. What is easy is the mind of faith; then ten thousand *li* feel like a few inches.
As for the statement that one attains birth by cultivating the subtle contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*), this is merely one gateway among the superior modes of rebirth.

However, one must not open one gate while blocking many. The *Anle ji* (Collection on Peace and Bliss) states: "There are two types of those who are born in the Pure Land: first, those with signs (*sanimitta*)."
The first is the mind that clings to signs and delights in them. The second is the signless mind, which corresponds to contemplation of principle (*yuanli*).

In this present age, those of middling or inferior faculties who are deluded and burdened by heavy obstacles—such that they must wait for their contemplation of principle to correspond before the [signless] mind arises—are few indeed.

Originally, the Buddha’s compassion in receiving sentient beings provides many gates of skillful means (*upāya*): there are wholesome practices of both meditative concentration and non-concentration, and there is the power of the Buddha-dharma.

There are those who possess merit yet rely on the power of aspiration to dedicate it toward rebirth; there are those who face the intense terrors of the moment of death and depend upon seeking rescue.
Of such types, numbering in the hundreds of thousands and tens of millions, one need only rely upon a single instance to surely attain rebirth.

As for "concentrated goodness," it refers to the cultivation of the wondrous contemplation of the mind, of which the Śūraṅgama Samādhi is an example. As for "scattered goodness," it is as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* regarding the ten moments of mindfulness.

The Buddha also attains birth in that land; this is so. As for "the power of the Buddha," it is because Amitābha Buddha’s power of great compassionate vows embraces those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Sentient beings, by relying on the power of the Buddha’s vow, immediately attain birth there.
It is like a weak man who, following a Wheel-Turning King, travels around the four continents in a single day and night—not by his own strength, but by the power of the Wheel-Turning King.

Regarding the power of the Dharma (*dharmabala*): as the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Padmaprabharāja, one should cause [the deceased] to recite the consecrated divine mantra (*abhiṣekamantra*), sprinkle it upon the corpse of the deceased or their tomb;
by virtue of this true mantra, even if that deceased person has fallen into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, they will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Regarding the merit of worldly affairs being dedicated [for others]: [this refers to] compassion...

It is this: with a mind free from killing, possessing all the virtues of the precepts, upholding secret mantras, and reciting the Mahāyāna sūtras, one dedicates these various merits and virtues toward the adornment [of the land], creating the causes for attaining birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. As for those who seek salvation at the end of life:

when the time of death approaches and the signs of the hell of the iron chariots appear, by the power of invoking the Buddha’s name, the fierce flames are transformed into a cool breeze, just as in the case of Sengxiong.
Jun and Zhang Zhongqi each invoked the name of the Buddha once and were both reborn in the Pure Land; this is proof of it.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that the various bodhisattvas of minor practice and those who have cultivated minor merits are beyond counting, and all shall attain rebirth there.

The Buddha said it is "easy to go," while the Master [Zhiyi] said it is "difficult to be born. One may temporarily follow the teaching and speak of its ease of access to open the gate of liberation for people.
There was no need to persist in delusion and claim that [rebirth] is difficult to achieve, for such views block the path to Bodhi.
On the first day of the early summer month in the first year of the Jianguo era, a celestial deity descended from the midst of the air and said to him, "Master, your pure karma has been perfected.

Furthermore, he dreamed of a great lotus flower in a pond, surrounded by celestial music. He then composed a poem of self-farewell to show to the assembly. Seven days later, he sat in the full lotus posture and...
Huà (from the *Fozu tongji* and *Lebang wenlei*). Miaosheng, Miaosheng:
a native of Kuaiji. He studied the Vinaya and diligently cultivated the practices of the Pure Land. Together with Chan Master Datong Ben...
Residing at Xiangwu on Mount Chao, he together with others clarified this Way.

One night, while gathered with his disciples to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he sat upright upon his mat, burned incense, joined his palms, and passed away in a state of profound stillness (*Zuǎnfǔ Tǒngjì*).
Tanyi, whose secular surname was Du, was a native of Yuyao. He received full ordination during the Huangyou era and studied the teachings and contemplation under Mingzhi of Tianzhu.
Later, he entered the quarters of Guangci at Leifeng, where he applied himself with diligent inquiry for twenty years without ever flagging in his resolve. Thus, he perfected his learning.

He returned to his native village and resumed his lectures at Mount Gu (Hugeshan). He devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land cultivation, reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* five thousand times and the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-buddhānusmṛti-sūtra* and the *Amitābha-sūtra* ten thousand scrolls each.
In the autumn of the first year of the Chongning era, he manifested illness. Gathering the assembly, he announced: "The time has come for me to be born in the Pure Land;
I shall ascend the golden platform and follow the Buddha westward. He then bathed his body, sat upright, formed a mudrā, and passed away. After the cremation, [the relics were collected].
The tongue-relic [of Shanben] was like a string of pearls (Fozu Tongji).

Shanben, whose secular surname was Dong, was a native of Kaifeng. His mother had no children until she prayed to the Buddha, whereupon he was born. Upon reaching adulthood, he sat for the examination on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
He attained liberation and became a disciple of Yuanzhao’s teacher. At that time, he was known as "Daoben" (the Elder Ben) or "Xiaoben" (the Junior Ben).

By imperial decree, he resided at Fayun Monastery in the Capital, where he was granted the title Dàtōng (Great Penetration). Later, he returned to Xiangwu Monastery in Hangzhou, where he shut his door and swept away visitors to devote himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land.
During his meditation, a monk beheld Amitābha Buddha manifesting a golden body within the abbot’s quarters. In the tenth month of the third year of the Daguan era...
On the day of Jiazi in the second month, he bent his three fingers and told his disciples, "Only three days remain.
When the time arrived, he sat in the lotus posture facing west and passed away (from the *Fozu tongzai* and *Fozu tongji*).

Zongtan, whose secular surname was Shen, was a native of Licheng in Luzhou. At the age of sixteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination. In his youth, he was proficient in the study of doctrine;

as he grew older, he traveled extensively to seek out renowned masters for nearly fifty years, until his fame resounded throughout the monastic academies. In his later years, he resided in the regions of Tang, Deng, Ru, and Ying.

During this interval, he lectured on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, exhorting people to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). Those who listened gathered like clouds, all of whom devoted themselves to the practice of pure karma.

Later, at Qingtai Town in Tangzhou, he vowed to seek rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing; he maintained the recitation of the name and practiced visualization, never for a moment forgetting them.
On the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Zhenghe era, he saw Amitābha Buddha in a dream, who told him:
He said, "If you preach the Dharma for six days, I shall be reborn in the Pure Land. Upon waking, he informed the assembly. The following day, he continued his lectures and chanting without ceasing.

On the night of the fourth day of the fifth month, knowing that the time had arrived, he struck the bell to gather the assembly and announced: "The meeting and dispersal of causes and conditions must indeed occur at their appointed time;
how could one afford to miss such a superior opportunity for the Pure Land? I pray that the assembly will recite the Buddha's name to assist me."

He attained rebirth in the Pure Land. It was further reported that he lived to the age of seventy-six. At the moment his four elements separated, he performed prostrations to Amitābha in the Pure Land and spoke:

"May I forever transcend the sufferings of the three realms. Having said this, he sat upright and passed away. A roar like thunder filled the room, and white clouds came from the west, covering the ground.
It was only on the third day that he ceased [his practice] (*Lianzong baojian*).
Zhongli, whose secular surname was Chen, was a native of Ning County in Mingzhou. At the age of nine, he left the household life at Qixin Temple in Yongdong and received the various...

He could read through a volume of scriptures and never forget them. During the Zhìpíng era, he passed the scriptural examination and received ordination. Initially, he relied upon Guǎngzhì to study the teachings and contemplation;
later, when Shénzhì succeeded him as the head of Nán-hú, he again relied upon him. Among the two hundred disciples under his tutelage, none surpassed him in standing at his right side.
When Shenzhi retired from his duties, [Shou]li succeeded him on the seat. He constantly used the practice of purity (*śubha-karman*) to exhort others.

He instructed his disciple Jieran to establish the Hall of the Sixteen Contemplations (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā-śālā*) to welcome those devoted to pure practices. Later, he retired; not long after, he restored Baoyun Temple and subsequently withdrew to Baiyun Hermitage.
There, he daily propagated the Dharma-gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. His writings were numerous, as he responded to the requests of the multitude.

He once again took charge of Nanhu. Ascending the seat to preach the Dharma, he opened the window to the infinite. Before and after, he recited the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Prabhāsa* sutras dozens of times;
he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* more than ten thousand fascicles. Whenever he performed prayers for people’s benefit or avert calamities, there was always an immediate response.

On the evening of the *xinhai* day in the fourth month of the fifth year of the Zhenghe era, he suddenly said to his disciple Fawei, "Do you smell a strange fragrance? He then gathered the assembly and spoke with a smile.
He said, "The time for my rebirth in the Pure Land has arrived," and he passed away sitting facing west (*Fozu Tongji*).
Yuanzhao, whose courtesy name was Zhanran, was surnamed Tang and was a native of Yuhang. Initially, he relied upon the Vinaya Master Huikan of Dongzang to study exclusively.

Regarding the *Vinaya*, he later followed Master Shenwu Qian to lecture on the Tiantai teachings and contemplations. Qian exhorted him that the thorough investigation and elucidation of the *Lotus Sūtra* should be his primary task.
He further received the Bodhisattva precepts from Dharma Master Guangci Cai; the radiance of the precepts manifested within him, leading him to extensively study the Nanshan school.
Carrying his staff and bowl, he went begging for food in the marketplace. In his later years, he presided over Lingzhi Monastery for thirty years.

He transmitted the precepts and ordained monks at sixty assemblies. He devoted himself earnestly to the practice of pure karma (*śukla-karman*), often saying: "In life I shall propagate the model of the Vinaya; in death I shall return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*).
Throughout his life, he attained nothing more than these two Dharma gates. He once compiled a ritual for the liturgical repentance of pure karma and wrote its own preface, stating:
"Since my ordination on the lower platform, I have known how to study the Vinaya; yet, being of mediocre and shallow disposition by nature, my conduct has been unworthy."

Later, he encountered the Dharma Master Shenwu of Tiantai, who exhorted and instructed him with earnest persistence. Only then did he realize the need to change his ways; he sought deeply into the ancestral teachings and extensively investigated the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).

Thereupon, he made a great vow: "May I always be born in this Sahā world of the five turbidities and evil ages to act as a great guide, leading and transforming the multitudes so that they may enter the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, he saw in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) the account of the Dharma Master Huishi, which says:

"Although that land is pure, it is not what I desire. If one were to experience pleasure within lotus flowers for twelve kalpas, how could that compare to saving sentient beings in the places of extreme suffering within the three miserable realms?
For this reason, he steadfastly maintained his view and passed many years without the slightest inclination toward the gate of the Pure Land.
Seeing others cultivate the practices for the Pure Land, he even gave rise to contempt and slander. Later, he suffered from a grave illness, and his complexion..."
His strength failed and his body grew emaciated; his consciousness became clouded, and he knew not where he was headed. Later, when his illness subsided, he suddenly realized his former errors.
He wept with grief and remorse, deeply reproaching himself. Although his resolve was vast, his strength was as yet insufficient to sustain it.

He then consulted the *Ten Doubts* (Shiyi lun) of Tiantai, which states that a bodhisattva at the initial stage who has not yet attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) must never be separated from the Buddha. It further cites the wisdom of...

The *Dulun* (Treatise on Crossing Over) states: "It is impossible for an ordinary person bound by all fetters to possess a heart of great compassion and vow to be born in an evil age to save suffering sentient beings.
It is, for example, like an infant who cannot be separated from its parents; or like a fledgling with weak wings, which can only cling to a branch."

From that time on, he completely abandoned all that he had studied throughout his life and devoted himself exclusively to seeking the teachings of the Pure Land school for more than twenty years, never ceasing for even a moment.
He investigated the principles and doctrines in depth, examining both ancient and modern sources; thus, he suddenly resolved all his doubts and his deepening faith grew ever stronger.

Furthermore, he encountered the two modes of practice—exclusive and mixed—taught by Master Shandao: that those who practice exclusively will be reborn [in the Pure Land] one hundred out of every hundred, whereas those who practice in a mixed manner...

Out of ten thousand or a thousand, perhaps one or two may have their mental consciousness distracted, making it difficult for them to accomplish the practice of contemplation. With single-minded devotion, I have upheld the four-character name;

Amitābha is the awakening of the fruit, while we are the delusion of the cause. When the mind of joy and aversion arises, one follows the Buddha’s exhortation to go [to the land]. Therefore, it is said to be "mind-only."
Furthermore, it is called the "Pure Land. One might ask: "In that case, since there is both taking and rejecting, as well as joy and aversion, does this not result in falsehood? I reply:

It should be understood that for a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*), when they reject, they reject the defiled to its ultimate end; the three lands and nine realms are all rejected. When they take, they take the pure to its very source;
they directly take the supreme *jìguāng* (quiescent light). Thus, the *Miaozong* says: "If taking and rejecting reach their limit, they are no different from neither taking nor rejecting."

This is not a divergent path. It is truly because the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhā*) is not separate from the three lands, and the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) are nothing other than the four lands.
If one observes with the four eyes and two wisdoms, then although the myriad phenomena are manifold, the three lands and nine realms must be relinquished.

If one observes with the Buddha-eye, then the true emptiness is profoundly still; it is not that the tranquil light exists apart from the three lands and nine realms as something distinct. It is not [separate].
Outside the light, there is another Sahā world. As the ancient masters have said: "Precisely because the mind itself is Buddha, one must rely upon cultivation"—this is the meaning of those words.

If one realizes that the nature of the mind is solely this single, fused, and wondrous Dharma of the three thousand worlds, then even the hundred thousand distant regions will not constitute an obstruction.
Why is this? Because the mind is all-encompassing; because it is the three thousand worlds; because it is fused.

Because it is subsumed [within this], one attains such as this. The above is a brief summary of the general outline. If you wish to deeply realize this principle, you must eliminate worldly attachments and conceptualizations.
One day, while in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he saw an old monk sitting upon a meditation platform who looked at him and said to Zhen:
"I am Fazhi of Siming. Startled and joyful, Zhen prostrated himself and asked: "Regarding the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the various schools, I have not yet..."

He was able to attain thorough penetration. He requested instruction, and the old monk nodded his head in approval. Upon awakening, his mind became suddenly expansive and clear; his wisdom and eloquence progressed daily from then on.
From that time forth, all who studied the teachings and contemplations received their guidance from him. In the twelfth year of the Shaoxing era, he presided over Nanhu.

While practicing the Lotus Samādhi, he was moved by the manifestation of light from Samantabhadra. He established a monthly assembly for the recollection of the Pure Land on the twenty-third day of each month.
On that day, he gathered monastics and laypeople to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha until ten thousand had assembled.

On the sixteenth day of the twelfth month of the twenty-third year, he gathered the assembly to chant the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Guānjīng) without ceasing day or night. The multitude perceived a wondrous fragrance filling the hall. Huichén said, "The Buddha has come to welcome me."

He immediately bathed and changed his robes. He wrote a verse, saying: "The Land of the Mind is inherently free from delusion or enlightenment; when not a single thought arises, one enters the first stage (Prathamā-bhūmi).

He then had [his disciples] recite the "Chapter on Peaceful Conduct" (*Anrakugyō-hon*); before it was finished, he sat down and passed away with a sigh of contentment. His remains were kept in the coffin for an entire month.
His appearance was as if he were alive (*Fozu tongji*, *Lebang wenlei*). His secular name was Ziyuan;
he was a native of Kunshan in Pingjiang. His father was surnamed Mao and his mother was surnamed Chai. One night, she dreamed that a Buddha entered her door. Next...

He was born at dawn, and thus named Fulai (Buddha-Come). He entered the monastic life at Yanxiang Temple and practiced *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight). While in meditative concentration, he heard the sound of a crow and attained great enlightenment.
Thereafter, he settled his mind in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and styled himself Wanshi-hui (All Affairs Rested). Amidst circumstances of both adversity and favor, he never once stirred a thought.
Admiring the legacy of Master Huiyuan’s Lotus Society on Mount Lu, he exhorted others to take refuge in the Triple Gem and to uphold the five precepts.
Regarding the precepts: by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha five times, one attests to the Five Precepts and universally establishes pure conditions.
This is intended to enable worldly beings to purify the five faculties, attain the five powers, and emerge from the five turbidities.

He thus compiled essential passages from the Great Canon to compose this Ritual for Morning Repentance, performing prostrations and repentance on behalf of all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm, aspiring to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). Later, he went to Mount Dian.

He established the White Lotus Repentance Hall at Lake [Hu] and practiced the Pure Land path together with others. He composed the *Selection of the Buddha-Path Diagram for the Four Lands and Three Contemplations of Perfect Interfusion*, providing an exposition on the essential insights of the Lotus School.
Furthermore, he wrote a verse to encourage others to make vows, saying: "The myriad dharmas arise from the mind."

All phenomena are extinguished within the mind; this is what our Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, has constantly taught. If one upholds the precepts but lacks faith and aspiration, one shall not be born in the Pure Land;
one will only obtain the blessings of gods and humans, and when those blessings are exhausted, one will undergo saṃsāra, revolving through it with difficulty and unable to escape.
Reading the sutras without the eye of wisdom, one does not recognize the Buddha’s profound intent. Though one may attain cleverness in future lives, a distracted mind makes liberation difficult.

It is better to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; in this present life, there will be no fame or profit. Whether walking or sitting, if one does not engage in manifold discursive thoughts, that itself is Amitābha.

Through the power of making vows and upholding the precepts, one dedicates [merit] toward rebirth in a land of bliss. If one practices and maintains this in such a manner, not even one in a thousand shall fail.
Thus spoke the golden mouth of Śākyamuni; Amitābha personally embraces them; all Buddhas protect and mind them; and all devas skillfully guard and sustain them.

Seeing such a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha, one knows they are not far from the Buddha. They shall sit at the site of enlightenment and turn the great wheel of Dharma, universally delivering boundless multitudes.
It is like a woman of a poor household who is pregnant with a Wheel-Turning King; the devas will always protect her.
The poor woman herself did not know that within her womb was a noble child; likewise is the mind of this person who recollects the Buddha.
Constantly mindful of the Buddha and remembering him, they shall before long attain Buddhahood. All Buddhas will skillfully protect and sustain them, yet that person themselves does not know it.
I shall be born in the Pure Land, yet I must return to future lives to be born once more among human beings.

It is like a poor person’s house where there is a hidden treasure buried in the ground; the deity of the treasure constantly guards it so that it is not lost, yet the poor person themselves remains unaware of it.
Within one's own home there is a treasure storehouse, yet day after day one seeks work as a hired laborer to provide for oneself with food and clothing.
It is the same with this person who recites the Buddha’s name: though they possess the Tathāgatagarbha in its fullness, they do not know it and say of themselves, "I have no share."
Instead, one is reborn among humans, like a patient in whose home there is a truly wondrous medicine; yet, not knowing the nature of that wondrous medicine, one cannot cure one's own illness.
Day after day, by one’s bed and pillow, one suffers immeasurable pain. Such is the case for this person who recites the Buddha’s name.
The meaning is likewise so: one who does not know how to recollect the Buddha with the mind cannot extinguish greed, anger, and delusion.

[But the one who knows] can act as a great King of Physicians, can act as a great Treasury of Jewels, can benefit and deliver all people, and can act as a Great Dharma King who protects and shelters all sentient beings.
They think, "As an ordinary person, I shall not be able to be born in the Pure Land. Thus they observe the precepts and fasts for themselves, vowing that in future lives they may become human beings;
only after practicing the path through successive rebirths can they finally be born in that land. I have often seen practitioners constantly making such statements.
Not praising the vows of Amitābha and not conforming to the Pure Land sutras, one’s mind is shrouded by false views; thus, it will be difficult indeed to attain liberation.
This is not the obstruction of others, but entirely the obstruction of one's own mind. If one fails to be reborn in this life, it is a failure that will lead to a hundred more.
I exhort you, practitioners: believe what the Tathāgata has spoken. The Buddha’s words are never unreal; how could they be false or deceptive?
You should simply exert yourselves with diligence and seek the Pure Land with a single mind. It is like fanning a fire with the wind; not much effort is required.

Fortunately, you possess the mind of *nien-fo*. Turn this merit toward the vow to transcend the three realms. To encounter treasure yet fail to take it, or to meet with food yet suffer from long-term hunger—alas for such great men!
You do not perceive the true meaning. I now offer this brief exhortation and praise; may it be passed on and transmitted to others.
"Disseminate this widely on my behalf; act as the Tathāgata’s messenger. You are truly the children of all Buddhas; this is truly called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

May you all practice according to these teachings and be reborn together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. In the second year of the Qiandao era, he was summoned by imperial decree to the Deyou Palace to expound the Pure Land dharma-gate.
He was granted the title "Patriarch Cizhao. On the twenty-third day of the third month, at Duocheng...
Ni Pu built a residence and addressed his disciples, saying, "My work of transforming conditions through my vows is now complete; it is time for me to depart.
With palms joined, he took leave of the assembly and suddenly manifested parinirvāṇa. On the twenty-seventh day, his body was cremated, yielding countless śarīras.
He once compiled the *Essentials of Amitābha* (*Míttó jiéyào*), which has been circulated in the world (as recorded in the *Lianzong baojian*).

Miaoyun (妙雲), courtesy name Cishi (慈室), surnamed Yang, was a native of Mingzhou. He studied under Dharma Master Jiuqiu (久) of Qingxiu Temple and attained mastery in both the doctrinal teachings and meditative contemplation.
In the nineteenth year of the Shaoxing era, he succeeded him as the abbot of Qingxiu. He subsequently served at Nannhu in Cixi before eventually retiring to Xi.
At the Wu Family Hermitage, he went one day to bid farewell to Master Wu. Upon returning, he bathed, sat in the lotus posture, and said to his attendant:
"I have kept a fragrant incense stick hidden for thirty years. I intended to burn it at the time of my death to repay the Buddha’s kindness;
now that moment has arrived, and I am about to depart. As the incense smoke rose in full intensity, he rose, addressed the Buddha, and requested permission to return home.
He passed away peacefully while seated with palms joined (Fozu Tongji).

Xiyen Xiyen, whose courtesy name was Shengtú, was a native of Fànhuà in Míngzhōu. Having successfully passed the scriptural examinations in his youth, he received full ordination and studied under Dharma Master Jiǔ.

His writings on the contemplation of dharmas were elegant and sublime; those of later generations admired them. In his later years, he examined himself and realized that residual habits had not yet been purified.

He consequently resided at the Li family hermitage in Taoyuan, where he devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of *nianfo* for over ten years. He said to others, "As for the Way of the Pure Land, how could there be a single dharma to be attained?
If one perceives not a single dharma within the midst of cultivation, then the supreme grade of the *Jiguang* (Dharmadhātu) realm is attained without being realized."
He attained realization. The small window in Bian’s residence was named "Recalling the Buddha. Once, while walking through a vegetable garden, he saw various insects devouring the plants;

fearing he would harm their lives, he ceased eating vegetables altogether, purchasing only sea algae to provide for his daily meals. At the time of his death, he took leave of the monastics and the laity in advance.
Having bathed and changed his robes, he faced west and practiced contemplation. Suddenly, he exclaimed, "The Buddha has come! and passed away with palms joined (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Daoyin, whose courtesy name was Cao’an, was surnamed Xue and a native of Mingzhou. At the age of seventeen, he received full ordination and studied under Master Fazhi Falü.
Thereafter, he traveled extensively among lecture halls and frequently visited Zen meditation chambers. He also studied the *Ten Gates of Non-duality* by Siming.
