Upon reading the *Zhijyao chao* (Essential Commentary), he attained realization and subsequently paid remote obeisance to Fazhi as his teacher.

He served in succession as abbot of Yongming, Baoyun, Guangshou, and Zhiping, and later presided over Yanqing. On the seventeenth day of the fourth month in the third year of the Qiandao era, he addressed his disciples, saying:
"The world of Avatamsaka is profoundly penetrating and luminously clear; it perfectly accords with my heart's desire. I am now about to depart. He then ordered that his writings be recited.
The Praise of Amitābha says: The boundless ocean of lands contains the void; that ocean and void are entirely the Lotus Palace. The Lotus Palace pervades everywhere throughout the void;
within this ocean of space, the countenance of Amitābha alone is revealed. Amitābha Buddha is neither born nor extinguished;
he is as difficult to find and grasp as the moon reflected in water. He is by no means a body apart from words; such is his resonance and response, and such is his teaching.

I and Amitābha are fundamentally non-dual; through the latent arising of deluded perception, we suddenly became separate. From this moment forth, I shall sweep away all dust of emptiness and existence;

as father and son, we shall naturally meet again. I vow to cultivate the three blessings and diligently practice the six remembrances, ensuring that my actions of body, speech, and mind remain free from flaw or blemish.
Now, with these thoughts, I shall contemplate Amitābha; until I behold him, I shall never grow weary. Having finished the praise, follow the assembly.

He chanted the name of the Buddha several hundred times and recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* up to the section on the "Highest Birth in the Highest Grade. He then composed his mind and passed away while seated.
Three days later, both his crown and his feet were warm (from the *Fozu Tongji*).

There was a friend named Mù'ān (牧庵), a native of Jīnhuá. By nature he possessed a powerful memory. He visited the Dharma Master Chēxī Qīng, attending upon him day and night to inquire after the teachings until he had mastered the Way in its entirety.
He presided over Xiāntán and lectured on the *Zhìguān*. At that time, the Master Tīānyī Chí arrived in the region while wandering for alms.
He entered the monastery to attend the lecture. Startled, he said, "This is something I have never heard before," and after performing a prostration, he departed.

The wife of the Xu family from Hu Lake had died early; she was frequently seen appearing in her room. Her family held a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

They invited friends to expound upon the meaning of the sutra. The woman relied on their words and said, "Thank you, grandfather and grandmother, for this one scroll of scripture; I have now attained liberation. Grandfather—

Question: "When a thousand monks recite together, why do you say it is 'one fascicle'? Answer: "It is that which Master Peng recited. He moved to Nengren Temple and later presided over Yanqing Temple.

On the day he opened the lectures, the assembly was flourishing. On the third day of the twelfth month in the fourth year of the Qiandao era, while seated in the Qingyu Pavilion, he requested a ritual master to chant the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.
When they reached the 'Contemplation of the True Dharma Body,' he ordered the great assembly to chant the Buddha’s name and remained [in meditation]."
The verse concerning his passing away (from the *Fozu tongji*):
"Only Yue, Only Yue.
It is not detailed where he originated from. He resided at Huacheng in Zhuji, where he elucidated the Vinaya studies and cultivated the practice of Pure Land. One day...

A monk came to welcome him. Two days later, he suffered a slight illness and urgently called his fellow resident, Daoning, saying, "I see Amitābha Buddha, eight *zhang* in height, stationed in mid-air;
I may now depart. Having finished speaking, he passed away (*Fozu tongji*).
Simin, Simin.

It is not known from whence he originated. Following the *Zhao* Vinaya Master of Lingzhi, he received the expanded precepts and devoted himself single-mindedly to pure practices, remaining as constant as a single day for twenty years.
Once he fell ill, he requested the assembly to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Guānjīng) for half a month. After three days had passed...
He saw transformation Buddhas filling the room. At the time of his death, he chanted the Buddha’s name; the sound emerged beyond the assembly.
During the intense heat of summer, his shrine remained for seven days, filled with a pervasive and fragrant aroma (from the *Fozu tongji*).

Huìhéng, whose courtesy name was Qīngzhào, is of unknown origin. Initially, he relied upon Línzhī to study the Vinaya; subsequently, he resided at Yánshòu Monastery in Hángzhōu, where he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
Having spent sixty years in this pursuit, whenever he encountered others, he invariably urged them to recite the Buddha’s name.
He exhorted [others] to construct a precious pavilion and erect statues of the Three Sages, which were most exceptionally magnificent.

There was a man named Jiang Ziren who suddenly dreamed that a jeweled throne descended from the sky, saying, "Dharma Master Heng shall ascend this throne. Just then, his fellow associate, Layman Sun, informed Heng of his impending departure;
he had already prepared his seal while still at home and passed away. When Heng went to offer incense and pay his respects, he returned and told his [family]:
Tudu said, "Master Sun has already departed; I too shall go. He then gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name and spoke this verse for them:

"Recite the name of Amitābha with every word; contemplate his white ūrṇā-hair with every thought. By maintaining this heart of non-retrogression, one will certainly be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
He then sat upright and passed away (Fozu Tongji).
Xing Xingxian.
It is unclear from where this name originates. When he received full ordination, he recited the *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Vinaya Manual) and mastered it thoroughly in three days.
He studied the Vinaya under Dharma Master Dazhi and resided at Mingqing Temple for twenty years. Once, while suffering from an illness during sleep, he immediately established [a ritual] to the west.
He faced the Buddha image and instructed his disciples to chant the Buddha’s name. After several days, he suddenly rose and requested his three robes.
He personally chanted the *Amitābha Sūtra* and called upon the Buddha with a resolute voice. Sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Yongqin—whose origins are not detailed in detail—resided at Qiantang Qibao Monastery. He relied upon Dazhi to study the Vinaya. He heard Dazhi address the assembly, saying:
"To propagate the *vinaya* while alive and to return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) after death; when one leaves the household life to study the Way, one’s duties are then complete."

He immediately focused his mind on the Pure Land with single-minded resolve, never wavering. He recited the Buddha’s name thirty thousand times daily. He once traveled spiritually to the Pure Land, where he beheld the various extraordinary manifestations of the Buddha and the Great Beings (Bodhisattvas).
Addressing his attendant, he said, "I shall depart for the West tomorrow. He then gathered the assembly to chant the Buddha’s name.
At dawn, he joined his palms facing west, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Weiwo, Weiwo.

A native of Qiantang, he retired from public affairs and secluded himself at home. He read the Tripitaka three times and recited the *Avataṃsaka*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and other sutras totaling twenty thousand fascicles.
In his later years, he recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* twenty sets. One night, while he was suddenly ill, he faced the west.
He sat upright, performed a mudrā, and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).

"Zhongming, Zhongming"—his origins are unknown. He resided at Ba'en Temple in Shan-yin; he had never previously observed the precepts or maintained moral discipline. Once, due to a sudden realization...

When he fell ill, he said to his fellow practitioner Dao-ning, "My mind and consciousness are scattered; what medicine can cure this? Dao-ning replied, "Simply follow the breath and recite the Buddha's name;

this is the supreme medicine. Ming followed this instruction and practiced it. When the seventh day arrived and he was extremely exhausted, Dao-ning further instructed him to visualize the image of the Buddha.
After a long time, Ming suddenly said, "Two Bodhisattvas have arrived," and then added, "The Buddha is coming. He then closed his eyes and passed away.
(*Fozu tongji*). Chongyi, Chongyi—his origins are not clearly known.
He resided at Jingguang Temple in Qiantang and drew blood to transcribe the seven scriptures of the Pure Land.

Furthermore, he transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra* in golden script and carved images of the Three Holy Ones of the Western Quarter. Relying on the methods for seated meditation according to the *Mohe Zhiguan*, he practiced the mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha.
One day, he fell ill; refusing to take medicine, he offered incense before the Buddha to repent and invited the assembly to join him in chanting the Buddha’s name and reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the words "the world of the West," he passed away peacefully (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Benkong (Zi Xutang) was surnamed Xu and was a native of Fenghua in Mingzhou. His mother dreamed that divine light circled her chamber before she gave birth to him.
From his youth, Kong frequently practiced vegetarianism and recited the sutras. At the age of fourteen, he left the household life and followed the Dharma Master Zhi Yongran.
He received instruction in contemplation. During the Chunxi era, he presided over Zijiao Temple; later, he moved to Bailian Temple, where he greatly propagated the teachings of the school.

Daily, he took rebirth in the Pure Land as his primary mindfulness. On the third day of the third month in the third year of the Shaoxi era, he took his seat before the assembly, wrote a verse, and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Fayin, whose secular surname was Gu, was a native of Cixi in Mingzhou. He studied under the Dharma Master Ca’ān Yin and mastered the essential tenets of his teachings;
he was thus known at the time as "Little Yin. He presided over Guangshou Temple for thirty years, devoting his mind to pure practice day and night. During the day...
He gave lectures at night. He never visited the homes of the laity for even a single day. When donors arrived, he could not refuse them; he would accept a small portion from each.
As for the room where he lived, when others urged him to renovate it, he said, "This very body is impermanent; why concern oneself with external things?"
In the eighth month of the fourth year of the Shaohui era, he manifested illness.

While in a state of meditative concentration, he beheld two Bodhisattvas of the Pure Land and said to those around him, "I have seen the Dharma-Flower (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka) assembly hall; it is vastly different from what I have seen before. I am about to depart.
He immediately gathered the assembly to chant the *Amitābha Sūtra* and recite the Buddha’s name. When some requested that he leave behind a verse, he wrote: "I and Amitābha originally have no..."
"Two, and both two and non-two are equally transcended. Thus do I now behold Amitābha; the resonance between the Way and its response is inconceivable.
He sat upright and composed, performed the mudrā, and passed away" (Fozu Tongji).
Zhili, Zhili. His origins are not clearly known. He resided at Huadu Monastery in Shangyu. By nature he was simple and honest; matters of right and wrong never touched his lips.

Initially, he traveled extensively to study under various masters of the Chan school, but in his later years, he focused his mind solely on the Western Paradise. In the eighth month of autumn, the first year of the Qingyuan era...
In the month of [Month], while free from illness, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying: "In a dream, I beheld Amitābha Buddha.

His body was seven or eight chi in height, adorned with the marks and signs of a golden-purple hue, and manifesting the light of the white tuft between his brows. He stood surrounded by a great multitude as he preached the Dharma.

The Buddha said, 'All you virtuous people, you should give rise to great faith and cultivate all wholesome dharmas; then you shall be reborn in my land. Having spoken these words, the Buddha immediately vanished. Since I...
He beheld the Buddha; his rebirth there was certain. He then wrote a verse, saying: "A wild goose flies across the vast sky; its reflection sinks into the cold water.
Neither ceasing nor arising—within the land of the lotus. Having finished writing, he turned his body toward the west, performed a mudrā, and passed away at the age of eighty-two (*Lèbāng wénlèi*).

Huiming, whose courtesy name was Wuhui, was a native of Yanguan in Hangzhou. He entered the monastic order at Xiangfu Temple and studied under Huiguang of Upper Zhushan for twenty years, whereby he fully realized the principles of the single mind and the three contemplations.
In his later years, he resided at Changzhao Temple on Jing Mountain, where he cultivated the practice of Pure Land.
He performed his daily recitation of the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as well as the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Yuanjue-jing*, reciting them in cyclical rotation.

He maintained the name of Amitābha Buddha at ten thousand recitations per day. In the spring of the fifth year of the Qinyuan era, he manifested illness. Summoning his disciples, he said: "I have studied the Mahāyāna and sought rebirth in the Pure Land;
now it shall surely be fulfilled. When his disciples requested that he compose a verse, he rebuked them, saying: "When facing death, how could I further offer riddles?"
When asked [what he wished to say], he could not bear to refuse and wrote out the five characters: “My bones shall merely be roasted. He then sat down with his feet crossed and passed away.
The assembly heard celestial music coming from the west, hovering above his head for a short while before ceasing.
Upon cremation, they obtained countless *śarīra* relics of five colors (from the *Lèbāng wénlèi*).
Liaoyi Liaoyi, styled Muden, was the great-grandson of the Junior Master Zhongli. At the age of fifteen, he took the jinshi examination and traveled to Jinling, where he met Master Baoning Ji.
Upon hearing the Dharma, he attained awakening and immediately underwent tonsure and ordination. Wherever he went, he inscribed [his name].
He said, "In my dreams last night, every thought was directed toward the Western Land without interruption. When Master Xiang went to Huangbo, I urged him to travel with me.
One night, Master Xiang dreamed that Master Yi came to bid him farewell, saying, 'I am returning to the West. He then saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who presented him with a golden platform."

Three days later, he sat in meditation with incense burning and passed away with a smile on his face. He once visited Mount Wutai and suddenly perceived himself walking in the procession behind a multitude of bodhisattvas.
Two men wearing purple sashes and golden seals followed behind him.

When Dao-yi questioned them regarding their names, a monk led him to the side of a hall where he saw two jade plaques inscribed in gold with the names Wang Gu and Ge Fan; both men had cultivated themselves through practice.
Pure Deeds. The details are found in his original biography (*Fozu Tongji*).
Huicheng:
his origins are not clearly known. He resided at Zisheng Temple in Qiantang, where he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and paid homage to the Western Paradise.
The Buddha once traveled spiritually to the Pure Land and personally beheld the countenance of the Buddha.
He then returned to a mountain grotto, used firewood as a funerary shrine, sat within the shrine, recited the Buddha’s name, and set himself on fire (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Zunang, Zunang.

It is not known from whence he originated. He resided at Mount Nanyue and, drawing blood from his own body, transcribed five hundred fascicles of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, one hundred fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṃitā Sūtra*, and ten sets of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Over a period of twenty-seven years, he maintained this practice for a long duration while constantly reciting [the scriptures].

The Buddha vowed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturance (An-yang). Toward the end of his life, his blood dried up and he stood as mere bones; yet the sound of his recitation of the Buddha’s name never ceased.
One day, he went to the abbot’s quarters, ascended the seat, and passed away. Śarīras burst forth from within his body, appearing wherever they were taken. (From the *Fozu Tongji*)
Xi Zhan (d. ca.
540) was a native of Shanyin. In his youth, he was a Confucian scholar, but he suddenly grew weary of the world and left the household life.

Together with the lay practitioner Ying, he constructed a hall for Amitābha Buddha at the monastery and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. He never sat with his back turned toward the west. After a long time, he frequently saw three...
The Venerable Xiang (Shengxiang). One night, facing west, he recited the sutras; sitting upright and forming mudrās, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*). Fachi:
his origins are not detailed. He resided at Huadu Temple and practiced the Amitābha Repentance for three years, until two of his fingers were consumed by the flames.

He increased his observance of the precepts and fashioned images of the Three Sages of the Western Paradise. He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Contemplation Sūtra*, and the *Rucigati-cakra-mantra*, vowing to shorten his life in Jambudvīpa so that he might be reborn early in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*).
One day, while suffering from a slight illness, he wept and prayed before the Buddha, wishing for the Buddha’s compassionate guidance.
As he chanted the name of the Buddha, the sound reached a hundred paces away. Suddenly, he beheld the Buddha’s body, sixteen feet tall, standing upon a lotus pond.
He then spoke of himself, saying, "I have already attained birth in the middle grade. He sat upright facing west and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Liaoxuan, whose secular surname was Pan, was a native of Fenghua in Mingzhou. He pursued his studies at Nanhu and thoroughly investigated the Three Contemplations and the Ten Vehicles.
Regarding this principle, he read Mahāyāna sūtras until there was nothing he did not thoroughly understand. He practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* repentance ritual for twenty-seven years.
He was on intimate terms with Shi Shanrong; whatever spiritual cultivation he undertook, he invariably engaged in it together with Rong.

Rong once transcribed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Śūraṅgama*, *Vimalakīrti*, and *Awakening of Faith* Sūtras in gold ink, and [the Master] assisted him in its completion. At other times, he would provide the materials for others to hand-paint images of Avalokiteśvara. II.
Xuán made a vow to be reborn [in the Pure Land] and exhorted others everywhere to follow suit; consequently, those who practiced mindfulness of the Buddha increased day by day.

One day, Xuán went to see Tányǒng’s residence and said, "The time for my departure has already arrived; we shall surely meet again in the Pure Land. Tányǒng laughed and said, "I was precisely wishing to see your strategic resolve.
Xuán immediately gathered the assembly to bid farewell, commanding them to recite the sutras and chant the Buddha’s name. He wrote a verse, saying: "Nature..."
He forgot his emotions and merged with the One; he had no reliance on the three realms. His breath ceased and did not circulate. Mahāśrī joined his palms and passed away.

It was the height of summer, yet his remains stayed in the shrine for seven days; his complexion remained rosy and lustrous, a slight saliva flowed from his mouth, and a wondrous fragrance wafted toward people.
This was the tenth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Jiatai era. When cremated, the *śarīra* relics were beyond counting. Three years had passed since he entered *nirvāṇa*.

Rong took the scriptures and images and distributed them among his old friends and acquaintances. He recited the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra* and the *Shorter Amitābha Sūtra*, and led the assembly in chanting the Buddha’s name.
Then, sitting in the full lotus posture, he said, "I go now to fulfill Master Xuan’s appointment. Having finished speaking, he passed away with a serene transformation.
(*Fozu Tongji*; *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Ming*)
Tanyi, Tanyi.

His origins are unknown. He resided at Jingzhu Monastery in Qiantang and made his living as a physician. In his later years, he paid homage to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and practiced the *nienfo samādhi*.

He distributed the provisions he had accumulated throughout his life to make offerings to the Buddha and provide meals for the monks, and he commissioned the creation of Buddhist images and ritual implements.
He bathed in this manner for twenty years. Later, he fell slightly ill; he set aside medicine and food, inviting seven monks to chant the Buddha’s name to assist him in his rebirth.
On the following day, he saw a lotus flower as large as a house. Another day, he saw a monk from India approach his bedside to offer greetings.
At midnight, the assembly heard the sound of chanting the Buddha’s name gradually fade away. Looking at him, they saw that he had passed away peacefully (from the *Fozu Tongji*).

Zulang, whose secular surname was Li, was a native of Jizhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of nine and took the National Teacher Yuantong of Dashing’ansi Temple in Yanjing as his preceptor.
During the Dading era of the Jin dynasty, he successively resided at various temples, including Chongshousi and Xianglin Monastery. During the Zhenyou era, he was granted [imperial honors].
He was titled Great Master Yuantong. He recited the name of Amitābha several tens of thousands of times daily. At the age of seventy-four, as he was about to pass away, he announced to his disciples:
"My karmic ties to this life have come to an end. His disciples were surprised by this. Seven days later, he composed a verse by dictation:
"Alas, this skin-bag! It is a constant source of affliction and harm. Unable to succeed in continuing the ancestral lineage, one must rely on mindfulness of the Buddha.

Coming, there is no coming; going, there is no obstruction. The four elements and five aggregates will all at once fall into ruin. But tell me, is there anything that does not perish? After a long silence, he said:
"When the floating clouds have dispersed, the moon rises into the sky; within the light of Sukhāvatī, one is forever free. He then sat in the full lotus posture.
He passed away while sitting in the lotus posture (*dhyāna-paryaṅka*) (from the *Zhanran Jushi Ji*).
"Taweī" (Great Subtlety) appears repeatedly, though its origin remains unclear. During his childhood, he entered the monastic life under Dharma Master Fǎ'ān of Qiántáng. Initially, he was [ordained].

He was able to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* from memory. Upon receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he made a vow to shut himself in his room to practice mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*) and became a monk of non-retrogression.
Once, while strolling on the mountain behind the monastery, he suddenly heard the sound of a flute; he attained sudden enlightenment (*satori*). Thereafter, he kept a flute to amuse himself with.
There was a man named Lin Jianbo who also cultivated the practice of purity. He styled himself "Village Head of the Pure Land" for Wei.
One day, he knocked on the door and said, "Brother from the Pure Land Village, let us meet. Wei replied, "We may meet in the Pure Land; today I am busy reciting the Buddha's name.

The next morning, people marveled that he had not gone to the morning gruel. When they went to look for him, they saw his *dizi* (flute), *pātra*, and meditation chair already there. He had passed away beforehand.
He passed away while sitting cross-legged on the ground amidst a mass of embers (*Fozu Tongji*).
As for Sincong, his origins are not well-documented. He resided at Fa'an Temple in Qiantang. In his youth, he delighted in composing poetry; later, upon reading the *Mahā*...

He studied various sutras and attained realization, subsequently retiring his mind to a pure land. Daily he recited two sections of the Lotus Sutra and maintained the chanting of the Buddha’s name, never speaking of worldly affairs.
One day, he suddenly said to his disciples, "Last night I saw the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas coming together to welcome and guide me.
A disciple asked, "I fear this may be a demonic trial; what should we do? Zong replied, "After I have passed away, you need only look at my chest."

This may be verified from earlier accounts. Two nights later, he ordered the sounding of the *qing* gong and the chanting of the Buddha’s name. With a joyful expression, he said, "The Buddha is coming!
He then passed away suddenly. Upon examining his chest, an area about the size of a palm was seen to be marked with a red, lustrous pattern resembling a lotus flower (*Fozu Tongji*, *Xihu Zhi*).

"Pure Contemplation, Pure Contemplation. It is not clear from where this phrase originated. She resided at Jiguang Hermitage in Jiaxing and practiced the Pure Land Repentance Method for over ten years.
She said to her disciples, "I shall depart after twenty-seven days. Two days before that date, she saw [a vision of] red...
A lotus flower appeared. On the following day, he again saw yellow flowers filling the sky, with a transformed youth seated upon a flower.
On the third day, he entered his shrine and sat upright. He commanded the assembly to chant the Buddha’s name, and shortly thereafter, he passed away (from the *Jiaxing County Gazetteer*).
Lixian, Lixian—no one knew his origins. He resided at Fahui Temple in Xincheng, where he recited the Lotus Sūtra daily while also maintaining the chanting of the Buddha’s name.
Every time it reached midnight, his voice was mournful and piercing, as he vowed to be swiftly liberated from Saṃsāra and reborn in Sukhāvatī. In his later years...
Having frequently experienced auspicious dreams, he suddenly manifested illness. He instructed the assembly to chant the Buddha’s name together;
facing westward with a fixed gaze, he sat upright and passed away (Fozu Tongji).
The master’s name was Anshi; its origin is not clearly known. He studied at Pujing Temple in Wuzhen and attained mastery of the *Avataṃsaka* school’s fundamental tenets.
For twenty years, he practiced the Amitābha Repentance, contemplating the Pure Land day and night without ceasing. Throughout his life, he suffered from many illnesses. At the time of his death...
Suddenly, his spirit and clarity became extraordinary; he said to his disciples, "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have already descended. I am about to depart.
He then sat upright and passed away (*Fozu tongji*).
He was like a treasure, yet the origin of his lineage remained unknown. He received his monastic training at Juehua Temple in Xiachuan.

Having heard that ancient virtuous masters had dedicated the merit of bathing the sangha toward rebirth in the Pure Land, he subsequently established a bathhouse and provided for the assembly of monks. After twenty years had passed, he constructed [a hall].
He was a devotee of Western Pure Land imagery who vowed to seek rebirth there. At the age of eighty-one, he invited the assembly to drink tea as a parting gesture.

Upon hearing the tolling of the bell, the assembly was struck with wonder; he immediately sat in the full lotus position facing west, joined his palms, gazed intently, and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).

Xianchao of Bozhou received the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* from the Tripiṭaka Master Zongchi. He maintained the mantra rites of the Vajra of Impure Traces (*Vaiśravaṇa*), curing illnesses and resolving grievances.

He calculated that the offerings he received amounted to fifty thousand strings of cash, which he dedicated to the permanent endowment of Yongshou Monastery. Later, while ill, he beheld the Buddha and Bodhisattvas.

Sakyamuni came forward to meet him; lotuses filled the air, and various musical instruments played in harmony. His disciples entreated him with great sorrow, praying that he remain in the world to save suffering sentient beings.
As the transformation scene of the Pure Land gradually faded away, [the Buddha] remained for another fifteen years, reciting mantras to save people.
One day, he suddenly heard celestial music and extraordinary fragrances; the Buddha and the assembly of sages all appeared in the sky. He then immediately turned his face toward the west.
He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) (Fozu Tongji). There was also one named Kai;
his origins are not detailed. He resided at Qianbu Temple in Xiachuan and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, never flagging from morning until evening.

Wang. On the first day of the year, he invited the assembly to chant the Buddha’s name and recite sutras. When they reached the section on the Western World, he immediately closed his eyes and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Daosheng, Daosheng—his origins are unknown. He resided at Xingfu Temple in Changshu. He commissioned a sixteen-foot statue of Amitābha;

having obtained financial support and materials for its gilding and painting from Mei Ruren, the Magistrate of the County, he immediately gathered the assembly to chant sutras and invoke the Buddha’s name, offering his prayers while weeping bitterly.
He took his leave of the Buddha and returned to his quarters; there he wrote a verse and passed away while seated (*Fozu Tongji*).
"If one contemplates, if one contemplates"—the source of this phrase is not detailed. He resided at Jiahuai Temple in Wuzhen and gathered ten thousand people to chant the name of the Buddha together.
Each person chanted ten thousand times, vowing that those who attained rebirth first would successively lead others upward.

They recited and studied the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* until they had completed several hundred thousand copies. They vowed to adorn pure karma together with all sentient beings.
One day, he took up his brush and wrote a verse, then sat in the lotus position and passed away (*Fozu tongji*).
Yingke, Yingke.
His origins are unknown. He studied under Yaoshan of Xichuan and was indiscriminate in his consumption of wine and roasted meat.
One day, he suddenly reflected that his pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) had been deficient and that he was destined for the evil realms. He then went to his fellow resident, Master Jiezhu, and...

He read the *Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth* (*Wangsheng zhuan*) and was deeply moved. He selected a room, set up a seat facing west, and abstained from food while reciting the Buddha’s name.

After three days had passed, he dreamed that the Buddha and a Great Being (Bodhisattva) told him: "Your lifespan still has ten years remaining; you should continue to exert yourself. Zheke replied to the Buddha, saying:
"The world of Jambudvīpa is turbid and evil, making it easy to lose right mindfulness. My only wish is to be born early in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī)."
He served the assembly of sages. The Buddha said, "Your aspiration is such; three days from now, I shall welcome you.

When the appointed time arrived, he commanded the assembly to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. He declared, "The Buddha and the assembly of sages have all arrived," and then passed away in silence (*Fozu Tongji*).
Zhijin (Wisdom Seal), Zhijin. It is unclear from whence he originated. Residing at Jiyuan Monastery in Xiachuan, he constantly practiced the meditation on purity without interruption day or night.
While ill, he gathered the assembly to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*. As soon as it was finished, he sat in the full lotus position with palms joined and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Regarding "Jiedu jiedu" (Precepts and the Perfection of Precepts), its source is not clearly known. He received his monastic training at Qixinsi Temple and studied the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Later, he resided at Jile Temple in Yuyao, where he focused his mind entirely on returning to the West [the Pure Land]. While ill, he composed a poem in the style of Tao Yuanming’s “Return to the Plow” (*Guiqulaili*) to express his resolve. During his illness...

He wrote a letter bidding farewell to his fellow practitioners and parting from his old friends. He then instructed the assembly to recite and contemplate the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Upon reaching the section on the contemplation of the Dharma-body, he called out "Buddha!
in a forceful voice and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture (*fuzutongji*).
Zuhui, Zuhui.
His origins are unknown. He resided in the Buddha Pavilion within the city of Mingzhou; whenever he encountered anyone, he would simply say, "Amitābha Buddha.
Wang Yongxiang, the Magistrate of Yinqian County, and his wife served him with reverence. One day, he went to their home and told them:
He said, "I shall depart tomorrow. On the following day, those who had come to see him off gathered together; he then entered his coffin and sat upright.
He requested a sweet melon, ate it entirely, and passed away while chanting the Buddha’s name (*Fozu Tongji*).
Like a mirror, like a mirror—its origins unknown—he resided at Tashan in Mingzhou. He read through the Tripitaka twice and recited the Lotus Sutra daily.

Devoting himself single-mindedly to the mindfulness of the Buddha, he never slackened day or night. In his later years, he lived in a hermitage; suddenly falling ill, he invited the monks from neighboring huts.
He chanted the name of the Buddha, sat in the full lotus position facing west, and passed away with a smile (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
As for Zu Xin, his origins are unknown; he studied under the master at Fuyuan Temple in Siming and maintained a life of plain clothing and coarse food, strictly observing his monastic discipline.

Living a life of pure austerity, he resided at the Fang family hermitage. He established the Jingtu (Pure Land) Cloister separately from the Chan Yuan, where he fashioned images of the Three Holy Ones and planted lotuses in a pond.
On the third and eighth days of every month, he gathered monastics and laypeople for a session of collective mindfulness.

One day, he went to the abbot’s quarters of Biefuluan and said, "On the fifteenth day of the second month, I shall depart for the Western Paradise. I have come specifically to bid you farewell; I wish to beg for a bowl of noodles to satisfy my empty stomach."
"Is this permissible? The host acted according to his words. When the meal was finished, [the Master] went before the image in the Jōdo-in and paid homage, saying:
"The Patriarch is about to depart; I pay my respects to the Honored Image. He then returned to the hermitage to take leave of the assembly, saying: "I am now leaving.

I pray that you, virtuous ones, will diligently practice *nien-fo* so that we may soon meet again. He then sat in the full lotus posture and chanted the Buddha's name. Suddenly he cried out, "The Buddha has arrived! and passed away.
Zhang'er Huihua (Fozu Tongji). Miaowen, whose secular surname was Sun, was a native of Weizhou.
He entered the monastic order at the age of nine. At twenty-one, he traveled to Yanjing and relied upon Master Dade.

O Illustrious Lord, you studied the Way of Complete and Sudden Enlightenment. Later, you resided at Yunquan Temple in Ji, where you practiced diligence and frugality, such that your granaries held surplus grain;

during years of famine, you used this to relieve the hungry, for which the people of Ji were deeply grateful. You presided over the lecture seats on numerous occasions, extensively propagating the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings.

He vigorously proclaimed the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong). In his later years, he retired from public life as an "elegant elder" and devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of the *nien-fo* samādhi.
In the sixth year of the Yuan Yanyou era, he manifested illness and instructed his disciples to chant the Buddha’s name aloud.
Suddenly rising, he sat in the full lotus posture (*kaḍa-pada*) and formed the seal of samādhi, passing away peacefully at the age of eighty-three (*Fozu Tongzai*).

Shanzhu (also known as Shanzhuzi) was surnamed Yunwu and was a native of Suzhou. He confined himself within a single room, reciting the Buddha’s name throughout the six periods of the day. Though he suffered from chronic illness for a long time, he did not falter.
At the time of his death, a rare fragrance filled the room. His *Anyang chuan guyang ji* (Anthology of the Echoes of the Tradition of Rebirth) is still extant in the world.

Master Zhigong, whose courtesy name was Biezong, was a native of Hangzhou. His observance of the precepts was extremely rigorous. He established a meditation hall on the southern slope of Longshan Mountain and practiced the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).
Although he lived through times of upheaval and separation, he never abandoned his practice for even a moment. At the time of his death, he was free from illness; having bathed, he sat upright.
He passed away while sitting (from the *Wangsheng ji*).
Xing Cheng, whose courtesy name was Zhandang, was surnamed Sun and was a native of Kuaiji. His mother dreamed that a solar disc fell from the sky when he was born. At four [years of age]...
Every year he would take up his brush to paint images of the Buddha and was taught Buddhist scriptures, which he was able to recite from memory immediately.

In the thirteenth year of the Yuan Dynasty, he went to Shimen Temple to receive the tonsure and full ordination under Master Shu. Thereafter, he relied upon Master Xian Fojian to study the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school.
In the ninth year of the Dade era, he resided at Dongzhu Temple in Hangzhou. In the eleventh year, when Wuyue suffered a great drought, he prayed for rain, and it fell.

He established [the practice]. During a famine, the people died and there was no means to provide coffins for their burial; he therefore gathered their remains to bury them and performed a Great Water and Land Assembly to universally deliver them.
In the first year of the Zhizhi era, he was summoned to the capital by imperial decree and ordered to reside at Qingta Temple to collate the Tripitaka.
He was conferred the title of Great Master Fohai. He resided at Upper Tianzhu Monastery and later returned to Foguo Monastery.
Devoted to the Pure Land, he practiced the threefold contemplation in a single mind for seven days and nights, frequently experiencing auspicious responses.
On the first day of the month, while greeting the assembly, Cheng suddenly bowed and said, "Had I not been urgent in taking the step back, I would have nearly failed midway. Today, however—"
"There is [a chance] today; I fear there will be none tomorrow. Can the passage of time be grasped and toyed with? Please trouble yourself to point out my robes and bowl to represent impermanence.

The assembly recited the Buddha’s name for him, but he stopped them, saying, "The Buddha must be contemplated within oneself. Tomorrow morning, I shall come for one last farewell. At dawn, the assembly gathered;
he sat upright and passed away at the age of seventy-eight (*Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Ming Dynasty*).
Mengrun, whose courtesy name was Yugang, was surnamed Gu and was a native of Haiyan. At the age of fourteen, he entered the monastic life at Bailian Temple under the tutelage of Dharma Master Guyuan.
Just as he was about to prostrate before the temple guardian deity, all the statues toppled over. Guyuan then bestowed upon him the *Tiantai Zhiguan* (The Great Calming and Contemplation).
By reading the *Gangbi Shibuermen* and other such works, one can immediately comprehend their general meaning. When Guyuan returned to stillness, he served Dharma Master Zhuan at Zhutang Monastery.

Due to his arduous studies, he fell ill; he then performed the Seven-Seven-Day Repentance of Invoking Avalokiteśvara, through which his illness was cured and his mind became even more clear and sharp.
Subsequently, he presided over Dezang Temple in Haiyan, where he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* daily. He later moved to Yanfu Temple in Nan Zhu. Once there—
He retired to the Bailian Hermitage at Longjing, where he devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of the *nienfo* samādhi. Those who followed him increased daily.
He subsequently emerged to preside over Xiazhu, leading the assembly in the practice of the *Fahua* Samādhi. Thereupon, Samantabhadra emitted light, and various auspicious signs appeared.

After he had lived there for three years, one day he summoned his disciples, including Shifa Mingce and others, and revealed the essential principles of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calming and insight) and the stabilization of the mind (*anxin*).
He then said, "The conditions for my life have come to an end; now is precisely the time. Suddenly, he recited the Buddha’s name several hundred times and passed away in stillness.
Run spent his entire life practicing with vigor, without ceasing day or night, constantly performing the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Present Buddhas). By means of the nine...

There were seven instances where he set a period of ten days; during these, he performed various repentance rites for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Mahākaruṇā*, and the Pure Land sutras.
There were also cases where he set a period of forty-nine days (*saptasapta*), which are too numerous to enumerate (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty*).

Mingben’s secular surname was Sun, and he was a native of Qiantang. At the age of fifteen, he resolved to leave the household life. He prostrated before the Buddha and set his arm on fire, vowing to uphold the five precepts.

Daily, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and other scriptures; at night, he constantly practiced walking meditation and did not lie down. Thereafter, he went to seek instruction...
Tianmu Gaofeng Miaogong subsequently received him into the monastic order. After consulting and resolving his doubts repeatedly, he attained a profound realization of the source of the Dharma.

Once Gaofeng had passed away, Yuan resided between the rivers and lakes; wherever he went, students gathered like spokes converging at a hub. He soon returned to the mountains and lived in a hut beneath the stupa of Gaofeng.
In the tenth year of the Dade era of the Yuan dynasty, he emerged to preside over Shizi Monastery. His disciples called him Zhongfeng He.
Zhenzhou Shouhang then took his leave. Many high-ranking officials wished to invite him to reside at the various famous mountains in Zhejiang, but Zhenzhou firmly declined and did not accept.

When Emperor Renzong desired to have him come to court, he could not be persuaded. The Emperor bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Foci Yuanzhao Guanghui and granted him a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*.
He also renamed Shizi Monastery as Shizi Zhengzong Chan Temple. Since Zhenzhou upheld the "upward direction" (the ultimate teaching) alone, he focused exclusively on this.
At times he further extolled the Pure Land, often saying that Chan is the Chan of the Pure Land and the Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan.
He composed one hundred and eight poems on the aspiration for the Pure Land, which circulated widely throughout the world. Furthermore, he once wrote the "Record of Baoyuan Monastery," stating:
"To uphold the single mind is Chan; to illuminate the myriad dharmas is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). As for this mind, it is perfectly profound, empty, and still."
It penetrates all things without obstruction; it cannot be sought through marks, nor can it be reached through words. When unfolded, the myriad dharmas manifest in accordance with it;
when rolled up, the myriad dharmas subside in dependence upon it. Ordinary beings are deluded and ignorant, thereby giving rise to the cycle of saṃsāra.
Suffering and pleasure, rising and sinking—none can release one from them. Therefore, without *dhyāna* it is insufficient to accord with the minds of all Buddhas;
without sublime contemplation it is insufficient to shatter the delusions of sentient beings.

Thus, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* establishes twenty-five cycles (*cakra*) through the mutual application of the three contemplations, while the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* divides the observation of a single Buddha across sixteen locations. At the outset, one sits upright in a quiet chamber.

Focus the mind on a single point. Maintain this focus without ceasing until thought and its object both vanish together. Thus, one wheel perceives the Truth; wondrous contemplation becomes clear and luminous.
When the function of a single locus is perfected, all Buddhas are fully realized. It is like a mirror upon a high dais, or like pearls in an Indra’s net:
the myriad phenomena appear, yet there is no merit of "illuminating"; a thousand lights converge, yet there is no trace of "gathering. One who contemplates in this manner—
He immediately beheld the King of Pure Vows, whose white brow-hair reached to the heavens and whose deep blue eyes were like a tranquil sea.

His towering radiance and extraordinary marks and signs pervaded the entire world; this light transformed into fragrant terraces, jeweled trees, palatial towers, ponds, and various articles of adornment.
At that time, the practitioner of samādhi hears, sees, perceives, and knows immediately:
every word and silence, every movement and stillness, all merge seamlessly with non-action and pure, wondrous contemplation.
Thereafter, from this wondrous contemplation, at all times, they manifest boundless adorned Buddha-activities, thereby repaying the grace of the state. Thus—
May the sacred reign be preserved for boundless eternity. To repay the kindness of one’s parents through this means, their arduous labors shall transcend the fetters of outflows (*āsrava*);
furthermore, all enemies and kin of the past, present, and future shall simultaneously attain liberation. How could such a repayment ever be measured?
Moreover, he once led his colleagues to observe the Buddha’s birthday and the days of the Three Primal Origins at Guanshiyin [Temple].
Before the image of the Bodhisattva, he made forty-eight vows. One of these vows stated:

"From this life until the end of the future, at the time of my death, may I be free from all illness and suffering; may right mindfulness manifest before me and my mind remain undistorted, so that I may be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
There, having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, may I immediately realize non-arising. Furthermore, may I go to the Inner Court of Tuṣita to pay homage to Maitreya. Thus...

Later, he stepped down from his position and was born into this Sahā world to extensively deliver the deluded masses, leading them all to the other shore. In the third year of the Zhizhi era, he stayed on the eastern ridge of Mount Tianmu.
On the thirteenth day of the eighth month, he wrote by hand a letter of farewell to his various lay patrons and Dharma relatives.
Rising at dawn the following day, he wrote a verse, saying: "I have one phrase to entrust to the great assembly. If you ask further how it is, there is no original text to rely upon."
He set down his brush, sat upright, and passed away at the age of sixty-one. On that day, a white rainbow pierced the mountain peak.
His shrine remained open for three days; his countenance was as if alive. (From the *Zhongfeng Guanglu*, "Biography" and "Vow Text")

Youtan (優曇), whose secular surname was Jiang (蔣), was a native of Danyang (丹陽). His family had served the Buddha for generations. When he reached the age of twenty, he left the household life at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu.

Later, he resided at Miaoguo Temple in Danyang. At the beginning of the Zhizai era of the Yuan dynasty, an imperial edict abolished the Lotus School (Lianzong). Youtan was greatly terrified and said: "I..."
"I have received its teachings for nearly thirty years. Will it then perish in my lifetime? He then addressed the Buddha and made a vow that he would surely restore those teachings.
Thereupon, he composed the *Lianzong baojian* (Precious Mirror of the Lotus School) in ten fascicles. Now, I shall record those passages therein which are most exhortatory.
One version says: "In general, those who cultivate the Pure Land must clearly intend to confront birth and death themselves; it is not a matter of merely speaking of it and then leaving it at that.
One must contemplate that impermanence is swift and that time does not wait for anyone; one must treat this as a single, vital undertaking.
If one is half-advancing and half-retreating, or half-believing and half-doubting, what benefit will there be when the end comes? As it is said:
How does one escape from saṃsāra? If you have sufficient faith, then from this very day forth, arouse great courage and great diligence.
Do not concern yourself with whether you understand or not, nor whether you have seen your nature or not;
simply hold fast to the single phrase, "Namo Amitābha Buddha," as if leaning against Mount Sumeru, unshakable and immovable.
Concentrate your mind and unify your intention. Whether through recollecting, contemplating, mindful recollection, or ten-fold recitation;

or through silent recitation, focused recitation, continuous mindfulness, or reverent recitation—let your mindfulness dwell upon this very object. Constantly remember and constantly recite: recite in the morning and recite in the evening;
recite while walking and recite while sitting. Let your mind not pass by in vain, and let the Buddha-recitation never depart from your heart. Day after day, at every moment, do not...
Relax and let go. Be continuous and dense, like a hen brooding her eggs, constantly ensuring that the warmth remains uninterrupted;

this is precisely what it means for pure mindfulness to succeed one another. Further augment this with the illumination of wisdom, so that you may know the Pure Land is none other than your own mind. This is the method of cultivation and progress for those of superior intelligence.
If you can grasp this firmly, act as its master, and rely upon it securely, then even when encountering suffering or joy, adversity or favor, [you will remain steadfast].

When sensory objects appear before you, simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Do not have a single thought of wavering mind, do not have a single thought of indolence or sloth, and do not have a single thought of distracted or mixed thoughts.
Continue thus until the end of this life, never harboring another thought, with the firm resolve to be born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
If you can apply yourself with such diligence, then the ignorance and birth-and-death of kalpas—

Karmic obstructions will naturally dissolve; the habitual outflows of worldly toil will naturally be purified until nothing remains. One will personally behold Amitābha without departing from one's original mindfulness.
When merit is perfected and practice fulfilled, supported by the power of one's vows, at the time of death, one will certainly be reborn in the highest grade.
One version states: If a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha has not yet purified their defilements and evil thoughts arise, they must examine themselves.

Whether there be a mind of stinginess and greed, a mind of anger and resentment, a mind of deluded attachment, a mind of jealousy, a mind of deception, a mind of "I" (ego), a mind of arrogance, a mind of flattery and crookedness, a mind of false views, a mind of contempt, a mind of subject and object, or various conditions of adversity and favor—[in all such cases, one must self-examine].

Whenever any unwholesome thoughts arise following the influence of defilements, one must immediately call the Buddha’s name with a loud voice, collect the mind, and return to correctness, ensuring that evil thoughts do not continue.
One must directly strike them down until they are completely purified and exhausted, so that they never arise again.
All hearts of profound faith, hearts of utmost sincerity, hearts of aspiration and dedication, hearts of compassion, hearts of humility, hearts of equanimity,
hearts of skillful means, hearts of patience, hearts of upholding the precepts, hearts of joyful relinquishment, hearts of meditative concentration, and hearts of diligence.
One should always protect the bodhicitta and all wholesome states of mind. Furthermore, one must distance oneself from unchaste conduct and sever evil vows.
One should take great care not to keep poultry, dogs, pigs, or sheep, and one must never engage in hunting, trapping, or fishing.
Know that the noble and virtuous beings within the land of Sukhāvatī have attained rebirth there precisely because they abandoned negative conditions and cultivated wholesome deeds.

The Pure Land. Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha and do not regress from Bodhi should follow the teachings of the Buddha; they must take the abandonment of evil and the adoption of good as their primary task.

One source states: "All who cultivate the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and desire to be born in the Pure Land should constantly reflect that everything in this world is impermanent—what is formed must inevitably decay, and what is born must inevitably die. If one has not personally heard the Buddha-dharma, then upon casting off this body..."
I have received this body and transmigrate through the three realms, the four modes of birth, and the six paths, with no foreseeable end to my liberation.

Now, having met with the necessary conditions, I am able to hear the True Dharma and cultivate pure karma. With the Buddha alone as my refuge, when I cast off this retribution-body, I shall be born in the Pure Land, enter the lotus womb, and experience all manner of bliss.
There, I shall forever escape birth and death and never regress from Bodhi. This is the vow of a great man.
This is the essential task for one who has been born. As soon as illness occurs, one must press forward, keeping the body and mind broad and open, and harbor no doubts.

One must sit upright facing west and single-mindedly contemplate Amitābha Buddha, along with the Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and countless transformation Buddhas, all appearing before one. With undivided heart, recite: *Namo Amitābha*.
Recite the name of the Buddha continuously, without interruption. Regarding all worldly affairs, do not harbor thoughts of them, nor feel any attachment.
Should a thought of such things arise, simply and urgently recite the Buddha’s name; within every single moment of mindfulness, the obstacles of karma will be extinguished.
By this single thought alone, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land. As long as life has not yet ended, one will naturally find peace and security. Be careful!
Do not give rise to vain attachments to this world. You must live as you live; you must die when it is time to die.
Simply prepare for rebirth—why harbor doubts? If you understand this principle, it is like casting off tattered clothes to don fine garments:
once you abandon the ordinary body, you immediately ascend to the stage of Buddhahood. Is this not magnificent? One says: True faith is the very essence of the practice of cultivation.
If you wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, focus your mind on a single thought and hold the name of Amitābha Buddha.
This single thought alone is my original teacher; this single thought alone is the manifested Buddha;
this single thought alone is the fierce general who shatters hell; this single thought alone is the precious sword that slays all evils; this single thought alone is...
It is the bright lamp that dispels the darkness. This single thought-moment alone is the great vessel for crossing the ocean of suffering.
This single thought-moment alone is the excellent remedy for birth and death. This single thought-moment alone is the path for exiting the triple world.
This single thought-moment alone is Amitābha, one’s own original nature. This single thought-moment alone reaches the Pure Land of Mind-Only. However, it is only when...
Remember this one phrase, "Amitābha Buddha," as you recite it. Do not let it be lost. Let it be ever-present in every thought-moment;
let it never depart from the mind. Recite it thus when there is nothing to do, and recite it thus when there is something to do.
Recite it thus in peace and happiness, and recite it thus in the suffering of illness. Recite it thus at birth, and recite it thus at death. Thus it is.

This is a single moment of clarity and non-delusion; why, then, must one ask others for the way home? Once the treatise was completed, he presented it for universal verification across all quarters, and not a single character could be altered.
He submitted a petition to Emperor Renzong requesting the restoration of his sect, which was granted.

An imperial decree appointed him as the Head of the Teaching (Jiaozhu) and bestowed upon him the title "Venerable of Tiger Creek" (Huxi Zunzhe). He passed away at the beginning of the Zhishun era (*Zhenjiang Fu Zhi*, *Lianzong Baodian*).

Hongji (弘濟), whose courtesy name was Tongzhou (同舟), was surnamed Yao and was a native of Yuyao. In his youth, he left the household life at Baoji Temple. At the age of sixteen, he received the tonsure and ordination;
he was extremely diligent in upholding the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Later, he relied upon Master Quan of Bāngshān to study the Tiantai teachings for a long time.
He thoroughly mastered their essential meanings. He once practiced the repentance rites of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and the Pure Land sutras.

One day, while in meditative concentration, he beheld the Venerable Siming, who bestowed upon him a rhinoceros-horn *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling) scepter. From that time on, his eloquence overflowed daily.
In the first year of the Taiding era, he went forth to reside at Wanshou Yuanjue Temple. The following year, the coastal cliffs of Yanguan collapsed, leaving the local residents trembling with fear.
Prime Minister Tuo Huan was concerned about this. He ordered Ji to go to the seashore and establish a great vegetarian feast for both land and water.

Entering the *maitrī-samādhi*, he took sand from the sea, recited the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī*, and scattered it everywhere across that area. Wherever his footsteps reached, the shore became firm once more; people marveled at his divine power.
Later, he moved to various temples such as Jiqing, Xianci, and Yuantong. In his later years, he returned to Baoji Temple to devote himself exclusively to the practice of mindfulness.
The Buddha entered samādhi. Suddenly, his illness flared up, and he immediately summoned his disciples to instruct them in the doctrine of the Pure Land of the Mind-Only.

When some had not yet fully understood, Zhi [Ji] raised his voice forcefully and said, "Birth and death are difficult to transcend," whereupon he passed away. This was on the tenth day of the third month in the sixteenth year of the Zhizheng era.
He was eighty-six years old. (From the *Hufa lu*)
Bi Cai (Bi Cai), courtesy name Dayong, surnamed Qu, was a native of Linhai in Taizhou. His mother, Lady Zhao, was a devout follower of the Buddha;

she dreamed that a foreign monk entered her hall, and upon waking, she gave birth to him. At the age of twelve, he followed Dharma Master Ju of Baoyuan Temple to receive the precepts of renunciation. Not long after...

He received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and subsequently studied under Dharma Master Yungang Run. He read widely across the various scriptures and possessed a profound understanding of the teachings and contemplations (*jiaoguan*).

Yungang sighed in admiration, saying, "This youth is surely one who was present at the assembly on Vulture Peak. In the first year of the Taiding era, he succeeded Yungang as the abbot of Decang Temple in Haiyan.
Subsequently, he served at Xingfu and Yanfu Temples in Hangzhou; he was a man of grave and profound character.

He remained silent and diligently cultivated meditative practices. When he came to expound the meanings of the sutras, his discourse was unhindered in its breadth and depth; there were none among the listeners who did not submit with admiration.
Emperor Shun bestowed upon him the title Fojian Yuanzhao. One day, his head and eyes became sunken and dull, whereupon he said to the assembly, "My karmic conditions have come to an end.
He then burned incense, faced westward, and chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha for an entire day and night. He then announced:
The assembly said, "Do not say that your practice has yielded no results; our affinity for the Pure Land has ripened, and samādhi has manifested before us.
He then requested a bath and changed his robes, wrote a farewell letter to his acquaintances, and passed away with palms joined. He was sixty-eight years old. His body was cremated.
There were five-colored lights radiating from within the shrine. Of the remains that did not perish by fire, there were two:
the tongue-root was like a red lotus flower, and the teeth were like white conch shells; the śarīra relics were beyond counting (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*).

Yueke Yueke (悅可悅可), whose secular name was Zhongting (中庭), is of unknown origin. He resided at Xiyin Temple in Jiading and constructed the Sixteen Contemplations Hall (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā-śālā*) to cultivate the Pure Land practice.
During the Yuanyou era, he was granted the title Great Master Guanghui (廣慧大師). In the Zhizheng period, he passed away while sitting in meditation without illness.
He passed away. His body was cremated; his teeth and tongue remained unburnt (according to the *Suzhou Fu Zhi*).
Weize, whose courtesy name was Tianru, was surnamed Tan and was a native of Yongxin. After he left the household life, he inherited the Dharma from Chan Master Zhongfeng Ben.
At the beginning of the Zhizheng era, he resided at Shizi Lin in Suzhou. Although summoned repeatedly for audiences, he declined to attend on the pretext of illness.

Having attained a profound and secret realization of the single transmission of the Dharma, he further propagated the principles of Tiantai and Yongming, while simultaneously extolling the teachings of the Pure Land.

He authored the *Jingtu huo wen* (Questions on Doubts Regarding the Pure Land) to dispel various misconceptions and encourage spiritual practice. Herein, I have recorded those passages that are most striking and urgent. [From] the *Jingtu huo wen*: "A Question on a Single Lifetime..."
"One commits evil deeds, yet at the moment of death recites the Buddha’s name and is reborn [in the Pure Land] while still carrying one's karmic burdens; furthermore, there is no falling back.

Therefore, I shall attend to worldly affairs for now and wait until the end of life to recite the Buddha’s name—is this permissible? The answer was: "Alas! Alas! This deceives oneself and deceives the world.

Monastics and laypeople, men and women alike, all speak these words. That an ordinary person of perverse evil can recite the Buddha’s name at the hour of death is due to what they have cultivated in past lives."

Because of one's roots of goodness, one encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and attains the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). Such fortunate circumstances occur but once in ten thousand cases.

The *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) states that there are ten types of people who, at the time of death, will not be able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. First, they may not necessarily encounter a virtuous friend.

There are ten circumstances that prevent one from reciting the Buddha’s name: first, being exhorted by others to do so; second, being bound by the suffering of the two karmas such that one has no leisure to recite; third, losing the power of speech due to a stroke; fourth, losing one's mind through madness;
fifth, encountering water or fire; sixth, meeting with jackals or wolves; seventh, having one's faith destroyed by evil friends;

eighth, dying in a state of delusion; ninth, passing away while in prison; and tenth, falling from a high cliff. These are all matters commonly heard of and seen, regardless of whether the person is a monk or a layman.
This is common to all worldly people. Summoned by past karma and triggered by present karma, it suddenly manifests before one, leaving no room for avoidance.
Once you have suddenly encountered such a state, you can no longer manage yourself; even a spiritual friend or a living Buddha cannot save you.
You will then follow your karma to undergo suffering within the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties. When that time comes, you will wish to hear [the Dharma], but—

The name of the Buddha cannot be heard or fully realized. Even if one avoids such evil conditions and dies from a "good" illness, one still cannot escape the wind-blades that dismember the body and the separation of the four elements, like a live turtle being pulled from its shell;
oppressed by such agony, terrified and trembling with fear, one is unable to recite the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, even if one dies without illness, if worldly attachments remain unresolved and mundane thoughts do not cease, driven by greed—
Fear of birth and death agitates the breast; furthermore, one’s private affairs remain unsettled and final matters unattended.
With a wife weeping and children crying, one is tormented by a hundred kinds of anxieties and finds no peace even while reciting the Buddha’s name.
Moreover, prior to death, should even a slight illness afflict the body, one cannot avoid enduring pain and suffering, wailing and groaning, seeking medicine and physicians, and offering prayers.
I repent. Distracting thoughts fly about; I am unable to recite the Buddha’s name. Even if it were before I fell ill, I am merely old in years;
signs of decay have appeared, I am exhausted and decrepit, filled with sighs, lamentations, and distress.
Amidst this aging body, I can only patch things together here and there; I am unable to recite the Buddha’s name. Even if it were before I grew old—precisely...

In youth and vigor, if one’s wild mind has not yet subsided and remains entangled in worldly affairs—climbing here and clinging there, with distracted thoughts and a vast expanse of karmic consciousness—one will be unable to achieve success in reciting the Buddha’s name.
Furthermore, even if one enjoys leisure and independence and possesses the aspiration to practice, [these obstacles must be overcome].

If you cannot clearly perceive worldly phenomena, if you cannot let go, if you cannot maintain composure, and if you cannot remain settled, then when even a slight境 (objective condition) manifests before you, your master will follow it into delusion; even reciting the Buddha’s name will not suffice.

Observe that whether it be at a time of old age and illness, or during the leisurely days of youth, if there is even a single matter that hangs upon the mind, it already renders the recitation of the Buddha’s name ineffective.

If you cannot attain it now, how much less so at the time of death? Furthermore, you say, "I will attend to worldly affairs. You are truly a fool; you speak the words of a fool. I dare say that you have applied your mind in error.
Moreover, worldly affairs are like a dream; what real efficacy do they possess? Which single thing can take the place of birth and death?

Even if you were to build monasteries, increase the permanent endowments, pursue fame and status, or form alliances with the powerful and noble—thinking these things to be many [in merit]—[they are of no avail].

One performs good deeds, yet fails to realize that one has violated the precept against failing to embody the fundamental nature of the Way and instead extensively constructing monasteries and such things.
Such conditioned merits harbor many faults; before heaven is attained, hell is already established. While birth and death remain unclarified, all such acts become the root of suffering.
Only when the light of the eyes falls to the ground and one undergoes suffering will one finally realize that all one’s daily actions were merely adding more shackles to an existing collar.

Adding shackles to those already on their necks; adding locks to those already upon them. Adding more firewood and charcoal to the boiling cauldrons; assisting the swords and spears atop the sword-trees.
Having lost the human body beneath the monastic robes (kāṣāya), it will be difficult to recover for ten thousand kalpas. Even an iron-hearted man would shed tears upon hearing this.

Did the Patriarchs, speaking with such bitter urgency, ever permit others to merely recite the Buddha’s name at the moment of death? Master Sijian said: "The wealth and treasures of worldly people..."
Like a mountain, with wife and concubines before one, enjoying joy day and night—what can be done? One’s future path is limited; it secretly urges one on.
When the tally arrives, it must be executed; no lingering or delay is permitted. Lord Yama does not follow human sentiment; the King of Impermanence is relentless.
What face do you have? Consider for a moment what everyone has seen and heard in the streets and alleys before and behind us:
how many relatives, kinsmen, friends, brothers, and sturdy youths have already died? The people of the world often say, "One should recite the Buddha's name when one grows old."
Do you not know that on the road to Guangquan, there is no distinction between old and young? An ancient said: "Do not wait until old age before you recite the Buddha's name;

most solitary graves belong to the young. Such was the resolve of Siji (Sixin); he exhorted people with such bitter words. Did he ever grant you permission to wait until the end of life to recite the Buddha's name?
How much time can a person have while living in this world? It is like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning—gone in the blink of an eye.
It is too late. While you are not yet old and not yet ill, shake off your body and mind, cast aside worldly affairs, and for every moment of daylight you obtain, recite the Buddha’s name;
for every period of effort you find, cultivate pure karma. When your life comes to an end, your provisions will already be prepared and your future path will be secure.
If you do not act in this way, it will be difficult to remedy your regrets later. Someone may ask:
If the power of concentration has not yet been achieved and the mind lacks a master, then in the mere blink of an eye, it has traveled a thousand or ten thousand miles away.
Or, should one be touched by even a hair’s breadth of worldly affairs, one will be unable to shake them off for five or ten days, or even half a month or a full month.
"What strategy should be employed to govern this? He replied, "Alas! This is a common affliction among scholars throughout the world.

When you are experiencing interruptions [in your practice], if you do not apply the whip with great severity, then even if you cultivate uninterrupted mindfulness, there will never be a time of accomplishment.
I have heard that the ancients had three strategies for the severe whipping: first, gratitude; second..."

First is resolving one's will; third is seeking verification. Regarding the first, repaying kindness: having already cultivated the Pure Land, one should contemplate repaying the kindness of the Buddhas and the kindness of the state;
this need not be discussed further for now. Even considering the upbringing of one’s parents and the education provided by one’s teachers and elders—how can this kindness not be profound?
Since you left the household life, you have claimed you wish to repay these great debts of gratitude. You have left your hometown and its familiar surroundings... two.
For thirty years, you have utterly disregarded the hardships and sufferings of your parents and teachers.
When your parents grew old and fell ill, you did not care for them; even upon hearing of their deaths, you did not return.

Now they may be undergoing punishment and suffering within the three miserable realms (trāya), hoping that you will rescue them and deliver them. Yet, moment after moment, your mindfulness is interrupted; thus, Pure Land is not achieved. Pure...
The earth will not support you; you cannot even save yourself. How then can you save others?
Since you cannot help one another, you are ungrateful, ingrate, and a person of great filial impiety. As the Sūtra says: "The sin of filial impiety shall cause one to fall into hell.
Thus, a single thought of interruption is itself the karma of hell. Furthermore, you wear clothes without weaving and eat food without plowing.

Regarding the bedding and furnishings in the monastic quarters, which you currently enjoy and use: you should diligently cultivate pure karma to repay the kindness of those who provide offerings of faith.
As the Patriarch said: "This is the portion belonging to the donors' wives and children; to use it while diminishing its value is for one whose 'eye of the Way' is not yet clear.

Even a drop of water or a thread of silk must be repaid by pulling the plow and dragging the handle before one may be free. Yet you allow your mindfulness to be interrupted moment by moment. [Pure...]

Neither the [ordinary] land nor the Pure Land will be accomplished; you will merely have a portion of karmic retribution to repay. Thus, a single moment of a distracted mind is itself the karma of an animal.
Second, regarding the resolution of one's will: if you study the exclusive practice, your resolve must be determined.
You may spend a lifetime practicing Chan, yet if you do not awaken to Chan, and then turn to the teachings, yet do not clarify the teachings—having fumbled until now, you must contemplate...
Your head has not yet died, yet you wish to speak several words of Chan, write several characters, and compose several poems.
Your emotions hang between two ends; your thoughts divide into four paths. The Patriarch said: "A hair’s breadth of attachment is the karmic cause for the three realms of suffering;

a fleeting stir of emotion results in ten thousand kalpas of bondage. Yet your resolve lacks determination, and your thoughts are manifold. It is because of these manifold thoughts that [you are thus bound].
This interrupts right mindfulness. Thus, even a single moment of an interrupted mind constitutes the karmic shackles of the three miserable realms (*trāya*).
Furthermore, if one guards the roots of the precepts but lacks resolute intent, or if one pursues objects through body and speech at every thought-moment, the scriptures state:
"It would be better to pour molten copper into one's mouth than to use a mouth that has broken the precepts to receive food and drink from others; it would be better to..."
Heated iron is wrapped around his body. One cannot, with a body that has violated the precepts, accept the clothing of others;
how much less so when, due to the lack of strictness in the various precepts, the deviant mind moves recklessly? Because of this reckless movement, one interrupts true cultivation.
Thus, a single thought of interruption is not merely the karma of heated iron or molten copper. Furthermore, if one cuts off hatred and attachment while the will remains undetermined, every...

Regarding empty fame and floating profit, if one does not examine oneself and break through them, then when fame and profit belong to oneself, greed and attachment arise; when fame and profit belong to others, hatred and envy arise.
An ancient said: "Those who crave fame and profit move toward the same class as ghosts; those who pursue love and hate [move toward the same class as spirits]."
We enter the same pit of fire together, yet you, because of this, create attachment and aversion that sever your connection to the Pure Land.

Thus, a single thought of interruption is itself the karma for the pit of fire of the hungry ghosts. Third, regarding the seeking of spiritual efficacy: having studied the practice of exclusive cultivation, one should seek its miraculous efficacy.
Now that your hair has turned white, your face is wrinkled, and the signs of death appear before you, you know that you are approaching the end. Furthermore—
In a few days, you must have [the Buddha] before your eyes; you must see the Buddha immediately. For instance, Master Yuan of Mount Lu saw the Buddha three times in his lifetime.
Furthermore, Master Huai-gan called upon the name of the Buddha and immediately obtained a vision of him.
Again, when Master Shao-kang chanted the name of the Buddha once, a Buddha immediately flew out from his mouth. Such spiritual manifestations are ten thousandfold.
"Ten thousand, ten thousand! If your mind is without interruption, it will not be difficult to see the Buddha. If an interrupted mind arises, you will certainly not see the Buddha.
Since you do not see the Buddha, you lack the affinity with the Buddha. Lacking the affinity with the Buddha, it is difficult to be born in the Pure Land.
If you are not born in the Pure Land, you will inevitably fall into the evil realms. Thus, a single thought of interruption is itself the karma for the three miserable paths."

Furthermore, regarding the three aforementioned strategies, you should personally lash yourself with remorse so that your mindfulness does not depart from the Buddha, and the Buddha does not depart from your mindfulness.
When response and resonance meet in this way, you will see the Buddha before you. Having seen the Buddha of the Land of Bliss, you will see all Buddhas of the ten directions;
having seen all Buddhas of the ten directions, you will see the Buddha of your own original nature. Having seen the Buddha of your own original nature...
The Buddha immediately attains the manifestation of great function; thereafter, he dedicates his compassionate vows to extensively transform all sentient beings.
This is called "Pure Land Chan," and it is also called "Chan Pure Land" (from the *Su Zhou Fu Zhi: Inquiry on Pure Land*).

Shanjì (善繼), courtesy name Juézōng (絕宗), was surnamed Lóu (婁) and was a native of Zhùjì (諸暨) in Yùe (越). His mother dreamed that a divine monk bestowed upon her a lotus flower, and she subsequently conceived.
Upon birth, he was able to speak; whenever he saw his mother recite the names of the Buddhas, he would immediately join his palms in homage and chant along with her. Great...

Dejian received the tonsure and ordination; the following year, he advanced to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*). He subsequently followed Dharma Master Huai of Dayan Temple in India to study the Tiantai teachings.
