Later, he traveled to South India to visit Master Tanzang Cheng, who held him in high esteem. During the Zhizheng era, he presided over Jianfu Temple at Tiantai, and later moved to Nengren Temple.
In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land, fixing his mindfulness on Amitābha Buddha day and night.
He did not cease his practice. One day, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "I am about to depart. He then sat upright and passed away at the age of seventy-two.
When his body was cremated, his tongue remained unburnt (from the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Ming Dynasty*).
Ziwen, whose courtesy name was Zongzhou, was a native of Xiangshan in Mingzhou. He studied under the Dharma Master Wen of Beixi and emerged as the presiding abbot of Baoyun Temple.

He was profoundly learned in both doctrinal teaching and contemplative practice (*jiaoguan*), and his adherence to monastic discipline was extremely rigorous. When conversing with others, he seemed almost reluctant to speak; yet when ascending [the dais],...

He sat upon the seat and preached the Dharma, flowing forth without restraint. One day, having finished his lecture on the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*, he took his place upon the seat to bid farewell to the assembly before entering parinirvāṇa.
Someone asked, "Master, you have not yet entrusted us with matters for after your passing;

why do you depart so suddenly? He replied, "In the monastic community, when one wishes to act, one simply acts. Do not employ the tactics of a worldly person. The assembly’s entreaties became even more earnest, whereupon he descended from the seat.
He returned once more to his quarters and recorded each detail in writing. He then joined his palms and recited the sacred names of the Western Paradise;

having completed his dedication of merit and vows, he passed away. His body was cremated, yielding countless *śarīra* relics, and an extraordinary fragrance permeated the air for many days before it finally subsided (*Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Ming Dynasty*).
Pangu, Pangu.
His courtesy name was Lishui. A native of Haiyan, his aspirations were transcendent and he was extensively versed in the classics and histories.

He expounded the general meaning of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra at Huizhen Temple in Hangzhou; his eloquence was unimpeded, and the seven assemblies were all moved to submission. Later, he traveled to Songjiang and constructed—
In the vihāra, he diligently cultivated pure karma and daily recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. At over seventy years of age, he was free from illness;
having set a date in advance, he sat upright and passed away in peace (*Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Ming Dynasty*).
Wenhui, Wenhui.

It is unclear from where he originated. He resided at Qinglong Temple in Jiahe and was skilled at composing poetry. Later, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, becoming increasingly diligent as he grew older.
One day, while ill, he heard a voice in the air saying, "You shall be reborn in the Middle Grade of the Upper Birth. Thereupon...
Shi (from the *Fozu tongji*). Miaoye, Miaoye. A native of Yinqian County, Mingzhou.
During the transition between the Yuan and Ming dynasties, he left the household life to become a monk. He specialized in the study of the Tiantai teachings. Dedicated...
He practiced the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) and authored the two volumes of the *Nien-fo chih-chih* (Direct Pointing at the Mind through Nien-fo).
Among these, the essay "Direct Pointing to the Essential Heart" (*Chih-chih hsin-yao*) refutes delusion and reveals the truth; it is his most refined and profound work. The text states:

"The Great Hero [the Buddha], observing that in this Sahā world there are the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and bondage by karma, taught people to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Since the Sage departed..."

As time has passed, the ways of the world have become increasingly corrupt. People mistakenly understand that all dharmas reside within the mind; they take the six sensory objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) reflected within the chest to be the mind itself, claiming that the Pure Land exists therein.
Thus, they do not seek rebirth there. These six reflected images belong entirely to external objects (*pūrvaviṣaya*) and possess no inherent substance of their own.
If the external objects do not exist, this mind ceases to exist. How, then, could a land exist within this [mind]? Some may claim that through awakening—

The Way is precisely the Buddha-land within the mind. Once you have seen your nature, how could there be any principle of persisting in attachment to the shadows of conditions? Such a view does not exist in the world;

it is most base and inferior. If you wish to awaken to your true original mind, you should observe that the mind you recognize as the shadow of the six sense objects is fundamentally within your chest.
The chest resides in the body, and the body dwells in the land, extending to all pure realms.
The oceans of defiled lands all exist within space; space is boundless, and the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—are entirely contained therein.
Although this space is vast, I do not stir from my true, fundamental mind. It is not that this [mind] is greater than the greatest, but rather that space itself resides within my own true mind.
Like a small fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity of the sky, how could the oceans of pure and impure lands not reside within the fundamental mind?
Thus, when the Buddha says that all dharmas are in the mind, he does not mean within the mind of deluded thoughts and reflected images in the chest;

rather, they reside within the fundamental true mind of the present single thought-moment. This mind is detached from cognition and perception, transcends hearing and seeing, and has forever severed [all attachments].

Regarding all phenomena of arising and ceasing, increase and decrease: since all bodies and lands are entirely contained within this mind, one knows that realms such as Sukhāvatī and Sahā are the complete manifestation of my own mind.

To arbitrarily within them—abandoning the east and grasping at the west, loathing the defiled and delighting in the pure, or fervently clinging to signs in pursuit [of the goal]—none of these escape my own mind. Therefore, the marks and embellishments of Amitābha in Sukhāvatī...
At this very moment, it is one's own mind that manifests; when one's own mind manifests, that Buddha appears.
My mind is the Buddha’s mind, and the Buddha’s mind is my mind; they are of one essence and non-dual. Therefore, it is said: "The Pure Land is Mind-only; Amitābha is one's original nature.

This does not mean that there is no land or Buddha in the West, nor that one need not seek rebirth there. Rather, it means that [the Buddha] exists within the conditions and shadows of your own arising and ceasing. This is called...
This is because it is the very nature of Mind-only. To seek that Buddha is to seek one’s own mind; to seek one’s own mind, one must seek that Buddha.
Why, then, do you now destroy the Dharma and disperse the Sangha? Wandering idly among the paths of Confucianism, you fail to realize that the environment is identical to the mind.
Seeking the principle of non-obstruction within the True, you instead divide the internal from the external within the Non-dual Dharma.
They distinguish between objects and mind, instructing people to abandon the external and grasp the internal, turning their backs on objects and directing themselves toward the mind.

This causes attachment and aversion to increase and discrimination to become even more extreme. They divide up objects, treating the Pure Land as something external and teaching that one need not seek rebirth there.
They divide up the mind, falsely pointing to the illusory shadows of the six sense-objects and deluded thoughts as being the true mind, claiming that the Pure Land exists [only within them].
Furthermore, he reflects that this mind has no substance and is fundamentally devoid of all dharmas of cause and effect, good and evil, cultivation, or realization.

From this point on, he will arbitrarily and falsely involve himself in worldly conditions, teaching others that they need not prostrate to the Buddha, burn incense, light lamps, recite sutras, or perform repentances and vows, claiming such acts are "attachment to signs.
Yet, regarding the heavens and hells, as well as the lands of bliss and the dust-motes of worlds, although he has heard of them...
Because they do not perceive it, they simply declare it to be non-existent. Conversely, they claim that happiness is heaven and suffering is hell;
how base is their view! The Tathāgata calls them objects of pity, for they do not know that my mind is in truth of the same principle as the Buddha-mind.
The power of Amitābha’s vows, his majestic virtue, and his radiant light abide within my own heart.
By the power of my own deluded mind, all Buddha-works are performed; there is no time when [the Buddhas] do not guide me.
My mind, moreover, within the vow-mind of Amitābha, cultivates all virtuous practices for mindfulness of the Buddha and seeking rebirth.

There is no practice that does not fully contain the Buddha’s virtues. Realizing those Buddha-virtues, one accomplishes my samādhi. Thus, one knows that the power of Amitābha’s vows first gives rise [to awakening].
The mind: ultimately, there is not a single dharma that does not directly course toward my own mind, because my own mind is itself the Buddha-mind.
I, too, from beginningless time until the end of the future, shall cultivate all samādhis;

there is not a single dharma that does not gather back into the ocean of the Buddha, thereby realizing the primordial Buddha, because the Buddha-mind is itself my own mind. Thus, regarding both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind—

Although cause and effect, purity and impurity, are of one and the same mind, they do not actually obstruct one another; each remains distinct within its own category, abiding in its respective position.
Because they are of one mind, although purity and impurity differ, that which is sought does not transcend the true mind. Because they are distinct categories, [they remain as they are].

Although one possesses a single mind, one must necessarily abandon defilement and take up purity. When one abandons defilement and takes up purity, the path of resonance and response intermingles, and one beholds that original nature, Amitābha.
Upon realizing and awakening to this single mind, purity and defilement become naturally distinguished; thus, one can awaken to the Pure Land as being solely of the mind.
Practice in this manner: like a single drop cast into the ocean, it immediately becomes of one taste; only then does one realize that the great ocean is oneself.
How could there be a single practice that is wasted or fails to become merit and virtue?

Even a foolish husband and wife from a village, though they do not understand the principle, because they believe with sincerity that that land exists, attain rebirth there at the time of their death. To fear that existence might fall into emptiness is a grave error.
Such people mistake the shadow of conditions for the mind; because they claim there is no external world, they continue to undergo birth and death despite practicing the path.

Therefore, those who seek rebirth [in the Pure Land] should, with a profound mind, give rise to superior vows and practices—whether by invoking the name or reciting mantras, circumambulating and prostrating, burning incense and scattering flowers, or repenting during the six periods of the day—and exhaustively casting aside worldly attachments to focus their minds single-mindedly.
Contemplating the mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows with an undistracted and unflagging mind, one will, at the end of life, be reborn in that land.

Furthermore, one should practice filial piety toward parents, serve teachers and elders, maintain a compassionate heart and refrain from killing, cultivate the ten wholesome actions, uphold the Three Refuges, and be fully endowed with the various precepts.
One does not violate the rules of dignified conduct; one has deep faith in cause and effect; one does not slander the Mahāyāna;

and one encourages practitioners to cultivate such dharmas, thereby being born there as well. To seek birth in that place in every thought-moment is precisely non-thought, non-seeking, and non-birth. Why is this?

To cultivate this with such intensity is itself non-cultivation; it is not that one does not cultivate that constitutes non-cultivation. Human life is impermanent, shifting from breath to breath into the next world.
Mundane affairs are like a chain of links, a succession of hooks and locks that never ceases.

If, amidst these entangled defilements and when one’s ambitions have run their course and there is nowhere left for the hand to rest, one cannot sever them all at once with a single stroke, then how can one hope to respond by rousing the power of aspiration and exerting every ounce of strength in a single leap? How could such a response ever be achieved?
"Mindfully recollecting that [Pure Land], I now prostrate. I exhort the children of the Buddha: you should practice with single-minded devotion. (From *Direct Pointing to Mindfulness of the Buddha*).

Fanchi’s courtesy name was Chushi; his secular surname was Zhu, and he was a native of Xiangshan in Ningbo. His mother dreamed that the sun fell into her bosom when she gave birth to him.

At the age of nine, he left home to become a monk at Yongzuo Temple; at sixteen, he received full ordination. Relying on Master Jinweng Xun, he studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and attained a realization.

He then traveled to Mount Jing to consult with Master Yuansou Duan, but they did not reach a mutual accord. Subsequently, responding to an imperial summons to transcribe scriptures, he arrived in Yanjing.

Upon hearing the sound of the drum at the Western Tower, he attained a sudden and complete enlightenment. He returned to Mount Jing to visit Yuansou, who subsequently granted him formal certification (*yinke*).
During the Yuan Tai ding era, he went forth to preside over Fuzhen Temple in Haiyan, then moved to Yongzuo.
He served successively at Benjue in Jiaxing and was bestowed the title Chan Master Furi Puzhao Hui bian. He was later transferred to Ba’en Guangxiao, after which he retired to Yongzuo.

He built a dwelling he named Xizhai (Western Studio) and devoted himself single-mindedly to the cultivation of pure karma. While in meditative concentration, he beheld a great lotus flower filling the world, with Amitābha seated within it, surrounded by a multitude of holy beings.
He composed a poem on longing for the Pure Land that was circulated throughout the world. Now, his hundred-line poem is recorded here as follows:
"If you wish to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, And serve the King of Drum-Sound, Join your palms facing westward, And bow your head in prostration."

That direction—the gateway of contemplation—is truly easy to enter; the ritual procedures are indeed immeasurable. The Buddha’s vows are especially profound and vast; the human heart must be steadfast and enduring.
Like an infant longing for its nurse, like a traveler far from home yearning for his native land, one should respectfully welcome the new moon and earnestly bid farewell to the setting sun.
Having clearly received guidance, do not forget it even in a moment of haste. Among all forms of sustenance, the pure meal is supreme; through this practice, one exerts oneself toward cultivation.
This is most excellent. Completely sever the five pungent roots; forever dam the ten evils. Do not seek fame or profit;
do not weary yourself in debating right and wrong. A coarse cloth robe covers this illusory body; wild herbs and millet fill the empty belly. Shake off the debts of many lifetimes;
prop up the leaking bag of the nine apertures. When the spirit is but slightly indolent, joy and anger erupt in chaos. Like water drops suddenly filling a vessel, the river’s current begins—

The source of the stream has overflowed; having accumulated merit and practice until they are full, seize the strength of this physical body. Place a thousand-flower throne within the chamber, burn a hundred kinds of incense in the burner.
Offer new robes for them to wear and prepare exquisite delicacies for them to taste. Do not light torches with leftover oil;

it is better to boil bath-water for the images. Their forms are like earth and wood; their discipline and restraint are like ice and frost. With thoughts free from all delusions, sit in the *paryaṅka* posture.
Upon a single couch, in an instant, one ascends to the Pure Realm. From within the square inch of the heart, a profound light radiates forth.

Flesh and bone are entirely dissolved; heaven and earth become infinitely vast and remote. The Great Void encompasses both the interior and exterior, and the Buddha-field occupies the center. Lotuses unfurl their lush calyxes; ripples surge across the shimmering ponds.
Fresh breezes follow the swaying movements; colorful banners flutter at will. Resplendent is the Golden Hall; its white [walls] stand in alternating rows.

The Jade Hall: its towers are joined with the four treasures, and its terraces are adorned with the seven rarities. Mirror-like surfaces spread across the steps and paving; lotus hearts form the inner chambers.
Coral is carved into the railings, and agate is fashioned into the beams. The ground is laid out in lapis lazuli, and the gardens are draped in brocade.
Within, exquisite carpets are spread; without, silver walls encircle it all. Above, there is a latticed net; below, the floor is level without any protrusions.

On Mount Wugang, jade groves stretch out everywhere; Gems-like trees stand in orderly rows. The fruits are large and as dense as clusters of gems; Their sounds are pure and wondrous, like the music of reed pipes.
Tall branches naturally face one another; Lush green leaves stand precisely opposite. Every single tree resounds with the song of a parrot; Pairs of phoenixes gather upon them.

In the Jasper Pond there is no distinction between day and night; The jeweled waters naturally harmonize in the *gong* and *shang* scales. The channels are bright with golden sand at their base; The breeze is light over the treasures.
Along the banks, lotuses in full bloom spread across the high and low ground; mandarin ducks play in waters deep and shallow. Their extraordinary colors swallow the flocks of common birds;

their rare blossoms eclipse the multitude of fragrances. A thousand branches divide into crimson and white; ten thousand clusters intermingle green and yellow. For a moment, one draws in the refreshing scent that cools the body’s faculties;

subtly, it opens the nostrils to a sense of coolness. The *piṅgala* bird dances before them, while the *saṃjīva* bird soars behind. All day long the orioles tune their throats; the cranes ascend toward the heavens.
Stretching out his neck, he realized that how could there be a self? He knew that all suffering is impermanent. The Great Being expounded the ultimate principle;

the Śrāvakas gathered at the Jewel Monastery. The Sūtras proclaimed the twelve divisions; the verses unfolded in hundreds of thousands of chapters. Directly pointing to the path of Bodhi, they all floated upon the raft of Prajñā.
He turned back the seeker of the sword and awakened the madman who had lost his head. The nine grades distinguish the coarse from the subtle; the three vehicles interact...
Elevating and suppressing; refined to the depths, all dross is finally severed. Winnowed clean, how could chaff remain? He manifests as the true Maitreya; he consults and studies with Mañjuśrī.
Holy sages gather like dense clouds; celestial music resounds daily. A magnificent and pure youth, his manner is free from the affectations of a maiden.
His speech is skillful in question and answer; his comings and goings are graceful in every step. Like fire-jade, his radiance flows constantly; like a *maṇi* jewel, it ever increases.
His radiant brilliance does not require the hanging of sun or moon; where could boundaries or frontiers limit him? His food is celestial delicacies, and his meal is not of worldly rice or grain.

A *cintāmaṇi* robe hangs from his shoulders, and he holds a bowl of naturally occurring nectar. His entire being is exceptionally pure, and as it contains the radiance of the sun, it shines even more brilliantly.

The *kāṣāya* robes enshroud auspicious mists, while necklaces provide a foundation for his immortal garments. He travels everywhere through lands as numerous as motes of dust, wandering throughout the [ten] directions.
At the site of enlightenment, I beheld his compassionate countenance with reverence; bearing offerings to sustain him, I listened closely to the teachings of the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni).

Yet, even what was attained has been made to vanish. Returning in the mere blink of an eye, I now laugh at my former frantic pursuit of worldly paths. May I always enjoy the bliss of walking meditation; who would say that sitting or lying down hinders it?
May conflict be removed from all under heaven, and may calamities be stilled across the earth. May its majestic spirit pervade the south and north, and its virtue spread to the east and west.

The manifestation of transformation endures; though several times the kalpas of fire have scorched the earth and the four seas have turned to fields of grain, this realm suffers no loss, and these people merely enjoy increasing longevity.
No longer are householders’ names registered for conscription, nor are their ages scrutinized for service. Their ears hear nothing but the Dharma, and they need no grain to satisfy their hunger.

Forever cherishing this grace, it enters their very marrow; at least they are spared from the invasion of poison upon their sores. If one were to describe the sufferings of this Sahā world, who could restrain their tears?

Tears flow profusely. Who among the inner circle of disciples can understand this? Your false views are truly lamentable; you endure being bound by greed and anger, willingly casting yourselves into the pit of profit and desire.

Thieves dwell within the same village, yet their spears strike at one another inside the very house. You may have money enough to fill your rooms, yet you still long for rice to overflow your granaries.

You hunt pheasants and rabbits in the mountains and herd oxen and sheep in the wilds. This will result in the retribution of having your life taken in another birth, as you carry your grievances through successive lifetimes.

In this world, one repays debts; in times of peace, one encounters bandits; amidst disorder, one meets swords and spears. One who loves drink becomes addicted to wine; one whose passions are deluded becomes infatuated with courtesans.
The mind-monkey abandons its tethering rope; the horse of the will is let loose from its halter. Noble ambitions are crushed midway; heroic souls depart for the Northern Mounds.
As weapons of war eliminate rites and music, the courtesy of Yao and Tang has vanished. Battles and conquests bring sorrow to the borders, and the smoke of alarms reaches far and wide.
Above, the azure heavens look down as entire villages suffer slaughter; bleached bones fill the city moats. The wailing of ghosts is heard amidst the dark rains;

men mourn for the fallen heroes of the state. The harvest is poor and many die of hunger; coffins are precious and few can be buried. Broken tiles and rubble heap upon the monasteries; thorns and brambles overgrow the schools of learning.
Military levies and taxes alike press hard; the grain fields yield less than in times of plenty. The conditions for reciting the Buddha’s name remain obstructed; the quest for the scriptures...
It is likewise desolate. Your simple breast is like a dragon leaping forth; your lofty stride is like a crane soaring aloft. Look back upon your companions as a flock of geese;

do not be like a solitary jumping deer. I have already perfected the holy embryo; you, my Dharma-fellows, gaze toward one another. Together we are elegant upon the jeweled ground; together we soar high upon the golden terrace.

Our diligent aspirations rise like towering peaks; our accumulated virtues are vast as the ocean. Through kalpas of eternity, merit has become ever more manifest; yet even the slightest transgression—

He immediately performed rites of expiation. With a threefold resolve, he looked toward the distant goal; with ten recitations, he prepared for the long journey. Determined to transcend the realm of Māra, from this day forth he would serve the Buddha-King.
In the first year of the Hongwu era, an imperial edict summoned him to the capital, where he preached the Dharma at Jiangshan. Soon thereafter, he was summoned once more.

In the autumn of the third year, the Emperor issued an edict inquiring about the nature of ghosts and spirits; Zongqi resided at Tienjie Monastery and others, where they compiled a treatise based on the sūtras and śāstras.
Just as he was about to enter the palace to present his memorial, he suddenly manifested a slight illness. After four days had passed, he bathed, changed his robes, and wrote a verse, saying:
"The true nature is perfectly luminous; fundamentally, it is without birth or extinction. A wooden horse neighs in the night; the sun rises in the west.

He then summoned the monk Mengtang E and said to him, "I am going. E asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "To the West. E said, "There is a Buddha in the West, but there is no Buddha in the East."
The Buddha appeared as a phantom; Qi let out a single stern shout and it vanished. He was seventy-five years old.
When his body was cremated, his teeth, tongue, and prayer beads remained unharmed (*Fahualu*, "Western Chamber Pure Land Poems").

Ke-shou (可授) was a man whose given name was Wu-zhi (無旨) and whose family name was Li. A native of Linhai in Taizhou, he entered the monastic life at the age of twelve and received full ordination at nineteen.
He devoted himself to profound investigation and study until he met Master Pu-jue Ming at Lingyin Monastery; during their brief exchange of questions and answers—
His doubts were suddenly dispelled. During the Zhizhi era of the Yuan dynasty, he went forth to preside over Ansheng Temple on Mount Daxiong.
After five years, he was transferred to Long’en; another two years later, to Zhenru. The following year, the Xuanzheng Yuan selected him to preside over Longhua.

He built Xiuan (the "Hermitage of Rest") in the western valley and daily cultivated the *nienfo sanmei* (Buddha-remembrance samādhi). In the sixth year of the Hongwu era of the Ming dynasty, he was again summoned to preside over Jingci Temple in Hangzhou.
He resided at Cisi for two years. Suddenly, he assembled the community to proclaim the precepts of diligent progress (*vīrya*). He personally struck the drum and then withdrew.

Manifesting a slight illness, he sat upright facing west and said, "I am about to depart. His attendants requested that he write a verse of farewell, but he waved them away, saying, "Our school is fundamentally without words or explanations.
He then joined his palms and recited the Buddha’s name; the sound gradually grew faint until he passed into stillness. (From the *Fahualu*)

Huiri (Wisdom Sun), whose courtesy name was Dongming and whose secular surname was Jia, was a native of Chicheng in Taizhou. He entered the monastic life at an early age at Guangyan Temple in his home county and studied the teachings under Baziting.
Having traveled to Upper Zhushan, he relied upon Zhantang of Zhuwu and subsequently emerged as the abbot of Wusong.
At Mount Shengshui Temple, in the fourth year of the Yuan Zhizheng era, the Lower Tianzhu Monastery suffered a disaster.

Daying responded to the requests of the multitude and renovated it anew. Once the temple was completed, he moved to Upper Tianzhu. Emperor Shundi specially bestowed upon him the title "Compassionate Light, Wondrous Response, Universal Salvation.

At the beginning of the Ming Hongwu era, he was summoned to the capital; by imperial decree, he established the founding of Tianjie Monastery and restored the ancient ruins of Waguan Monastery. Furthermore, he was ordered...

He presided over the recitation of the precepts at Zhongshan. Thereupon, he took his leave and returned to Shangzhu, where he resigned from his monastic duties and practiced the Amitābha repentance ritual.
On the first day of the seventh month in the twelfth year, he said to his disciples: "In my dream, blue lotuses grew from a square pond; their pure fragrance permeated all who encountered it."

The auspicious signs of the Pure Land were manifest. Four days later, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture with palms joined. He was eighty-nine years old (*Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Ming Dynasty*).

Puzhi (普智), whose courtesy name was Wuai (無礙) and whose secular surname was Chu (褚), was a native of Hangzhou.

He entered the monastic order at Longjing Temple and studied under Master Rimeng (日蒙) of Dongming, receiving the teachings on the inherent nature (*xingju*) of the Tiantai school. His expositions were unimpeded, and he presided over four monasteries, causing his spiritual influence to flourish greatly.

In his later years, he taught and expounded the Dharma at Yanqing Temple in Songjiang, where he eventually spent the remainder of his life. He devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land, remaining undeterred by cold or heat.

He ceased [his activities]. On the second day of the first month in the sixth year of the Yongle era, he fell slightly ill. He assembled the congregation and, sitting upright facing west, passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name.
He once annotated the *Amitābha Sūtra* in one fascicle (as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Ming*).

Jinglong, whose courtesy name was Zuting and style name Konggu, was the son of the Chen family of Suzhou. From childhood, he abstained from meat and enjoyed sitting in meditation as if in a state of *dhyāna*.
Upon reaching a slight maturity, he followed Master Lanyun of Mount Bian to inquire into the Great Dharma. At the age of two...
18. He left home at Mount Huqiu. During the Hongxi era, he was granted official documents to become a monk.

He relied upon Master Shigan at Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou, and subsequently went to Mount Tianmu, where he studied with great diligence. Suddenly, he attained realization and hurried to visit Lanyun, who then granted him formal approval (*inka*).
Having upheld the supreme teaching, Longyun also exhorted others toward the practice of Pure Land; he composed one volume of *Pure Land Poems*.
Chapter One Hundred Eight. Someone asked about the meaning of the "Fourfold Simplification" (Sì Liǎojiǎn) of the Yongming era. He replied:

"A practitioner of Chan who clings to the *huatou* (critical phrase), claiming it is his own practice of maintaining stillness and that there is nothing else to do, will not engage in the rebirth through reciting the Buddha’s name (*nianfo wangsheng*) or in morning and evening liturgical services.
This is what is meant by 'having Chan but no Pure Land. Such a form of Chan practice is also not of the correct spirit."

This is what is meant by "guarding the dead phrase" (huatou). It is no different from earth, wood, tiles, or stones; those who sit in this manner fall ill in eight or nine cases out of ten, and none can save them.
One who has truly grasped the essence of Chan is like a gourd upon the water: it turns as soon as it is pressed down, remaining lively and agile.

Practicing Chan in this way does not disparage the path of reciting the Buddha’s name for rebirth in the Pure Land; performing liturgical recitations at dawn and dusk is likewise that which one should follow.
Whether walking left or right, there is nothing that is not the Way. This is what is meant by "having both Chan and the Pure Land. It is further said:
The single gate of Buddha-recitation (*nien-fo*) is a swift path for cultivation. One must discern that this body is unreal and that the world is illusory;

only the Pure Land is where one can return, and only Buddha-recitation is what one can rely upon. Whether reciting with urgency or slowness, in a loud or low voice, there are no constraints whatsoever. It is simply...
Render body and mind tranquil and serene. Recite silently without forgetting. Whether in stillness or clamor, leisure or haste, let it be one and not two.

Suddenly, upon encountering a situation or circumstance, strike the single phrase that turns the body; only then will you know that the Land of Peaceful Light is not separate from this very place, and that Amitābha Buddha does not transcend one's own mind.
However, if you seek awakening with a calculating mind, it will instead become an obstacle. Simply rely on faith.
The mind is the root. Do not follow any distracting thoughts whatsoever.

If you practice in this manner, even if you do not attain awakening during your lifetime, after death you will still be reborn in the Pure Land, where you will progress through successive stages of cultivation without ever falling back.
Master Yudam had people call out, "Who is it that recites the Buddha’s name? Some replied, "That which is my original nature is Amitābha. This is called "gathering" (shō).
"Mindfully reciting the Buddha's name" and "investigating through reciting the Buddha's name"—these methods need not be employed now; simply continue with ordinary recitation.

When Master Long was over fifty years old, he composed his own funerary inscription (taming). There is no record of when he passed away. At that time there was also Master Qin, whose courtesy name was Guyin.
He was the son of the Cai family of Fujian. He once composed a verse titled "An Exhortation to Mindful Recitation of the Buddha," which begins: "A single phrase of A..."
"Amitābha Buddha. This is the primary koan of the Chan school. It is like riding a horse while holding a staff; it is a complete segment of a secure livelihood.

Regardless of whether one belongs to the four classes of practitioners, whoever maintains this will find it efficacious. Amidst walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, do not let this single phrase "Amitābha" be interrupted.
You must believe that when the cause is deep, the fruit is deep. Directly cause the non-recitation to become self-recitation. If you are able to recite...
Contemplate non-emptiness; ensure that your contemplation becomes a single, unified whole. While contemplating, recognize the one who contemplates; Amitābha and you will appear together.

You will then enter the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation and personally realize the Inner Court of Sukhāvatī. Those who have perfected this practice will see their own names inscribed upon the lotus womb.
They will personally behold Amitābha bestow upon them a prophecy of enlightenment, and from then on, they shall become companions to the Bodhisattvas. From this point forward, they depart.

Departing from this Sahā world, there is a single path entirely free of sorrow and affliction that leads directly to unsurpassed Bodhi. For eternal kalpas, one may roam at ease according to one's heart;
having returned by relying upon this Way, one will certainly attain Buddhahood without deficiency. (From the *Míngsēng Jílüè*, *Kōnggǔ jí*)
Baobao (Precious Jewel) was of unknown origin. He once traveled between Hangzhou and Jiaxing in Zhejiang province, wearing a single robe through both winter and summer.
He sustained himself by begging for food and had no fixed dwelling. He never ceased reciting the Buddha’s name, responding to those who spoke with him with only a word or two.
He immediately recited the Buddha’s name continuously. Later, at Haimen Temple, he suddenly became like one who had gone mad for about half a month.
A monk scolded him, saying, "In your daily practice, you should serve as a model for the world;
how can you act like this? Zhuzhu replied, "It is so. I am going. After requesting a bath, he passed away peacefully (from the *Wangsheng ji*).
Benming, Benming.
His origins are not clearly known. He resided at Jingjia Temple in Tongzhou, where his religious practice was pure and he was diligent in his lecturing on the scriptures.

Later, he ceased his lectures and devoted himself exclusively to the Pure Land, performing the six-period rites of worship and recitation without fail for many years. Suddenly, he fell slightly ill. From [himself]...
Knowing that the time had come, he calmly informed the assembly and passed away. A rare fragrance lingered for seven days (*Wangsheng ji*).
Yi Xiu, whose courtesy name was also Yi Xiu, was a native of Wenli. At the beginning of the Jiajing era, he resided at Zantan Hermitage in Pu. Daily, he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha.

The sound of over one hundred thousand voices continued day and night without interruption for more than fifty years. At the place where [Dao]xiu practiced walking meditation, the brick-paved ground had become hollowed out.
When people attempted to fill it, after some time it would return to being hollow as before. Initially, there was a poor man who could not support himself; he came to rely on Daoxiu, who took him in.
After a long while, [the man] proved to be ill-suited to his duties, so Daoxiu rebuked him, saying, "You are truly a thief. Not long after, [the man] disappeared.
Guo led his faction and attacked Xiu under the cover of night. At the first assault, Xiu’s chanting of the Buddha’s name was still loud;

at the second assault, the chanting of the Buddha’s name did not cease, though it had become faint. When his breath failed, the sound of the Buddha’s name finally fell silent (from the *Collected Works of Elder Master Zibo*).
Xue Mei, Xue Mei.
A native of Suzhou, his traces were extraordinary and he did not adhere to the monastic precepts. He was fond of composing poetry.

During the Jiajing era, he traveled to Nanjing and stayed at Ba’en Temple. Whenever he saw a Dharma Master preaching the sutras, he would invariably laugh and say, "Nonsense, nonsense! He specialized in...

He practiced the cultivation of the Pure Land with uninterrupted diligence, both in motion and stillness. He soon recovered his health and resided at Zhutang Temple. When he was over eighty years old, he suddenly took leave of the assembly and set a date for his departure.
The monks used their funds to prepare his funerary shrine. On the appointed day, those who came to see him off gathered like clouds.
Mei Xiao said, "You lot have only contributed a few coins as offerings, yet you already wish to take away this old monk’s life. It is still too early, it is still too early. The assembly...
They dispersed in dejection. Several days later, he sat upright within his shrine and passed away in stillness (*Xuemei Jilüe*). His name was Xingzhuan (專), with the style name Shou’an (守庵).
He was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Kunshan in Suzhou. Having shaved his head in youth, he traveled extensively to seek out realized masters. He paid his respects to...
Miaofeng received the precepts and attended the lecture series on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Later, he took his leave and went to the mountain peak to practice the *dhūta* austerities.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, he recited only the *Lotus Sūtra* and practiced profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Once, while in the air, he beheld a jeweled pond in the west that had turned the color of lapis lazuli, vast and deep beyond measure. He reported this to Miaofeng, who said, "This is merely the beginning of your contemplative practice."

As for the signs of its completion: he did not give rise to attachment. This was a virtuous omen. Zhuan kept it strictly secret and did not speak of it. In Shicheng, there was a Maitreya statue one hundred feet high;
during the Jiajing era, it had been stripped of its gilding due to military conflict. Zhuan restored it anew and constructed a stone hall to match the scale of the image.
He was moved by the Buddha’s emission of light, which illuminated the night as brightly as day. In the autumn of the twenty-third year, he invited the Dharma Master.
While Chuan-deng was lecturing on the *Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, there was one who lectured on the *Sūtra on Maitreya’s Ascent to Tuṣita* and insisted, "It is not so.
I have heard that Amitābha and Maitreya are one body and one wisdom; their powers and fearlessnesses are likewise identical.

He continued, "I shall cause the assembly of the sea to realize together that the Amitābha of one's own nature is none other than the Maitreya of one's own nature, so that they may first travel to the Pure Land of Lotus-Bloom."

Thereafter, he was to participate in the pre-assembly for the Dragon Flower (Nāgapuṣpa) festival. On the middle winter month of the twenty-fifth year, having bathed and changed his robes, he commanded the assembly to strike the bell and recite the sutras.
He then sat in the lotus position and passed away. A few days prior, a single miraculous *lingzhi* fungus had grown from the folds of his robe;
it was as large as a fist and red-and-white in color (a testament to the efficacy of upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*).
Zuxiang, whose secular surname was Zuxiang, was a native of Xinyu on the banks of the Yangtze River. He cultivated the Pure Land practices with great diligence at Longtan Temple in Shandong.
A layman named Wang Jie built a hermitage and invited him to stay; Xiang told Jie that he would return home on a certain day, though the assembly earnestly tried to detain him. Xiang—
It is said that he returned to the home of An-yang. When the appointed time arrived, he arranged his seat facing west and passed away.
His coffin was carried into the mountains, where fire spontaneously emerged and consumed it (from the *Wangsheng ji*).

Yuan Guo Yuan Guo (圓果圓果). His style name was Qiyuan (祇園). One character, Huan Kong (幻空). It is unclear from where he originated. In his youth, he served as a Commandant (指揮使) for the Imperial Tombs in Fengyang.
He subsequently resigned his office and entered the monastic life on Mount Wutai. He was profoundly versed in the sutras and treatises, attaining sudden enlightenment directly.
Finger. He traveled east to Su and Hangzhou, where he ascended the Dharma seat to preach the Dharma; heavenly flowers fell during the day, falling profusely like rain.
In the thirty-fourth year of the Jiajing era, the Japanese incursions in Zhejiang reached Beixin Pass. At that time, Zhixu was at Fohui Temple in Hangzhou.
Hearing that Zhixu’s Way was sublime, the Provincial Commander-in-Chief Hu Zongxian invited him out of the mountains to consult on strategies for repelling the rebels. Zhixu...

He spoke, saying: "There is no need for concern; after three days, the rebels shall withdraw of their own accord. Three days later, the soldiers saw thousands of divine spirits within the clouds striking the Japanese.
The Japanese retreated and fled in disarray, and all took it to be the result of his spiritual power. On the day he passed away:

He instructed his disciples that he should be cremated ten years later. When the appointed time arrived, they carried his coffin to the wilderness. Suddenly, it spontaneously burst into flames, leaving no ash or residue behind.
Among the thousand monastics and laypeople who witnessed this, all beheld the manifestation of the Western Realm within the clouds:
sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, sevenfold rows of trees, jeweled ponds, ground of golden sand, and palatial towers.
The halls were all adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, *śukti*, ruby, and agate. From within the ponds, blue, yellow, red, and white lotuses blossomed.
White cranes, peacocks, parrots, *śārikas*, *kalaviṅkas*, and *saṃjīva* birds of various wondrous kinds were present, no different from those described in the Buddhist sūtras. After a short while—
Celestial music resounded through the sky and only subsided after some time.
Zhenqing Zixian, whose secular surname was Luo, was a native of Xiangtan in Changsha. From his youth, he possessed a memory far superior to that of ordinary men; at the age of fifteen—

He completed his monastic training. At nineteen, he encountered a family tragedy and subsequently retired to Fuhu Rock on Mount Nanyue. There, he relied upon Master Baizhu to shave his head and receive full ordination.

He took up the "Mu" (No-Character) koan for contemplation; while his boat was touching the shore, he attained a realization. After Master Baizhu passed away, Qing stayed at Juehuang Temple, where he suffered from a back ailment.
In a dream, Guan Yunchang bestowed medicine upon him, and his illness was cured. He then traveled south to Tiantai to establish [a retreat].
He lived in a thatched hut. He moved to the Tianzhu Peak of Huading Mountain and practiced the Great and Small Amitābha Repentances for six years.

In his leisure time, he expounded upon the Ten Vehicles and elucidated the Three Contemplations. Students flocked to him by the day, and at the request of the layman Wang Taichu, he accepted their invitation.
He retired to the Yongming Meditation Hall and lectured on the *Miaozongchao* (The Sublime Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra) for one hundred days.

He habitually practiced the five repentances with diligence and secretly recited the *Contemplation Sutra* and the "Mind-Ground" chapter of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. One night, he dreamed of a magnificent palace of eternal purity, where jeweled trees grew in intricate patterns.

He beheld Amitābha Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta. While he was in the midst of prostrating himself, a novice monk appeared by his side and handed him a tablet inscribed with the words:
"Perfumed by the cultivation of the fragrance of the precepts; awakening, one knows this as the sign of rebirth in the Middle Grade.
In the first month of the thirty-first year of the Wanli era, he fell ill. He disposed of all his accumulated possessions, entrusting them to Wutai, Yunqi, and Xixing.

When various monasteries offered him a meal for the assembly of monks, he declined it, saying: "The conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have matured, and the sacred realm has manifested before me in secret.
Before long I shall depart this life; what would be the use of [this food]? On the seventh day of the first month, he ceased eating grain, consuming only sandalwood-scented water.
He announced that he would pass away on the twenty-ninth day and preached the Dharma of non-arising to the assembly with great earnestness.
On the night of the twenty-ninth, he rose and addressed the assembly, saying, "I am departing. The assembly entreated him, saying, "Venerable Master, may you be reborn in the Pure Land."

"Where among the nine grades does he dwell? They replied, "He is born in the middle grade of the middle level. The assembly asked, "Why was he not born in the upper grade? He said, "I have been perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts;
my station stops at the middle grade. Having finished speaking, he passed away peacefully. Five days later, his complexion remained rosy and moist as if he were alive.
On the day of his cremation, a fragrant aroma filled the air, and his bones made a tinkling sound. He was fifty-seven years old. (From the *Ming*)
From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*:

Mingzheng’s courtesy name was Wuchén; his secular surname was Wei. He was a native of Kuaiji. By nature he was upright, simple, and taciturn. From his youth, he took no pleasure in meat or pungent flavors.

He had always desired to leave the household life. When he was in his early twenties, he visited a neighboring temple and encountered an elderly monk with thick eyebrows on Mount Wutai, who appeared to him as an old acquaintance.
The monk expressed a wish for them to rely upon one another, with the elder acting as his disciple. The old monk said, "Three years from now, you may have your hair shaved;

first, you must practice asceticism and study the various scriptures. Having received this instruction, he went to a monastic community to perform heavy labor and studied the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* every day.
He recited only a single character. At night, he prostrated before Avalokiteśvara, remaining awake until dawn. After three years, his recitation of the dhāraṇī was finally completed.

Suddenly, he fell ill for seven days, with pain erupting throughout his entire body as if his bones were being replaced. When the illness subsided, his innate wisdom suddenly opened up, and the monk from Mount Wutai arrived once more.
He shaved his head and received full ordination, being instructed to recite the Lotus Sūtra for the rest of his life; thereupon, he unfurled the scripture.
He recited them without hesitation. Subsequently, he mastered the *Avataṃsaka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras by heart.
He then said to the old monk, "I wish to spend the remainder of my life begging for food as an offering to repay the virtue of my teacher. That night, the old monk did not know where he had gone.
He had realized the daily recitation of one *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. He took only two meals a day; apart from his three robes, a sūtra, and an alms bowl, he possessed nothing else.
When people offered him gifts, he would accept them and immediately give them away. Even when speaking with others, he would merely smile. He remained thus for thirty years.
One day, while reciting the sūtra, he appeared sullen and displeased. When his disciples asked the reason, he said: "I have maintained this recitation for one..."
Born with the aspiration to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, how could he possibly fall back into the dust of the mundane world? Thereupon, he redoubled his diligent recitation for three years.
One day, he struck the desk and laughed aloud, saying, "I shall not go to the dust of the mundane world now. He then went to visit Master Yunqi Hong.
He returned to the mountain stream and said to his attendant, "Go and inform the assembly that I shall depart tomorrow.
The next day, when the disciples arrived, they asked, "At what time [will he leave]? He replied, "At noon. Thereupon, he ordered them to prepare hot water for him to bathe.

Sitting upright and reciting the name of the Buddha, he chanted the names of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta until reaching the words "Great Purity," at which point he closed his mouth. The assembly heard [voices] from the air.
As he chanted the names of the ocean-like assembly of Bodhisattvas, a rare fragrance wafted forth; with palms joined, he passed away in stillness as if entering meditative absorption.
Seven days later, when the coffin was opened, it was a time of intense heat, yet his countenance remained as if alive. He was fifty years of age;
this was the twenty-first year of the Wanli era. His disciple, Zhending, styled Jingming, followed his teacher’s instructions after ordaining and applied himself with diligent mindfulness.

The Buddha [Foyan] sought rebirth in the Pure Land while simultaneously prostrating before various sutras such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. He commissioned the creation of Buddhist images, provided offerings for the Sangha, and practiced various ascetic disciplines.
At the age of seventy-two, he set a specific date in advance and passed away facing west while reciting the name of the Buddha (from the *Lian'an Si Ji*).

Mingyu, whose courtesy name was Wuxia, was surnamed Liu and was a native of Western Shu. After entering the monastic order, she traveled extensively across famous mountains to seek instruction from spiritual teachers.

Her ascetic practices were peerless; she performed prostrations before the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, bowing once for each character. This was in the twenty-third year of the Wanli era.
In the first month of that year, he suddenly said to his disciples, "I have been bound by my karma in this Sahā world for seventy-two years;

now I am about to return. Thereupon, he ceased eating. For ten days he recited the Buddha’s name without interruption, his voice sounding like a great bell. As his end approached, he bathed and sat upright;

holding his prayer beads, he recited the Buddha’s name with increasing urgency and sorrow. After a while, he cried out in a loud voice, "Buddha! Buddha! Buddha! and then, "I shall drive the iron ox backward."
He returned to the Buddha-land, his voice ceasing as he passed away (*Han-shan Meng-you Ji*).

Fa-xiang, whose courtesy name was Rui-guang, was surnamed Zhou and was a native of Sheng County in Shaoxing. From a young age, he possessed the aspiration for world-transcendence and studied under Xiao Yan.

The Elder Ruo Yan instructed him in the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation (nianfo), whereupon he left the household life. He resided at Side Peak on the side of Mount Nanyue, his shadow never leaving the mountain as he dedicated himself solely to the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
He kept count of his recitations using beans, practicing with such diligence day and night that his ribs never touched his mat.

People called him "Bean-Child Buddha" (Dou'er Fo). Before long, a monastic community was established there. On the sixth day of the second month in the thirty-eighth year of the Wanli era, he passed away.

He requested a bath and paid homage to the Buddha, then addressed the assembly, saying, "The melon seeds have ripened. At the very moment the stalks were falling, none of the assembly could understand his meaning.

He entered his room and sat in the lotus posture, instructing the assembly to chant the names of the Buddhas; with palms joined, he passed away. Before the mountain peak, the sound of music was heard.
(From the *Ham-shan Meng-you Ji*)

Zhu Hong, whose courtesy name was Fohui and pen-name Lianchi, was the son of the Shen family of Renhe, Hangzhou. At the age of seventeen, he passed the examination for the status of a *zhusheng* (local scholar), becoming renowned for his learning and conduct.
A neighboring elderly woman was reciting the Buddha’s name several thousand times daily; when [Zhu Hong] asked her the reason for this, the woman—
He said, "My late husband recited the Buddha’s name; at the time of his death, he was free from illness and bid farewell to others with a single bow.
Thus, one knows that the merit of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) is inconceivable. From this point on, Hong settled his mind upon the Pure Land.

He wrote the four characters "The Matter of Life and Death is Great" (*shēngsī shì dà*) upon his desk to exhort himself. At the age of thirty-two, he left the household life and visited the great masters Bianrong and Xiaoyan.

He asked, "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? Upon this, he attained awakening. In the fifth year of the Longqing era, he went to Yunqi to beg for alms; seeing that the mountains and waters were secluded and sublime, he took up residence there.

As the mountain was naturally infested with tigers, he performed the *yoga-agnikula* (the fire-offering ritual) for them, and the tigers ceased to cause him harm. During a severe drought that year, [he prayed for rain].
The residents prayed for rain. He said, "I know only to recite the Buddha’s name; I have no other skill.

When the crowd pressed him earnestly, he took up his wooden fish and went out, walking along the ridges of the fields while chanting the Buddha’s name. Rain poured down immediately, following wherever his feet reached.

The people were delighted and together gathered materials to build a hall. Monastics flocked there daily, and it eventually became a great monastic center (conglin). Hongzhu advocated the Pure Land school.

He vehemently denounced the "mad Chan" (kōzen) and authored the *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* (*Amidakyō soshō*). This work harmonizes principle and phenomena and encompasses the three capacities [of practitioners], reaching a depth of profound subtlety.
At that time, there was one named Sō Ruzen who sent a letter to Yunqi, stating briefly:
"The Buddha Śākyamuni possesses the teachings of the Three Piṭakas and the Twelve Divisions of the Canon; these are what are called 'casting many nets across the vast ocean' and 'the great granary.'"
Regarding small granaries, one should simply discuss the great to encompass the small; how can one raise up a single instance and thereby discard the many?
Among our own school, there are those who advocate that becoming a sage over successive kalpas must necessarily be gradual and not sudden.

Now, the "gradual" is also a teaching of the Sages and has never been incorrect; yet to discard the sudden for the sake of the gradual is erroneous. The Venerable One secretly harbors the sudden and perfect within, while outwardly...
It is manifest that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land exists; all Buddhas have it, so there is no room for doubt.

Yet, as for the audiences of recent times, they wish to discard the fifteen princes entirely on account of the single sage Amitābha, and to discard the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon entirely on account of a single Pure Land sutra.
This is something I, your humble servant, do not wish to hear. Although this is an age of the Final Dharma, such...
Regarding the faculties of people, how could they not vary in sharpness or dullness? As it is said, when the World-Honored One taught Kāśyapa and Kauṇḍinya, his discourse was such;
yet when he taught Sudhana and the Dragon Girl, his discourse was otherwise. Thus, twenty-five sages each realized their own perfect penetration.
What Mañjuśrī described is just like that: what was called "fixed" yesterday is not fixed today;
furthermore, what was called "I am empty" is not actually empty, and what was called "I am existent" is not actually existent.
This is why it is the skillful master of impermanence, lively and vibrant, like a gourd floating upon water. Were one instead to stake a post and guard a den, [one would be lost].

How beneficial this would be for humans and devas! It is our wish that the Venerable One, for the sake of the great assembly, provide a broad and pure teaching; that you, encountering those of sharp faculties, point toward the Supreme Vehicle;

that you be perfectly integrated and thoroughly penetrating, without being hindered by partiality or sectarianism; and that you enable both the great Peng bird and the small sparrow to find their own proper place—would this not be utterly good and utterly beautiful?
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the unsurpassed, perfect teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the ultimate discourse of the Tathāgata’s realization of his own nature (*dharmatā*).

To place it on an equal footing with the *Amitābha Sūtra* already seems somewhat inappropriate; thus, some have composed treatises to elevate it, even attempting to position the Pure Land school above the *Avataṃsaka*.
How can one allow the colors of red and purple to be so confused? I also pray that the Venerable One will [consider this].
To those whose spiritual capacity is suited to the Pure Land, one speaks of the Pure Land; to those whose capacity is suited to the Avataṃsaka, one speaks of the Avataṃsaka.

Do not mock one another, nor do let them become confused with one another. This is how the Buddha-vehicle is propagated, and this is how the five teachings are presented side by side so that all three capacities are fully encompassed.
Alas, why must one seek a sword by marking the spot on a boat, or drive away a hawk merely to catch a sparrow? In his reply, Hong wrote: "Now, as for the Avataṃsaka..."
The *Yanjù wúliàng mén* (The Gate of Immeasurable Adornments) is but one gate among the immeasurable gates of the *Huáyán*.

It is according to the capacities of beings at this particular time that they enter the *Huáyán* through this single gate; it is certainly not the case that by citing this one gate, the *Huáyán* as a whole is discarded.
Your letter suggests that because I have placed Amitābha and the *Huáyán* on equal footing, you consequently harbor a misconception.
Regarding the claim that this treatise supersedes the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: who composed this treatise? The *Avataṃsaka* is like a celestial sovereign;
who could possibly place feudal lords, kings, great ministers, or officials above a celestial sovereign? Nevertheless, even I, an unworthy person, have never made such a comparison.
In my commentaries (*shu* and *chao*), I specifically state that while the *Avataṃsaka* represents the ultimate perfection, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* attains that same perfection.
This is but a small portion; it is a member and derivative of the *Avataṃsaka*, not its equal.

Furthermore, your letter suggests that one should preach the teachings according to the capacity of the listener—that those suited for the Pure Land should be taught the Pure Land, and those suited for the *Avataṃsaka* should be taught the *Avataṃsaka*.

This intention is indeed excellent. However, there are two points herein: first, that the simultaneous cultivation of a thousand capacities is the very purpose of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world; it is not...
Each is according to what is capable. Thus, while Caoxi was dedicated exclusively to the Chan of direct pointing, was he not conversant with other teachings?
Huiyuan presided over the community at Donglin; did he not also receive those of duller faculties?

As for Yunmen, Fayan, Caodong, Guiyang, and Linji—though these five schools share a single origin, their lineages of transmission differ slightly, as do their pedagogical methods and doctrinal arrangements. Regarding the principle...
This is naturally so; there is nothing strange about it. How much more so for an unworthy, ordinary person like myself!

If one recklessly imitates the ancients—claiming that what was fixed yesterday is not fixed today—and acts without any lineage of transmission, resulting in inconsistent and chaotic changes, this is called "benefiting others" in name, but in reality, it is "misleading others.
Why is this? I am the Dharma King, sovereign over the Dharma; among commoners, such a title is called "King."
One must not fail to be cautious regarding these two points. To speak of the *Avataṃsaka* is to encompass the Pure Land; to speak of the Pure Land is likewise to penetrate the *Avataṃsaka*.
Therefore, those who speak of the *Avataṃsaka* do so as the *Avataṃsaka*, and those who speak of the Pure Land do so as the Pure Land;

they proceed in tandem without contradiction. People today know only that the *Avataṃsaka* is more expansive than the Land of Ultimate Bliss, yet they do not realize that [the latter]... [is also vast].
"Dha" (Dhā) is precisely "Vairocana. Furthermore, Nāgārjuna retrieved the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* from the Dragon Palace, yet he vowed to be reborn in Sukhāvatī.
Samantabhadra is the eldest son of the *Avataṃsaka*, yet he vowed to be reborn in Sukhāvatī. Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra together assist Vairocana;
they are known as the Three Sages of the *Avataṃsaka*, yet they all vowed to be reborn in Sukhāvatī. There is clear evidence for all of this, as manifest and bright as the sun and stars.
That you, Layman, intend to propagate the *Avataṃsaka* throughout the four quarters while contradicting Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Nāgārjuna—this is something this unworthy one cannot understand.
Moreover, Fangshan enumerated ten types of pure lands;

although he stated that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is provisional, the *Avataṃsaka* integrates the provisional and the real, such that principle and phenomena are unimpeded, and all phenomena are mutually unimpeded. Therefore...
Even brothels and places of slaughter are nothing other than pure *maṇḍalas*; how much more so is the Ultimate Bliss Land, adorned with the seven treasures?
Even the insatiable *Vasudhārā* is the manifestation of an ancient Buddha; how much more so is Amitābha, who is fully endowed with myriads of virtues?
That you, Layman, sport within the unimpeded gates of the *Avataṃsaka* yet remain obstructed from the Pure Land—this is something I, this unworthy one, cannot understand.
I and you, Layman, are like inseparable, close friends within the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra* (Huazang).
Yet you fail to perceive my humble sincerity; you further wish to drag me into being a brother of flesh and blood within the lotus womb, and look toward...
"The Layman has not excluded me from his circle. Lu Chuan further sent a letter saying:

"Various sutras and treatises of provisional meaning, such as the independent *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*, and treatises like the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, all proclaim the Pure Land. How could this be without cause?"
However, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* never mentions this; indeed, the tenth pure land listed by Fangshan provides even clearer evidence.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the sixteen princes are arranged in succession, among whom Amitābha is included, yet he is never definitively established as a single, distinct Buddha.

When it praises the merit of upholding the sutra, it incidentally cites the *Anle* (Peaceful Bliss) [Pure Land], and when it truly explains the causes and effects regarding women, it refers to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* twenty times.

Regarding the five holy ones’ realization of perfect penetration, Mañjuśrī shows no partiality or preference; he merely states that "the gates of skillful means are many" and further says that "both following and reversing are skillful means.
However, since this is followed by the observation that "their speed differs," there is, within this absence of partiality, nonetheless a pointed direction.
Thus, while reaching the ultimate in the Universal Gate (Pumen), he does not extol the power of Avalokiteśvara (Śìzhì) to the exclusion of others.
They further disparage and denigrate it, calling it "impermanence" and "arising and ceasing.

As for the masters of the Xianshou and Qingliang traditions, they repeatedly set forth the five teachings—Initial, Final, Sudden, Complete, and Perfect—and all agreed upon them as authoritative; yet they never once ranked Pure Land among them.
Those belonging to the lineage of the Mind-Only school were especially dismissive of it. As the Chan Master Qi Ji said: "There is only the shortcut of cultivation; follow the old [path]..."
He beats him and pursues him around, yet he only chants the name of Amitābha Buddha. Even when his chanting fails to save him, he cries out:
"Perhaps, as before, he abandoned his father and fled, wandering through foreign lands, bumping into things here and there—how bitter it is! Amitābha Buddha!
While such words might be considered harsh, how could they have been spoken without reason? There must surely be a deeper meaning behind them. What is said...
The realized one says that the arduous practice of many *kalpas* is not equal to attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, he says that a single thought-moment of dependent origination as non-arising transcends the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles; how much more so when one disregards even the distinction between the Three and One Vehicles?
Ultimately, there is no "mine" (*mamakāra*). For those who now attain rebirth in the Pure Land, I am the one who gives birth, and the land is...
What arises is distinct between self and other; arising and ceasing are vividly apparent; joy and aversion are in disarray.

Regarding all that has not yet been fully understood, when looking back at those who have traditionally discussed the Pure Land, they invariably say: "Upon the blossoming of the flower, one sees the Buddha and awakens to non-arising.

This implies that one must first attain rebirth to see Amitābha, and only then—whether from Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, or Amitābha himself—is one instructed in non-arising. It is only at this point that...
Awakening seems, for the time being, to be a remote and slow process. Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of the entire body within the ocean of nature of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:

it is as if there were eighty-four thousand pores upon a human body, and within each pore dwell the Medicine Buddha of the East and Amitābha of the West, each preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
If one were to cast this entire body into a single pore, it would not only be like inverting the ocean and its bubbles, but would be like a fly throwing itself [into a trap].

Regarding the window paper: what can be said of it? What the unworthy one [the author] wrote in his own hand yesterday was that it is appropriate for those devoted to the Pure Land to speak of the Pure Land, and for those devoted to the *Avataṃsaka* to speak of the *Avataṃsaka*.
He considered this not to contradict the various Dharma-gates of the Buddhas, and it was also intended as a sincere offering of his heart to the Venerable One.
Yet, the Venerable One now wishes to lead me into the lotus-womb; thus, as the ancients have said: [The text ends here.]
To grasp at things is to enter the mired ford; this is what is meant by "discarding gold to carry grass.
Among the assembly under the Venerable Master, those who have traveled from Hangzhou to Suzhou are all eloquent in their discourse on the Nine Grades of Rebirth.

When I speak with them casually and they encounter even a slight mention of the Supreme Vehicle, their hearts are startled and their eyes stare wide, or they even laugh at it. Is this fault in the disciples, or in the teacher? Great Man!

Now, one whose spirit and bearing reach toward the heavens must take the salvation of sentient beings as their primary urgency. Having left the mundane world, having opened the hall, and having ascended the seat,
if one does not possess the strategic maneuvers of a great man, but merely acts with the gestures of an old layman or laywoman from the village lanes,
then when suddenly questioned by a clever person or pressed by one with clear eyes, would you attempt to hide yourself within the Big Dipper, or perhaps behind the Iron Ring Mountains?

To hide oneself within the mountains is a heterodox practice. The Great Matter of the Buddha-Dharma is no trivial affair; I pray that you, Venerable Sir, will reconsider this with renewed earnestness.
Hong replied again in a letter, saying: "I have received your gracious letter. Its original phrasing and subtle eloquence are vast and layered; I truly admire and look up to it.
However, I venture to think that while your affection for me is deep, your words are somewhat excessive. If you truly wish to propagate the Chan school and suppress..."
Regarding the Pure Land, there is no need for many words. Why not say: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time have been swallowed by me in a single mouth"?
Since not even a single Buddha remains, who else could possibly be Amitābha? Furthermore, why not say: "If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not an inch of earth in the great world"?
Since not a single inch of earth exists, where else could there be a Land of Ultimate Bliss? These two phrases alone suffice.
Your recent communication encompasses everything exhaustively. Now, were I to respond to each point one by one, I fear it might lead to contention;
yet if I do not respond, a matter of the Great Way cannot remain unaddressed. I venture to set forth my views briefly. Regarding your statement concerning the *neyārtha* (provisional) sūtras:

He then spoke of the Pure Land, taking the "Chapter on Vows and Conduct" (*Pranidhāna-paṭala*) and the *Awakening of Faith* (*Bodhicitta-utpāda-śāstra*) as its basis. Let us set aside the *Awakening of Faith* for a moment;

as for the "Chapter on Vows and Conduct," it subsumes the entirety of the eighty-fascicle sutra within a single chapter. From antiquity to the present, who would dare to claim that it is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)?
Yet you, Layman, alone hold the *Avataṃsaka* in high esteem while disparaging the "Chapter on Vows and Conduct. If the "Chapter on Vows and Conduct" were not of definitive meaning, then...

The *Avataṃsaka* is likewise of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). Furthermore, regarding your letter’s claim that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* records the rebirth in the Pure Land as the cause and effect for women:
would it then follow that the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood is also merely the cause and effect for women?
And if you claim that Amitābha was one of the sixteen princes, would it then follow that Vairocana is merely one of the twenty layers of the Flower Treasury World (*Huānzàng*)?
Thirteenth, you are mistaken. You hold Vairocana alone to be supreme; how can it be that Vairocana is equal to Amitābha?
Furthermore, in your letter you claim that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* selects Avalokiteśvara while omitting Śrī-ghoṣa, and further degrades him as subject to impermanence and birth-and-death.

If so, then when Kauṇḍinya realized the two terms "guest" and "dust," he could be said to have attained the understanding of impermanence and conformed to the non-arising and non-ceasing. Why then did he not enter [nirvāṇa]?
The selection of Yuan Tong truly marks the passing of Guanyin in the imperial examination and the failure of Shizhi.
Have you not heard the analogy of "receiving a mark on the forehead at Longmen"? Is it merely the talk of a rustic from Qidong?

Furthermore, in your letter you mention that the Chan Master Qi Ji provided word-by-word commentary on an ancient verse for reciting the Buddha’s name, stating: "There is only the path of direct cultivation," to which he added: [commentary].
He continued to strike him as he circled around him. The monk said, "I am merely reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha.
The master then remarked, "Reciting it will not save you. The layman was well-versed in the Chan school;

why did he not realize that this was a master acting directly to untie the tangles and remove the bonds for the sake of others, yet instead took it to be a substantial teaching and died caught under the words? Indeed, as an ancient said: "Tread upon..."
"If Vairocana’s practice on the crown of the head is not sufficient, then would even Amitābha not suffice? Would even Vairocana not suffice?
Such words appear by the hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions in the recorded sayings and biographies.
Forty years ago, when I was still old and decrepit, I too used such expressions to sharpen my tongue and bolster my writings. Later, I came to feel shame and dared not do so again. Until—
Even now, he remains deeply ashamed. Furthermore, Qi Ji said to one who was seeking the Western Land:
"To abandon one's father and flee, wandering lost in a foreign land, bumping into things here and there—what suffering! Amitābha Buddha! The man replied to him:
"Right now, it is rather like a son remembering his mother, returning to his native home, and casting aside the east to find the west—what joy! Amitābha Buddha! Now tell me: [which of these is it?]

How does this statement differ from what Qi Ji has said? Furthermore, your letter suggests that practicing over many kalpas is not as good as attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in a single thought-moment.
Has the Layman already attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas?
If you have, then you should not regard me as the producer or the land as the produced. Why is this? Because the mind itself is the land; who then could be the producer?
That which is capable of producing is precisely the mind; what, then, is produced? One does not see a producer or a produced, yet one proceeds by way of birth.
Therefore, although birth occurs throughout one's entire life, it has never truly occurred. This is precisely why it is called "true non-birth" (*anutpāda*).

It is certainly not the case that one must first deny birth and only then call it non-birth; such would be a nihilistic emptiness, and not the principle of non-birth. Furthermore, regarding your letter:
To see the Buddha only upon the blossoming of the flower and only then realize non-arising would be a circuitous and delayed path. Layman, you are proficient in the Chan school;

surely you know that attaining enlightenment from delusion is like waking from a dream or the blooming of a lotus flower. Among those who practice the Buddha-recitation, there are those who realize their nature in the present life;
this is the blossoming of the flower in an instant. There are those who realize their nature after death; this is the blossoming of the flower over a long duration.
Faculties may be sharp or dull, and effort may be diligent or lax; thus, the blossoming of flowers has its own pace, whether slow or swift. How can one categorically dismiss this as being circuitous?
Furthermore, in your letter, you compared the Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng*) to the entire body and the Western Land to a single pore.

To claim that those born in the West are like taking the entire body and thrusting it into a pore is to invert the analogy of the ocean and the bubble. Such is the nature of analogies concerning size.
However, Master, you are a master of the Huayan school. Why do you permit only the small to enter the great, yet not allow the great to enter the small?
Furthermore, the mutual interpenetration of the great and the small is but one of the ten mysterious gates of the Huayan.
Consider how the unspeakably unspeakable, infinite worlds of the Flower Treasury (Huazang) enter into a single lotus flower within the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī), yet do not even fill it.
If it is but a single petal of a flower, or a space within a single mustard seed, what harm is there in the entire body entering a single pore?
Furthermore, regarding your letter, you state that when you speak of the Mahayana to a mountain monk, he is struck with awe and stares in amazement.
You previously remarked that one should speak of the Avatamsaka to those suited for the Avatamsaka, and of the Pure Land to those suited for the Pure Land; now, as for this—
Those of dull faculties are precisely those for whom the Pure Land is most suitable. Why then do you not provide medicine appropriate to their ailments, but instead insist on lecturing them?
Furthermore, your letter states that since I have left the secular world and ascended the hall [as a master], I lack the grand strategy of a great man and behave like an old layman or laywoman;
when pressed by clever people or cornered by those with clear eyes, I point toward the Big Dipper.
Are you hiding within the Iron Ring Mountains? I, an old and decrepit man, have never dared to assume the title of one who has transcended the world;
naturally, I lack the strategic insight of a great man. Let us set that aside for now.

To disparage those who cultivate the Pure Land as "laymen and laywomen" (zhāigōng zhāipó) is, as the ancients said, not to disparage the ignorant husband and wife, but rather to disparage Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
The "Worthy Horse" (Bhadra-aśva) refers to Nāgārjuna. Are Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Aśvaghoṣa, and Nāgārjuna alone [to be so honored]?
