In fact, all the Bodhisattvas and spiritual friends—such as Master Huiyuan, Shandao, Zhiyi, and Yongming—as well as the great gentlemen such as Liu Yimin, Bai Juyi, Liu Zongyuan, and Su Shi—all observe the *gongzhai* (public fast). All these great men observe the *gongzhai*.
Poxie! Even laymen and laywomen who merely recite the Buddha’s name and attain rebirth in the Pure Land immediately reach the stage of non-retrogression;
how could they possibly be held in contempt? Furthermore, these laymen and laywomen are those who, though simple, dull, and lowly, strictly observe the prescribed rules.
They may be ignorant, but as for those who are clever and eloquent, who speak recklessly of Prajñāpāramitā and have already eaten their fill of meat—come here!
Those who seek out monks to discuss Chan are demons. A fool values his own folly; I truly examine myself in this way.
I would rather be an old layman or an old laywoman than be an old male demon or an old female demon.
As for those so-called "clever people" or "those with clear eyes," when they come to question or press me, those laymen and laywomen need not ascend high to the North.
A measure of distance; he seeks the Iron Ring Mountains afar, yet settles his bedding right at the throat of the clever one.
He spreads his seat upon the pupils of the clear-eyed person. Why? It is merely to cause him to temporarily close the samādhi of the mouth and turn the light back to reflect within.
Furthermore, you, Layman, hold the *Avataṃsaka* in high esteem while forcefully disparaging the Pure Land; I, an old man, practice the Pure Land while offering my utmost praise for the *Avataṃsaka*.
Layman, try to reflect upon this in stillness: what indeed could be the reason for such a state of affairs?
Moreover, in your letter you stated that my exhortation for you to seek rebirth in the Pure Land is like abandoning gold to carry hemp—an inverted act of conduct that deeply offends me.
This is indeed a disgrace. However, this analogy is not yet apt. Let me now offer another:
suppose a farmer were to send a visiting card to the gate of a great and wealthy householder, and that householder were to invite him into his estate. Those who heard of this would all laugh at him.

The farmer, however, would sweep the path and plan to issue a formal invitation once more. Those who had laughed would say: "It was fortunate that the master did not reprimand you before; he now wishes to..."
"Are you like Feng Fu? The farmer replied, "I have seen among the wealthy families those who possess riches but lack benevolence;
those whose wealth is external while their inner substance is poor; those who are not yet wealthy but are already arrogant;
and those who serve as stewards at the gates of the rich, considering themselves wealthy themselves. Moreover, where are the Jingu Valley and the Meiwu Mound today? And as for me..."
"The old country fellow was enjoying the peace and prosperity of the era; thus he forgot his station and acted as he did. Now he realizes his error.

Thereupon, they laughed together and dispersed. Daohong, in his daily life, extensively cultivated all manner of wholesome deeds to support his pure karma. At that time, the ordination platform had long been forbidden and unused.
Daohong ordered those seeking the precepts to prepare the three robes before the Buddha to receive them, acting as their witness.
Furthermore, he composed ritual texts for the rites of land and water, as well as the *Yogācāra-bali*, to rescue those suffering in the dark realms;
he established ponds for the release of living beings and wrote essays on the prohibition of killing. Consequently, those who were transformed by his teachings were exceedingly numerous.

At the end of the sixth month in the fortieth year of the Wanli era, he suddenly entered the city and took leave of his disciples and old friends, saying, "I am about to depart elsewhere. He returned to the mountain to prepare tea and bid farewell to the assembly.
The assembly could not fathom this. On the evening of the first day of the seventh month, he entered the hall and said, "Tomorrow I shall depart.

The following evening, he entered his private quarters and manifested a slight illness; he sat with eyes closed. When all the disciples from the city had arrived, he opened his eyes again and said, "Everyone, recite the Buddha’s name with sincerity.
Do not engage in eccentricities; do not violate my rules. Facing west, he recited the Buddha’s name and passed away at the age of [blank].
81 (Cloud Dwelling Collection of Dharma).
Rongrong, whose given name was Da-xian, was a native of Haining, Hangzhou. In his prime, he worked as a butcher; having been bitten by a pig, he was subsequently moved to remorse.

Wu went to the Northern Monastery of the county, where he shaved his head and received the precepts to become a monk. Later, he returned to Yunqi at the age of sixty. During the day, he joined the assembly in manual labor;
at night, he recited the Buddha’s name with diligent and tireless devotion. In the ninth year of the Wanli era, on his birthday, he prepared a vegetarian feast for the monks.
Prostrating himself before the Buddha’s seat, he called out with a resolute voice three times, vowing to be reborn in the Western Paradise. The assembly gathered around him and sang in chorus.
The Buddha passed away with palms joined (from the *Yunqi Jishi*).
Rucheng, whose courtesy name was Fayuan, was surnamed Ruan and was a native of Shangyu in Shaoxing. He first left the household life at Longjing on West Lake.

He later entered Yunqi Monastery, where he applied himself with keen resolve to the practice of Buddha-recitation (*nienfo*). He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and performed prostrations during the six periods of the day.

In the eleventh year of the Wanli era, he fell ill and remained bedridden for several months. When his condition reached its terminal stage, he heard the sound of Buddha-recitation from within the hall;

suddenly, he sat up in a state of startled alertness. At midnight, he joined his palms, gazed intently at the golden countenance of the Buddha, and passed away while looking upward in devotion (*Yunqi Jishi*).

Guangzhi (廣製), courtesy name Anlu (安廬); his origins are unknown. In his youth, he dreamed of entering Jinpan Hermitage (金盤庵), where he stood with hands clasped beneath a lapis lazuli lamp, facing the statues of the Three Sages of the West;
there was not a single person in sight, and his inner mind was crystal clear. Upon waking, he took joy in this experience.
When he was somewhat older, he again dreamed that he entered the An-yin Hermitage and saw the Great Being Avalokiteśvara manifesting the aspect of one who contemplates sentient beings.
From this point on, he conceived the aspiration for world-transcendence. At the age of twenty, he left the household life and visited the Great Master Yunqi.

Upon hearing that the Western Pure Land is free from the sufferings of saṃsāra, he immediately leaped with joy and said, "From this day forward, I know where my place of rest and refuge lies. Thereupon—

He devoted himself to the profound study of the Pure Land Dharma-gate, composing poems on the longing for the Pure Land as well as various prose pieces and rhymed compositions, most of which were elegant and worthy of recitation.
Now, I record his "Fu on Longing for the Pure Land. Its preface states: "The Land of Purity and Sovereignty is truly a rare realm in the West."
When crossing the waters, there are jade ponds and gemstone pools; when ascending the land, there are jewel-strewn streets and golden paths.
These are all places where the great Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body wander and transform, and where the most virtuous beings linger and dwell. Such is the splendor of its capital city.
The beauty of its palaces surpasses the primordial void of the Immortal Capital and exceeds the magnificence of the celestial palaces.
That it is thus praised throughout the ten directions and its fame recorded in the various canons is surely because its land is exceptionally sublime and its path is the direct shortcut.
Whether its name transcends that of other monasteries or its substance differs from all other regions, it marks the point where one first departs from the realm of saṃsāra.
To finally tread upon the ground of non-arising—were it not for one who loathes the world and its desires and fears impermanence, how could such a state be yearned for and delighted in?

Were it not for one who exhausts the profound and explores the subtle, whose faith in the Dharma is steadfast, how could they conceive of it in distant contemplation and seek it with earnest devotion?
Thus, my spirit races and my thoughts engage; my reflections are bound and my feelings remain fixed. Between waking and sleeping, it is as if I have already gone there.

As for those who are born [into this state], they wash away the defilements of the sense-faculties and entrust their minds to this realm. Unable to bear the intensity of their singular contemplation, they have briefly transcribed this scene to give vent to their sentiments.
The赋 (fu) says: The true source is vast and empty, remaining unchanging while following conditions. There are those whose flow is turbid and defiled, becoming silt and sand;
there are those whose accumulation is pure and clear, becoming gold and jewels. How magnificent is the adornment of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, brought forth by the true practice of vows!...
Supported by these [teachings], King Śīlāditya set forth upon his journey; relying upon the Dharma-treasury, he established the foundation of his reign.

Some have praised the secret scriptures, while others have eternally sung pure verses. One should verify these through the Tathāgata’s own words as expressed from the Sage’s mind, rather than harboring doubts based on ordinary sentiments.
Far away lies that wondrous realm, profound, mysterious, and remote; those who cling to their own narrow views do not believe, and those whose faith is shallow...
Stalled by lingering emotions, one remains unenlightened. The quail soars among the *péng* and *hǎo* grasses, unable to fathom the majestic majesty of one who strikes the wind.

When principles are subtle, affairs do not manifest; when fruits are minute, causes leave no omen. One may worry over lost sheep and weep at the forked path, yet cling to the single Way of mere names.
Seeing spiritual efficacy, one travels westward; suddenly realizing that one’s life is about to depart, one still adheres to the legacy of the former sages.
I have arrived at the courtyard of the long life of immortality. If one may indeed reach out to grasp the highest goodness, what need is there to fear the City of Doubt?

Having cast off the shackles of birth and death, I give full expression to my lofty sentiment of non-arising. I am robed in the fluttering of fine silken garments, shaking the bells and clappers of my golden staff.
I pass through the dense foliage of precious leaves and tread upon the towering heights of rare blossoms. Ascending the crystalline void, I desire to—
Ascending, he gallops swiftly across the azure void, treading upon the soaring pavilions of the high heavens and overlooking the profound darkness of the lower realms.
He takes the azure sky as his canopy and points to the verdant forests as his screen. Grasping the green branches that brush against the wind, he touches the purple stalks that hold the morning dew.
Though he has not yet reached the inner hall, he has already attained the secret of longevity; having brought his mind into accord with the profound mystery.
The essential point is this: having entered the profound source, all is leveled and even; one attains a leisurely pace upon the ninefold thoroughfares.

The paths are free of obstructions and unimpeded, allowing the mind and eyes to roam in vast clarity and permitting movement to be unhurried and composed. One treads upon the *kṣānti-grass* that brushes against the hem of the robe and tramples the fallen crimson petals of the *padma*.
Beholding the swarms of *śuka-parrot* birds and hearing the resonant cries of the *kalaviṅka*, one passes by the sacred pond to test [one's virtue].
I bathe; the water flows at will, submerging my chest. It washes away the turbidity of the eight impurities and cleanses the obscurity of the five hindrances.
I follow the noble path of Master Huiyuan and tread in the original footsteps of Master Shandao. This alone is the sacred realm where the King of Emptiness resides.
Rows of trees flank the way, and lotus flowers cluster to form dwellings. Azure halls tower amidst the central grove, and vermilion pavilions...
Exquisite in every quarter, the flowing rosy clouds cast their radiance upon the winged windows; they receive the shadows of the morning sun through the ornate lattices.

The birds cry out by day and rest by night; the flowers close at evening and bloom at dawn. Celestial music is as abundant as the rustling wind-blown leaves; the sounds of the Sūtras harmonize with the flowing streams.
The courtyard abounds with jade from Lantian, and the deep pool holds pearls from the Crimson Waters. Raising the *kaṣāya* robe to hold them...

Flowers [fell] as he listened to the preaching of the Dharma while soaring through the void. In a trance-like state, he vanished from here to appear there; in profound stillness, he emerged from existence to enter non-existence.
He displayed such divine transformations in an instant that he was as one with ten billion stupas. His body was serene and his breath tranquil; he had completely cast aside both mind and environment.

There was no trace of hesitation or difficulty; his spiritual encounter was total and complete. He drank from the vast surging waves of the ocean of wisdom and inhaled the hundred [streams] of the great leviathan.
Crossing the river, they travel upon the wind; the corners of their robes flutter aloft. The Dharma drums resound with a clear ringing, and extraordinary fragrances waft like rising smoke.
The multitude emerges from the forest to perform their circumambulations; scattered flowers descend from the realm beyond the void as immortals arrive.

They listen to the Dharma-sounds of waterbirds, which harmonize with the gushing springs from the rock caverns. Thus, the teachings on both emptiness and existence are first presented, and the Noble Truths are eloquently expounded.
This chapter delves into the realm where one is both immersed in and detached from [phenomena], and wondrously emerges from between existence and non-existence.

It unifies the principles of emptiness and existence within a single void, and by transcending the distinction between the true and the false, it attains the primordial source. Since the Middle Way cannot be grasped as a fixed entity, the perfect contemplation is extinguished in three turns.
At Vaiśālī, he spoke of non-duality, valuing the silence of Vimalakīrti; he integrates the myriad things to constitute the self, returning to the inherent identity of the same essence.
However, the details of his later life are not recorded (*Pure Land Miscellaneous Verses with Preface*).

Zhényuán (真緣), whose courtesy name was Huìguǎng (慧廣), was surnamed Yáo (姚) and was a native of Wúxī in Chángzhōu. He left the household life at the age of thirty and traveled extensively to consult various masters.
He spent sixteen years in retreat until he attained the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).

In the twenty-second year of the Wanli era, while residing at Ayuwang Temple in Mingzhou, he personally witnessed a relic emit light, within which appeared the Buddha Śākyamuni. He then vowed to offer his own body by means of self-immolation.
He invited the assembly of monks to solicit firewood and straw; each person contributed a bundle, which were piled up to form a high pyre. Thereupon, he took [the vow].
He anointed his body with fragrant oil, sat cross-legged atop a pile of firewood, and recited the Buddha’s name with palms joined. When the fire reached his body, he was instantly reduced to ashes.
The assembly saw a five-colored light emerge from the crown of his head; within the light appeared the golden body of a Bodhisattva.
It was about two chi in length and shone brilliantly in all four directions; only after a long time did it finally extinguish (*Guǎiyuán*).

According to various records, he was a native of Yīn County, Nìngbō. By nature he preferred living alone, making it his practice to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* daily until he had completed nine thousand recitations.
He produced over one thousand seven hundred works. The world called him Master Fahua.

In the fourteenth year of the Wanli era, Yu Chunxi, Director of the Office of Merit, compiled the *Record of the Dharma Flower Samādhi Repentance*, noting that he had three occasions of observing the *jinzu* (foot-binding) retreat for the long-term practice, enduring nine cycles of cold and heat.

He repeatedly received auspicious responses. Later, while resting on the path at Xixi in Hangzhou, he performed various acts of Buddhist service by carrying water on his shoulder and bearing firewood on his back.

Someone remarked, "Venerable Master, why do you still perform such conditioned meritorious deeds? He rebuked him with a stern voice, saying, "How could the unconditioned exist outside of the conditioned?
In the seventh month of the forty-first year, he took leave of his disciples and recited the names of the Buddhas three thousand times.
He chanted the title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* several times, then passed away while facing west with palms joined.
On the following day, the crown of his head was still warm, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room (a testament to the efficacy of upholding the *Lotus Sūtra*).

Deqing, Deqing—whose courtesy name was Chengyin and whose late sobriquet was the Elder Hanshan—was the son of the Cai family of Jinling. His mother dreamed that Guanyin brought forth a child in her arms before she conceived.
At his birth, he was encased in two layers of white clothing. He left the household life at the age of nineteen and devoted himself single-mindedly...
He practiced the recitation of the Buddha’s name. One night, in a dream, he beheld Amitābha Buddha manifesting his body, standing in the sky at the place where the sun sets;
the features of his face and eyes were vivid and distinct. From then on, the sacred form shone brilliantly, appearing before his eyes from time to time.

He subsequently went to Mount Wutai to practice meditative concentration and realized his inherent nature. He drew blood to transcribe the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; with every stroke of the brush, he recited [the Buddha’s name].

The Buddha uttered a single sound; for a long time, movement and stillness remained as one. In the tenth year of the Wanli era, while Qing resided on Laoshan, Empress Dowager Li ordered the delivery of gold to construct a temple, which was granted the title Haiyin.
At that time, the Empress Dowager frequently dispatched palace eunuchs to repair various pagodas and temples.

A powerful official who harbored a grudge against these eunuchs had a Daoist priest strike the "Denwen Drum" (the drum for reporting grievances) to lodge a complaint regarding the encroachment of their interests.

Upon hearing that the matter involved Qing, he was sentenced to penal servitude at Leizhou for privately constructing a temple. Qing followed him wherever he went, wearing a scholar’s cap and gown while preaching the Dharma.

He further made a vow to propagate the Mahayana sutras, composing commentaries and treatises on the *Laṅkāvatāra* and *Śūraṅgama Sūtras*. In the forty-second year [of the reign], by imperial decree, he was permitted to return to monastic robes.
Upon returning, he passed through Mount Lu and established a hermitage at the foot of Wuru Peak, where he emulated Master Huiyuan by practicing the six periods of meditation.

[The Master] was leaking [semen]. He cultivated pure practices with even greater diligence. At that time, there was a Chan practitioner from Haiyang who sought to receive the precepts and asked about the essentials of cultivating the Pure Land.
Qing said: "The Buddha taught many expedient methods for practicing the Dharma to transcend birth and death.
Among them, none is more swift and essential than reciting the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. This Dharma gate was spoken by the Buddha spontaneously, without being asked. Three...
The faculties are universally encompassed, and the fourfold assembly is gathered equally; this is not merely a provisional teaching established for those of inferior capacity.

As the Sūtra says: "If you would purify a Buddha-land, you should first purify your own mind. Thus, in practicing pure karma now, one must take a pure mind as the foundation. It is essential to purify one's own mind.

First, one must ensure that the roots of precept-keeping are pure. Regarding the three actions of the body, four of the mouth, and three of the mind—these ten unwholesome karmas are the causes of suffering in the three miserable realms.
Now, the essential point of upholding the precepts is that the three karmas must first be purified; when they are pure, the mind will naturally be pure.

Within this pure mind, one should cultivate weariness for the sufferings of *saṃsāra* (Sahā world), resolve to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), and establish the correct practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
However, for the practice of nianfo to be essential, one must have a sense of urgency regarding birth and death. First, sever external conditions and single-mindedly maintain the one thought-moment.
Take the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" as the root of life; let every thought be without delusion and every mind be uninterrupted throughout the two periods of day and night.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining; picking up the spoon or lifting the chopsticks; turning, moving, bowing, or looking up;
whether in motion or stillness, leisure or haste—at all times, one is neither deluded nor obscured, and there are no divergent conditions.

If one applies the mind in this manner for a long time until it becomes thoroughly refined, such that even in dreams there is no further loss, and waking and sleeping are as one, then the practice will become continuous and dense, forged into a single whole; this is called "attainment."
This is the time of power. If one’s mindfulness reaches the state of "one mind, not distracted," then at the moment of death, the realm of the Pure Land will manifest before them.
Naturally, they will not be detained by birth and death, and they will be moved by Amitābha Buddha to emit light and welcome them.
This is the definitive efficacy of attaining rebirth there. While single-mindedly holding the name is certainly the primary practice, it must also be supported by visualization.
Contemplate further with greater stability and confidence. For Vaidehī, the Buddha taught the sixteen sublime contemplations, whereby one may achieve completion in a single lifetime.

Now, from among these sixteen contemplations, you should select whichever one you prefer—whether it be the singular contemplation of the wondrous marks of the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, or the contemplation of the pure land’s environment, such as the jeweled ground of lotus flowers as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Contemplate according to your inclination.
Contemplation. If one’s visualization is clear and distinct, then throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, it will appear before one as if in the Pure Land.

At the moment of death, one will be reborn there instantaneously with a single thought. Using the mind in this way and diligently maintaining the precepts, one forever severs evil thoughts and afflictions.
With such a pure mind, maintaining the visualization in continuous succession is nothing other than the true cause for the Pure Land. Furthermore, there is the abiding of the pure mind...

The practitioner asked: "I am unable to achieve a continuous state of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo*). Please grant me instruction. Qing replied: "The foremost requirement for cultivation is a sense of urgency regarding birth and death.
If the sense of urgency regarding birth and death is not keen, how can one achieve a continuous state of mindfulness of the Buddha?

Furthermore, since sentient beings have come from immeasurable kalpas ago, every thought has been deluded and false, with the faculties of emotion and intellect firmly obstructed. Even having now entered this present life, when has there ever been..."

To regard a single thought with such urgency as if it were birth and death, yet in daily life to follow after emotions moment by moment without ever reflecting inward—now wishing to sever the cycle of birth and death accumulated over many kalpas with a superficial and floating faith—is this not like attempting to extinguish a fire of faggots with a cup of water? Is there any such principle?
If your concern for birth and death is truly urgent, and every thought is like that of one whose hair is on fire, you must fear only losing [this resolve] for a single moment.
A human body is difficult to regain even in a hundred kalpas; one must therefore firmly "bite down" upon this single invocation of the Buddha's name.
One must resolutely oppose delusive thoughts so that they manifest before one in every situation, moment by moment, without being obstructed by them. Practice such diligent and earnest cultivation.

After a long time, through constant refinement, one naturally attains resonance; without seeking to form a continuous state of mind, it spontaneously becomes so. This matter depends entirely on one’s own exertion.
If you merely use the recitation of the Buddha's name as a superficial mask, then for ages like that of a donkey, there will be no time of realization.
You must be courageous and resolute; do not hesitate any longer. Having lived at Mount Lu for several years, I went to Caoxi. (Recorded in the third year of Tianqi.)
In the tenth month of that year, he manifested a slight illness and said to those around him, "The worldly ties of this old monk are about to come to an end.
He bathed, burned incense, and passed away while sitting upright. A light shone forth, illuminating the heavens. He was seventy-eight years old (*Mengyou ji*).
Chuandeng (傳燈), whose secular surname was Ye (葉), was a native of Quzhou (衢洲). In his youth, he received the tonsure under Master Ying’an (映庵) of Jinxian (進賢).

He subsequently visited Master Baisong (百松) and heard him lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*, at which point he experienced a sudden spiritual resonance. He then inquired about the essential meaning of the "Great Samādhi" (*mahāsamādhi*) of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Master Bai...
Song opened his eyes wide and looked around; at once, Deng entered into realization. Baesong bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya* robe with golden clouds.
Throughout his life, he practiced the repentance rites of the Lotus Sutra, the Great Compassion Mantra, the Radiant Amitābha, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and others without a single idle day.
He chose to reside at Gaoming Temple in Youxi. Previously, the venerable master Ye Qi had buried his parents behind the temple and dreamed of a deity who said, "This is the Path of the Sages."

Regarding the site: "There will be an incarnate Bodhisattva who shall perform great Buddha-work here; you should move quickly. Qi did not believe this. Suddenly, his entire family fell ill and was in distress. Frightened, he moved away.
The following day, Zhi arrived and established the ancestral temple of the Tiantai school on that very spot. Disciples gathered there like spokes converging at a hub.
He once ascended the seat to expound the principles before the Great Buddha of Xinchang. The assembly heard the sound of [the Dharma] from within the stone chamber.

The music was resonant and rhythmic; when the lecture concluded, it fell silent. He once composed the *Treatise on Birth and Non-Birth*, which harmonizes the three contemplations and elucidates the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
Furthermore, there is an essay of his spiritual instructions (*dharmapada*) that is most essential, which states: "Yang Cigong said: 'If attachment is not heavy, one will not be born in Saha;
if mindfulness is not single-minded, one will not be born in the Pure Land. In Saha, there is at least one love that is not slight."
Thus, at the moment of death, one is led away by these attachments; how much more so when there are many attachments!

If there is even a single moment of mental distraction regarding the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one will be turned away by that thought at the time of death; how much more so when there are many such thoughts!

Now, these attachments may be slight or heavy, thick or thin, pertaining to the primary retribution or the secondary environment. To list them exhaustively, they include parents, wives, children, brothers, and so forth.

Friends, official rank, fame, wealth, nobility, literary works, poetry, arts, crafts, clothing, food and drink, dwellings, fields, gardens, groves, springs, flowers, precious gems, and articles of play—these are too numerous to enumerate. There is not a single thing among them that one does not forget.
It is love. To have not a single thought neglected is love. When there is even one vestige of attachment remaining in the breast, thoughts will not be unified.
When there is not a single thought that returns to oneness, then life cannot be born. Someone asked: "Is there a way to diminish attachment? He replied:

"To diminish attachment, nothing is more essential than a single thought. He was asked: "Is there a way for a single thought? He replied: "For a single thought, nothing is more essential than diminishing attachment. This is because...

Thought is not unified because it is caused by the distraction of the mind toward various objects. This distraction of the mind toward various objects is caused by its frantic pursuit of sensory realms.
When there is one realm in the Sahā world, there is one mind among sentient beings; when there is one mind among sentient beings, there is one realm in the Sahā world.
As myriad conditions sway within, they rush outward; mind and objects race against each other, as chaotic as dust motes in a river of sand. Therefore—
If one wishes to diminish their attachments, there is nothing better than to block off their objects.

When all objects are empty and all conditions are utterly still, and when all conditions are utterly still, the single thought-moment is spontaneously perfected. Once the single thought-moment is perfected, then both attachment and its conditions are exhausted.

It is asked: "Is there a way to block off these objects? It is replied: "To block off objects does not mean to eliminate the myriad existents, nor does it mean to close one's eyes and not look. Rather,"

The objective realm is understood to be empty; by realizing the fundamental source, the derivative is emptied. The myriad dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; their appearance as existent is due to mental afflictions (*kleśa*).

Thus, when afflictions exist, objects exist; when afflictions are empty, objects are empty. When the myriad dharmas are empty, the original nature manifests; when the original nature manifests, afflictive thoughts cease.
This occurs spontaneously and naturally, without the application of effort. As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, this is what is meant by "seeing and that which is seen."

Conditions, as well as the perceived characteristics, are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent. This seeing and these conditions are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi.
How could there be "is" or "is not" within them? Therefore, to block external objects, nothing is better than realizing that things are empty.
When one realizes that things are empty, emotional attachments naturally cease. When emotional attachments cease, craving does not arise; thus, it is simply mind-only.
Manifesting now, a single thought is perfected. Thus, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "To know that it is an illusion is itself to leave it; no expedient means are required.

To leave the illusion is itself awakening; there are no gradual stages. There is neither departing nor remaining, and no room for shifting or turning. The speed of its efficacy is like that of a drum struck by a mallet.
Those who study the Way should devote their full hearts to this. [The questioner] asks: "I have heard your instructions regarding 'lightening attachment,' but what of 'a single thought'?
[The Master] replies: "The Way of a single thought has three aspects: faith, practice, and aspiration. To seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must begin by strengthening faith.
One must read extensively the Mahāyāna sūtras and study broadly the teachings of the patriarchs; all those works that elucidate the Pure Land..."
In the scriptures, one must investigate each point thoroughly. One must realize that the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is originally the pure land of one’s own mind, not some other land;
and that Amitābha is originally the self-Buddha of one’s own fundamental nature, not some other Buddha.

Second, regarding the gates of practice, there are two types: the primary and the auxiliary. Within the primary practice, there are again two: first, the invocation of the name; second, meditative visualization. As for the invocation of the name...

This is known as the "Shorter Amitābha Sūtra. Recite the name for seven days with single-mindedness and without distraction. There are two types of single-mindedness: single-mindedness regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and single-mindedness regarding principle (*tattva*).
If you recite the Buddha’s name vocally, bind your mind to that object so that the sounds follow one another in succession and the moments of mind do not become distracted.
Even if the mind wanders toward external objects, withdraw it and bring it back. This requires the development of a resolute mind, severing thoughts of the future and casting them aside.
Regarding worldly affairs: set aside the mind of attachment so that the mind of mindfulness gradually increases.
From gradual to prolonged, from few to many—whether for one day, two days, or even seven days—one must ultimately achieve a state of single-mindedness without distraction before ceasing.

This is the single-mindedness of practice (*shi-ichinen*). Once this is attained, the pure cause for rebirth in Sukhāvatī is perfected; right mindfulness at the moment of death will surely be secured;

one will personally behold Amitābha, who will extend his hand to welcome and guide one; and birth in the Pure Land is certain. As for the single-mindedness of principle (*ri-ichinen*), there is nothing else to it:
it is simply to realize, in every thought-moment of the single-mindedness of practice, that the mind which contemplates and the Buddha who is contemplated are [non-dual].
The three periods of time are equal; the ten directions mutually merge. It is neither empty nor existent, neither self nor other.
There is no going and no coming; it is neither arising nor ceasing. This very thought-moment before one is precisely the boundary of the future Pure Land.

To contemplate while not contemplating, to contemplate within non-contemplation; to arise within non-arising, to be non-arising within arising. Amidst that which is beyond contemplation, [it] blazes forth.
However, one should reflect: within that which is fundamentally unarisen, to ardently seek birth is the first matter; this is the single mind that clarifies principle.

Second, as for the visualization, it is fully detailed in the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*. There are sixteen objects of contemplation, but the visualization of the Buddha is most essential.
One should visualize the body of Amitābha Buddha, sixteen feet in height, appearing like an image of purple-golden hue.
Standing upon the lotus pond, he assumes the posture of reaching down with his hands to welcome others.

His body possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), and each mark is adorned with eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). These two types of correct practice must proceed in mutual dependence:

at all times—whether walking, standing, sleeping, or reclining—one should single-mindedly recite the Name; when sitting cross-legged, one should maintain contemplation in every thought-moment. When weary from walking, one should sit cross-legged.
When sitting, one contemplates the Buddha; when rising from sitting, one performs walking meditation while reciting the name.
If one practices this without interruption throughout the four modes of deportment, rebirth in the Pure Land is certain. Second, there are two types of auxiliary practices:

first, mundane practices, such as being filial to one's parents, practicing worldly benevolence and compassion, maintaining a compassionate heart that refrains from killing, observing all the precepts, and performing every kind of beneficial deed.
Regarding these matters: if one can dedicate [the merit] toward the Western [Pure Land], there is nothing that does not assist the path.

Second, as for supramundane practices—such as the various merits of the six perfections and myriad practices, the recitation of Mahāyāna sūtras, and the cultivation of various repentance rites—one must likewise employ a mind of dedication to assist in their cultivation;
thus, they are all practices of the Pure Land. Furthermore, there is another kind of subtle and wondrous auxiliary practice.
Whenever you encounter various conditions or objects, apply your mind in every instance. For example, when seeing your kinsmen, regard them as spiritual kin from the Western Land;
guide them through the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, causing them to diminish their attachment so that their thoughts may become unified, and forever serve as your birthless kin in the future.
If feelings of affection arise, you should then call to mind the kin of the Pure Land, where there is no emotional attachment. When will this be?
One shall attain birth in the Pure Land and remain far removed from this craving. When anger arises, one should contemplate the retinue of the Pure Land, who are free from provocation and affliction;
one should think, "When shall I attain birth in the Pure Land and be freed from this anger?

When experiencing suffering, one should contemplate the Pure Land, where there are no manifold sufferings, but only the reception of all joys. When experiencing pleasure, one should contemplate the bliss of the Pure Land, which is without...
The center has no dependence. Whenever one encounters conditions or objects, one should extend this principle to all of them;
thus, at all times and in all places, there is nothing that does not serve as an auxiliary practice for the Pure Land. Regarding the third vow:

the vessel of the Pure Land takes faith as its rudder, and practice as its oars, sweeps, mast, and cables; the vow serves as the wind-sail. Without a rudder, there is no direction to guide one; without oars...
Without masts, rigging, and ropes, one cannot move forward; without wind and sails, one cannot break through the waves to reach one's destination swiftly.

Therefore, the subsequent section on practice is intended to clarify the vows. Now, these vows have both general and specific aspects, as well as broad and narrow dimensions, and universal and limited scopes. The general aspect is exemplified by the "Text for Transference and Aspiration" established by ancient masters.
The specific aspect follows the individual’s own intention. The broad aspect refers to the Four Great Vows: seeking the supreme above and saving those below...

Transformation. "Narrow" refers to measuring one's strength and resolving to be reborn in the Pure Land, being restricted like a fixed liturgy performed at specific times or in concert with the assembly.

"Universal" means making vows at all times and directing the mind toward the goal in every place. One must simply ensure that the essence conforms to the Four Great Vows and not arbitrarily establish one's own whimsical methods.
Through these three dharmas, one may expect rebirth in the Pure Land and swiftly behold Amitābha. This is the method for all Pure Land practices.
The gates [of the Dharma] are all contained within this. Every year, Master Deng cultivated the four samādhis, personally leading the assembly with diligent and courageous vigor.
He annotated the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, and other scriptures; whenever he took up the brush, he was invariably clad in his monastic robes.
Over his career, he presided over more than seventy lecture series. At the age of seventy-five, knowing that his time had come, he wrote out the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* by hand.
Five characters. Again, chant the title of the sutra twice more. Then, settle into profound stillness (*Fahua Chiyen Jingtu Fayu*).
"Ancient pines, ancient pines.
Gu Song was a native of Pingyang in Shanxi. He left home to become a monk at Lohu Monastery on Mount Wutai in his youth and attained the practice of *nianfo*.

Samādhi. The mountain was infested with tigers. [Shan]duo preached the precepts to them and gave them names. Consequently, the tigers no longer harmed people; whenever called, they would immediately arrive.

In the thirteenth year of the Wanli era, he traveled to Jingkou and established the Jingye Chan Monastery. At that time, he lived in deep valleys, sitting beneath trees to enter meditative absorption.
He resided there for thirty-nine years. One day, he joined his palms, raised his hands, took leave of the assembly, and passed away. His body was placed in a stone sarcophagus.
The stupa had not yet been constructed. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Chongzhen era, a five-colored light suddenly appeared from within the shrine.
Upon opening the shrine, it was seen that [the image] sat upright and composed upon a pine-wood pedestal, its features appearing as if alive.

On the second day of the tenth month in the fifteenth year of the Shunzhi era of the Great Qing, a precious light appeared once more, and a wondrous fragrance filled the chamber; it ceased only on the third day (according to the *Zhenjiang Fu Zhi*).

Zhongguang, whose courtesy name was Fayu and pen-name was Foshi Shanong, was the son of the Dai family of Qiantang. His mother dreamed of a monk covering his body with a *kāṣāya* robe and giving birth to light.
From childhood, he loathed the smell of meat and pungent foods. At the age of fourteen, he entered the service of Master Jingming.

He shaved his head and donned the dyed robes. At eighteen, he received the precepts at Yunqi. He traveled extensively among the lecture halls, studying the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school until he deeply penetrated the One Vehicle.
In the twenty-second year of the Wanli era, he visited Zen Master Zibo in Jinling, where he personally received the transmission of the prediction of enlightenment.

He returned to Wulin and reached the Eighteen Streams (*Shiba Jian*). Admiring the secluded and extraordinary beauty of its groves and valleys, he cleared away the thatch, piled up stones, and constructed a small cottage.
One day, while digging the earth, he discovered a fragment of an ancient stele and learned that the site had once been the ancient Lian'an Temple; he therefore rebuilt it.

Monastics gathered there in great numbers, and it eventually became a flourishing monastic center (*conglin*). Master Guang guided them according to their individual capacities, establishing a separate practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) outside the meditation hall.

In the Hall, he met Master Hanshan Deqing, with whom he consulted on establishing regulations. They divided the day into twelve periods, assigning six shifts to each person; each shift lasted six hours.

During these times, they practiced walking meditation while chanting the Buddha’s name, prostrations for the dedication of merit, and remaining seated in stillness, silently reciting what they had heard or practicing the gates of contemplation.
Thus, they attained mastery in both movement and stillness. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the ninth year of the Chongzhen era, he suddenly manifested [his passing].
Suffering from a slight illness, he said to his disciples, "Today the weather is clear; I wish to travel far away. A disciple asked, "Master, you are ill; where do you wish to go?
Daguang replied, "Do you think I am ill? He then leaned on a staff, left his chamber, and sat in the lotus position. He gathered the assembly to entrust them with his final affairs.
Just then, Layman Cai arrived, and Daguang clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "Layman, bear witness for me; there is nothing more to say."
He waited. Then he wrote a verse, saying: "A single phrase of Amitābha for fifty years— Clearly digging through the earth to seek the blue sky.
Now there is this truly excellent news: The midnight bell reaches the traveler’s boat. Having finished writing, he looked around at those nearby.
He threw down his writing brush and passed away (*Jingtu quanshu*, Lianansi ji).
As for the monk of Jintong Temple, his name has been lost. The temple was located at the North Gate of Changshu; the monk would daily strike a wooden board.
In the streets and alleys, he cried out at the top of his voice that impermanence is swift, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name. The crowd did not find this particularly strange.

In the third month of the thirteenth year of the Chongzhen era, he took leave of all his neighbors, saying, "Recite the Buddha’s name well; the old monk is departing. No one understood the reason for this.
The following day, he offered incense before the Buddha, joined his palms while chanting the Buddha’s name, and passed away sitting upright. (From the *Jingtu shengxian lu*)
(From the Epilogue at the end of the *Tuyue*).
Haibao, Haibao.
His place of origin is unknown. He resided at Tiantong Monastery in Changzhou. His appearance was very plain; when people spoke with him, he did not...

He replied with but a few words, merely laughing. His tattered robes were full of lice; when he had leisure, he would sit on the ground before the Buddha, picking up the lice and tossing them up and down without ever letting them leave his body.
He constantly solicited money to purchase vegetables and fermented bean curd to provide for the monks of the temple, and he also accumulated offerings of gold.

He earnestly exhorted the assembly to recite sutras and perform repentance rituals, while he himself focused on the Buddha and dedicated the merit toward their liberation; he continued in this manner for many years.

During the Chongzhen era, the Hanlin scholar Zheng Zuchang invited Bao to travel to the South Sea (Nanhai), but Bao declined. After the boat had set sail, Zheng frequently saw Bao walking ahead of him on land, unable to catch up with him.
When they reached the mountain and entered the hall, Bao was there once again. Zheng then dispatched a messenger to invite the Master.

On that same occasion, he again failed to obtain [the scripture]. When Zheng arrived at the commandery, he went directly to the temple to wait for Bao. A disciple said, "The Master has been lying in bed for over a month;
he only just rose yesterday. Zheng recounted the Master's spiritual wonders, and from this point on, the people of the commandery revered and believed in him.
One day, while sitting in meditation, he chanted the Buddha’s name and passed away (*Jingtu chenzhong*).
Dayun Dayun, whose courtesy name was Wanan, was surnamed Guo and a native of Renhe. He entered the monastic order at Yongqing Temple and received full ordination at Yunqi.

Residing in the northern suburbs, he was devoted to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism; many people relied upon him for guidance. He solicited donations to build Jixiang Temple, the monastic quarters of which were magnificent and radiant.
Thus, a monastic community was established, and its communal regulations were entirely based on the system of Yunqi.

Before long, he manifested a slight illness and immediately ceased all food and drink, devoting himself solely to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. After one month had passed, someone went to visit him;

Yun said, "If Amitābha does not remember me, what is the point of my remembering him? At the time of his death, he spoke to his disciple Zhijing, saying, "Sweep and clean for me; the Buddha is coming."
He welcomed [the end]. Sitting cross-legged, he recited the Buddha’s name and passed away at the age of fifty-nine (*Lingfeng Zonglun*).
As for the "Nameless Monk," he resided in Huangzhou, Hubei, where he single-mindedly upheld the name of Amitābha Buddha, never ceasing day or night. Following...
Everything he saw was called upon as Amitābha Buddha. In the sixteenth year of the Chongzhen era, the General Huang Ding was defending the state city.
A monk chanted the Buddha’s name with a loud voice, disrupting the vanguard; they seized him. It happened that Zhang Xianzhong was attacking Huangzhou.

While seated atop the city wall at night, the monk chanted the Buddha’s name in a high voice. The soldiers could not sleep and resented him, so they bound him and threw him down from the wall. Suddenly—

He further ascended the city wall and chanted the Buddha’s name. He did this four times, each time descending at the eastern wall and ascending at the western hall, then descending at the southern wall and ascending at the northern wall.
When the commanding general heard this, he finally paid him respectful homage. During a great famine in Huangzhou, people were eating one another.

A monk went outside the city, and a starving person, holding a knife, begged the monk to sacrifice his body. The monk untied his robes and showed them to the crowd, saying, "Wait while I chant the Buddha’s name."

He recited [the name] a thousand times; they were about to devour him. When he had reached three hundred recitations, the crowd was in such haste to strike him with blades that suddenly divine soldiers descended from the sky.
The starving people scattered in terror, and the monk was already within the city. A hunter in the mountains caught a large tiger;
the monk wished to redeem it and release it, but the hunter demanded thirty pieces of gold. The monk managed to obtain only four pieces of gold. The hunter—
The Master said, "If you can grasp the tiger’s ears and circle it three times, I shall give you the tiger. The monk was granted the tiger by the Master;

he grasped the tiger’s ears and circled it three times, whereupon the Master released it. The tiger followed the monk and would not leave. The monk and the tiger went together to the Vajra Cave on Mount Huangma.
When the Provincial Governor Lu Xiangsheng led his troops past Huangzhou, he visited the mountain to seek him out and wished to see the tiger. The monk spoke...
The tiger poked its head out the window; Lu wished to see its full body, so the tiger let out a great roar and leaped out.

Lu then presented his offerings and departed, calling himself a disciple. One day, as the monk was walking through the streets, he saw a rooster; he chanted the Buddha’s name aloud, and the rooster also chanted along with him.
In the seventh year of the Shunzhi era of the Qing dynasty, he was traveling to Wulin and passed through the White Gate (Nanjing), where he stayed.
At the Qinhuai River pavilions during the Dragon Boat Festival, [the Master] saw Qian Sheng among the pleasure boats; he was the Master’s disciple. He then called out, "Qian Amitabha!
Qian stepped ashore and saw the monk, who asked his fellow travelers if they knew who he was. They replied that it was such-and-such a person.
He wailed aloud, saying, "How can sentient beings take suffering for pleasure? Is it truly like this? He earnestly entreated him to show him the essentials of spiritual practice.
The monk said, "Single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. He further said, "After I have passed away, if you have any doubts..."
One may consult Juelang; he was a man of clear vision. His final whereabouts are unknown.

Juelang, whose name was Daosheng, served in succession as the presiding master at various monastic centers including Tianjie in Jinling, Chongguang in Hangzhou, and other locations. His dharma style flourished greatly (*Jingtu chenzhong*).

Zhi Xu, whose courtesy name was Ouyi and whose secular surname was Zhong, was a native of Wu County. His father, while reciting the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* as a lay practitioner, dreamed that a Bodhisattva brought him a son, and thus Xu was born.
In his youth, he took up the study of the Confucian sages and authored several thousand words of writings to refute Buddhism. However, upon...
Upon reading *Cloud-Abode: Notes from the Bamboo Window*, he burned his own previously composed treatises.

At the age of twenty, while reading the *Sutra on the Original Vows of Kṣitigarbha*, he gave rise to the aspiration for world-transcendence and began reciting the names of the Buddhas daily. In the first year of the Tiānqī era (1621), at the age of twenty-four, while listening to a Dharma Master lecture on a sutra, a state of doubt suddenly arose within him.
He applied himself to investigating this with all his heart, and after some time, he attained sudden enlightenment (*huòrán*). Subsequently, he withdrew into seclusion at Wú.
Jiang was stricken by illness and was on the verge of death; he then resolved his mind single-mindedly to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.

When his illness subsided slightly, he established an altar and recited the *Wǎngshēng zhòu* (Rebirth Mantra) for seven days. He then spoke this verse: "I prostrate to Amitāyus, who uproots the very foundation of karmic obstacles;

To Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the ocean-like assembly of Bodhisattvas. I was deluded regarding the light of original wisdom, and falsely fell into the suffering of saṃsāra; For kalpas beyond measure, not even for a moment [have I been free]."
Stop! There is no rescue and no refuge; having obtained this inferior human body, one still encounters the chaos of the *kalpa*-defilement (*kaṣāya*).

Although you have joined the ranks of the Saṃgha, you have not yet entered the stream of the Dharma. Witnessing with your own eyes the decay of the Wheel of Dharma, you wish to pull it back, yet your strength is insufficient.
This is truly because from time immemorial you have not planted superior roots of goodness. Now, with a resolute mind, seek birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, riding upon my original vow.
A boat to ferry across the masses submerged in suffering; if I do not go to be born there, I shall not be able to fulfill my vow.

Therefore, within this Sahā world, I must certainly depart. Just as a person drowning first seeks to reach the shore quickly, I shall then employ the power of skillful means to rescue all those swept away by the violent current.
With a heart of utmost sincerity, a profound heart, and a heart of dedication, I shall burn my arm as an offering of incense.
Lighting incense, establish a pure altar for one week and single-mindedly recite the *Wǎngshēng Zhòu* (Rebirth Mantra), except during times of eating and sleeping.

By the power of this merit, I seek certain rebirth in An-yang (Sukhāvatī). If I should retreat from my initial resolve and fail to head toward the West, may I immediately fall into hell, so that I may quickly give rise to repentance.
I vow never to cling to the realms of humans and devas, nor to the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). I look up with aspiration to Your Great Majesty...
May the divine powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unshared qualities of the Three Jewels, along with their boundless virtues, bestow their grace upon Zhixu and others.
May they subdue those who would cause us to regress and sustain us so that we may flourish.

Thereafter, he resided successively at Wénlíng, Zhāngzhōu, Shíchéng, Chéngxī, Chángshuǐ, and Xīn'ān, widely propagating the Tiantai teachings before retiring to Língfēng. At that time, many Chan practitioners from various regions [practiced] the Pure Land...
The *Tuzan* (Earthly Contemplation) is a provisional teaching; whenever it encounters a person who practices nianfo, it invariably requires them to investigate the meaning of the word "who" (*shui*).

Master Xu, however, alone maintained that the single method of holding the name (*chiming*) is itself the Perfect and Sudden Mind School (*xinzong*). There was once a man named Zhuo Zuocheng who posed a question, saying:
"What is the upward path within the gate of nianfo? How can one transcend the four propositions and sever the hundred negations? What is nianfo?"
The Buddha is the ultimate pinnacle for human beings. What is the point of confusion? A single blow behind the head!

I hope you, Venerable Master, will cast aside all talk of the original self-nature Amitābha and the pure land of the mind-only, personally behold the realm of the Tathāgata, and swiftly deliver a discourse that shakes the great trichiliocosm. Xu replied: "As for this 'one step beyond,' it is not—"
Meditation is not separate from purity; meditation itself is purity. To even speak of "investigating" [the mind] is already a concession made for those of inferior capacity.

A true great man should naturally believe with deep conviction that this very mind creates the Buddha and that this very mind is the Buddha. Were there to be even a single thought separated from the Buddha, [one would fail].
This is not called the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). If every thought-moment is uninterrupted by the Buddha, why labor further to ask who it is?
Regarding the ultimate reality of the Pure Land: there is no Buddha outside of mindfulness to be the object of remembrance, and there is no mindfulness outside of the Buddha that can remember him.
At the very moment of truly applying oneself, one does not fall into the four propositions or the hundred negations; one penetrates through and enters entirely, seeing only [Amitābha].
From a single pore of light of Amitābha Buddha, one immediately perceives the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions;
by merely being born in the single Buddha-land of the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss, one is immediately born in the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions. This is the upward path.
If one abandons the Amitābha present before one and speaks instead of a "self-nature Amitābha," or abandons the pure land of the West and speaks instead of "mind-only," [one has strayed].
"Pure Land. This is a public case of confusion. The Sūtra says: "The Three Worthies and Ten Sages dwell in the retribution realm; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.
This is a blow to the back of the head. One need only have deep faith in this gate, and based on that faith, give rise to the vow.

When one acts in accordance with their vows, then in every thought-moment there flow forth immeasurable Tathāgatas, who sit pervasively throughout lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, turning the Great Dharma Wheel and illuminating both past and present; this is not beyond their capacity. How could it stop at merely shaking the great trichiliocosm?
Furthermore, he once said to people: "As for the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation, there is nothing particularly marvelous about it; it is simply the power of deep faith."
What matters is practice. The Buddha said: "If a person merely recollects Amitābha Buddha, this is called the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna.
Tiantai said: "The four kinds of samādhi are all equally named 'recollection of the Buddha. The *Nianfo Samādhi* is known as the king among samādhis. Yunqi said:
"A single phrase of 'Amitābha Buddha' encompasses the Eight Teachings and perfectly subsumes the Five Schools. It is truly a pity [that people do not realize this]."
Nowadays, people regard the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha's name) as a trivial matter, a task for the ignorant and the unlearned.
Consequently, their faith is not deep and their practice is not diligent; they spend their days drifting idly, failing to achieve any realization of pure merit.
Some, wishing to profoundly clarify this Nianfo Samādhi through skillful means, instead direct themselves toward the investigation of the word "Who? (shuizi).
Superior! Little do you realize that the mind manifesting in a single thought is fundamentally beyond words and transcends all designations;

it does not require deliberate effort to become detached from them. Even the Buddha who is the object of recitation in this present moment is fundamentally beyond conceptualization and free from views.

Why labor to speak of "wondrousness" or "the primordial source"? It is simply a matter of being able to believe and remaining steadfast. Proceed directly with the recitation—whether ten thousand times by day and night.
Whether it be fifty thousand or thirty thousand [recitations], take the definitive and unerring standard as your measure. Vow that throughout this one lifetime you shall never change your resolve;
if, despite this, you fail to attain rebirth, then the Buddhas of the three periods would be speaking falsehoods. Once rebirth is attained, there shall be no further regression.
All manner of Dharma gates will manifest before you. You must by all means avoid the error of saying today it is Zhang’s turn and tomorrow it is Li’s.

Fourth: When encountering those of the Scriptural Teaching (Jiao), one again thinks of searching for chapters and selecting phrases; when encountering those of the Zen School (Zongmen), one again thinks of investigating questions and answers;
when encountering those who maintain the Vinaya, one again thinks of donning the robe and using the alms bowl. In this way, the head is never finished and the accounts are never settled.
How could such a person know that the recitation of Amitābha Buddha has become mature, or that the ultimate principles of the Tripitaka and Twelve Divisions of the Canon have been mastered?
All are contained herein. The pivotal mechanisms of the seventeen hundred koans are also contained herein.

The three thousand modes of dignified deportment, the eighty thousand subtle practices, and the three clusters of pure precepts are likewise contained herein. To truly practice the Buddha-remembrance (nienfo) by laying down the world of body and mind is itself great giving.
To truly practice the Buddha-remembrance so that greed, anger, and delusion no longer arise is itself great upholding [of the precepts].
To be truly able to practice Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*) without calculating right and wrong or self and others is itself great patience (*kṣānti*).

To be truly able to practice Buddha-recollection without even slight interruption or admixture is itself great diligence (*vīrya*). To be truly able to practice Buddha-recollection without the mind wandering in discursive thoughts is itself great meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
To be truly able to practice Buddha-recollection without being deluded by other paths is itself great wisdom (*prajñā*). Examine this for yourself.
If, regarding the body, mind, and world, you have not yet let go; if thoughts of greed, anger, and delusion still arise spontaneously;

if notions of right and wrong, or self and others, still linger in your heart; if interruptions and intermingling with worldly concerns have not been entirely eliminated; if discursive thoughts still pursue their objects without ceasing forever;
or if various divergent paths can still distract your will—then this cannot be called true mindfulness of the Buddha. You must reach [the state where...]
The state of "single-mindedness without distraction" has no other technique. When first beginning, you must use a counting rosary to keep the count clearly distinct.
Set a fixed schedule and ensure there are no omissions. After long practice until it becomes pure and mature, you will reach a state where you do not need to think of anything else;
at that point, whether you count or not does not matter. If you attempt to recite "fine words" from the very start, you will fail to achieve this.
You are attached to signs. You wish to study the perfect fusion and sovereign freedom, yet it is all because your faith is not deep and your practice is not diligent.
Even if you can expound the twelve divisions of the teachings or resolve a thousand and seven hundred public cases, these are all matters pertaining to the shore of birth and death.

At the moment of the end of life, they will certainly be of no use. In the winter of the tenth year of the Shunzhi era, I fell ill. I left instructions that after my cremation, [the ashes] should be ground into powder.

He ground his bones into powder and distributed them to birds and fish to form karmic connections with those in the western direction. On the twenty-first day of the first month of the following year, he rose at dawn;
his illness was completely cured. At noon, he sat cross-legged upon a rope bed, raised his hands toward the west, and passed away. He was fifty-seven years old.
Two years after his passing, he was cremated according to the Dharma. Upon opening the sarcophagus, his hair was long enough to cover his ears and his face appeared as if alive.
His disciples could not bear to follow his final instructions; they collected his remains and enshrined them in a stupa at Lingfeng (as recorded in the *Lingfeng Zonglun*).

Ruohui, whose courtesy name was Miaoyuan, was surnamed Tan and a native of Shuntian. He abstained from meat from his youth. At the age of twenty-nine, he left the household life and vowed to practice the dhūta austerities, never letting his side touch the mat.
Throughout his life, he burned a total of six fingers as an act of repentance for past karma, including the practice of "refining the crown" through burning.

His arms were countless. When he first arrived in the south, he practiced only asceticism. Later, moved by his fellow practitioners, he focused his mind on the Buddha until he completely forgot his own body and the world.
Upon seeing anyone—whether monastic or lay—he would not exchange pleasantries such as inquiries about their health.

He instructed others with fierce intensity and earnest sincerity. He traveled alone without companions and did not accumulate any extra possessions; he discarded his winter clothes in summer and gave them away entirely in winter.

In the summer, while staying at Suicao Hermitage, he said to Liu Daocheng, "To single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and exclusively seek rebirth in the highest grade of the highest level is the foremost primary meaning of spiritual progress. You will come to believe these words only on a future day.

In the autumn of the fifth year of the Shunzhi era, he passed through Qingjiangpu in Huai'an; the assembly there requested that he remain, but before long, he presented a single robe to Wande Hermitage.
The master addressed him, saying, "I shall depart before long; I have one matter to entrust to you. The master replied, "The Venerable One has only just arrived;
why speak so suddenly of departure? He said, "I am going to the West. You may cast my body into the current of the river."
He wished to universally establish karmic conditions for the attainment of a Pure Land with even the fish and insects; however, the host declined, saying he did not dare.

Huì said, "In that case, after my cremation, why do you not take my bones and mix them with flour to establish karmic conditions for me? How about that? The host replied, "Yes. He then ordered the purchase of large candles and fine incense.
None of the assembly could fathom his intention. On the nineteenth day of the tenth month, at the fourth watch of the night, he called out loudly to the host:
The main gate was quickly opened, incense was burned, and candles were lit. When the master had finished lighting the candles, he looked upon him; he sat there in silence and passed away.
A wondrous fragrance was perceived by those both near and far. In accordance with his final instructions, his body was cremated, his bones ground into powder, and they were cast into the river.
He was seventy-one years old (*Lingfeng Zonglun*).

Daqíng (Great Powerful One), whose courtesy name was Chōngfú and whose surname was Biān, was a native of Zhùjì in Shàoxīng. He entered the monastic life at the age of seven at Dàxióng Temple in his hometown.

Upon reaching adulthood, he heard of the reputation and teachings of Yúnqī; consequently, he crossed the river to pay his respects to him. Their spiritual affinities were perfectly harmonized, and thus [Daqíng] devoted himself entirely.
The Pure Land of the Mind. In his later years, he rested his staff at Dashaan Chan Hall. He held the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in high esteem and recited one fascicle daily.
He composed one hundred and eight poems on the aspiration for the Pure Land; here, four are recorded. The first says: "The seeds of the Buddha arise from conditions;
my great capacity is vast. My livelihood now is to close my door. Having refined my body until it is as light as a crane, I cross freely to the Land of Ultimate Bliss."
Flying straight on. One says: "I laugh at myself; this mountain monk can do nothing about it. Drifting through the world with a fervent heart, whenever I meet someone I speak of the West.
Pointing it out clearly takes but a single moment. Another says: "Suffering ends and sweetness comes as one reaches old age; the sound of the Buddha’s name flows like water from the teeth.
Few have seen the golden platform, yet the omen was in the courtyard locust tree; apply yourself once more with diligence."
"Do not resent Heaven. One version says: "Suddenly, thoughts arise like waves on a windless plain;
moment by moment they dissolve back into the state of no-thought. Who would know that even 'no-thought' is still too much? November, the sixth year of Shunzhi.
He manifested illness and personally wrote the inscription for his funerary casket, entrusting it with his final affairs.
When the appointed time arrived, he sat up, donned pure robes, and facing west, recited the name of Amitābha Buddha before passing away (from *Chan Master Chongfu’s Pure Land Poems and Postscript*).

Da Zhen (Great Truth), whose courtesy name was Xinyi and whose secular surname was Zhou, was a native of Wuling in Changde. While still in his swaddling clothes, he was already able to join his palms and recite "Namo Buddhāya.
Upon reaching the age for external studies, he did not associate with other children; instead, he gathered sand and drew figures on the ground to create Buddhist stupas.
Sometimes he sat cross-legged and observed his nose. At the age of nine, he went to Lianju to receive the precepts from Master Jiao and subsequently relied upon him as his teacher.
At fifteen, he shaved his head; at twenty, he entered Yunqi to receive full ordination. Zhen’s parents passed away one after the other, and he performed the funeral rites for them.
Zhen attended to his teacher with boundless care, remaining as devoted for several decades as he had been on that first day. After the master passed away, Zhen took charge of Lianju.

He composed the *Weishi heyang* (Echoes on Consciousness-Only) and simultaneously conferred the Vajra Jewel Precepts. He established the Great Compassion Maṇḍala and concurrently practiced both the ritual and principle-based repentances.
At the age of seventy-one, in the autumn, he manifested a slight illness; he gathered his lay disciples and instructed them to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
After seven days had passed, he bathed and changed his robes. Sitting cross-legged and holding prayer beads, he recited the Buddha’s name together with the assembly.
Shortly thereafter, both his voice and breath became still; a stream of tears flowed from his nose for over a chi. When more than an hour had elapsed, the crown of his head was still warm.

Previously, the lay devotee Zhou had dreamed that celestial music welcomed the True One as it departed toward the west; he hurriedly came with several kinsmen to receive the precepts at the hermitage.
Master Daosheng. Previously, on the first day of the New Year, he dreamed of Zhen sitting upon a lotus pedestal (from the *Lingfeng zonglun*).
Daoshu, Daoshu.
A native of Renhe, he mastered the Tiantai teachings and was devoted to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. He did not involve himself in worldly affairs. Shunzhi 10th year...
In the second year, he dreamed that he ascended the summit of Mount Yuping with a divine monk. In the sixth month of the following year, he suffered from a slight illness.
On the twenty-sixth day, rising early, he said to the assembly: "Last night I dreamed that a divine monk came to welcome me; could this be the same one who ascended Mount Yuping with me?
When all was quiet, he suddenly saw banners and canopies filling the sky and lotus flowers carpeting the ground. He then sat cross-legged and joined his palms.
He recited the title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* seven times and chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha more than a hundred times before passing away peacefully.
His complexion remained unchanged, and between his coffin and the table, a rare fragrance wafted intensely (*Complete Record of the Pure Land*).
Chongwen, Chongwen.
It is not known from whence he originated. He was a disciple of Master Yunqi Hong and resided in a quiet chamber in Nanzhu Village, Changshu.
Having lost the sight of both eyes, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Every night, he would ascend the seat to perform *yoga* rituals.

He ate [only once] every three days without ceasing. On the fourteenth day of the third month in the fifteenth year of the Shunzhi era, he sent his disciple Xingxian to inform the monastics and laypeople within the city, saying:
"Tomorrow I shall return to the West; I have specially dispatched you to bid me farewell. The next morning at dawn, a crowd of more than thirty people gathered.
Wén sat upon his bed and commanded his disciples to recite one scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra*. As they recited...
He entered nirvana. A fragrant aroma remained within his chamber for three days without dispersing (*Postscript to the *Jingtuyue*).
Jujong was a native of Wuxi, Changzhou. He lectured on the Tiantai *Zhi guan* and practiced the *Nianfo sanmei*. In instructing others...
Exhausted. In the sixteenth year of the Shunzhi era, he manifested illness. Having prepared warm water for a bath, he put on a single sandal.

Upon finishing the recitation of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he chanted the Buddha’s name ten times and wrote eight characters: "Vast and empty spiritual void; no place of coming or going. He then cast down his brush and passed away.
He remained seated in the lotus position for three days, his countenance unchanged (from the *Complete Record of the Pure Land*).
Du Ti (杜體), style name Yuejian (月見), surnamed Xu (許). His ancestors were from Jurong (句容) in Jiangnan.

Having served in the military in Dian and Qian, he inherited the rank of Commandant (指揮使) for his meritorious service and subsequently settled in Chuxiong. Ti did not wish to inherit the official post and departed for Chidang in Jianzhou.

Yan practiced the Way for three years. One day, he encountered an elderly monk who bestowed upon him the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. Upon reading it, he attained great enlightenment and subsequently left the household life.
He received full ordination from the Vinaya Master Samadhi Guang. Samadhi was the abbot of Baohua Mountain; when he was about to pass away, [he entrusted Yan with the lineage].
He was invested with the robe and bowl as the second patriarch of Baohua.

He practiced the Pratyutpanna Samādhi in seclusion, neither sitting nor lying down, nor leaning against anything, remaining standing upright day and night for ninety days. Monastics and laypeople from all quarters flocked to him in great numbers.

Throughout the year, there was not a single month in which he was not invited from both north and south to preside over the ordination ceremony. One day, he manifested a slight illness and said, "Do not bring me any medicinal decoctions;
seven days from now, I shall depart. When the appointed time arrived, he passed away in silence at the age of seventy-nine.
Upon his cremation, the form of a lotus flower was seen emerging from the midst of the flames, and more than one *sheng* of five-colored *śarīra* relics were recovered (from the *Baohua Shan Zhi*).
Lingu Gu (Forest Valley) was a native of Shaoxing. He resided to the southwest of Mount Luo, wearing tattered robes and hempen sandals, and did nothing but exhort others to recite the Buddha’s name.
One day, he saw a Buddha coming from within white clouds to welcome him, whereupon he passed away. The local people named his hermitage "White Clouds" (Baiyun).
Yun (from the *Complete Collection of the Pure Land*):
Wanyuan Wanyuan, surnamed Qiao, was a native of Changxing in Huzhou. He was by nature dull-witted; when people reviled him, he did not become angry, yet when they praised him...

He did not take pleasure in this. He devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the Buddha’s name for several decades. In the seventh month of the second year of the Kangxi era, he suddenly bound together a grass hut for himself.
Yuan Renzhi, who was well-acquainted with him, said to him, "Since you have already bound the hut, I shall go to Suzhou to sell tea;
upon my return, I will provide you with a mat. Yuan replied, "I appreciate your kind intention, but I fear I shall not wait for you. This continued until the ninth month.
One day, he suffered a slight illness and took nothing but plain water. On the sixth day, at noon, he entered his grass hut, sat cross-legged, and passed away (from the *Jingtu quanshu*).
Shengci (勝慈), whose courtesy name was Yule (與樂) and whose family name was Yang, was a native of Beiqiao in Chuzhou. He entered the monastic order at Jiuming Temple at the age of fourteen.

There he visited the Great Master Xizhu and studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, but he did not yet attain realization. At that time, the Great Master Bikkong was lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He went to the Siṃhaguhā (Lion’s Cave) to rely upon Master Ci. He once used the great matter of birth and death to awaken his parents;

they were moved to realization and both left the household life. At the age of twenty-nine, he was entrusted with the robes and bowl by the master from Western India. The following year, he presided over Jīfēng Temple (Chicken-Crowing Temple).
Later, he resided at Shàngshèng Ān (Supreme Vehicle Hermitage), taking only the Pure Land as his ultimate refuge. Before long, he manifested illness. As he approached the end of his life, he said:
Her mother said, "The boat of Amitābha can ferry one across the sea of suffering. Having spoken these words, she passed away.
This was on the seventh day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Kangxi era. She was fifty-seven years old. (From the *Xianshou zongcheng*).

At the time of his ordination, he was named Jiānmì (Firm and Dense). His secular surname was Wú, and he was a native of Shè County in Huīzhōu. In his youth, he served as a student of the Confucian classics.
