It was the beginning of spring (Lichun). He said, "In four days' time. He asked again, "What day is today? He replied, "Jiazi. [Huangbo] declared, "Today is auspicious.

He then rose from his seat, finished giving instructions for his final affairs, and lay down upon his pillow. At dusk, he arose, called the assembly together, and ordered them to prepare hot water for him to wash his hands twice.
He repeatedly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. When the assembly requested that he speak a verse, he composed it extemporaneously, saying: "Successor to the Ancestors."

The lamp of transmission receives empty echoes; opening the hall to preach the Dharma is like ghosts striking a gong. Today his nostrils have been straightened; upon the lotus pond he beholds Amitābha.
When the verse was finished, he became silent. The assembly called out, "He has passed away! He was sixty-seven years old.

His Dharma heir was Ji-hui, whose style name was Lüting; he also practiced the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance. At the end of his life, he composed a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, which ended auspiciously.
He passed away (from the *Houji* of the *Erlijuju*). Shiyuan, styled Shiyuan, was a native of Songjiang.
From his youth, he harbored aspirations for the transcendence of the world. When he was eighteen or nineteen years old, his parents were about to arrange a marriage for him.
Some days later, he fled to a temple at night and requested the abbot to shave his head; having done so, he proceeded to Baohua Mountain to receive full ordination.
His family reported the monk’s whereabouts to the authorities, who dispatched officers to track him down. Yuan returned wearing monastic robes and said, "My hair has already been removed;
it is too late for them. His parents confined him in a single room, where he sat in meditation daily and refused to eat.

He did not sleep; there was no end to it. Finally, he was permitted to leave the household life. In the city of Songjiang, there was a monk who established a ritual enclosure and prostrated himself before the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Before he had finished, he passed away, thereby completing his final task. Having done so, he went to Mount Jinshan and practiced the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* for a full hundred days.
In the twenty-fifth year of the Qianlong era, he resided at Tiantong Temple in Changzhou. Upon entering the Buddha-recitation hall, he chanted the name of the Buddha day and night without ceasing.

In the third month of the twenty-eighth year, he manifested a slight illness. He gathered the assembly to chant the Buddha’s name and emptied all the money from his pouches as offerings for three full days.
Having bathed and prepared his ceremonial regalia, he joined the assembly in entering the hall, where he sat in the lotus posture and continued chanting the Buddha’s name.
*Shi* (composed by the Vinaya Master Qi).
Hengyi, whose courtesy name was Shengxue, was surnamed Shen and was a native of Wujin in Changzhou. He left the household life at a thatched hut on Mount Qionglong.

He first visited Gaomin Temple in Yangzhou, where he subsequently studied the Tiantai school and mastered its teachings. He once stayed at Wensheng Pavilion in Suzhou, where he contracted a disease that caused him to cough up blood.
He moved to Xianyi Monastery on Bāngshān in Hangzhou, where his illness became severe. On a set date, he prepared a vegetarian feast to bid farewell to his fellow practitioners;
chanting the names of the Buddhas of the Western Paradise, he passed away. He once remarked that a monk from a certain hermitage had fallen... [text fragment].

Tuo did not observe the precepts. His fellow practitioner of the precepts tried to admonish him, but he would not listen. Later, when his illness became severe, he summoned his friend and said, "Because I did not listen to your words, I have come to this state.
Now, what shall we do? The friend replied, "In the West, Amitābha Buddha has made a fundamental vow:
that sentient beings who create karma need only recite the Buddha’s name ten times to be fully received and guided by him. Can you believe this, monk? The monk [replied], "I can."

He replied, "I believe it is so, but my strength cannot sustain me; what shall I do? His friend said, "It is no matter. Set up an image to the west of the bed and have him fix his gaze upon it without moving.
Burn incense in the burner and chant the Buddha’s name while holding the sick man's hand and commanding him to listen attentively.
After three days and nights, the sick man suddenly sat up and thanked his friend, saying, "Having been received by the Buddha, I have attained rebirth in the Middle Grade."
Raising his hand in farewell (as recorded by Seng Jingyun).
Huiduan—Huiduan.
His origins are not clearly known. He resided at Lian’an Temple in Hangzhou and daily recited the name of the Buddha tens of thousands of times. Later...
He resided at Shanfu Hermitage in Shaoxing. One day, he invited his fellow practitioner, the monk Chenggu, along with five or six other monks to the hermitage to chant the Buddha’s name.
When it was noon, he suddenly raised his hand and chanted several times in a loud voice; then, standing firm, he passed away.
He was over twenty years old. (Recorded by the monk Chenggu.)
Fazhen, whose courtesy name was Langru, was a native of Gaoyang County in Ruizhou. He received the tonsure under Master Guanxi Yuanwen.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled to Lingnan, where he resided at Danxia for the longest period. In his daily life, he devoted himself deeply to the Pure Land teachings. One day...

Once, while discussing the "Mu" (No-Character) kōan with a Chan practitioner, he harbored doubts for a long time until, suddenly, he attained a profound realization. He went to Haichang to pay respects to the Elder Zhengmu;
their spiritual resonance and words were in perfect accord, and he subsequently received the transmission of the Dharma.

In the twentieth year of the Qianlong era, the assembly requested him to preside over Haichang, where he propagated the Chan school while simultaneously promoting the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. In his later years, he resigned from his monastic duties and entered seclusion behind closed doors.
In the eastern part of the temple, he devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the Buddha’s name for eight years, never flagging despite the cold or heat. He once composed a verse that says:
"Holding the hundred-and-eight-bead rosary day and night, The lotus flower gradually emerges from the deep mud. Cast aside the rosary and let the lotus flower go."
The ancient Buddha has never been in the West. On the ninth day of the ninth month in his thirty-eighth year, he manifested a slight illness.
At dusk on the eleventh day, he summoned his disciples to entrust them with his final affairs. At noon the following day, he gathered the assembly to chant the Buddha’s name.
After the incense had burned more than two inches, he himself recited the *Xiao jingtu wen* (Short Text on the Pure Land); before it was half-finished, he passed away. (Narrated by Monk Gao Tang)

Fonian (n.d.), whose courtesy name was Shiyuan, was a native of Suzhou. When he was over thirty years old, a neighbor slaughtered a pig; as the entrails were being removed, the characters "Cao Cao" appeared upon them.
Startled, Fonian conceived the aspiration for enlightenment and entered the Tianzhu Hermitage at Shangjin Bridge to become a monk. Thereafter, he resided there.

At the Shrine of King Bohao, he took the recitation of the Buddha’s name as his daily practice. Whenever he received money, he would immediately purchase incense and flowers to offer to the Buddha and release various fish and birds.
In the third month of the forty-first year of the Qianlong era, he fell ill.

He dispatched his disciples to Shilin Monastery to invite monks to perform the *Jingtu chan* (Pure Land Repentance) for three days and to conduct one session of the *Yogācāra-yānaka-yamaka-mukha* (Yoga Fire-Feeding Ritual). When the period was complete, he prepared a vegetarian feast for the following day.
He summoned his disciples for a final farewell and recited the names of the Buddhas; his followers joined him in harmony. At noon, after burning three incense sticks, he sat upright and passed away.
During his ordinary life, he occasionally composed poems to encourage others to dedicate their merit toward rebirth in the Pure Land. His final poem reads:
"In the Western World, upon the wondrous lotus throne, Within the vision, a single flower clearly blooms. Red, white, blue, and yellow—no different colors; The mind..."
"May my heart only wish to behold the Tathāgata. It is further said: "Do not say that the path to the West is far; this very moment, with a snap of the fingers, one ascends the golden bridge.
Amitābha receives and guides with a subtle smile, praising you for your high observance of the precepts in this Sahā world.

(From the *Sengxiuxue Shu*) The Commentary states: Since the Buddha-dharma entered China from the Han through the Jin dynasties, those who transmitted the scriptures and explained their meanings have generally been the priority. Until...

Master Huiyuan first established the White Lotus Society and practiced the *nien-fo* samādhi, benefiting both himself and others; those who later spoke of Pure Land practice looked to him as their model.
When the Patriarch came from the West, he pointed directly to the original mind; when he taught at Caoxi, he simplified and prioritized the teaching of the Pure Land.
This is the supreme, ultimate pivot, transcending all expedient means.

From the masters of Tiantai, Yongming, Tianru, and Chu-shi onwards, having realized the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*), they further opened the gate of Buddha-recitation (*nien-fo*). Is this not the perfect fusion of nature and phenomena (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), which simultaneously encompasses the three vehicles?
Now, what is called "leaving home" (*pravrajyā*) does not consist merely of parting from one’s kin and severing attachments; it is truly...
This is to leave the home of the triple world. To be able to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is true renunciation.

If you gentlemen, by means of Chan enter the Pure Land, or through the Buddha-dharma clarify the mind, casting off your bodies amidst the mud and shedding the shell of saṃsāra like a cicada, this too is the great achievement of a true man of stature.
The fourth bhikṣuṇī to attain rebirth was Huìmù.
Her surname was Fù.
At the age of eleven, she left the household life and resided at Zhùgō Village Temple in Liángjùn. She recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily.
There were many miraculous occurrences. He once dreamed that he traveled to the Western Land, where he saw a bathing pool filled with lotus flowers.

Within it sat various beings born by transformation, who subsequently requested the Master to receive the precepts for them. Suddenly, at the site of the altar, he beheld heaven and earth radiantly bright, entirely the color of golden-yellow.
On one occasion, while prostrating before Amitābha Buddha together with the great assembly, he remained prostrate on the ground and did not rise. Or...

He kicked him and questioned him. [The monk] said: "When I was prostrate on the ground, I felt my body arrive in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). The Buddha preached the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* for me;
I had already mastered four fascicles when I was awakened by the kick. I deeply regretted this. This was during the fourteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
This year he was already sixty-nine; his end thereafter is not detailed (*Fayuan zhulin*).
Fasheng, whose secular surname was Nie, was a native of Qinghe. In the fourteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, at the age of about seventy, he left the household life.

At Jianfu Temple in Jinling, his talent and insight were sharp and awakened. He said to his colleagues Tanjing and Tanai, "My conduct in life and my practice of the Way have been directed toward the Western Land.
On the twenty-seventh day of the ninth month of the sixteenth year, he prostrated before the Buddha beneath a stupa.

In her later years she was no longer at ease, and her illness grew daily more severe. On the evening of the last day of that month, while dozing, she saw the Tathāgata descend from the sky, where he was discussing the Dharma of the Two Vehicles with two Great Beings.
His radiance shone brilliantly, and the members of the monastery were all struck with wonder. She related her vision in great detail;
having finished speaking, she passed away at the age of seventy-two (*Biqiuni zhuan*).

Jingzhen (淨眞), a person of the Tang dynasty, resided at Jixian Temple in Chang’an. Wearing patched robes, he lived by begging for alms and recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred thousand times.
He was devoted in his resolve to practice mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*). One day, he said to his disciples: "Within the fifth month, I have seen the Buddha ten times. Two...
He said, "I have witnessed the Bodhisattva-child playing upon a precious lotus flower; I have already attained rebirth in the highest grade.
Having spoken these words, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture, as auspicious light filled the temple (from the *Fozu Tongji*).

Fazang (Fa-zang), a person of the Tang dynasty, resided in Jinling. He was diligent in his resolve to practice the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). One night, he saw the radiance of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas illuminating the monastery.
He then passed away suddenly. (From the *Fozu tongji*)
Wuxing was a person of the Song dynasty who lived on Mount Lu. He was devoted to the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) and sought rebirth in the Western Paradise.

Suddenly, he heard the sound of celestial music from the sky and said to those around him, "I have already attained rebirth in the Middle Grade. I see all my fellow practitioners reciting the Buddha’s name with such diligence."
For those who advance [toward rebirth], there are always lotus flowers awaiting their birth. Having finished speaking, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Nengfeng of Qiantang was one who exclusively cultivated the Pure Land practices. He frequently saw the light of the Buddha illuminating his body. One day, without illness, he announced...
His disciple said, "The time for my rebirth in the Pure Land has arrived. A short while later, the assembly heard the sound of him reciting the Buddha’s name with great intensity.

When they went to look, he was already sitting facing west with palms joined, having passed away. A wondrous fragrance filled the room, and the faint sound of music drifted westward (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Huian, whose secular surname was Yang, was a native of Mingzhou. He resided at the hermitage of Xiaxi and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Western Pure Land.

He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* without ceasing, regardless of cold or heat. He frequently saw the light of the Buddha descending and illuminating his room. One day, manifesting illness, he sat upright and exhorted the assembly.
"Do not speak. After some time, he said, "The Buddha has arrived. He ordered the assembly to chant the name of the Buddha, and suddenly he passed away at the age of ninety-six (Fozu Tongji).
Zhu Jin (祩錦), courtesy name Taisu (太素), surnamed Tang, was a native of Hangzhou. He married Shen Sheng (沈生) of the same district, who was none other than Master Lianchi Hong (宏公).
When Master Hong left the household life, Jin was only nineteen years old. Some advised Jin to dissuade him, to which Jin replied: "I have thoroughly..."
Hearing that he [the Master] spoke of the great importance of the matter of birth and death, [the official] tried to dissuade him; this was a mistake on his part. It could not be.

When the Master reached the age of forty-seven, he also left the household life and received full ordination. He maintained a strict and solemn conduct and devotedly cultivated the practice of Pure Land. In the forty-second year of the Wanli era, he fell ill.
As he neared the end, he suddenly said to his attendant, "The sutras speak of rebirth through ten recitations. Quickly help me to rise. He rose.
He then sat upright in meditation, reciting the Buddha’s name, and passed away at the age of sixty-seven (*Xiaoyi'an Lu*).

Guangjue, whose secular surname was Gong, was a native of Chongming, Suzhou. At the age of twelve, he immediately abstained from meat and began to receive and uphold the sutras and dharanis. Each morning...
In the evenings, he paid homage to the Buddha with the utmost reverence. He vowed not to take a secular surname. At the age of twenty-eight, he shaved his head and donned the dyed robes.
He went to Hangzhou and resided at Xiaoyi Hermitage under Master Taisu. He maintained the Brahma-faring life with precision, remaining pure and unadulterated.

Being physically frail and delicate by nature, he disciplined his mind and mortified his body, never sparing himself of toil. Suddenly, he fell ill; he declined medical treatment and waited for his end with single-minded devotion. His breath grew faint and feeble.
He shook himself and suddenly rose, sitting upright in the full-lotus posture. The abbot set up an image of Amitābha Buddha for him;

Jue fixed his gaze upon it with intense concentration and, with palms joined, took refuge in the Buddha. Thereafter, he washed his hands, donned clean robes, and took up his prayer beads. With body erect, he faced the Buddha as if entering a state of meditative absorption.
A servant, fearing he might fall over, propped him with two pillows on his sides, but he waved them away, saying, "There is no need for this. The assembly—
He circumambulated while reciting the Buddha’s name. Again, he waved his hand and said, "I have my own master; do not trouble the assembly.
He sat cross-legged without moving for two full days and nights, softly chanting the Buddha’s name. His breath gradually grew more labored, and he passed away peacefully.
This was on the seventh day of the second month in the thirty-ninth year of the Wanli era; he was thirty-three years old (*Xiaoyi'an Lu*).

Chengjing Chengjing, whose secular name was Shixiu, was a native of Donggang in Guangzhou. From his youth, he observed the fasts and precepts; later, he left the household life and received full ordination.

He recited the Buddha’s name without ceasing for even a moment. He once exhorted the assembly to create a sandalwood image of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Great Compassionate One. [This occurred during the] Ming dynasty.

In his later years, he contracted a slight illness. Foreknowing that the time had come, he said to his disciples, "The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion, with a thousand hands and a thousand eyes, has come here to receive me.
I am departing. He then closed his eyes and passed away (*Guanyin Cailin Ji*).
Chaoyin (Tidal Sound), surnamed Jin, was a native of Changshu, Suzhou. She married into the Gong family and remained a widow, maintaining her vows of chastity.
Together with her son, Duanwu, she resolved to leave the household life. Once Duanwu had become a monk, Chaoyin also went to Suzhou and paid homage to the nun Zhenru as her preceptor.

The Master subsequently returned to his native village, where he repaired his dwelling to practice ascetic cultivation. Day and night, throughout the six periods, the sound of the Buddha’s name resounded vast and continuous.

One day, manifesting a slight illness, he bathed, donned his robes, and sat firmly in the central hall. At the hour of *rāhu* (the afternoon), he calculated the time, saying, "The hour of *hai* has arrived.
He drew his hands back into his sleeves and passed away while sitting upright. He was seventy-three years old; these events took place during the Shunzhi era of our dynasty. (Chao)
*Yinsi lüe* (A Brief Account of Sound Matters).
The treatise states: I have compiled records of ancient bhikṣuṇīs who cultivated pure practices and attained renown; they are but a few scattered individuals.
I suspect that those who transmitted these accounts may have been lost, or perhaps most remained submerged and followed worldly customs, with few capable of exerting themselves to rise above them.

As for those few who were able to be transmitted [as examples], they were generally those who could carefully maintain their recitations, uphold their firm vows, and manifest various auspicious signs at the time of death;
these were recorded and passed down as the orthodox path of practice.
Record of the Holy and Wise of the Pure Land, Volume Six;
Record of the Holy and Wise of the Pure Land, Volume Seven;
Section Five: Those Who Attained Rebirth as Human Kings.
The King of Ujjayinī was deeply devoted to the Buddha-dharma. He once said to his attendants, "Though I am a king who enjoys prosperity and pleasure, I cannot escape impermanence.
I have heard that the Pure Land of the West is a place where one may lodge the spirit; I shall now make a vow to seek rebirth there."

In that kingdom, he practiced the Way and meditated on the Buddha during all six periods of the day. Whenever making offerings to the Buddha or providing meals for the Sangha, the King and his consort personally served the food.
They did not cease this practice for thirty years. At the time of his death, his countenance was joyful and serene, and various auspicious signs appeared. (*Wangsheng ji*) The Commentary states:
Since the Buddhist teachings came to the East, there have been rulers of various nations who protected them with profound sincerity; such individuals have appeared in every generation without fail.
As for the auspicious signs of rebirth there, they are rarely recorded and cannot be described in detail.

In ancient times, when Yao governed the people of the world and brought peace to the administration of the realm, he went to visit the four sages on Mount Gaosheshan; he then became profoundly detached, as if losing his hold over the empire.
Indeed, for one who can truly take the Pure Land as their ultimate refuge, their attitude toward the world shall be just like this.
It is finished.
The sixth and seventh tens of thousands of Śākyas, both kings and ministers, have been reborn.
The Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove at Kapilavastu. He commanded his disciple Kālodāyin to go and convert his father, the King.
Upon arriving at the city of Kapila, Kālodāyin traveled through the air while sitting cross-legged by means of his supernormal powers.
There he praised the rare and marvelous virtues of the Tathāgata for King Śuddhodana, who then gave rise to a heart of reverence and faith, leading all [his followers]...

The Śākya went to where the Buddha was. After the Buddha had bestowed predictions upon each of the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, he then extensively expounded the three gates of liberation for the sake of the king. He further said, "All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma.
The king asked, "If all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, then all sentient beings should also be Buddhas. The Buddha replied, "If they are not inverted..."
To see sentient beings is to see the Buddha; what is called the Buddha is to see sentient beings as they truly are.
To see sentient beings as they truly are is to see the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). The limit of reality is the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
All phenomena are unborn; this is the gate of dhāraṇī. One should settle the mind within this Dharma and not rely on others.

At that time, King Śuddhodana and seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan heard the Dharma and attained realization; they attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha manifested a smile and spoke these verses: "The Śākyas possess decisive wisdom; therefore, within the Buddha-Dharma, their minds dwell with certainty.
Having ended their lives among humans, they shall be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, where they will personally attend upon Amitāyus and achieve fearlessness."

*Bodhi* (*Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*; *note: according to the supplementary record of the *Śuddhodana-rāja-parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the king was reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, therefore he is not included in this record).

Liu Chengzhi, courtesy name Zhongsi, was a native of Pengcheng. He lost his father at a young age and served his mother with filial piety. He was well-versed in the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi and did not abandon them.

At that time, Shi was serving as a military aide (*canjun*) in the local administration. Although high officials recommended him for office both before and after, he declined all offers with great resolve.
At that moment, Dharma Master Huiyuan was residing at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu, practicing the *nienfo sanmei* (Buddha-remembrance samādhi). Chengzi went there to rely upon him.

Huiyuan said, "Official rank and emolument are towering and magnificent; why would one not pursue them? Chengzhi replied, "The Jin house lacks the stability of a bedrock foundation, and the state of affairs is as precarious as a tower of eggs.
What could I possibly do? Because Liu Yu could not bend him, he styled him "Yimin" (The Left-Behind Man) to honor him.
At that time, there were the lay devotees Zong Ke, Lei Cizong, Zhou Xuzhi, Zhang Ye, and Zhang [Zhan].
Quan Pi, Ying, and the others all came to Mount Lu. There, before the statues of the Three Sages of the West, they established a fast and formed a society to collectively cultivate the pure karma.
Cheng Zhi engraved these words upon stone as a vow, which said: "Now that the principle of conditioned transformation is clear, the signs of coming and going become manifest.
Since the laws of shifting responses correspond, the retribution for prior good and evil must surely follow."
Thus it is. By reflecting on how those who once stood side-by-side have silently sunk away, one realizes that the arrival of impermanence is pressing;

by examining how the three retributions urge one another along, one knows that the perilous realms are difficult to escape from. This is why our fellow practitioners, the various worthies, are vigilant at night and diligent by day, looking upward in thought for a means of salvation.
For the spirit can be reached through resonance, but cannot be summoned by physical traces; it is essential that this resonance be present.
Regarding these objects, though the dark path is but a few feet away, if one seeks them without a guiding master, how can there be any ford across the vast, boundless expanse?

Now, fortunately, through a resonance that requires no prior consultation, our collective minds are directed toward the Western Realm. As we strike upon these verses to open our faith, our sincere sentiments burst forth from heaven.

Thus, the signs and images are communicated even in dreams; our joy exceeds that of a child returning home. Thereupon, the celestial designs manifest their brilliance, and their shadows match the work of the Divine Creator; this merit arises from—
The principle is harmonious, yet the matter is not within the scope of human effort; this is truly the manifestation of Heaven’s inspiration, where the dark workings of destiny have converged.
Nevertheless, their illustrious achievements vary and their merits are not uniform; though our morning prayers are identical, our evening returns are separated by distance.

This is truly lamentable for those who share the bonds of teacher and friend. Therefore, with deep sighs we have gathered by mutual command, straightening our robes in the Dharma Hall, and equally bestowed [our offerings] as one.
With a mind that harbors the profoundest depths, he vowed to join with fellow seekers to travel together into the remote realms. His extraordinary emergence was beyond compare;

as he first ascended to the divine spheres, he did not seek solitary excellence upon the cloud-capped peaks, nor did he forget the preservation of all beings within the secluded valleys. Thereafter, he wondrously beheld the celestial countenance, and his mind was opened to pure illumination.

Through awakening, his consciousness transformed the heart; through transformation, his physical form was renewed. He took refuge upon the lotus flowers amidst the flowing waters, seeking shelter beneath their shade.
With jade-like branches for his song, he let his cloud-robes drift to the eight extremities of space; floating upon fragrant breezes, he forgot the passage of years.

Facing the three miserable realms, he offered a distant farewell; looking up at the celestial palaces, he took his long leave. He succeeded the various spirits to continue their path and pointed toward Great Enlightenment as his destination.
To investigate this Way—how could it not be magnificent? Measuring out the ground north of the West Grove stream, he established a separate meditation hall.
He delved deeply into the fundamental principles and concurrently observed the prohibitive precepts. He composed the *Nianfo Sanmei Shi* (Verses on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection).

After residing there for half a year, while in meditative concentration, he beheld the Buddha’s light illuminating the ground, all of which turned to a golden color. Fifteen years later, while in the midst of reciting the Buddha’s name, he saw Amitābha Buddha;
his jade-like halo radiated light as he lowered his hands to comfort and welcome him. Cheng [the Buddha] said to him: "How can you obtain the Tathāgata?"
I rubbed his head and covered him with my robe. Suddenly, the Buddha rubbed his head and drew out his *kāṣāya* to clothe him.
On another day, he again dreamed of entering a pool of the seven treasures, where he saw lotuses of blue and white hues and water that was deep and clear.

A person with a halo around the neck and a *svastika* (*śrīvatsa*) emerging from the chest pointed to the water of the pool and said, "This is water of eight virtues; you may drink it. He drank of it.
The water he drank was sweet and delicious. Upon waking, a wondrous fragrance issued from his pores.
He then said to others, "My karmic connection with the Pure Land has reached its fulfillment. He invited monks to recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Lotus Sutra) for nearly several hundred times.
As he burned incense before the Buddha image, he prostrated twice and prayed, saying, "By the bequeathed teachings of Śākyamuni, I know that Amitābha Buddha exists. This incense..."
One should first make offerings to Śākyamuni Tathāgata, next make offerings to Amitābha Buddha, and furthermore make offerings to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It is by virtue of the merit of this sutra that one attains birth in the Pure Land.
Vowing that all sentient beings may likewise be born together in the Pure Land, one then parts from the assembly, lies upon the bed, faces west with palms joined, and passes away in serene stillness.
At that time, in the sixth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he was fifty-nine years old (according to the *Chusanzang jiji* in the *Donglin zhuan*).
Yu Chang—whose place of residence is unknown—served as a Recorder (*lushi*) during the reign of Empress Wu of the Tang dynasty; by day, he adjudicated official affairs.
At night, he would judge the underworld offices and always foreknow calamities and misfortunes, making secret preparations for them. This continued for six years.
Upon the death of his mother, he took up the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as his daily practice and no longer served as an official of the underworld.

At the age of eighty-four, as he was about to pass away, he suddenly smelled a wondrous fragrance and said to those around him, "The Sage of the West has come to welcome me. He then faced westward and repeatedly called out [the Buddha's name].
The Buddha’s Name and His Departure (*Baoying ji*). Maziyun:

his place of residence is unknown. He was recommended as a filial and incorrupt official (*xiaolian*) and served as the Magistrate of Jing County. He was appointed to lead the grain transport convoy for his local commandery.

He was appointed to oversee the transport of grain to the capital. His boat capsized, and ten thousand *hu* of rice were lost. He was imprisoned, during which time his son Yun concentrated his mind on reciting the Buddha’s name.
After five years had passed, he was released by imperial amnesty and lived in seclusion at a temple on Mount Nanling, observing the one-meal-a-day fast. This was in the tenth year of the Tianbao era.
He passed away at Jing. Previously, he had said to others: "Because my destiny was unfortunate, I have devoted myself to the practice of the Inner Teaching.
Now that my karma in the West is perfected, I shall be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. The next day, he bathed, donned new robes, sat upright with palms joined.
Suddenly, a strange fragrance filled the room. Ziyun said, "The Buddha has arrived," and he then passed away (*Jiwen*).
Wei Wenjin—whose origins are unknown—served in the Tang dynasty and rose to the rank of Observation Commissioner (*Guancha Shi*). He established a Western Path (Pure Land) center.

Chang was devoted to the practice of pure karma and sought rebirth in the Western Paradise. One day, while reciting the Buddha’s name, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room (Fozu Tongji).

Zhang Kang, Zhang Kang. His origins are unknown. During the Shijin (Later Jin) dynasty, he served as a Hanlin Academician. He recited the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* one hundred thousand times, seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land.
One day, while suffering from illness, he maintained only the chanting of the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, he said to his family members: "The West..."

The Pure Land was located right beside the main hall. Amitābha Buddha sat upon a lotus flower, while the old man and his son were on the golden sand of the lotus pond, prostrating and playing together.
After a long while, as soon as the Buddha’s voice fell silent, they passed away. The old man and his son were descendants of Kang;
at that time, they had already been deceased for some time (from the *Fozu tongji*).

Wen Yanbo, courtesy name Kuānfú, was a native of Jiexiu in Fenzhou. He served through four successive reigns—the Song emperors Rénzōng, Yìnzōng, Shènzōng, and Zhézhōng—occupying positions as both general and minister for over fifty years.
His official rank reached that of Grand Preceptor (Tàishī), and he once concurrently held the office of Commissioner for the Translation and Polishing of Scriptures.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lu. Having long placed his faith in the Buddha-dharma, he applied himself even more diligently to the Way in his later years.

He focused his mind exclusively on Amitābha Buddha, never slackening for even a moment whether walking or sitting from morning until evening. He made this vow: "May I always be diligent, assiduously cultivating all virtues;
may I realize the essence of the Mind and broadly deliver all sentient beings. While residing in the capital, he gathered with Master Jingyan.
One hundred thousand people gathered for a Pure Land assembly; at that time, many officials followed him and were converted.
He passed away at the age of ninety-two (*Dongdu Shilüe*, *Fozu Tongji*, *Fofa Jintang*).

Yang Jie, courtesy name Cigong, was a native of Wubei. He styled himself the "Man of Non-action" (Wuwei Zi). During the Yuanfeng era, he served as an official in the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Taichang).

Initially, he was devoted to the Chan school and studied under the Chan Master Tianyi. He investigated the kōans and teachings of Master Pang. Later, while serving as a ritual attendant at Mount Tai, he beheld—
As the sun rose like a platter surging from the sea, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. At the end of the Xīníng era, he returned home due to the mourning for his mother.

Living in seclusion, he read the Tripitaka and subsequently turned his heart toward the Pure Land. He painted a sixteen-foot Amitābha Buddha to keep by him for constant contemplation. These were his writings throughout his life.
Most [masters] point toward the Pure Land. The preface to the *Ten Doubts about the Pure Land* by Tiantai states:
"If one's attachment is not heavy, one will not be born in Saha; if one's mindfulness is not single-minded, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī. Saha is a defiled land; Sukhāvatī is a pure land.
The lifespan in Saha is finite; the lifespan in that land is infinite. Saha is replete with all sufferings; that land..."
Then there will be peace and no suffering in Sukhāvatī. In the Sahā world, one transmigrates through birth and death according to karma;

yet by going once to that land, one eternally realizes the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If one wishes to deliver sentient beings, one may do so at will with sovereign ease, no longer being driven by various karmic forces.
Regarding such distinctions as purity and defilement, lifespan and its duration, suffering and joy, and birth and death, sentient beings remain in profound ignorance;
how lamentable this is! Amitābha Buddha is the sovereign who embraces the Pure Land; Śākyamuni Tathāgata is the teacher who guides one toward the Pure Land;
and Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are those who assist the Buddha in propagating his transformation. Therefore, the Tathāgata...
Throughout the various scriptures of this one lifetime, there is earnest and repeated exhortation to aspire for rebirth [in the Pure Land].

Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, boards the vessel of the Great Vow to traverse the ocean of birth and death; they do not cling to this shore, nor do they linger on the far shore, nor do they halt midway.
Their sole buddha-activity is that of salvation. Therefore, the *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "If there be sons of good family..."

O virtuous woman, if one hears the teaching of Amitābha Buddha and upholds his name for one day, or even up to seven days, with single-mindedness and without distraction, then at the time of that person’s death, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings, will appear before them.
At the moment of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Furthermore, there is no...

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "If sentient beings of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should remember my land, plant roots of virtue, and with a sincere heart dedicate their merits toward rebirth in my land, yet fail to achieve it, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

For this reason, the Anityatā-śālā (Hall of Impermanence) was established within the Jetavana Vihāra, wherein the sick were instructed to face west and form the thought of rebirth in the Pure Land; this was because of Amitābha’s light.
The light universally illumines the Dharma-realm, mindful of sentient beings and embracing them without abandonment. The holy and the mundane are of one essence;

when the capacity and the response coincide, the sentient beings within the hearts of all Buddhas find every dust-mote to be Sukhāvatī, and the pure land within the minds of sentient beings finds every thought to be Amitābha.
Observing it from this perspective, those with wisdom easily attain birth, for they are able to sever doubt; those in meditative concentration also easily attain birth.
Because they are not distracted, those who uphold the precepts are easily born [in such states]. Because they distance themselves from all defilements, those who practice generosity are easily born.

Because they are free from the notion of "mine," those who practice patience are easily born. Because they are without anger, those who practice diligence are easily born. Because they do not regress, they are easily born.
It is easy for those who have neither committed good nor performed evil to be reborn there, because their mindfulness is single-minded.
It is also easy for those whose various evils have already been committed and whose retribution has already manifested to be reborn there, because they possess genuine shame and dread.

Even if one possesses many virtues, if one lacks a sincere heart of faith and a heart that dedicates merit and makes vows, then one shall not attain rebirth. Alas! Amitābha is very easy to hold in mind; the Pure Land is very easy to go to.
Sentient beings are unable to uphold [the precepts] and unable to travel [to that land]. What can the Buddha do for them?

Now, to create evil karma and enter the realms of suffering, and to mindfully recite Amitābha’s name to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—both are words of the Buddha. For worldly people to fear falling into hell yet doubt rebirth in the Pure Land—is this not a delusion?
During the Yuanyou era, he served as the Provincial Commissioner for Judicial Review in the Two Zhe circuits. When he was on the verge of death, he...
He spoke in verse, saying: "In birth there is nothing to cling to; in death there is nothing to abandon. Within the vast void, what 'zhi', 'hu', 'ye', or 'ra'?
To follow error with error—this is the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Previously, there was one named Wang Zhonghui, who served as a Counselor of the Ministry of Personnel.
Zhong Hui was from the same hometown as Jie. He once followed Jie to receive instruction in the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation. Zhong Hui asked, "How can one ensure that there is no interruption?
Jie replied, "Once faith has been established, not to doubt again is itself a great interruption. Zhong Hui leaped for joy at these words.

The following year, while Jie was serving as the magistrate of Danyang, he dreamed one night that Zhong Hui said to him, "Previously, I was fortunate enough to be guided by you toward the Pure Land; now..."
"I have attained rebirth there; I have come specifically to express my gratitude. Having prostrated himself twice, he departed.

Shortly thereafter, he received a letter of condolence regarding his son, which stated that Zhonghui had foreknowledge of the time of his passing and, after bidding farewell to all his relatives and friends, had passed away.

After Jie had died, later on, the consort of the Prince of Jing dreamed of traveling to the Western Paradise, where she saw a person sitting upon a lotus flower, their robes billowing, wearing a jeweled crown and necklaces.
He adorned his body. When asked who he was, he replied, "Yang Jie" (*Dongdu shilüe*, *Lèbāng wénlèi*).
Wang Gu (courtesy name Minzhong) was a native of Dongdu and the great-grandson of Wenzheng Gong Dan. His lineage goes back seven generations...
He maintained the precept against killing. In the past, he had further resolved to release one million living beings.

While traveling in Jiangxi, he investigated the matters of the Chan school with various senior masters such as Huìtáng and Yángqí. Subsequently, he composed the *Zhǐzhǐ jìngtǔ juéyí jí* (A Collection for Resolving Doubts Regarding Directly Pointing to the Pure Land).

He propagated the teachings of the Western Land. While living in seclusion, he never let his rosary leave his hand; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, he practiced pure contemplation (*śubha-vipaśyanā*) without interruption.

Furthermore, he once composed the "Preface to the Collection of Jewels on the Pure Land" (*Jingtu Baozhu ji xu*), in which he said: "When the minds of sentient beings are pure, the Buddha-land is pure.
The Dharma-nature is unborn, yet there is nothing that is not born. There is a Buddha, the World-Honored One, who now currently preaches the Dharma in the [Western] Ultimate..."
There is a Land of Bliss named Amitābha. Its conditions are supreme and its eon is long; its compassion is profound and its vows are vast.

It gathers all beings with boundless radiance and is adorned with inconceivable purity and wondrous beauty. Jeweled nets beautify the sky, and jade forests rise from the earth; its waters are pure, possessing the eight virtues.

Flowers bloom, emitting fourfold radiance; celestial music resonates throughout the six periods of the day. Petals scattered from the robes fill billions of lands, while all Buddhas join in praise and beings from the ten directions come to take refuge.
Within the mind of Amitābha, sentient beings are continuously gathered and transformed; within the minds of sentient beings lies the Pure Land.
In every thought-moment one is reborn, resting upon a precious lotus; yet without leaving one's current location, the spirit wanders through many lands. How could this arise from the self-mind?
It is like a mirror containing ten thousand images without coming or going, and like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers, fundamentally neither rising nor setting.

For those with the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden [teaching], all shall attain the stage of "one-life-to-enlightenment" (*ekajātipratibaddha*). To clarify the gate of skillful means, there are nine grades of distinction.
By recollecting the immeasurable light of one's original nature—which is fundamentally without thought—one is born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), which is truly non-arising.

Thus liberated from the wheel of suffering, even ten recitations transcend the Jewel Ground (*Ratnabhūmi*) and converge in the Ultimate Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). As for the Two Vehicles... [the text ends].
One realizes Bodhi; it is like a great ship carrying stones that avoids sinking, or like sailing with the wind at one's back where no obstacles remain.
To realize this, there is neither far nor near; to be deluded by it, even what is near becomes remote.

Alas! Learning is meager while hindrances are many; doubt is deep while contemplation is shallow. To dismiss [the Mahāyāna] as provisional or Hinayāna is as silent as if one were dead—thus did Aśvaghoṣa [lament].

Nāgārjuna [warned] against what has not yet occurred; Tiantai Zhiyi [lamented] those who do not understand. Failing to believe that one shall receive the prediction of Bodhi, they refuse to be born suddenly into the family of the Tathāgata.
Like caged birds or fish in a cauldron, they suddenly find themselves at play; like a horse in a crack or a candle in the wind, they falsely calculate their existence to be long-lasting.

In vain they receive a single retribution-body, and pointlessly they cast themselves into various realms of suffering. How could they know the praise and exhortation of the Great Hero, the golden mouth [of the Buddha]?

He was meticulous. He associated with sages and worthies in a single moment; he manifested the primary and secondary marks in an instant. When experiencing joy, he forever cast aside the five turbidities;

when increasing his compassion, he turned back to rescue those in the three miserable realms. Not knowing this is truly pitiable. During the reign of Emperor Huizong, he served as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue.
Due to the calamity of political factionalism, he was dismissed from office and soon passed away. A monk who traveled spiritually to the Pure Land saw an ancient...
Ge Fan was also among them. Fan was a native of Chengjiang and held the official rank of Chao-san-dafu.

Whether at his official residence or his private home, he invariably established a pure chamber where he set up images of the Buddha. One day, while he was engaged in ritual recitation, śarīra relics descended from the sky.
Subsequently, he passed away without illness, sitting upright facing west (from the *Song shi*, *Lebang wenlei*, and *Faxi zhi*).
Zhongli Jin.
A native of Kuaiji, his mother was Lady Ren, who practiced the Pure Land teachings with great devotion. As she approached her death, she exhorted Jin to cultivate the pure karma of the Pure Land.
From then on, Jin was moved to exert himself; he performed twenty acts of benefit daily. Later, while serving as an official in Western Zhejiang, he [associated] with Ciyun...

Master Shi composed the *Essentials for Rebirth* (*Wangsheng zhiyao*), and his pure cultivation became even more earnest. Lady Ren possessed a sandalwood Buddha image, which she used to wear upon her head while practicing the Way.
During this time, as Sengjin paid his respects and made offerings, several grains of śarīra suddenly burst forth from between its eyebrows.

Not long after, he was appointed as the Prefect of Kaifeng. One night at the hour of midnight, he suddenly rose and said to his family members, "The Lady informs me that the time for my rebirth has arrived.
He then sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. On the day before this, the entire family had dreamed that Jing was riding upon a blue lotus flower.
Surrounded by celestial music, he ascended into the air and departed toward the west. His disciple Jingrong held the official rank of Chaoling Dafu.
He constantly recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and cultivated the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. Having resigned from office, he built a thatched hut beside the East Garden in Yizhen. He once said:
To recognize Amitābha—Amitābha, Amitābha! Not to recognize Amitābha—what can be done? What can be done!
If you do not recognize Amitābha, Amitābha remains further beyond the Western Land. If you recognize Amitābha, Amitābha is simply within your own home. One evening.
He requested the monk Miaoying to recite the "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra. After burning incense and listening to the conclusion, he performed mudrās with both hands and passed away.
His great-grandson, Song, resided in Suzhou; together with Baoji, Shigong, and others, he formed a religious society to practice nianfo.
Without prior illness, he suddenly sat upright facing west, joined his palms, and passed away (from the *Fozu Tongji*).

Ma Xu, courtesy name Zhongyu, was a native of Hefei in Luzhou. While his father, the late Minister of Rites Ma Liang, was serving as the Governor of Hangzhou, the Venerable Shikun of Ciyun Monastery instructed him in the Dharma-gate of Pure Land.
Consequently, the entire family came to revere the Buddha. During the Yuanfeng era, Xu encountered a monk...
Guangchu initially obtained the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (Shiyi lun) of Tiantai and said with joy, "I have now found my place of refuge.

He subsequently followed the method of the Ten Recitations and Dedication (shinian huixiang fa) taught by Ciyun, practicing it for over twenty years. Later, he further corresponded with Wang Gu and became even more diligent in the recitation of the Buddha's name.
He constantly took the release of living beings (fangsheng) as his Buddhist service. Having served in succession as governor of Zichuan and Xinding, he governed with compassion and benevolence.
As for his administration, he was diligent in reciting sutras and dharanis and contemplating the Western Paradise according to a daily routine.
At that time, the consort of the King of Jing dreamed of wandering through a lotus pond and saw someone dressed in court robes sitting upon a flower. She said, "This is Yang Jie of Maxu.
By then, Jie had already passed away, yet Xiu was still alive. In the first year of the Chongning era, he fell ill; he bathed, changed his clothes, and sat upright.
She passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name. A vapor like a blue canopy rose into the air.

Shortly thereafter, some dozen family members all dreamed together that she said, "I have already attained rebirth in the Pure Land in the highest grade. That autumn, a maidservant fell ill while lying in bed;
she also passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name. Her son, Yongyi, likewise practiced the method of ten recitations and cultivated the sixteen contemplations for over thirty [days].
In his later years, he fell ill. He beheld Amitābha Buddha and two Bodhisattvas coming to welcome and guide him.

He formed mudrās and passed away peacefully; a fragrant aroma filled the room. After the body was enshrouded, five-colored flowers grew upon the coffin, their radiance brilliantly shining. (From *Lèbāng wénlèi*)
Jiang Gongwang, courtesy name Minbiao, was a native of Yanzhou. He passed the jinshi examination and, in the first year of the Jianzhong Jinggu era, was appointed as Left Censor-in-Chief.

Shortly thereafter, he was sent out to serve as the Military Governor of Huaiyang Commandery. When Cai Jing administered the government, he harbored resentment toward those who offered remonstrances and subjected them to persecution.
He governed Annam. In his daily life, he and his wife, Lady Yu, maintained a vegetarian diet and observed pure fasting, practicing the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).

He composed the "Essay on the Expedient Means of Buddha-Recollection," which states: "Regarding the dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane worlds, if one wishes to achieve them with ease and efficiency, there is nothing like binding the mind to a single object.
This is as when reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha: there is an expedient skill in this that does not require the movement of the mouth."
A sound issues forth. Subtly striking the front teeth with the tongue-root, the mind’s thought accords with it, and the sound becomes distinct.

The sound does not exceed the cavity, yet the faculty of hearing merges inwardly. The mind seals the mechanism of the tongue; as that mechanism draws out the root of thought, one enters the stream through hearing and turns the hearing back toward one's own nature.

These three elements—sound, hearing, and mind—converge, becoming perfectly integrated in every thought-moment. After a long time, this eventually results in the contemplation of mind-only consciousness. If...

These are people of keen faculties. Moment by moment, nothing arises; thought after thought, there is nothing to be grasped. The six sense-faculties are profoundly still, and the various consciousnesses are eliminated.
Every phenomenon is entirely true, and every gate is free from dependence. In a mere flash, they thus achieve the contemplation of reality as it is.

Beginners and later students should single-mindedly collect their thoughts upon the Tathāgata; even while attending to household affairs or performing various types of labor, they likewise do not [disturb this state].

They mutually obstructed one another. [The Master] completely restrained the six sense faculties, maintaining pure mindfulness in succession. Within no more than ten days or months, he attained samādhi.
This is what is meant by "the mind itself creates the Buddha," "the mind itself is the Buddha," and "the mind itself sees the Buddha.

His son had died young and appeared to him in a dream, entreating his uncle to go to Tianning Temple and recite the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* to pray for rebirth in a good realm. Furthermore, [the son] said that he had seen...

An inscription on a stone stele in the underworld states: "Master Jiang Gongwang held the office of censorial responsibility, yet his aspirations were directed toward the realization of suffering and emptiness.

He personally devoted himself to ascetic practice, his mind free from worldly attachments. In both movement and stillness, he did not violate the Buddha-dharma; whether speaking or remaining silent, he was always in accord with the essential spirit of the school.

His name shall be enrolled among those liberated from the dark gates of the netherworld, and his body shall surely return to the Pure Land. Later, having encountered a general amnesty, he was permitted to return to the world, where he passed away peacefully without illness. (From the *Song Shi*)
*Lebang wenlei* (The Literary Categories of the Land of Bliss; A Golden Bulwark for the Buddha-Dharma).

Chen Guàn, courtesy name Yíngzhōng, was a native of Shā County in Nánjiàn Prefecture. During the reign of Emperor Huīzōng, he served as the Left Palace Attendant Censor (*zuǒsìjiàn*) for his uprightness.

The Way had no place for him, so he soon left office to serve in a provincial post. Subsequently, he returned to serve as the Vice Director of the Right Bureau and acted as an Acting Secretariat Drafter.

Having offended Chancellor Zeng Bu, he was sent out to govern Taizhou. During the Chongning era, he was placed under administrative detention in Yuanzhou, later transferred to Tongzhou, and subsequently exiled to Taizhou.
Initially, Lü Guàn had been fond of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and styled himself the "Avataṃsaka Layman. Later, upon meeting Ming...
Dharma Master Zhi called upon the fundamental tenets of Tiantai. Mingzhi showed him the inconceivable object of the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* for those of superior faculties;

by subsuming cultivation within nature (*xing*), he perfected the practice of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). He attained a profound realization and, upon entering Taizhou, cast aside his books and no longer composed writings, devoting himself exclusively to the cultivation of the *nien-fo samādhi*.
In the postscript to the *Tiantai Shiyi Lun*, he wrote: "The human mind has no..."

The Dharma is eternally without fixed form; the myriad variations of mental phenomena all have their root here. To believe in this is to believe universally—this is why the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of the "Ten Faiths.
To doubt this is to doubt universally—this is why the *Zhizhe Sanmei Jing* speaks of the "Ten Doubts.
To emerge from doubt and enter into faith is to enter once and enter forever; one never departs from this and attains the ultimate state. The Pure Land is that ultimate state.
In this place dwells the Lord of Dharma named Amitāyus. This Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma has never ceased;
yet, if doubt obstructs one's ears, one will be deaf and fail to hear; if doubt obstructs one's mind, one will be muddled and fail to awaken.
Failing to hear and failing to awaken, one remains settled in evil habits, praising non-recollection, following along with a coarse mind, and falsely pointing to the lotus-womb as being empty.
Alas! One ultimately does not reflect upon this body of segmented existence—from where it was obtained, from whence it came, or where the impurities of the womb-prison truly reside.
Relying on karmic consciousness, one isolates oneself from the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Within a single illusory realm, failing to realize that "this" is not "that," one remains unenlightened through successive births, forever severing the path to the sages. For these reasons, Śākyamuni Tathāgata gave rise to great compassion.
Out of compassion for those within the defiled and turbid world, he utters a great voice to praise the sublime and wondrous bliss of that Pure Land.
Amidst birth and death, he acts as a great mariner, ferrying beings across upon the Dharma-boat to reach the other shore. Day and night he delivers sentient beings without ceasing.
Yet, the shore of Amitābha is fundamentally without "this" or "that," and Śākyamuni’s boat is truly not one of coming and going. This is an analogy.
It is like a single lamp illuminating eight mirrors; though the mirrors are positioned east and west, the light and its reflection are not two.

Amitābha’s preaching of the Dharma pervades all within these reflections, yet Śākyamuni, through his skillful means (*upāya*), points specifically to the western mirror. Therefore, those who have already reached the other shore can forget the distinction between self and other;
but for those who have not yet entered the *dharmadhātu*, how could they themselves obliterate the distinction between east and west? Within this Dharma, if...
It is not yet ultimate. Do not stagnate in partiality; do not distinguish between self and other. One need only maintain right mindfulness and sincere faith.
This is the intent of these two sages, and it is that by which the wise place their trust. Faith is the mother of all virtues; doubt is the root of all evils.
If one can follow its mother and weed out its root, then the various obstacles and conditions previously mentioned—
The deaf may regain their hearing; the obscured may regain their awakening. Those not yet born from birth-and-death shall attain birth from birth-and-death;

those not yet born into the Pure Land shall attain birth in the Pure Land. Following the instructions of Śākyamuni, they go to face Amitābha; following the vows of Amitābha, they come to assist Śākyamuni.
Remaining here while traversing the ten directions, they enter all mirrors from the West. From these two Sages...
Since its establishment, people such as these have been as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. How can one fail to believe? How can one harbor doubt?
Having attained self-confidence, one further employs skillful means to ensure that those who have not yet believed shall have no one left unconverted;
this is precisely why the wise act out of compassion. After five years, he again served as a Lang (Court Official) and moved to reside in Chuzhou. Passing through Lu...
Shanjia once said to his close associates, "In years past, when I encountered hardships and calamities, my only fear was death;
now, however, both life and death are cast aside beyond my concern. He subsequently passed away at the age of sixty-five (as recorded in the *Dongdu shilüe*, *Fozu tongji*, and *Li Zhongding ji*).
Wang Zhong, courtesy name Wang Zhong, was a native of Jiahe. He resided on Mount Gu at Qiantang. During the Zhenghe era, he was nominated as a recluse but did not accept the appointment.
Later, he attained the rank of Chao-san Dafu. He once studied under Chan Master Xiaoben but had not yet attained any realization. One day, he happened to hear a monk reciting:

Having been moved by the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, he subsequently devoted himself single-mindedly to pure practice. He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* seven times daily and chanted the Buddha’s name ten thousand times, never ceasing for nineteen years.
He established a Lotus Society at his residence, welcoming both monastics and laypeople, as well as those of high and low status, all of whom were permitted to join.
One day, without prior illness, he bathed, faced west, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
(Jilebang Wenlei). Zhang Di was a native of Qiantang.
He held the office of Assistant Teacher (Jiaozhu) and received the Bodhisattva precepts from Vinaya Master Yuanjing, specializing in the cultivation of the Pure Land.
Jiye made a vow before the Buddha by burning his arm as incense. Every time he invoked the Buddha’s name, his voice was forceful and resolute;
even when he lost his voice, he did not cease. Once, in a quiet chamber, he saw a white *piṅgala* bird dancing before him.
There was also a boy with green hair who joined his palms in greeting. Three years later, facing west and reciting the Buddha’s name, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Hu Yin, courtesy name Dafu, was a native of Qiantang. He held the official rank of Xuan-yi-lang and retired from public service in his later years.
He was a close associate of the Vinaya Master Qingzhao. One day, he fell ill; his son invited Qingzhao to visit him and said, "Dafu’s life-long [friendship] with..."
Huiheng and [Wang] Yin were good friends. [Huiheng] asked, "How can you not know of the great matter at the end?
Yin said, "I thought that if the mind is pure, then the land is pure. Qingzhao asked, "At all times, is there no defilement from discursive thoughts? Yin replied, "I am not yet able to do so.
Qingzhao said, "If this is the case, how can the mind be pure and the land be pure? Yin said, "The sutra says that one recitation of Amitābha..."
"Amitābha Buddha can extinguish the sins of birth and death accumulated over eight billion kalpas. Why is this? Qingzhao said:
'Amitābha Buddha possesses great vows, great majestic virtue, and inconceivable radiance and supernatural power, exactly as described in the sutras.
By reciting His sublime name even once, the defilements of sin naturally vanish; it is like the blazing sun at its zenith—how could frost and snow remain?'"
Liu Yin was greatly enlightened. He then single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name and invited monks to assist him for several months.
Finally, when Qingzhao arrived, Yin said, "Why have you come so late? You and Guanshiyin and Dashizhi have already graced me with your presence for a long time.
Qingzhao and the assembly of monks together raised the Buddha’s name, and Yin passed away peacefully (from the *Lebang wenlei*).

Feng Jie, whose courtesy name was Jichuan, was a native of Suining in Shu. He passed the imperial examinations through the Imperial Academy. Initially, he attended upon Chan Master Foyan Yuan and attained a realization.
He subsequently attended upon Chan Master Dahui Zonggao; entering the mountains to observe the summer retreat, he achieved profound awakening. Thus it was.

He concurrently cultivated the practice of purity and composed a ritual for the Repentance of Amitābha. During the Xiangshou era, when he was appointed as the regional commander of Luchuan, he led both monastics and laypeople in holding "Mindfulness Assemblies," taking the Western Paradise as their ultimate refuge.
At that time, following the military upheavals of the Jianyan era, many famous temples and their Tripitaka collections had been destroyed by war.
He therefore allocated his official stipends to produce forty-eight sets of the Great Canon and four sets of the Small Canon.
These [copies] were likewise produced in that same number and distributed among various lands. He recorded in his vow-text: "My gift of scriptures is twofold in purpose.
To produce the scriptures by means of wealth is called the gift of material things (*āmiṣadāna*); to transmit the Dharma by means of the scriptures is called the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*)."
The gift of material wealth shall bring the retribution of merit and fortune among devas and humans; the gift of Dharma shall bring the retribution of worldly wisdom, eloquence, and preeminence.
One should know that both types of retribution are causes for saṃsāra and the root of suffering. I now make this vow:
may these two types of retribution be transformed so that, at the time of death, I may be adorned and reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

With a lotus flower as her womb, she took up residence therein; there she beheld the Buddha and heard the Dharma, awakening to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and ascending the stage of non-retrogression to enter the rank of a Bodhisattva.
Returning once more to the realms of the ten directions and amidst the world of the five turbidities, she manifests her body everywhere to perform the work of a Buddha.
By virtue of her present causes of both material and Dharma-giving, she is like the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, endowed with great compassion.
I shall travel through the five realms of existence, manifesting forms according to the various classes of beings to preach and recite the wondrous Dharma.

I shall awaken those who have not yet realized it, causing them to leave the path of suffering forever and attain wisdom. May all sentient beings everywhere attain Buddhahood; this is my vow for bestowing this scripture.

Later, while serving as the Governor of Qiong Prefecture, in the autumn of the twenty-third year, I requested retirement. I informed my relatives and acquaintances, setting October the third as the date.
The announcement of his passing was made. When the appointed time arrived, he ordered a high seat to be set up in the rear hall. He received visitors as he had during his lifetime.

As noon approached, he donned his ceremonial robes and cap and performed a solemn prostration facing the imperial palace. He then requested the Transport Commissioner to assume the administration of the prefecture. Putting on his monastic robes, he took his place upon the high seat and addressed the assembled officials, both secular and clerical, saying:
"Each of you should turn toward the Way and establish the banner of the Dharma. Thereupon, he picked up his staff, rested it upon his knees, and sat in profound stillness.
The Canal Commissioner said, "In your coming and going as an Anfu [official], you are so free and easy. Why not leave behind a verse to commemorate this extraordinary feat?
Jie then opened his eyes wide, took up a brush, and wrote: "Three on the first, eleven on the last; nine in the middle, seven at the bottom.

The old man has spoken his fill; Guige’s eyes are red. There exists a record of his sayings (*yulu*) and verses on ancient cases (*songgu*) that circulate in the world (found in the *Wudeng huiyuan* and the *Lianzong baojian*).

Wu Bingxin, courtesy name Zicai, was a native of Mingzhou. During the Shaoxing era, he held office at court; having come into conflict with Qin Gui, he was expelled as a member of the political faction.
Upon returning home, he built a hermitage south of the city and sat in meditation day and night. He fashioned a coffin and slept within it every night.
At the fifth watch, he ordered a youth to knock on the coffin and sing: "Wu Xinsou, return! Return! There is no peace in the three realms; one cannot dwell there.
In the Western Pure Land, there is the lotus womb; return! Upon hearing this chant, [the deceased] immediately rose and practiced meditation and recitation. After a long time, Hui died.
He was summoned as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, but soon thereafter was sent out to serve as the Prefect of Changzhou. In the twenty-sixth year.
He was summoned once more to the post station of Xiāoshān. After sitting for a short while, he ordered his family members to listen quietly. They all heard the sound of celestial music.
He then said, "I have lost mindfulness and arrived here from the Pure Realm. Now that the golden terrace has arrived, I shall proceed."
Having finished speaking, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
As for Zhang Lun:
his origins are unknown. He served as the Vice Commander-in-Chief of the Western Zhejiang Circuit. He was a devout practitioner of the Pure Land and once requested—
Gaozong inscribed the two characters "Lotus Society" (Lianshe) and had them painted upon his residence. He composed a record for it, saying:
"I, your servant, have once read the scriptures of India and learned that there exists a world-transcending realm called Sukhāvatī. In that land dwells a Buddha named Amitābha.

When he first ascended the throne and assumed the reign, he renounced it and did not dwell therein; rather, he attained solitary awakening and realized sainthood through his mind. By means of the power of his great vows, he universally delivers all beings."
All of it. That land is entirely adorned with the most exquisite and wondrous jewels. The ground is all of pure gold. It is free from the dangers of mountains, rivers, hills, and valleys.
Its climate is perpetually spring-like, devoid of the fluctuations of yin and yang, cold and heat. There is no suffering of hunger, cold, old age, illness, birth, or death.
There is no turbidity of the mixed dwellings of the five destinies. By means of these various supernormal powers and skillful expedients, he skillfully guides the multitude.

Giving rise to joy and engendering faith, if one can, throughout daily life, produce a single thought-moment to recollect the name of that Buddha, then this single thought-moment—purified, matured, complete, and perfect—will merge with True Suchness (tathatā) and become one with the Dharma-nature (dharmatā). When the illusory body perishes, this nature does not cease;
in a single kṣaṇa, the Buddha-land will appear before one, like taking back a deposit by presenting the left half of a tally.

I, your servant, have respectfully heard his discourse. He has been diligent and resolute in his spiritual progress without interruption; for many years now, he has focused his mindfulness solely upon the Buddha.

All members of his household, from the young to the old, have followed his transformation. Consequently, he cleared the eastern wing of his humble cottage, excavated a pond, and planted lotuses, emulating the legacy of Huiyuan’s establishment of the White Lotus Society.
Daily, he leads his wife and children in reciting the name of the Buddha ten thousand times, and furthermore, throughout the year...
In the final month of spring or autumn, having selected an auspicious day, he gathered at the Pujing Monastery with those who shared his faith in the Way.
Thereupon, those who saw or heard of this rejoiced; they assembled like clouds and flocked like rivers, the sound of chanting the Buddha’s name surging forth like the tide rising upon the Yangtze.
Master Huiyuan founded this society in the past; from that time until now, several hundred years have elapsed, during which both monastics and laypeople have looked up to it with admiration.

Among the remaining followers who have inherited his lofty spirit, there has not been a lack of individuals throughout the generations; yet, for the most part, they remained obscure and unremarkable, as silent as wood or stone.

How fortunate I alone am to have received from His Majesty, the Most August Emperor Guangyao Shousheng, the personal gift of these two great characters, "Lotus Society" (Lianshe), written with the imperial brush.
These celestial calligraphic marks and divine strokes are something never before encountered; now, ten thousand eyes behold them together.
I, Zhan, am filled with joy and exultation. This is not merely to transmit and display [this record] within Yunlin, to celebrate a magnificent encounter spanning a thousand years;

rather, I truly wish that all those throughout the world and future generations who encounter or hear of this may universally attain the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) and ultimately achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.
How can the extent of such benefit be measured? I have therefore carefully engraved it upon metal and stone, to honor and proclaim this great and manifest glory.
Regarding Miñgan (from *Lèbāng Wénlèi*): his secular surname was Li.
It is not detailed where he originated from. At the end of the Shaoxing era, he served as an official of the inner court. He held office through three reigns and attained the rank of Wǔgōng.

The Grand Master served as the Director of the Imperial Pharmacy and requested a palace temple appointment to retire from office. In his prime, he developed a devotion to the Chan school and studied under Chan Master Zide of Jingci Monastery, where he attained a realization.
Subsequently, he turned his heart toward the Pure Land, carving copies of the *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* (Pure Land Text of Longshu) to exhort the world.

He maintained his recitations with such diligence and sincerity for over thirty years that his son, Yuanzhang, joined him and other like-minded practitioners to form a society for the cultivation of pure karma.

He was at Chuánfǎ Temple when he joined the assembly. In the autumn of the fourth year of Jiatai (1204), he fell ill; he reduced his food and rejected medicine, yet his countenance and spirit became even more alert.
When winter arrived, he suddenly saw the manifestation of Amitābha in a dream. Seven days later, at dawn, he saw golden flowers filling the room.
He called his two sons to help him up, bid farewell to his relatives and friends, and asked for a brush to write: "Sixty-one years have come to an end."

"His discourse was disordered; yet his slight insight was actually quite good. Now he has gone straight toward the Western Land, where for ten thousand kalpas he shall forever be free from the aging of birth and death.

He set down his brush, adjusted his hands into a mudrā, and passed away. (*Lèbāng Wénlèi*; [Note: In the *Wǎngshēng jí*, a eunuch official who held a ceremonial parasol and served in the inner court is mistakenly identified as a palace eunuch.
However, according to Song regulations, there was no precedent for eunuchs to petition for temple honors, and furthermore, how could such a person have had two sons?)]
Lu Yuan, courtesy name Ziyuan, was a native of Shanyin, Kuaiji. He served in successive offices until he reached the rank of Assistant Director of the Court of Palace Revenues.

Subsequently, he was transferred to an external post and served as the Commissioner for Maritime Trade in Fujian. Later, having incurred the displeasure of the authorities, he lived in retirement; his home was on the banks of the Hengxi River in Mingzhou.
He habitually upheld the Lotus Sūtra. Upon rising at dawn, he would bathe and burn incense, first chanting a verse that said:
"Washing my hands at early dawn, the palm-leaf scrolls unfold; I seek not the Buddhas nor do I ward off calamities. Where worldly conditions are severed, let them be severed by others;
amidst the flames of the kalpa-fire, I shall dance once more. Thereafter, he opened the scroll and read it, neither too slowly nor too hurriedly, his voice like a string of pearls. Day after day...
At first he recited one fascicle [of scripture] daily. In this manner, after thirty years, having reached the age of eighty, he increased his recitation to three fascicles.
He further recited the name of Amitābha Buddha, directing his mind single-mindedly toward the West. At the age of eighty-five, he bathed, changed his clothes, and passed away.

From between his mouth and nose there issued the fragrance of lotus flowers, rich and pervasive, which did not cease for an entire day. This event occurred in the fifth year of the Shaoxi era (as recorded in the *Wen'ei Manuscript Collection*, "Biography of the Dharma Master").
*Jixi Zhifa Hua Chi Yan Ji* (Record of the Efficacious Experiences of the Lotus Sūtra Upheld by Joyful Resolve).

Qian Xiangzu, courtesy name Tongbo, was a native of Taizhou. He began his official career as Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Taichang Cheng*) and, during the Kaixi era, served as a Vice President of the Council of State (*Canchi*).
In matters of statecraft, he conspired with Shi Miyuan to jointly execute Han Moxiu, upon which the realm relied on him for stability.

In the second year of the Jiading era, he was appointed Left Chancellor; shortly thereafter, he resigned and returned home. Initially, Xiangzu had sought the Way from Master Yuan of Cican, investigating the Great Matter until he attained realization.
Subsequently, he turned his heart toward the Pure Land. During his tenure guarding Jinling, he established a reception monastery in his native district.
There were ten locations, all of which were named after the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). He established a hermitage there and dwelt within it, engaging in discourse with eminent monks.

After his retirement from official service, he applied himself even more diligently to his spiritual practice. In the fourth year of the Jiading era, he happened to fall slightly ill and wrote a verse, saying:
"The fragrance of the lotus comes from the Buddha-land; Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, all dust and defilement are absent. My own mind is pure and transcends that very realm."
"Today I know from afar that one flower has blossomed. When a monk came to inquire after his well-being, he replied: "I do not crave life, nor do I fear death.
I shall not be reborn among the heavens, nor among humans; I shall only be reborn in the Pure Land. Having spoken these words, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away.
At that time, celestial drums resounded and extraordinary fragrances filled the air. The people of the district all heard a voice from the sky saying: "Qian..."
