The Chancellor should be reborn in the Pure Land of the West as the Bodhisattva Ciji (from the *Fozu tongji*, *Xugangmu wangsheng zhuan*, and the *Taizhou zhi*).

Zan Dingguo, styled Shengzhai, was a native of Mingzhou. He served as a lecturer at the Prefectural School and constantly cultivated the practices of the Pure Land. He established a "Society for Returning West" (Xigu She).
At the beginning of the Jiatai era, he constructed a Pure Land Cloister at Huiguang Temple in Xiajiang and erected stone stupas within its pond for the sake of his fellow villagers.

This is the place where the people store their bones. On the twenty-eighth day of every month, they assemble the clergy and the laity to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the Buddha’s name, creating wall-niches and paintings to encourage others to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
There was an ironworker named Mr. Ji who was nearly seventy years old and had lost his sight;

because he received from them the paintings for mindfulness of the Buddha, his two eyes became clear after he had recited up to the fourth painting. He continued in this manner for three years until he had completed all seventeen paintings.

One day, while he was reciting the Buddha’s name, he suddenly fell into a swoon. After half a day, he revived and said to his son, "I have already seen the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Western Paradise.
The Imperial Instructor Zan was the primary one who exhorted me; you should divide these six paintings and give them to him, and convey my thanks on my behalf.
He then sat facing west and passed away. In the fourth year of the Jiading era, Dingguo dreamed that a young attendant informed him: "The Buddha..."

"I now inform you: in three days, I shall be reborn in that land. On the appointed day, he bathed, changed his clothes, and while continuously reciting the Buddha's name, he sat upright and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Mei Ruren. A native of Changshu.
He served as a district magistrate and was devoted to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism. One night, he dreamed that a monk gave him a piece of paper with eight characters written in two lines.
He asked Master Dongling Zhao about them. Zhao said, "Two eights make sixteen. Could it be sixteen?"
This is what is meant by the *Contemplation Sūtra*. Once, as he was giving the sūtra to a monk, it suddenly vanished.

From then on, he recited the sūtra and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, adopting the name "Wangsheng" (Born in the Pure Land) to manifest his resolve. The monk Daosheng of Poshan Mountain initiated the creation of a sixteen-foot image of Amitābha.
"You were able to bestow a hundred thousand pieces of wealth and establish a vegetarian feast with rites of repentance. In the pond before the hall, twin-headed white lotuses grew;
each flower had a hundred petals. That winter, he passed away without illness" (Fozu Tongji).
Zhu Gang, Zhu Gang.
His origins are not clearly known. He was a *gongshi* (recommended scholar) of Shuntian who served as a District Vice-Commissioner (*futingzhi*) until his death.

He devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism, reciting the name of the Buddha thirty thousand times every day for fifteen years. One day, while sitting upon his couch, he was just about to take up his prayer beads...
While reciting the names of the Buddhas, a sudden extraordinary fragrance filled the room. It was said, "The Buddha has come," and he subsequently passed away (*Wangsheng ji*).
Chen Zan (courtesy name Tingluan), a native of Changshu in Jiangnan, was a jinshi of the thirty-fifth year of the Jiajing era. He served as an official in the Ministry of Punishments.
He was appointed as a Court Editorial Official (Ke-gishichō), but was dismissed for speaking frankly. While living at home, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
A guest visited him and rebuked him, saying, "Have you not heard the Great Mirror’s discourse on 'Mind-Only'? Why do you loathe impurity and delight in purity? He replied:
The Pure Land is Mind-only; this was proclaimed by Great Kāśyapa, yet it did not originate with him. "This mind creates the Buddha;
this mind is the Buddha"—the Buddha had indeed spoken these words long ago. It was likely because he feared that people would seek a pure land with an impure mind;
it was not to say that the land itself is devoid of defilement and purity. Furthermore, as for the delights of the Land of Bliss, they are not limited to lotus ponds and pearls alone.
The warbling of birds in the pavilion and the wind through the trees are merely such things.

I am fortunate to roam with the multitude of sages, clothed in immeasurable light, passing through incalculable kalpas, realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and attaining the Unsurpassed Way to deliver boundless multitudes—this is truly joy.
You, as a guest, find joy in meditation within this defiled land; I, as myself, find joy in meditation within the Pure Land. As for meditation, there is neither guest nor host.
"I delight in being neither defiled nor pure; you guests need not reproach me. In the early years of the Longqing era, he was reinstated as an official of the Ministry of Personnel.

During the Wanli era, he held successive posts culminating in his appointment as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice. In the seventh month of the sixteenth year, he lay ill with his illness; he recited the names of the Buddhas with increasing devotion.
According to custom, high-ranking officials of the third rank or above in the capital were granted ice during the hot months. Having placed the ice upon his bed, [he passed away].
Previously, the multitude saw a seven-storied pagoda with its railings and hooks interlaced emerge from within the ice; its window lattices were exquisitely intricate.
As time passed, the ice gradually melted and the shadow of the pagoda gradually thinned. After a short while, the breath [of the person] ceased and the shadow vanished.
At that moment, all the people of the capital spread word of this marvel (from the *Preface to the Ming Shi Lebang Wenlei Xutan Hui*).
Yan Cheng (嚴澄), courtesy name Daoche (道徹), was a native of Changshu. He was the son of the Duke Wenjing Yan Ne (嚴訥). From his youth, he possessed a pure character.

By virtue of his father’s patronage, he served as a Secretariat Drafter (Zhongshu Sheren). His official career culminated in the post of Prefect of Shaowu. In his later years, he retired to his home and devoted himself to the teachings of Yunqi.
His son, Pu, was simple, sincere, prudent, and fond of goodness. At the age of twenty-five, he fell ill. As he was about to die, Cheng said to him, "Do not harbor distracting thoughts;
simply focus your mind single-mindedly on the Buddha. Pu replied, "Yes. Cheng spoke again, "From this day forward, I too shall focus my mind single-mindedly on the Buddha.
Pu said joyfully, "If that is truly so, then I have no cause for concern. He then composed his countenance, joined his palms, and passed away. Cheng—
He then took the "Pure Land Text of Longshu" carved upon a block of wood and had it printed. He sent it widely to his relatives and old friends, attaching a letter that said:
"I, Chengyi, have been ill for some time and was nearly at the point of death. Unexpectedly, I have returned to life. Although I merely endure on, who knows what tomorrow holds?

When I look back upon my former schemes for worldly gain, they are like chewing wax. This single skin-bag must ultimately decay; as for the shadows of conditions within the six sense-objects, what [reliance can there be]?"

While residing in this firm and stable body, it would be better to exchange this ordinary mind for the aspiration to be born in the Pure Land. By reciting a single phrase of Amitābha’s name, one’s boundless karmic offenses will be extinguished.
I offer this brief exhortation to express my sincere intent. He passed away at the age of seventy-eight (from the *Changshu Zhi*, *Yunqi Fahui*, and the colophon to the *Jingtu Wen*).
Cai Chengzhi, courtesy name Huaiting, was a native of You County in Huguang. By nature he was solitary and aloof, indifferent to fame and profit.

When he was over twenty years old, he observed a strict vegetarian fast and devoted himself to the Buddha. He would recite the names of three thousand Buddhas, recording one name per day; this continued for three years.
Upon graduation, he never forgot [his studies] for the rest of his life. He passed the jinshi examination in the eleventh year of the Wanli era and served as the Governor of Jiaxing.
During his tenure in office, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāra-mitā Sūtra* daily. His chamber contained no superfluous items; there was only an incense burner, incense, and a scripture desk.
He restored the ancient Lengyan Temple and prohibited the common people from slaughtering livestock to sacrifice to the gods. He once sought the Dharma from Master Yunqi Hong. Thus...

He devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the *nien-fo* samādhi. Subsequently, he was appointed as the Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Taichang Siqing*). He requested leave to retire and returned home.

In his later years, he constructed a thatched hermitage to establish a *nien-fo* assembly, where he guided even vegetable sellers to collectively dedicate their merits toward rebirth in the Pure Land. He composed a verse to decline visitors, saying:
A traveler longing to return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, I am but a decayed Confucian by the Xiang River. I harbor no anxiety for tomorrow’s affairs; I seek only the talisman for rebirth.

I dwell as circumstances allow in a cramped room, Sustaining myself with thin soup from whatever comes my way. With hatred and love extinguished within my breast, I let others call me whatever they please—horse or ox.

In the year he was about to pass away, he styled himself the "Soon-to-Depart Wayfarer" (Bujiu Daoren). When he fell ill, he was carried to a Buddhist temple where he requested a monk to shave his head.
Upon returning to his bedroom, he saw a silver platform coming to welcome him; he repeatedly invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and then passed away.
His *Poems on the Pure Land* and his *Book on Cause and Effect* were circulated in the world (*Jingang Xin Yi Lu*).

Yu Chunxi (also written as Yu Chunxi), courtesy name Changru, was a native of Qiantang. From birth, he remained in a state of constant prostration and did not close his eyes. At the age of three, he chanted the names of the Buddhas without ceasing.
A lotus flower and jeweled trees appeared within his room, which he reported to his grandmother. His grandmother said, "This is the West..."
This was a manifestation of auspicious signs. Consequently, he was instructed to practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereupon he would frequently sit upright with his eyes cast downward.
His younger brother, Chunzhen (courtesy name Sengru), had been close to him since childhood. During the mourning period for their mother, they practiced the *Tiantai* *Zhi-guan* together.

As he grew up, he became a teacher in the village, instructing a group of children in the practice of *bigan* (nose-contemplation). Because of this, he incurred the displeasure of his host, who showed him no sympathy. Having already passed the provincial examination (*xiangju*), he soon...

He taught his disciples at Mount Bishan. While he and his fellow practitioners were reciting the *Lianghuang Chant* (the Imperial Repentance of Emperor Liang), on the following day, a cloud-like light entered through the pillars, sweet dew moistened the walls, and the heavens rained down golden grains, *yuan-shu* millet, and *shen-shui* incense.
Although it was midwinter, ten thousand flowers bloomed in full bloom.

In the Chunxi era, [Emperor] Gan was moved by these miraculous signs, and his practice of meditative concentration became even more steadfast; consequently, he attained the ability to know the future. When Master Hong of Yunqi heard of this, he rebuked him.
It was said: "Yusheng has fallen into the net of Māra. In the eleventh year of the Wanli era, he passed the jinshi examination and returned home due to his father’s mourning.

He lived in a thatched hut at the tomb for three years and received the precepts from Master Hong. While dwelling in the mountains, he daily offered rice porridge to deer and rabbits; whenever tigers approached, he would simply shout at them and they would depart.
Upon the completion of his mourning period, he was appointed as a Shushi (Director) in the Ministry of War. Shortly thereafter, he again requested leave to return home and satuated himself at Tianmu.
Before Gaofeng’s "Deadly Barrier," he exerted himself day and night. On the twenty-first day, being extremely exhausted, he wished to rest his head upon a pillow.
Suddenly, he saw Master Gaofeng severing his left arm. He attained sudden enlightenment and rushed to Yunqi to verify his realization.
Master Hong said, "One who awakens from sleep does not comb their hair or wash their face before returning to the quilt and pillow; they will surely fall back asleep. One who awakens from delusion—"

To fail to adorn oneself while instead associating with the defiled and turbid is certain to lead to further delusion. A fire-lotus easily withers; a young bamboo shoot easily breaks. You must devise your own plan;
do not allow a single moment’s distraction to obstruct the path of your spiritual cultivation. Consequently, he exhorted him to dedicate his merit toward the Pure Land to continue his prior causes.
Thus, Chunxi practiced this throughout his life. Should there be those who do not believe in the practice of *nien-fo* (reciting the Buddha’s name), [one should guide them accordingly].
He told them: "To awaken oneself and awaken others, with awakening perfected, is called a Buddha. To 'recollect the Buddha' (nien-fo) is to recollect awakening.
Is it possible to have every thought-moment not be constant awakening, while every thought-moment is constantly deluded? A person dwells within the capital; a bird dwells on the edge of a hill.
Is it possible to dwell not in the ground of ultimate goodness, but to dwell in a ground of non-goodness? Someone asked: "How does one recollect the Buddha? He replied: "Uphold..."
Awaken right mindfulness; let it continue in an uninterrupted succession. Among hundreds of thousands of skillful means, there is but the single word "knowing.

If every thought-moment is the light of the infinite, how could one not enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? When a student cultivates the Way, they focus solely on seeking liberation from birth and death.

Yet if every thought-moment is the life-span of the infinite, what birth and death is there to be liberated from? Subsequently, he returned to official service and was promoted to a position in the Office of Guest Reception.
Wailang was later appointed to the Office of Merit (Sikun). He again requested to return home, where he spent his days with Chunzhen strolling by the lakeside.

At that time, Master Hong was seated at Nanping, expounding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng) and soliciting funds to redeem Wàngōngchí for the establishment of a society for releasing living beings.

Tens of thousands of monastics and laypeople joined in, the sound of their chanting resonating through the valleys. Many men of pure integrity of the time attended these gatherings; indeed, it was Chunzhen who...

Xu led by example and subsequently restored the three ponds as *fangsheng chi* (pools for the release of living beings). He built embankments and constructed pavilions, releasing various fish and birds therein.
After a short while, he entered Mount Nanping and did not emerge. Chunzhen likewise retired to Lingjiu Peak to spend his final years there (*Deyuan ji*, Appendix).

Tang Shi, whose courtesy name was Yizhi, was a native of Huzhou. Having been recommended as a scholar to the National University, he later served as the governor of Shouyang and subsequently as the regional inspector of Xiangguo.
When rebel forces broke into Xiangyang, he threw himself into a well to the left of the Duanli Gate; his family members then pulled him out.

He emerged, having fainted and then regained consciousness. He submitted a memorial to the throne to exonerate himself. An imperial decree ordered the Three Ministries to investigate the matter; his innocence was established, and he was released to return home.
At that time, he first joined the Lotus Pond Society (Lianchi), where he was instructed in the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation. Consequently, he diligently cultivated Pure Land practices.

All his kinsmen were able to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Samantamukha-parivarta*) from memory. During the day, each practiced their respective duties, while at night they gathered together.
The Buddha previously dedicated his merit to establish this as a constant practice. He once said that for those who cultivate the Pure Land, the gate of contemplation (*guanmen*) is essential.

One must wear clothes and eat food while remaining constantly within contemplation—whether it be traveling spiritually through the lotus sea to prostrate before the Buddha amidst the flowers, or sitting in gazing upon the jeweled lands as the Buddha’s light illuminates one’s body.
Once pure thoughts are established, what need is there to wait for rebirth? Thus, he devoted himself exclusively to the contemplation of the Buddha. [He passed] southward...
At Changgan Temple in the capital, while he was prostrating before the stupa and reciting the Buddha’s name, he saw a white light radiate from the summit of the stupa;

it was as if the Buddha had manifested a physical form, golden in color. One day, while sitting in meditation in the hall, he suddenly looked out the window and saw a mountain emerge from the midst of the great ocean, upon which the Buddha sat, his radiance penetrating in all four directions.
The walls and the forest trees were entirely empty and invisible. Such was the response to his sincere devotion.
At that time, he was skilled in literary composition. Having turned his heart toward the Buddha-vehicle, he frequently employed worldly language to expound the essentials of the various dharmas.
He composed works such as the *Lotus World*, the *Fragrance of the Tathāgata*, and the *Kinnara’s Voice*, which were carved into woodblocks and circulated in the world.

He once prepared his own burial vault, but subsequently abandoned it to reside at Qixia Temple. He left a testament stating that after his death, he must be cremated according to the *te-p'i* (dhāya) rite. As he approached [the end]...
End. He manifested various auspicious signs and passed away with right mindfulness (*Jingangchi yanji Jingtu chenzhong*).
Yuan Hongdao, courtesy name Zhonglang, style name Shitou Jushi, was a native of Gong’an County, Hubei. His elder brother was Zongdao.
His courtesy name was Baxiu. His younger brother was Zhongdao, whose courtesy name was Xiaoxiu. The three of them passed the jinshi examination in succession, and all were devoted to the Chan school.
During the Wanli era, Hongdao served as the Magistrate of Wujiang and later as a Chief Clerk in the Ministry of Rites; he subsequently retired on medical grounds.
Initially, he studied Chan under Li Zuo’u, attaining deep understanding and proficiency. He delighted in debate, but later, through personal verification, he declared: "This is emptiness."

He spoke of this not as a mere matter of theory, but proceeded to dedicate his merit toward the Pure Land. Morning and evening he performed prostrations and recitations, while concurrently upholding the prohibitive precepts.

Having extensively studied the scriptural teachings, he composed the *Western Pure Land Synthesis* (*Xifang helun*), which harmonizes the schools of Nature (*xing*) and Characteristics (*xiang*) to enter the gate of non-duality.

Among its five types of practice gates, those most essential are briefly stated as follows: First, the practitioner of faith. As the sutra says: "Faith is the source of the Way and the foundation of its efficacy."
Venerable Mother, all conditioned phenomena have faith as their primary cause. Even until the fruit of enlightenment is perfected, it is solely through the completion of this faculty of faith.
It is like a grain of rice falling to the ground; until it matures into a fruit, it does not differ from its original seed. It is like a young bamboo shoot reaching the heavens.
This is fundamentally the original staff. For bodhisattvas at the initial stage of mind, there are none who do not achieve [enlightenment] by relying on the power of faith.

In the Lotus School, faith is especially relied upon as the root. First, one must have faith that Amitābha Buddha—the immovable wisdom, the fundamental wisdom—is no different from oneself, like the vast empty sky:
when the sun shines, it is bright; when clouds come, it is obscured. Yet the sky itself is fundamentally without these states. Furthermore,

Because clouds and the sun are themselves empty space. Second, one must have faith that the various practices of Amitābha Buddha—difficult to perform and difficult to endure over nayuta kalpas—I too am able to carry out.
Why? Because throughout beginningless time, I have drifted and drowned in the three miserable realms, enduring the suffering of birth and the suffering of death;
having been born with fur and horns, and having endured the iron beds and copper pillars—all such useless sufferings, I am now able to [endure them].
If one accepts [this], how much more so now for the Bodhisattva’s myriad practices and the work of saving sentient beings—how could one not be able to do this?
Third, one must have faith in Amitābha Buddha’s immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable supernormal powers, and the accomplishment of his immeasurable power of vows and other such matters.
I, too, shall attain it. The Tathāgata’s self-nature and skillful means possess such inconceivable matters as these.
Because my own nature and that of the Tathāgata are one and the same in their purity, fourthly, I believe that Amitābha Buddha neither departs nor arrives;
I, too, neither depart nor arrive. The Western Land and this world are not separated by more than the tip of a hair; if I wish to see him, I see him immediately. Why?
For this reason, all Buddhas take the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as their body and land.

Fifth, one must have faith that Amitābha Buddha’s cultivation throughout kalpas leads directly to the realization of the fruit without shifting for even a single *kṣaṇa*; I, too, shall not shift for a single *kṣaṇa*, and my status will be equal to that of all Buddhas.
Why is this? Time and divisions are gathered by karma; within the ocean of the *dharmadhātu*, karma cannot be found.
Therefore, such faith and understanding constitute the initial mind for entering the Way.

One who practices the path of all Buddhas’ Pure Lands through the dual cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā—according to the Three Contemplations of the Tiantai School—demonstrates the "fishing net and rabbit trap" of the single mind and grasps the essential pivot of all dharmas.

Each of the sixteen contemplations of the Western Quarter possesses these three meanings. The *Miaozongchao* states: "The substance of the three virtues within the nature is the three bodies of all Buddhas;

these very three virtues and three bodies are my own one mind and three contemplations. If it were otherwise, then the Buddha would exist externally to the contemplation, and the object would not be identical to the mind;
how then could this be called the contemplation of the Perfect Teaching’s absolute non-relation? This may also be understood in this way.
The three bodies of Amitābha constitute the Dharmakāya; my three contemplations constitute Prajñā; and the vision of the Buddha upon the completion of these contemplations is itself liberation.
A single [act] encompasses all three, like the character for "new" (新). Just as it is with the contemplation of the Buddha, so it is with the contemplation of all the environments and inhabitants.
The principle does not follow divergent paths; this is explained extensively in the commentaries (*śūtra* and *bhāṣya*), which I cannot describe in full detail here.

To understand this is to understand that the single recitation of the Buddha’s name (*nien-fo*) fully embodies the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). To realize that the mind which recites is neither the physical heart-mass nor a mere reflected image is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

To realize that the Buddha who is recited—whether as the support (*āśraya*) or the supported (*āśrita*)—is such that each principal figure and attendant is perfectly interfused, vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, is the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*).

When subject and object are understood as transcending all dependence, both are simultaneously negated and both are simultaneously illuminated; this is the Middle Way. Furthermore, that which contemplates is the single mind’s threefold contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), and that which is contemplated is the single mind’s threefold truth (*trisatya*).
Subject and object are non-dual; thus, the truths and the contemplations are non-dual. The three truths are the *dharmakāya*, and the three contemplations are *prajñā*.
The non-duality of the truths and the contemplations is the correspondence with the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), which is liberation. To raise up one [aspect] is to...
Third: It is like the character "new" (新). Thus, a single recitation of the Buddha's name can purify the four lands, just as picking up a single mote of dust.
Transforming the great earth into gold—this is called the inconceivable contemplation gate of the perfect interfusion of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

For the practitioner of the three [aspects of] the six perfections, as stated in the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, when the Bodhisattva’s profound understanding manifests before them, their practice becomes free from signs.

Because they know that the essence of the Dharma-nature is free from stinginess and greed, they practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) in accordance with it. The Dharma-nature is unstained and free from the faults of the five desires.

Therefore, one practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) in accordance with it; because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without suffering and is free from malice and affliction.
One practices the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) in accordance with it; because the nature of phenomena is without the characteristics of body or mind and is free from indolence.

One practices the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) in accordance with it; because the nature of phenomena is eternally concentrated and its essence is without distraction. One practices the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) in accordance with it.

The essence of the Dharma-nature is luminous because it is free from ignorance. Therefore, by practicing in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*, those who cultivate the Pure Land do not deviate from this single practice.
Possessing these six meanings, they practice giving in every thought-moment while remaining detached from action;

they practice precepts in every thought-moment while purifying them; they practice patience in every thought-moment while remaining tranquil; they practice diligence in every thought-moment while maintaining continuity; and they practice meditative concentration in every thought-moment while remaining focused on the one.
In every thought-moment, one practices the Buddha’s conduct through wisdom. One should know that this is detached from [dualistic] purity and quiescence, yet continues as a single unity.

While there must be phenomenal characteristics (*nimitta*) that arise in accordance with conditions, all of them flow forth from the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). Thus, the primary and auxiliary practices are non-dual; phenomena and principle are non-dual.

For this reason, the single practice of *nien-fo* (recollection of the Buddha) can encompass all practices, because *nien-fo* is the dharma-gate of the one mind, and there are no practices apart from the mind.

If one abandons all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*), it is equivalent to abandoning the mind. For those who practice the four types of compassionate vows, the ocean of the nature of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is inexhaustible;
their offerings are inexhaustible, their precepts and generosity are inexhaustible, and even their benefit to others is inexhaustible.

Therefore, in the *Five Gates of Mindfulness of the Pure Land* by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, the four practices of prostration, praise, making vows, and contemplation are established for the purpose of achieving entry [into that realm].

The Gate of Merit: dedicating it to all sentient beings afflicted by defilements to uproot their worldly suffering, and for the sake of accomplishing the gate of transcendent merit, the Bodhisattva cultivates the five gates of mindfulness and swiftly attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. An objection is raised: the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:
The Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings as being like echoes or like masses of foam upon water; thus, sentient beings are fundamentally empty.

Yet, he makes vows to benefit them—would this not be like seeing flowers in the sky with one's eyes? The answer is: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites the Buddha as saying, "There is no Buddha," in order to destroy attachment to the notion of a Buddha;
it does not mean that one should grasp at the mark of "no Buddha. One should know that the statement "there are no sentient beings" likewise destroys [attachment].

Regarding the "conception of sentient beings," it does not mean that one grasps at the signless nature of non-existence. Therefore, Vimalakīrti said that once a bodhisattva has performed this contemplation, they say to themselves:
"I shall preach the Dharma of the non-existence of sentient beings for the sake of sentient beings. This is called true compassion.

Thus, we know that when a bodhisattva employs various means to deliver sentient beings, it is because they have profoundly realized the meaning of the non-existence of sentient beings. If one perceives the existence of sentient beings, then [compassion is not true].
I am of inferior compassion; how could I possibly perform such deeds of benefit? Fifth, regarding "acting in accordance with the Dharma":
the ocean of the *dharmadhātu* is immeasurable and boundless, and the ocean of practice is likewise immeasurable and boundless.

Therefore, all the practices of a bodhisattva accord with the self-nature of reality, which is neither existent nor non-existent, neither practice nor non-practice; they accord with the self-nature of phenomena and are not attained by the initial resolve alone.

This is not attained by subsequent thought; its characteristics shall now be briefly set forth. First, although the Bodhisattva brings all sentient beings to ultimate *nirvāṇa* without exception, the realms of beings do not diminish.
It is like puppets on a stage whose laughter and weeping appear vividly, yet are nothing more than clay and earth, empty and devoid of anything real.
Second, although the Bodhisattva commits the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), they are free from affliction and anger. Up to...
In the hells, he is free from all stains of sin. Among animals, he is free from faults such as ignorance and pride;
like a woman’s *bhūta-graha* (spiritual essence) that departs and yet remains constantly before her mother until the birth of a child, so it is with him.

Thirdly, the Bodhisattva enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) within his own body and emerges within another's body; he enters absorption within a single body and emerges within many bodies; and he enters absorption within a sentient body and emerges within an insentient body.
It is like a fierce tiger causing a corpse to rise, kneel, prostrate, and dance; the corpse acts solely according to the tiger's will, for it is devoid of consciousness.
Fourth, within the body of a small sentient being, the Bodhisattva turns the Great Wheel of Dharma, kindles the great torch of Dharma, and thunders the great drum of Dharma.
The palaces of Māra are destroyed, the great earth trembles, and immeasurable, boundless sentient beings are delivered—yet this small sentient being does not [perceive it].
He perceives what is not perceived, just as when a musician of the Heavenly Emperor flees into the nostrils of a young girl, yet the girl neither knows nor perceives it.
Fifth, when a Bodhisattva wishes to remain in the world for a long time, he can expand a mere moment of thought into immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas;
and when he wishes to remain in the world for a short time, he can [contract] immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas [into a moment].
Eons are condensed into the duration of a single thought-moment, like a child watching horses gallop within a lantern; when one calculates their beginning and end, they cannot be grasped at all.
If one realizes such inconceivable practice, the pure lands of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are entirely subsumed within a single thought-moment.
This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of adorning the pure land, through the illumination of non-conceptual wisdom.
This is visible; it cannot be fathomed by the measures of ordinary intellect. Why? Because its self-nature transcends all measures.

Once the book was completed, he took the Middle Way as his primary path and simultaneously resolved his mind toward rebirth in the Pure Land. Subsequently, he was appointed to the post of Official at the Department of State Affairs (Hongdao).

He was later transferred to the position of Director of the Ministry of Merit (Jixun Si Langzhong), but again moved due to illness and returned home. Not many days after arriving home, he entered the Jing [Valley].

He stayed at a monastery in the provincial capital and passed away without illness. Zhong Dao-guan, the Court Gentleman of the Southern Bureau of the Ministry of Rites, requested leave to retire and live out his old age at home.

He was habitually diligent in ritual recitations. On the night of the full moon in the forty-second year of the Wanli era, after completing his daily recitation, he sat in the lotus posture with his body and spirit serene and refreshed;
he suddenly entered a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). His spirit emerged from the house, riding upon the clouds in a graceful manner, accompanied by two youths.

He led him westward, and in an instant they descended to the ground. The youth said, "Stop. As they proceeded along the way, they continued to descend until they saw the ground as level as the palm of a hand, radiant and smooth.
To the side was a channel, over ten *zhang* wide, filled with five-colored lotuses of extraordinary fragrance.
A golden bridge spanned the channel, its railings intricately interlaced, and its pavilions were exceedingly orderly and magnificent. He bowed to the youth and asked, "This..."
"What place is this? Who are you? He replied, "I am an attendant of Master Linghe. He asked, "Who is this Master?
He said, "He is your elder brother, the General of the Household (Zhonglang). He is currently waiting for you to have some words with him; you should go quickly.
They took another path to a certain place where there were over ten trees and the water of a pond gurgled. Above the pond was a gate of white jade. A young boy entered first.
A young boy led the way. Passing through more than twenty tiers of pavilions, they arrived at the foot of one pavilion where a man came down to welcome them.
His countenance was like jade and his robes were like clouds and mists; he was over ten feet tall. Seeing him on the path, [the man] said with joy, "My younger brother has arrived!
Looking closely, it was Hongdao. They ascended the pavilion and bowed to one another. Four or five other men came and sat together. Hongdao said, "This..."
The western borderlands are places where faith and understanding have not yet been perfected and the jewel of the precepts is incomplete; many are born there. It is also called the Land of Indolence.
Above, there are transformation-buddha towers and terraces, before which lies a great pond spanning a hundred *yojanas*.

Within it are exquisite lotuses, the birthplaces for sentient beings. Once born, they disperse to the towers and terraces, gathering with pure friends with whom they share a karmic affinity. By means of...

The resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) regarding the absence of licentious sounds and beautiful forms is easily accomplished; before long, one will advance to become a person among those in the Pure Land.
Midway through his life, he asked his elder brother where he had been reborn. Hongdao replied, "Although my pure vows were profound, my emotional attachments have not yet been eliminated.

At first, I was born here for a short time, but now I dwell in the Pure Land. Ultimately, because my observance of the precepts was lax, I merely attained a terrestrial rebirth and could not ascend with the Great Beings into the void."
"Though you possess the Jewel-Palace of Emptiness, you must still advance in your cultivation.

Fortunately, because your wisdom from previous lives was sharp and keen, and because you once composed a treatise on the West praising the Tathāgata’s inconceivable power to deliver sentient beings, you have attained mastery in flying through space.
You travel to various buddha-fields and are able to go and listen to the Dharma taught by all the Buddhas; this is truly excellent. Thereupon, he took him along the Middle Way.
Ascending, in an instant he traveled thousands of miles until he reached a place of unobstructed radiance.

Its ground was made of lapis lazuli, and it was bordered by trees of the seven treasures, all of sandalwood and auspicious wood, which produced various exquisite flowers of wondrous jewel-like colors.

Below, there were jeweled ponds with waves surging in infinite measure, emitting natural, sublime sounds. Within the ponds were clusters of precious lotuses, their petals glowing with light of five colors. Above the ponds, [the sky] was hidden...
Concealed behind the distant reaches of the perilous towers, galleries extend out to the sides. In each of these are immeasurable musical instruments that produce the sounds of all dharmas.
Hongdao said, "What you have seen is the dependent retribution of sentient beings practicing on the Pure Land grounds.

Beyond this lies the dwelling place of the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body, which is many millions of times more exquisite than this, and their spiritual powers are also many millions of times greater than this."
I traverse these realms by the power of wisdom; I cannot abide therein. Beyond this lies the realm inhabited by those of the Ten Stages and Equal Enlightenment, which I am unable to know.
Beyond this lies the realm inhabited by those of Wondrous Enlightenment; only a Buddha and a Buddha can know it.
Having finished speaking, they arrived at another place. There were no walls or fences, only railings, and its radiance surpassed that of the previous location.
After sitting for a short while, Hongdao said, "I did not expect such extreme bliss as this. Had I strictly observed the precepts during my life, it would likely have been even more than this.
Generally speaking, when both the Mahayana vehicle and the precepts are urgent, one’s rebirth is of the highest grade; next, when the precepts are urgent, the rebirth is most stable. If..."

There are those who possess the vehicle [of the Mahayana] but lack precepts; they are mostly dragged by the power of karma and flow away into the assembly of the eight classes of ghosts and spirits. I have personally witnessed many such cases.
My younger brother possesses a profound affinity for Prajna-wisdom, yet his discipline and concentration are very slight.

Now, if one realizes the principle but cannot give rise to discipline and concentration, it is "wild wisdom" (mad-prajñā); such a person returns to the five turbidities. While you are still strong and healthy, you must truly realize and truly practice, maintaining both [wisdom and discipline].

Purify your vows, practice with diligence, employ skillful means, and show compassion for all beings; before long, we shall meet again. Once you have entered another path, it will be terrifying and fearsome.
If you are unable to maintain the precepts, there exists the "Six Fasting Days Method" (Ṣaḍupavāsa-dharma) of Nāgārjuna; follow and practice it accordingly.

The precept against killing is most urgent. I entrust this message to my fellow students: there has never been one who, having daily raised the carving knife and greedily craved flavors with their mouth, was yet able to be born in this land.
Though one may preach the Dharma like clouds and rain, what benefit does it bring to the matter at hand?

You and I were brothers in every lifetime throughout the Kalpa of the Empty King, even as we passed through the six realms of existence; it has been no different for all. Fortunately, I have now attained this auspicious state.

"Fearing that you might fall back into the lower realms, I have used my skillful means and spiritual power to bring you here. Since the pure and the defiled are now separated, you may not remain for long.
At that time, Zongdao had already passed away; Zhongdao asked where he had been reborn, and Hongdao replied, "The place of your rebirth is excellent;

you shall know it for yourself later. Suddenly, Hongdao rose into the air and vanished. Zhongdao then stepped onto the edge of the pond and suddenly felt as if he were falling into the water, whereupon he leaped up and awoke.
He recorded this himself as follows. First: Zongdao had a son named Deng. At the age of thirteen, he suffered from abdominal distension (pi).

As his end approached, he said to Hongdao, "I am dying. Uncle, how can you save me? Hongdao replied, "You need only recite the Buddha's name, and you will immediately attain rebirth in the Buddha-land.
This world of the five turbidities is not worth lingering over. Thereupon, Deng joined his palms and invoked the name of Amitābha Buddha.
His attendants all joined him in chanting with one voice. After a short while, he smiled and said, "I see a lotus flower, its color slightly reddish.
Shortly thereafter, he said, "The flower is gradually growing larger; its color is so brilliant that nothing can compare to it. Again, he said, "The Buddha has arrived;
his marks and signs and radiant light fill the entire room. After a moment, his breath grew labored. Zongdao said, "You need only recite the name of the Buddha. Deng—
He recited the name of the Buddha several times, joined his palms, and passed away (*Ming Shi: Western Regions Synthesis*, *Baisu Zhai Ji*, *Kexue Zhai Waiji*, *Huayuan*).
Ding Mingdeng, whose courtesy name was Jianhong, was a native of Jiangpu. During the Wanli era, he received the Three Refuges from Yunqi. He styled himself the "Lotus Companion.
In his forty-fourth year, he passed the jinshi examination and served as a *tui-guan* (assistant magistrate) in Quanzhou, later being promoted to the post of Prefect of Quzhou.

Wherever he went, he exhorted people to the Buddha-dharma. For those who were legally required to be flogged, he permitted them to redeem their punishment by offering rice, using the proceeds to provide for the prisoners in the jails.
During the summer months, he repaired the prison cells and provided the prisoners with *xiangru* (patchouli) decoctions and *huai* (millet) fans. In the winter months, he gave them pepper and ginger.
He selected physicians to attend to the sick and provided each person with a string of prayer beads, instructing them to recite the Buddha’s name. This was Master Yunqi Hong.
He once recounted that his neighbor, who habitually recited the Buddha’s name, passed away while accompanied by his friend, Yiqing.
Consequently, he painted a portrait of Yiqing and hung it in his hall of offerings to exhort himself. During the Chongzhen era, he received the Bodhisattva precepts.

In the winter of the second year of the Shunzhi reign of our dynasty, his illness became severe. On the first day of the eleventh month, he prepared a memorial to inform the Buddha of his desire to be reborn in the Pure Land, burning incense daily.

One account states that on the tenth day, he consumed porridge as usual; his face was radiant with a brilliant glow, and he exhorted all his relatives and friends to cultivate the practice of the Pure Land.
Then, he lay upon his pillow and passed away (*Jingtu chenzhong*).
Huang Yisheng, courtesy name Ziyu, was a native of Taicang. He had long served the teachings of Yunqi and diligently cultivated the Pure Land practices.

During the Chongzhen era, he was recommended for office and appointed as the Magistrate of Xindu in Sichuan. He governed the people with compassion and benevolence, and frequently provided meals for the monastics.
In the magistrate’s hall, he personally attended to the serving of food with his own chopsticks and distributed alms, followed by prostrations.

When Zhang Xianzhong’s rebels invaded Sichuan and passed through Xindu, the thousand monks of Xindu, moved by the virtue of [Wang] Yisheng, led one another up the city walls to chant the Buddha’s name. At night, their voices shook the heavens;
the rebels warned one another not to disturb them and departed in silence. For his merit in defending the city, he was promoted to the post of Governor of Jizhou.

When the Ming dynasty fell, he resigned his official post and returned home. His cultivation of the Pure Land practice became even more steadfast. The hall where he lived was called the Lotus Calyx Hall (Lianrei Lou), and he styled himself the Lotus Calyx Layman (Lianrei Jushi).
He prepared vegetarian feasts to honor the Buddha and daily recited the Buddha’s name tens of thousands of times. Later, he lay ill for a full month;

he hung images of Amitābha on all four walls and invited Master Xianshan Hui to confer the Bodhisattva precepts upon him. As Master Xian conferred them, he spoke extensively on the nature of Consciousness-Only.
In the *Xinjingguan* (Contemplation of the Pure Mind), Yingsheng said: "My spiritual clarity grows ever stronger and my vows grow ever firmer;

I am confident that I will certainly be born in the Western Land. On the following morning, Master Xian was about to depart, having fixed the eighth day as the date for his departure. It subsequently turned out exactly so (*Xiangguo suilu*).
Advance, Golden Light! Advance, Golden Light!
I, a man of the Imperial Court’s Right Yellow Banner, having risen from the ranks of the military, see goodness and act upon it.
I command all soldiers: do not kill recklessly; do not violate a single woman; do not seize a single object; do not burn a single dwelling. [Seal] Qi.
He was able to recognize characters and recite sutras. In the tenth year of the Shunzhi era, while accompanying the military campaign to Fujian, they passed through Hangzhou.

Hearing that Master Gudé was preaching the Dharma at Lingyin Monastery, Guangqian went there with his wife to seek instruction. Having personally received the master’s guidance, he attained realization through the practice of nianfo from that time on.
In the summer of the twelfth year, they were returning north and were stationed on the banks of the Qiantang River when Guangqian suddenly fell ill.
Gong requested that a physician be summoned. Guangqian stopped him, saying, "In the past, I personally visited Lingyin with you.
Now I simply wish to prepare for my final transition and seek the Master’s certification. What need is there for medicine?
Gong laughed loudly and said, "I did not expect that you, sir, would also reach such a state. She then ordered two coffins to be made and said, "I shall go with you, sir. Shortly thereafter—
"I am delaying only to finish my final affairs for the Master. Upon hearing this, Guangqian immediately joined his palms and passed away.
Gong sent an envoy to Lingyin Temple to request that he serve as the torch-bearer for both men, and further instructed that offerings be made to the monks and repentance rites performed.

When the seven-day period concluded, [Gong] ceased all food and drink, did not lie down day or night, and single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name. On the afternoon of the seventh day, he observed whether the sun was rising or setting, then leaned against the coffin.
He fell asleep. After a short while, he awoke and said, "The time has come. He sat upright, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away (*Guobao Wenjian Lu*).
The commentary states: For kings and ministers to enter the Way is more difficult than for laypersons. Those who are urgent about fame and office prioritize advancement and acquisition.

Those who indulge in idle pleasures regard quiet cultivation as suffering; unless one has planted virtuous causes in the past and firmly maintained right aspirations, how could they possibly refrain from overstepping their boundaries?
As for these gentlemen, they did not abandon the toil of the mundane world but together returned to the pure realm.
This may be called manifesting in the body of a high official to preach the Dharma.
As for such figures as Liu Zhitou, Bai Juyi, Su Shi, and Zhao Mengfu, who praised and took refuge [in the faith], their merit in purifying their causal conditions was evident;

yet when the moment arrived for them to relinquish consciousness, auspicious responses were rarely heard. This is truly because their wisdom was deluded by many divergent paths, and illness arose from attachment to existence—a condition common among literary men.
This has been the constant rule since antiquity. When birth and death arrive, it is impossible to rely on mere luck. Later gentlemen should take this as a warning and a lesson.
*Record of the Holy and Sages of the Pure Land*, Volume Seven.
Record of the Holy and Wise of the Pure Land, Volume Eight:
Lay Practitioners Who Attained Rebirth,
Part Seven, Chama Jie.
In the city of Kapilavastu, there was a son of a Śākya elder named Kṣamākara. He went to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what practice does a bodhisattva swiftly attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path? How does he come to be fully endowed with the thirty-two marks?
How does he travel from one buddha-field to another? And at the time of his final passing, how is it that his mind remains undisturbed as he takes birth?"

They do not fall into the eight states of adversity. They always know the affairs of the past and future. They fully accomplish all dharmas and master all matters. They know all phenomena without any obstruction.
They believe in and understand the practice of emptiness and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Constantly with a sincere heart they desire to become śramaṇas; they never violate the precepts and take no pleasure in worldly dwellings. For them, the Buddha expounds the bodhisattva’s patience.
Regarding the practices of giving and so forth, he ultimately declared that there is no self and no person, and that all phenomena are like transformations.
At that time, Kṣamāgata attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), as did five hundred bhikṣus, five hundred upāsakas, and twenty-five upāsikās.
They shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression. At the end of their lives, they shall all be reborn in the pure land of the immeasurable Buddhas in the Western Quarter.
There, they shall constantly protect and uphold countless Buddha-dharmas, teaching and transforming all people to bring them to fulfillment, ensuring that none fall back.
In this manner, throughout infinite kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he shall successively become a Buddha in this land (*Bodhisattvajanmabhūmi-sūtra*).
Que Gongze—Que Gongze was a man from Zhao. During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty, he resided in Luoyang. He lived in a state of profound tranquility and detachment, day after day...
He constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Upon his death, his friend organized a religious assembly at Baima Temple.
When they began the recitation of the sutra at dusk, a voice suddenly resounded from the air. Looking up, they saw a person of radiant and magnificent appearance who said, "I am Geng Kuezhi.
I have been reborn in the Western World of Peace and Bliss, and I have come here with various noble beings to listen to this sutra. Those within the hall all [beheld him].
This was witnessed by Du, a soldier from Jiji County, who had studied under Gongze. His mother would regularly provide meals for the monks.
As noon approached on this day, a bowl suddenly descended from the air and landed directly before her. Upon examining it closely, she saw that it was the very bowl Gongze habitually used;
it was filled with rice, its fragrance permeating the hall. Those who ate it remained without hunger for seven days. (Recorded by Zhi Daolin)

I offer this eulogy for him: How great is Duke Que! He partakes of the void and receives the numinous; his spiritual transformations reached the Western Regions, while his traces responded in the Eastern Capital.
He lingered amidst the celestial heights, his resonant fame illuminating his form. How could I merely admire him with a single panegyric? He has shown me that he is not obscure.
(From the *Dàtáng nèidiǎn lù*, "Treatise on the Samādhi of the Precious King of Buddha-Recollection").

Zhang Ye, whose courtesy name was Laimin, was a native of Xunyang. By nature filial and fraternal, he gave away all his fields and houses to his younger brother and shared both the bitter and the sweet with his nine clansmen.
Although repeatedly summoned by the provincial and commandery governments, he did not respond; when appointed by imperial decree as an Attendant Censor of the Mounted Guard, he likewise declined.
He entered Mount Lu’s White Lotus Society and became a disciple of Master Huiyuan.
In the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, he took leave of his family, entered his room, sat upright, and passed away at the age of sixty-nine (from the *Donglin zhuan*).
Zhang Quan, whose courtesy name was Xiushi, was a descendant of Zhang Ye. He possessed a lofty and detached temperament, cherished antiquity, and delighted in the Way.

He labored in the fields with his hoe and never ceased carrying his scroll of the classics. When summoned to serve as an Attendant Censor, he did not rise to the post. Yu Yue recommended him for the post of [Governor of] Xunyang.
He was also not permitted [to remain]. Thereupon, he entered Mount Lu and relied upon Master Huiyuan. He investigated the Buddhist scriptures with great depth and attained profound realization.
In the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty, he faced west and recited the Buddha’s name, passing away without illness at the age of sixty-five (from the *Donglin Zhuan*).
He Tantuan, He Tantuan.
A native of Lujiang, he was the son of Wan Shou, the Court Counselor of the Ministry of Justice under the Song dynasty. From his youth, he honored the Dharma and observed the Bodhisattva precepts.

At the age of eighteen, while observing the mourning period for his father, he became so emaciated with grief that he fell ill. Consequently, he turned his heart toward the Pure Land and invited monks.
Several people were at his residence repenting for their past karma. As time passed, they became increasingly devout.

One night, after the recitation of the sutras had concluded and the monks had fallen asleep, Tan-yuan suddenly began to chant and recite by himself. The monks, finding this strange, questioned him, saying: "I see the Buddha’s body, golden in color, with a radiance over ten feet high.
He comes from the west, attended by banners and flowers that fill the void. The Buddha smiles serenely. He then summoned [the others].

"Tanyuan, depart quickly! Tanyuan had always been physically frail and weak; yet at this moment, his countenance became resolute and vigorous. He then took fragrant flowers and scattered them into the air.
At the fifth watch of the night, he suddenly passed away. A fragrant aroma filled the residence, which did not dissipate for several days (*Mingxiang ji*).
Wei Shizi was a native of Liangjun.
He was born during the Song dynasty and was a devoted and diligent follower of the Buddha. He led his children and grandchildren in practicing the pure karma of the Western Paradise.
Only his wife alone did not believe; when his daughter fell ill and died, she revived after seven days and immediately ascended a high seat.
He recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and addressed his father, saying: "I am going; I shall depart for the Land of Immeasurable Life.
Myself, my father, and my elder brother—each of us shall have a great lotus flower within the pond, and we shall be born therein. Only my mother alone has none; I cannot bear this grief."
Therefore, I have returned this report. Having finished speaking, he closed his eyes and passed away. From that time on, his mother also came to revere the Dharma (*Mingxiang ji*).

Yǔ Shēn, courtesy name Yànbǎo, was a native of Xīnyě. He was extensively versed in the classics, histories, and the studies of the *wèi* and *hòu* (astral and meteorological portents), yet by nature he cherished...

Yi Jian was particularly fond of forests and springs; he maintained a vegetarian diet and wore tattered clothes, never engaging in business or industry. He practiced patience and gentleness, delighting in the cultivation of virtue.

Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty had been on friendly terms with him since his youth; when the Emperor rose in arms, he appointed Yi Jian as Secretary to the Office of the Pacification of the West, but Yi Jian did not submit.
During the Putong era, the Emperor issued a decree appointing him as Palace Attendant, but he declined on the pretext of illness. In his later years, he resided within his own residence.

He established a site for the Way and performed repentance rituals during the six periods of the day. He recited the Lotus Sūtra once every day. One night, he suddenly saw a Daoist practitioner who called himself Master Yuan;
his appearance and demeanor were most extraordinary. He addressed Huixian as "Master Shangxing" and, after handing him incense, departed.
In the fourth year of the Zhongdatong era, while napping during the day, he suddenly woke up with a start and said, "Master Yuan has come again; I must not remain here long."
Having finished speaking, he passed away. The entire household heard a voice chanting from the air, saying: "Master Shangxing has already been reborn in the Pure Land of Amitābha.
He was seventy-eight years old at the time (Nanshi).

Songman, Songman, was a native of Hengzhou. He lived during the Sui dynasty and was devoted to the practice of pure karma. Every time he recited the Buddha’s name, he would mark the count with beans until they reached thirty *shí*.
He then prepared a vegetarian feast to make offerings to the Buddha. Suddenly, three monks arrived at the assembly to beg for food. After they had eaten, [the air was filled with] fragrance...
Flowers spread through the air, and he ascended into the sky and departed. Not long after, his face was turned toward the west as he passed away (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Zheng Muqing, a native of Yingyang, had his entire family practice the Pure Land path. During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, when he was critically ill, someone urged him to [advance].
Fish and meat were not permitted. Holding an incense burner in his hands, he faced west with single-minded devotion. Suddenly, a wondrous fragrance wafted forth in profusion, and he passed away.
His uncle, the Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Su Ting, dreamed of a precious lotus flower blooming, upon which the Prefectural Governor sat (from the *Fozu Tongji*).

Gao Haoxiang, a native of Dongping, lived in seclusion behind closed doors and recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* every day. Once, while in meditative absorption, he sat upon a red lotus flower floating in a pool of white jade.
Although he had not yet seen the Buddha, he immediately directed his whole heart toward the flower and paid him homage with deep reverence.
Gazing from afar at his golden countenance, its radiance shone forth in the four directions. One night, he saw a multitude of bodhisattvas coming to welcome him;
then, in silence, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Li Zhiyao, Li Zhiyao.
A native of Chang’an, he was deeply devoted to the Pure Land and led the assembly of faithful followers in the practice of *nianfo* in five sessions.
Late in life, he fell ill and suddenly said, “The Master has come! He washed himself, put on his robes, lit incense in the burner, and went out into the hall to prostrate in worship.
A voice was heard in the air reciting a verse: "I inform you, Li Zhiyao: merit has been achieved and its fruit is naturally summoned.

I shall lead you to birth in the Pure Land and carry you across the Golden Bridge. Thereupon, he sat upright upon his bed and passed away in stillness. A wondrous fragrance filled the room, which everyone present smelled.
(From the *Jingtu wen*)

Sun Zhong, Sun Zhong. A native of Mingzhou, he had long admired the Western [Land]. He abstained from meat and maintained the precepts. He built a hermitage east of the prefectural city, excavated two ponds, and planted white lotuses;
he constructed a pavilion overlooking the ponds. Every month he gathered the assembly to hold a Buddha-recitation assembly (*nianfo hui*). He once beheld the body of the Buddha.
He appeared in mid-air, stepped forward, and called his two sons to him; they prostrated together before him, and only after a long while did he vanish.

Later generations consequently named that place Zhufu Xiang (The Lane Where the Buddha Stopped). In the eighth year of the Yuanyou era of the Song dynasty, the monk Kejiu traveled spiritually to the Western Land.
He saw a golden platform bearing the name of Sun Zhong. After some time, Zhong fell ill; he invited a hundred monastics and laypeople to hold a Buddha-recitation assembly.
Suddenly, looking up into the void, he joined his palms in greeting, formed two mudrās with his hands, and passed away with a serene expression.
The entire city heard celestial music and extraordinary fragrances, which gradually faded toward the west. His two sons were able to carry on his legacy, and they likewise sat facing the west.
Huà (from the *Fozu tongji*). Zuoshēn was a native of Línhǎi in Tiāntái.
He received the Bodhisattva precepts from the Dharma Master Shénzhào and heard the Mahāyāna teachings.

He attained sudden and complete enlightenment. From that time forth, he strictly observed the precepts, fashioned images of the Three Holy Ones of the Western Paradise, and served them with devotion morning and night, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.
He recited the Lotus Sūtra three thousand four hundred times and the Diamond Sūtra twenty thousand scrolls.
In the autumn of the second year of the Shaosheng era, he fell ill. He instructed his son, the śramaṇa Jingyuan, to recite the opening verses of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Shortly thereafter, he dreamed of three majestic figures standing on the riverbank, who summoned him to board a boat. As they suddenly departed toward the west, Shen knew that the time for his rebirth was near;
he then requested monks to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* and suddenly said, "I have already seen the light of the Buddha," whereupon he bathed.
He changed his robes and instructed those around him not to weep and not to crowd before him;
sitting upright and forming a mudrā, he passed away (*Fahua chiyi ji* and *Fozu tongji*).
Sun Liang was a native of Qiantang. He lived in seclusion and studied the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*), gaining a profound mastery of the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

He once followed the Vinaya Master Dazhi to receive the Bodhisattva precepts. Daily, he recited the names of the Buddhas ten thousand times, never ceasing for twenty years. Suddenly, he ordered his family...

When people invited him to chant the names of the Buddhas for half a day, he joined his palms toward the sky and said, "World-Honored One and Bodhisattvas, you have already graced us with your descent.
He then withdrew from his seat and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Jia Chunren, Jia Chunren, was a native of Huzhou. He maintained a lifelong fast and cultivated the Pure Land practices. One day, manifesting illness, he faced west and recited the Buddha’s name.
Sitting peacefully in meditation, he passed away. A circular halo of white light appeared upon his crown, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Fan Yan, Fan Yan.
A native of Renhe, he habitually maintained a vegetarian diet and did not involve himself in worldly affairs. He said, "A hundred-year journey is but a temporary lodging;
what more is there to seek? Daily he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and transcribed a copy by hand, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. During the Daguang era, suddenly—
He saw Samantabhadra riding a six-tusked white elephant, emitting golden light, who said to Yan: "You have frequently recited the Lotus Sutra and been mindful of Amitābha Buddha;
you shall attain birth in the Pure Land, and thus I have come to inform you. After one night had passed, he beheld the various holy beings extending their hands to him.
He sat upright with palms joined and passed away (Fozu Tongji).

Sun Bian, whose courtesy name was also Sun Bian, was a native of Qiantang. Known as the Layman Wu-zheng, he secluded himself behind closed doors to conceal his traces, reading the Avataṃsaka and Vajracchedikā Sūtras daily.
Various sutras take the Pure Land as their ultimate refuge. Lady Gong, who had cultivated the practices of the Pure Land, fell ill by chance.
She invited the Vinaya Master Qingzhao to preach the Dharma for her; she sat upright and passed away. Not long after, she joyfully dreamed of arriving at a lotus pond and saw Qingzhao by her side.

A person standing nearby handed her a slip of paper with Sanskrit characters. Not recognizing the person, she said, "I have requested a vegetarian feast for thirteen days. At that time, it was precisely...
In the twelfth month, when the appointed time arrived, he suddenly fell ill. A monk came to inquire after his health and wished to perform prayers for him.

Fayan said, "Birth and death are already fixed; why pray? He then informed Qingzhao, saying, "I must now depart for a while. He then sat cross-legged, formed the meditative seal (*mudrā*), and passed away facing west.
The following day, Qingzhao arrived, preached the Dharma for him, sealed the coffin, and returned to the hermitage. Three days later, he too passed away. (From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*)
*Zutongji*. Tang Shiliang was a native of Kuaiji.
He observed the precepts and served the Buddha, diligently performing prostrations every day. When he grew old and fell ill, he never [ceased his practice].
He went to bed and recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* one hundred thousand times. One day, he said to his family members, "The Buddha has come to welcome me.
Having finished speaking, he prostrated himself and passed away while seated. At that time, the practitioner Zongli was at Daowei Mountain;

during the night, he dreamed that there was a wondrous light in the west, with banners, flowers, and celestial music. A voice from the air said, "Tang Shiliang has already returned to the Pure Land" (*Fozu Tongji*).

Lu Jun (陸浚) was a native of Qiantang. In his youth, he served as a minor official, but after some time, he abandoned that life. He joined the "Association for Mindfulness at West Lake" and took the Pure Land as his ultimate refuge.
Whenever he performed repentance before the Buddha, his voice and tears would flow together. On occasion, when meeting with friends, he would speak of it...

Whenever he spoke of the causes and conditions for the Pure Land, he could never help but feel moved to tears, fearing that he might not cross over in this life or that his pure karma would be difficult to accomplish.
At the end of his life, he requested the Vinaya Master Yuanjing to expound the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.

When they reached the chapter on the "Highest Birth of the Highest Grade" while chanting the *Amitābha Sūtra*, Yuanjing said to him, "It is time for you to depart. Li Jun replied, "The assembly of sages has not yet gathered; let us wait a moment longer."
After waiting for a short while, he rose and went to a bamboo bed, where he sat upright facing west. In an instant, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).

Wang Qian, whose courtesy name was Wugong, was a native of Cixi in Mingzhou. Having failed in his second attempt at the jinshi examinations, he lived in plain clothes and subsisted on vegetarian food.

He attended lecture halls extensively. In his later years, he specialized in the cultivation of the *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) samādhi and composed the *Jingtu Zixin Lu* (Record of Self-Confidence in the Pure Land).
Its preface states: "The Dharma-gate of our Buddha’s Pure Land can be summarized in a single phrase: it is simply for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to attain non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).

Why is this? Because in this land, those who practice—whether they be those at the first stage of faith (*śraddhā-pratilabdha*) in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), those at the first fruit (*phala*) of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), or those with wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—"
The poison shall never arise again. This constitutes the severing of delusions and the awakening of insight; one has newly entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Transcending birth, one does not obscure that which has been realized, thereby surmounting the four miserable destinies (*apāya*) and never losing the status of humans or devas.

Even among the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), although the bodhisattva who has subdued delusions and attained awakening may forget what has been realized and cultivated upon undergoing the extraordinary transformations of birth and death, for this reason—
There are those who, encountering adverse conditions, may regress and still fall into the realms of suffering.

However, as for the Pure Lands where ordinary beings and sages dwell together, such as the Land of Ultimate Bliss and others, although they are included within the three realms, there are only humans and devas; therefore, all sentient beings who attain birth therein—
One shall immediately take leave of the four realms of existence. Furthermore, the auxiliary conditions are fully provided, and the lifespan is immeasurable.

Even for those of dull faculties, if they practice through a single lifetime, there are none who do not realize the fruit of sainthood; how could there be any further possibility of falling back? Such is the fundamental intent behind the Tathāgata’s praise and exhortation.
Moreover, for those of complete capacity to embody the Way is the most supreme pure karma; if one earnestly applies the guidance of aspiration, [the goal will surely be attained].
They are thus included among the superior class. As for those who are simple and unsophisticated, if they can merely invoke the Buddha’s name and make a vow, there are none who do not attain rebirth.
Alas! By observing this single gateway of the Pure Land, we know that the Sage casts nothing away.

Those followers who cling to a deluded emptiness, emulating the "unimpeded" and "non-cultivation," give rise to self-obstructing minds and sever the path of others’ learning; is this not truly lamentable? (Shaoxing)
On the evening of the *dingmao* day in the fourth month of the sixteenth year, a rare fragrance suddenly filled the room.

He said to his disciple, the śramaṇa Siqi, "This is what has been evoked by my pure practice (*śuddhakarma*). Thereupon, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the lotus posture facing west before passing away.
When his body was cremated, one hundred and eight grains of *śarīra*, like millet seeds, were obtained (from the *Fozu tongji* and *Lebang wenlei*).

Wang Rihui, whose courtesy name was Xuchu, was a native of Luzhou. During the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty, he was selected as a Jinshi degree holder from the National Academy; however, he renounced his official post and did not serve.

He was extensively versed in the various classics and composed several hundred thousand words of commentaries and exegeses on the Six Classics, the Analects, and the Mencius. One day, he abandoned them all.

He devoted himself exclusively to the practice for rebirth in the Western Paradise, wearing simple clothes and subsisting on vegetarian food. He performed a thousand prostrations daily and authored a work titled *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu).
From princes, dukes, and scholar-officials down to butchers, beggars, servants, slaves, and even entertainers and courtesans—everyone was drawn to him.

He exhorted all to take refuge in the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land; his writings were composed with simple language and skillful metaphors, being extremely detailed and earnest, much like the instruction of a father or elder brother to his younger siblings.
Every morning when rising to worship the Buddha, Rihui would offer this prayer:
"I, the disciple Rihui, reverently burn incense and prostrate myself on behalf of all sentient beings throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space."
May all Buddhas, all the True Dharma, all the great Bodhisattvas, and the noble assembly of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, grant the fulfillment of all virtuous aspirations.
May they deliver immeasurable and boundless sentient beings so that, at the moment of death, in a single kṣaṇa, one may behold Amitābha Buddha,
realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and master the six supernormal powers, without departing from this world.
After one year, he came to this realm to teach and transform sentient beings.
Gradually, he transformed this Jambudvīpa, extending from the entire Sahā world to the infinite worlds of the ten directions, making them all pure and blissful worlds of Sukhāvatī.
He further prayed: "I, the disciple Rihou, for the sake of all sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa, whether great or small—"
I pay homage to all the devas, the celestial sovereigns, the sun, the moon, the Earth Goddess, and all spiritual beings.
For the sake of these sentient beings, I express gratitude for their grace in covering, supporting, illuminating, nourishing, and protecting them.
On behalf of these sentient beings, I shall recite "Namo Śākyamuni Buddha" one hundred and eight times to plant supreme roots of goodness. I shall recite "Namo Amitābha... [Buddha].
Recite the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred and eight times to form supreme and virtuous karmic conditions.

May these sentient beings always bathe in your great grace, facing one another with joy, neither contending nor killing, neither devouring nor oppressing. May they advance in the cultivation of the Buddha-dharma and escape the sea of suffering;
may this Jambudvīpa be transformed into a Land of Ultimate Bliss. Furthermore, he offered this prayer: "Disciple..."

Ri-hui. Out of deep respect for all sentient beings throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space, I prostrate before Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, and the assembly of śrāvakas and other sublime beings.

We look up with reverence to Your Great Kindness and Great Compassion. Moved by pity for sentient beings who are submerged in the sea of suffering with no prospect of escape, You have specially manifested Your majestic spiritual power to exhort one another.
You have divided Your body here within this land of Zhendan to teach and transform sentient beings, so that they do not contend with or kill one another, nor devour or oppress one another.
May the corrupt ways of the age be transformed, and may all together ascend to benevolence and longevity. And so it reaches this place...

Throughout Jambudvīpa, this Sahā world, and the turbid and evil worlds of the ten directions, may those who serve as kings, ministers, officials, and common administrators teach and transform sentient beings so that they together cultivate the Buddha-way and escape the sea of suffering.
May my own country, and likewise all the turbid and evil worlds of the ten directions, be transformed into pure and blissful worlds of Sukhāvatī. Furthermore,
The prayer says: "I, the disciple Rihui, am entangled in the net of worldly existence; my past karma is profound and heavy.

I pray that for the sake of all sentient beings killed by me in the past, those eaten by me, and all sentient beings killed or eaten throughout Jambudvīpa in the south, I shall daily recite the name of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, thirty-six trillion, one hundred and eleven thousand, nine thousand five hundred times."
Recite the name of Amitābha Buddha one hundred and twenty times. I look up with reverence to the Tathāgata’s great kindness and great compassion:
may each single recitation of the Tathāgata’s name by Riuhui deliver one sentient being;
until the number of recitations is exhausted, may all sentient beings be delivered and be born together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The details are recorded in the *Jing* [Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra].
In the *Tuzhong* (Records of the Soil): During the Qiandao era, Li Yanbi of Luling fell ill and was on the verge of death.
He dreamed of a man who called himself the Layman of Longshu, who said to him, "Rise and drink white congee; your illness shall be cured.
Furthermore, do you still remember Que Zhongya teaching you the shortcut to cultivation? Yanbi replied, "Every day I recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing. Upon waking, he sought [the congee].
He drank the gruel and was immediately cured. Yanbi had not previously known Rihui; however, upon seeing his portrait, it matched exactly with his dream.

He then sent his sons there to receive instruction from him. Three days before Rihui’s death, he took leave of all his dharma friends one by one, exhorting them to cultivate the pure practices with diligence, saying that he was about to depart and would no longer see them again.
When the appointed time arrived, after he had finished lecturing on the scriptures with his students, he passed away.
He performed his ritual recitations as usual until the third watch of the night, when he suddenly called out "Amitābha Buddha" several times in a forceful voice.
He then proclaimed, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and stood upright, passing away in a state of transformation. Hearing of this, Yanbi was moved by the event;
