he carved a statue of Ri Xu and composed an account of these matters to circulate far and wide. From then on, many people in Luling made offerings to him. During the Xianyou era, Lü Yuan...
Yizhong re-carved the *Jingtu wen* (Text on the Pure Land). When he reached the section on "Vows," three śarīra relics were found within the printing blocks.
His uncle, Shishe, recorded this event at the beginning of the text, titled *Lebang wenlei: Jingtu wen*.
Loufen, Loufen.
A native of Mingzhou, his elder brother Baozhou was fond of the Buddhist scriptures and would frequently discuss the Way with śramaṇas.
Loufen listened from the sidelines, his faith growing day by day. At the age of twenty-two, he fell ill and resolved to return to the West [India]. He said to his parents:
He said, "If one can merely attain birth in the Pure Land, see the Buddha, and hear the Dharma—what worldly excellence could surpass this?
He then requested that the monks recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Contemplation Sūtra). He set up an image opposite his bed and gazed at it for a long time, saying, "I am already in the Western Land.
Thereupon, he recited the names of the Buddhas and passed away while facing west (*Fozu Tongji*).
Zhang Yuanxiang was a native of Chang’an. He habitually recited the name of the Buddha without ceasing. One day he said to his family members, "The Sage of the Western Land is coming here;
wait for me until my meal is finished, and we shall go together to the Pure Land. When the meal was over, he burned incense, faced west, and sat in the full lotus posture.
He passed away while sitting in the lotus posture (according to the *Fozu tongji*).
Yuan Ziping—whose origins are unknown—resided at Guanyin Temple in Jingkou. He practiced mindfulness of the Buddha and recited the sutras. One day...
Suddenly hearing the sound of celestial music from the air, he sat facing west and passed away into transformation; a rare fragrance did not cease for several days (*Fozu Tongji*).
Yao Yue was a native of Xiantan in Huzhou. He devoted himself to the inner scriptures. When Master You of Juehai established a society for the cultivation of Pure Land practices, Yao Yue [joined it].

The Master was in fact presiding over these affairs. Suddenly, he told his friend, "I have long grown weary of this floating life; before many days pass, I shall depart for the West. You may assist me in reciting the Buddha’s name.
His friend then recited the Buddha’s name with him every day. One day, the Master took his seat and passed away.

Shortly thereafter, he appeared in a dream to his friend and said, "I have already been reborn in the Pure Land; this is due to the power of your assistance. The friend replied, "I wish to travel with you, sir; may I?"
Yue said, "The Master's worldly lifespan is not yet exhausted; Jingyi of this monastery shall arrive first. Jingyi was a fellow member of the monastic community.
Within a month, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Mei Fu, Mei Fu.
A native of Songjiang, he recited the sutras and upheld the precepts, fixing his mindfulness on the Pure Land.

As the time of his death approached, he knew it beforehand and immediately ceased eating grain, subsisting only on water. Upon reaching the seventh day, he bathed, changed his robes, sat upright, and addressed [his disciples]:
The assembly said, "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva has now come to welcome me," and he passed away while still seated (*Fozu Tongji*).

Hu Song, whose courtesy name was Hu Song, was a native of Huzhou. During his lifetime, he placed his faith in the Buddha-dharma and cultivated various meritorious deeds. One night, he suddenly dreamed of the Buddha.
A saying goes: "You may build a house to welcome me. Sōng then constructed a pavilion to enshrine Amitābha.
On the evening of his death, he suddenly said, "The Buddha’s light is illuminating me," and having finished speaking, he passed away (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Lu Wei, Lu Wei.
A native of Qiantang. Initially serving as a local official, he grew weary of the world in his middle years and diligently cultivated the Pure Land practice.

He established two congregations for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, each numbering about a hundred people. After twenty years, these eventually became a grand assembly. Lu Wei personally transcribed the Dharma...
Having changed his robes one day and sat upright,
he chanted the name of the Buddha and passed away (Fozu Tongji).

Yan Bangrong was a native of Qingyang in Chizhou. In his middle years, he encountered a monk who exhorted him to cultivate the Pure Land practice and to recite the *Wangsheng Zhou* (Recitation for Rebirth).
He subsequently abstained from meat and blood. Every morning, he would face west and recite the mantra a thousand times; he also led various men and women to chant it together with a single voice.

He recited it for twenty years. On the first day of the first month of the first year of the Shaohui era, while reading the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, he sighed and said, "Human life is but a dream and an illusion;
why should I have any attachment? On the first day of the third month, he smelled a wondrous fragrance that was rich and pervasive, which did not cease for an entire day.
His son dreamed of Amitābha Buddha emitting a great radiance that illuminated the entire hall, turning everything into the color of gold.
Five days later, he rose at dawn. Having completed his regular recitations, he looked at his family and said, "I shall depart today;
pray do not disturb me. He then faced west, closed his eyes, and sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). After midday had passed, he suddenly rose and said, "I am going.
He stood up, walked several steps, extended his hands to form a mudrā, and passed away with a smile (from the *Lèbāng wénlèi*).
Wu Keci, whose courtesy name was Fuzhi and who styled himself the Layman Kaian, resided in Putian, Wuzhou. He once suffered from severe eye disease.
Someone advised him to recite the name of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara; he followed this advice, and his illness was quickly cured. Thereupon, he conceived deep faith.

As for the mind: when he read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to the passage where emptiness arises within the mind—likened to a cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the sky—he felt as if his ignorance had been suddenly dispelled.

Later, after reading the *Zhongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the School) for a long time, he attained realization and composed the *Fahua shujian* (Key to the Lotus). He dedicated his merit toward rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, saying:

"Without reading the *Lotus Sūtra*, there would be no way to clarify that the wondrous Dharma is inherently possessed by my own mind; without being born in An-yang (Sukhāvatī), there would be no way to realize this mind."
The wondrous Dharma is inherently present. The Tathāgata has repeatedly and earnestly taught it; the wise have diligently propagated the sutras.

From the Buddhas and Patriarchs down to the present, their compassion has been consistent, never diverging from this single path. During the Qiandao era, while residing in Suzhou, he formed a Lotus Society with Master Shi of Baoji.

He commissioned artisans to paint illustrations of the ten realms and nine grades upon the two corridors: one to demonstrate that all phenomena are but the mind, and the other to point toward the Western Paradise.
The path [to his grave] was recorded by his fellow student Zhongli Song. In the winter of the seventh year of the Jiading era, he passed away at Baoshan.
His final instruction was that he be cremated according to the rites for a monk. He was seventy-five years of age (*Fozu Tongji*, *Lebang Wenlei*).
Chen Junzhang.
A native of Huangyan, he was born during the Yuan dynasty. At the age of forty, he turned his heart toward the Buddha-dharma.

Together with his wife, Lady Ye, he recited the Lotus Sūtra and dedicated the merit toward rebirth in Sukhāvatī. After twenty years had passed, when his illness became critical, he instructed his son, Jingxing:
He helped him sit up and said, "I am returning home. Jingxing asked, "Where do you go to return? He replied, "I am going to the place of extinction.

He then instructed that after his death, the *jhāpaka* (cremation) rites for a *śramaṇa* should be performed. With palms joined, he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha and passed away (*Wansheng ji*).
King Jiulian, King Jiulian.
His origins are unknown; he was also a man of the Yuan period. He devotedly cultivated the Pure Land practice and meditated according to the sutras.
However, the Buddhas who appeared in his dreams were all depicted as images, not living Buddhas. One day, he met the monk Jigong, who told him:
For this reason, Master Ji said, "This is easy. Can you recall the appearance of your late father? [The man] replied, "I can.

"Is what you saw in your dream different from his appearance when he was alive? [The man] replied, "It is no different. Master Ji said, "The Buddha is fundamentally without form; it is because of the mind that form arises.
If you wish to see the Buddha, simply regard your late father as Amitābha Buddha and visualize a white [light] between his eyebrows."
Visualize the light of the *ūrṇā*. Form the visualization that his face is like pure gold. Form the visualization that he is seated upon a precious lotus flower.

After visualizing this for a long time until it is perfected, you will gradually see his body; as the days pass, it becomes higher and larger until it pervades the entire realm of empty space. Then, you will behold the Living Buddha.

If one cultivates the Nine Lotuses according to the Dharma, from then on, one will see one’s father in every dream and will immediately think, "This is the Buddha. After a long time, the father will finally lead [the practitioner] to sit beside him.
Lianhua was given the essentials of the Dharma. The nine lotuses blossomed in her heart, and her diligent cultivation became even more earnest.
There was a paternal relative, Mr. Ma, who had returned from afar; seeing Lianhua, he said: "On such-and-such a day, I fell gravely ill and was seized by the officials of the underworld.
As I passed through various hells in a state of extreme terror, suddenly a golden light shone upon my body. Within that light was a person sitting upon a lotus flower, calling me by my name."
He gazed at him closely and recognized it was his own father. He ordered an official to escort him home, whereupon he was restored to life.

Not knowing what spiritual cultivation his father had practiced to reach such a state, Jiulian explained the circumstances to him. Mr. Ma was likewise moved and vowed to practice the Pure Land path together with him (from the *Langhuan ji*).
Yang Jiawei (also written Jiexi), courtesy name Banghua, was a native of Taihe County in Jixian Prefecture. During the Wanli era of the Ming Dynasty, he was a local scholar (*zhusheng*).

From his youth, he was fond of learning and investigated all branches of literature. Later, he devoted himself deeply to the Buddhist scriptures (*neidian*). At the age of thirteen, he observed the precept against killing.
He was not harmed by fleas or lice. When he reached his twenty-something years, he entered the National University (Guozi Jian) in Nanjing.
Suddenly, he fell ill and dreamed of wandering through hell, where he beheld Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva in the Hall of the Living and the Dead (Mingyang Dian).

Upon waking, he released all living creatures, invited monks to recite sutras, and after chanting the Buddha’s name, he said to those around him, "I am about to depart. A blue lotus has appeared before me. It was no ordinary [flower].
"Is this the realm of the Pure Land? he asked. Thereupon, he chanted the Buddha’s name day and night without ceasing.
He commanded his attendant to extinguish the candle, saying, "I am always within the light; there is no need for a candle. When asked what he saw, he replied, "Lotuses of four colors are blooming.

When asked whether he saw Amitābha, he said, "I see Amitābha manifesting a body one thousand *zhang* tall. When asked about Avalokiteśvara, he said, "His body is equal in size to that of Amitābha. Only...
"I have not seen Śrī-Ābhāsvara. Having finished speaking, he suddenly leaped up, took up incense, and said, "The merit of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* is unspeakable, unspeakable, unspeakable.
I have already attained rebirth in the highest grade. He then passed away in silence (*Wǎngshēng jí*).
Chen Daomin, whose Dharma name was Mingjue, was a native of Wujiang. From his youth, he maintained a vegetarian diet.

In the twenty-sixth year of the Jiajing era, he became a disciple of Master Zhiyuan, receiving the Upāsaka precepts. He recited the scriptures during the six periods of the day, his mouth never ceasing its chanting.
In the ninth month of the fifteenth year of the Wanli era, the Buddha [the Master] knew in advance that his time had come and took leave of his fellow practitioners.
On the night of the seventeenth day, while his wife was lighting a torch to spin silk, the Daoist layman bowed with joined palms to his wife to bid her farewell.

He sat upon the corner of the bed, removed his shoes and socks, and bound them together with a sash, saying, "Tomorrow morning you will not be able to put them on. Upon returning home, he hurriedly called for his children and grandchildren.
He looked around; at midnight, the sound of his reciting the Buddha’s name fell silent, and he passed away (from the *Huayuan*).
Tang Tingren, whose courtesy name was Tiru, was a student from Lanxi in Jinhua. By nature he was pure and sincere, personally practicing filial piety and fraternal kindness.
He practiced this conduct. Subsequently, realizing that the world is impermanent, he turned his heart toward the Ultimate Way.
He studied under Master Yunqi Hong and received the precepts for the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance, which he then practiced with great diligence. For thirteen years, they passed like a single day.

At the age of sixty, on the morning of the middle winter month, he said to his sons, "On the eleventh day of the New Year, I shall depart. When the appointed time arrived, he washed and rinsed his mouth and adjusted his robes.
She sat upright, formed mudrās with her hands, and recited the Buddha’s name; she passed away with a smile.
This event occurred in the thirty-first year of the Wanli era (as recorded in the *Wansheng ji*).
Ge Yi’an was a native of Qiantang.
He served Master Yunqi Hong as his teacher; his Dharma name was Guangtai. He was filial toward his parents and delighted in practicing hidden virtue.
In his later years, he served the Buddha with great devotion and established two seasonal assemblies—one for spring and autumn—with the monk Suanxue. For...
He held a Buddha-recitation assembly and recited the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. Afterward, he said, "My great limit has arrived; I must now prepare for my journey to the West.

He then shut himself in a room to practice meditation and recitation, never ceasing day or night. He predetermined the date of his departure. Two days prior, when his family came to visit him, they were deeply grieved.
He comforted them, saying, "Birth must inevitably end in death; why grieve? I am merely concentrating my spirit on the Pure Land."
He beheld Amitābha face-to-face. [The Master] said, "You all must not allow emotional attachments to disturb my right mindfulness. He then invited Yuanxu to join him in chanting the Buddha’s name.
When the appointed time arrived, he passed away (from the *Wangsheng ji*).
Sun Shuzi, Sun Shuzi.
A native of Tongcheng, Anqing. His father, Layman Jingwu, while reading Yunqi’s *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, sighed deeply and said:
"How sublime is this wondrous function! It turns heaven and earth; it is what is called the beginning and end throughout ten ages of past and present."
There is no practice that does not depart from the present moment; is it not solely the single gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha?
He cast an image of Amitābha Buddha, adorned according to the Forty-eight Vows. Once the image was completed, he sent it to Yunqi and requested the Dharma name Guangyu (Broad Abiding) for himself.
He was styled Disciple Shuzi. At the age of twelve, he followed [the master] and subsequently received the five precepts; his dharma name was Dawu.

Upon returning home, he abstained from meat and blood and abandoned his studies for the civil service examinations. He cultivated the *nien-fo samādhi* with such diligence that he spared neither body nor life.
Suddenly, he saw two bhikṣus standing before him holding lotuses and said, "Young man, well done! You have single-mindedly focused on the Pure Land. He further saw...

The transformed person recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for a full day and night. Then, he suddenly rose from his seat and said, "Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara have both come to welcome me.
He formed the *vajra-muṣṭi-mudrā* and chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha several times, whereupon he passed away in profound stillness.
A "Song of the Twelve Hours of the Pure Land" was transmitted to the world. Within his chamber, auspicious *reishi* mushrooms grew every year. In the year of his death, there was...
One [image] was as large as a peck-measure (*dou*). Its color was either like gold or like a red-white wheel (*Wangsheng ji*, *Yunqi fahui*).
Guo Dalin of Tangyin was also single-mindedly devoted to the Pure Land practice. At the age of seventy-six, one day he said to his son:
He said, "I shall depart at noon. Without illness, he passed away (*Wensheng ji*). Liu Tongzhi was a native of Shuntian.
He was diligent and devoted to the recitation of the Buddha's name. At the age of fifty-two, he fell ill; his mindfulness became even more earnest. His...
His dharma-fellow Bai-zhai died first. Tong-zhi fainted and then revived, saying to his family members, "Bai-zhai and I are destined to be born together in the Pure Land;
he has already moored his boat there waiting for me. Change my clothes for me.
He hung his prayer beads around his neck and followed [the deceased], whereupon he passed away (*Wangsheng ji*).
Hao Xizai, Hao Xizai.
A student of the local schools in Qiantang, he was a man of loyalty and integrity who never deceived others. In his later years, he returned to the teachings of Yunqi; his Dharma name was Guangding.
He lived at home, engaging in meditation and recitation without interruption. Subsequently, he fell ill. One day, he suddenly raised his head and looked toward the window.
Later, he said to his son, "Now, heaven and earth have parted. At midnight, he said, "The Buddha sits upon a lotus pedestal and appears before me;
I am going. He then passed away. This event took place in the thirty-ninth year of the Wanli era (as recorded in the *Wansheng ji*).
The Layman Du, Layman Du—his personal name has been lost—was a native of Wanping who followed Heaven. He lived in seclusion within an ancient hall beside Duan Guang Temple on the Western Hills.

For thirty years, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name; when encountering others, he would do nothing but join his palms and chant the Buddha’s name. He was able to know in advance that [he was about to pass away].

The ritual concluded after nine days of repentance. When reciting the earnest passages within the liturgy, she would suddenly shed tears and choke with emotion. She subsequently ceased eating, drinking only a small amount of water each day.
Upon the completion of the repentance ceremony, she sat upright and passed away. Ten days later, when the body was finally enshrouded for burial, her countenance remained as if alive.
Five-colored clouds swirled above her dwelling; those in the mountains spread word of this marvel (from the *Wǎngshēng jí*).

Wu Da’en, Wu Da’en, was a native of Renhe. He was compassionate and fond of charity; he showed mercy to the orphaned and the destitute and protected all living beings. His fellow villagers praised him for these virtues.

Subsequently, he turned his heart toward the Buddha-dharma, reciting sutras and chanting the Buddha’s name morning and night. One day, he took leave of the assembly and sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

When he passed away, his countenance was radiant and the room was filled with a fragrant aroma. This account is recorded in the *Wǎngshēng jí* (Collection on Rebirth), dated the fortieth year of the Wànlì era.

Wú Jìxūn, courtesy name Yòngqīng, was a native of Huízhōu in Jiangnán. He was grave and resolute by nature, and his thirst for doing good was like that for water. In his later years, he cultivated [the Way].
He purified his karma, maintained the recitation of the *Wǎngshēng* (Rebirth) Dhāraṇī, and chanted the Buddha’s name with a fixed daily practice. Once, he lost his footing and fell into the river;
a being supported him, and after drifting ten *lǐ*, he leaped up and boarded a boat. The multitude regarded this as divine.
Later, he suffered from a carbuncle on his back, yet he continued his recitations as usual. Suddenly, with right mindfulness, he passed away (*Wǎngshēng jí*).
Huajushi, Huajushi:
a native of Jianggan in Hangzhou. He was pure, simple, and free from artifice; he did not engage in formal social courtesies with others.

In his middle years, he lived alone in a single room, withdrew from worldly affairs, and devoted himself solely to the diligent recitation of the Buddha’s name. When his end approached, he knew the time of his passing by himself.
He arrived at his residence, changed his clothes, and entered the main chamber. He adjusted his cap with his own hands and sat upright. Departing from the assembly, he passed away (*Wansheng ji*).
Gu Yuan, courtesy name Qingfu, styled Baochang Jushi, was a celestial being who had been a *zhusheng* (junior scholar) during the Jiajing era. He was young... [text fragment ends].
Haojun was skilled in poetry and proficient in calligraphy and painting.

Upon reaching the age of forty, he completely abandoned his former studies, renounced wine and meat, and constructed a small pavilion where he sat alone to cultivate meditative contemplation with great diligence. He never allowed pigs, humans, or women to see his face.
Every night at the fifth watch, he would rise and strike a large wooden fish-drum, chanting "Amitābha Buddha" in a loud voice. Beside his dwelling lived a butcher.
Every time he heard the sound of the wooden fish, he would immediately rise from the butcher’s stall. One day he rose late; in a fit of rage, he rebuked his wife.
His wife said, "Do you not hear that practitioner beating the wooden fish and reciting the Buddha's name every day? He does not know his own faults, yet he rebukes me."
"Why is this? The butcher was startled; he immediately broke his knife and ceased slaughtering. At once, a great many of the butchers followed his example and changed their vocations.
Yuan was on friendly terms with Master Yun Gu of Xi Xia, with whom he established a Western Paradise Society.
One day, when Master Qing of Han Shan arrived at Xi Xia Temple, he saw from afar a practitioner who was as serene as a solitary crane. As he drew near, [he observed] that the man’s eyes—
He did not blink. As if casting off the world, he then entered the palace gate and paid homage at the Śarīra stupa. He gazed upon it for a long time;
suddenly, five-colored light appeared atop the stupa, as vermilion as if inlaid with jewels. Master Qing was struck by this marvel and spoke of it to Yungu. Yungu said, "This is a jeweled banner;
you are currently practicing the visualization of the Western Paradise. Shortly thereafter, he manifested a slight illness and requested several eminent monks.
The people there chanted the Buddha’s name together. Shortly thereafter, a palace attendant ran to report, "The fragrance of lotuses is being smelled throughout the entire residence.
The crowd was filled with wonder and joy, yet Yuan remained as tranquil as usual. He spoke slowly to the monk, saying, "I have been sitting within a lotus flower for more than half a month."
I beheld the Dharma-body of Amitābha pervading the worlds of empty space; all these worlds were golden in color.
The Buddha looked at me with a smile and took my hand, then covered me with his *kāṣāya*. "I shall certainly go to the Western Land," I thought.
My sons wept and pleaded, saying, "Father, if you depart at once, what will become of us children? Yuanxiao replied, "Do you think I am alive? Do you think I am dead?"
"But have you not observed the sun? It rises in the east and sets in the west. Does it truly vanish?
He then set a date, bathed, changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away; the fragrance of lotuses did not cease for three days (from the *Dream Excursion Collection* by Hanshan).
Zhu Yuanzheng, Zhu Yuanzheng, was a student at the local school in Haiyan. Throughout his life, he had been devoted to the study of the sages. He maintained a very strict discipline over himself.

When he reached his sixties, he immersed himself deeply in the joy of Chan meditation. He lived in a dilapidated room behind his house, closing the door to his retreat and no longer attending to household affairs. Every day...
At dawn he would recite one scroll of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and once midday had passed, he would sit in meditation.

His disciple Chen Ze-liang visited him and said, "Master, you are advanced in years; why not relax your prohibition against wine for a little? Yuan Zheng replied, "Do you think I need to nourish my blood and qi?
You do not realize that I have already drawn a line of demarcation regarding birth and death. Ze-liang was struck with awe. He was seventy years old at that time.
Yue said to his son, "I have no further business here; you may go. When asked where he was going, he replied, "To the West.
Although the son and grandson earnestly entreated him to stay, on the first day of the twelfth month, he manifested a slight illness and ceased eating.

His family members hurriedly prepared the funeral requisites. Yuánzhèng said, "Do not be anxious; after eight days from now, at midnight, the matter will be settled. When the time arrived, he sat upright.
He wished to depart. Again he said, "In my life, I have never failed anyone by even a hair’s breadth. Recently, a craftsman behind my house leveled a patch of ground for my back gate.
I intended to wait until the New Year of next year to go out through the pass and walk about;

since I have not yet repaid his kindness, I shall take this paper to compose a poem to thank him. Having spoken thus, he passed away silently while it was still cock-crow. At that time, he had already made his preparations.

Regarding the lay practitioner: when he was about to depart, he did not allow women to come near him. They were permitted to arrive only after two or three hours had passed, and even then they were not to weep.
By the break of dawn, his kinsmen arrived and all began to wail. Yuanzheng, however, opened his eyes again and shook his head, ordering the women to leave.
Only when they had all departed did he close his eyes once more (from the *Fahua chiyen jishi*).
Zhou Tingzhang, styled Chufeng, was a native of Yunnan. He was born during the Zhengde and Jiajing reigns. By nature he was simple and honest;

in managing his household, he did not calculate whether he had wealth or not. Whenever he possessed anything, he would immediately distribute it to the poor. When people spoke with him, he would simply smile. Or...

Though others mocked him or insulted him, he merely smiled. Having long turned toward the Buddha-dharma, he would invariably recite one scroll each of the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Amitābha*, and the *Avalokiteśvara* sūtras upon rising at dawn;
thus filled with self-satisfaction, he would say, "I do not depart from daily life, nor do I involve myself in craving and attachment—it is simply this.
At the age of eighty-seven, on the Qingming festival, while visiting his ancestral graves, he took his final leave of his ancestors.
He returned and said to his wife, "I am about to depart; Amitābha has come to welcome me, and both Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta have arrived together.
Shortly thereafter, he said, "Avalokiteśvara told me that I must abstain from meat for five days before traveling west. Thereupon, he ate only one meal of gruel and one dish of vegetables per day.

When the appointed time arrived, he bathed and donned his cap, and instructed his children and grandchildren to recite the names of the Seven Tathāgatas. Once the recitation of the sutra was finished, he passed away.
He sat upright and passed away. On the following day, a fragrance emanated from his body, and his countenance remained as if alive (*Jinganglingshenglü*).
Cheng Jienshan—his courtesy name was Chuan; he left behind no personal name—was by nature filial and fraternal. In his youth, he worked as a merchant, but later abandoned that life.
At home, he studied Buddhist principles with great precision. His ritual recitations followed a fixed schedule, which he did not neglect even amidst his busiest affairs.

In his later years, he became increasingly serene and silent, devoting his days to the practice of Chan meditation. When his illness grew critical and his family was in a state of frantic distress, he said to them, "Do not make a sound;
I am now clarifying my thoughts and taking the Western Paradise as my destination. My lifelong aspiration is now fulfilled. Thereupon, he passed away.
At the age of seventy-six (according to Liu Ziwei’s *Chan Yue Xiao Cao*).
Zhang Shouyue, a native of Xiushui County, Zhejiang Province, was poor yet fond of charity; he exhorted his fellow practitioners to widely perform acts of benefit.

He performed beneficial deeds in a hundred thousand ways. In his later years, he completely renounced worldly affairs, subsisting on a single vegetable dish and a single meal daily while reciting the names of the Buddhas of the Western Paradise.
He once composed three hundred poems modeled after those of Hanshan to exhort both the monastic and lay communities. He was single-mindedly devoted to the Pure Land as his ultimate refuge.
He said: "The Great Dharma-gate of the Pure Land and the Great Vow-power of Amitābha have come this very day after a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas."

Having first attained this realization, you should conceive the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find; be careful not to lose it again. Recite the Buddha's name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land;

what is precious is single-mindedness. One verse says: "Entrusting my idle body to that which lies beyond all things, let all conditions cease of their own accord. Unstained by even a speck of dust, I remain in silent stillness."
Meditate on the name of the Buddha with single-mindedness. Let your nature be as soft as cotton-wool, yet let your mind be as hard as iron.

To willingly engage in useless matters is like reaching down into the depths of water to grasp at the moon. One says: "Yesterday I entered the Lotus Society; my mouth was the Buddha and my mind was likewise the Buddha.

Today, amidst the burning house, affairs are manifold and thoughts are likewise manifold. Were it not for a profound capacity, one could not avoid being submerged in the turbidity of worldly toil. Thus, the ancients...
The Sage cultivated pure practices in the mountains. One version says: "Those of the superior grade see the Buddha quickly; those of the inferior grade see the Buddha slowly.

Although there is this difference in speed, in the end there is never a time of regression. To practice Chan is to be afflicted by attachment to signs; in the recitation of the Buddha's name, it is essential to sever doubt.
Truly, truly, there is the Pure Land; truly, truly, there is the Lotus Pond. One version says: "Seventy years are rare these days; there is not much ahead."

The day arrived. Hurry, hurry, to prepare the travel provisions; I fear we may not arrive in time. Whether he acts crookedly, let him act crookedly; whether he acts straightforwardly, let him act straightforwardly.
Where could one find the leisure to distinguish right from wrong for him? His wife, née Tao, had followed Shouyue since their marriage and likewise recited the scriptures without interruption.
When Shouyue went to Putuo to pay homage to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara), Tao said to her two sons: "In my daily life..."
"Sanzi, this mind is the Buddha. Only now have I finally realized this. My karmic ties to this Sahā world are exhausted; it is time for me to depart.
He sat upright and passed away at the appointed hour. The next day, Shouyue returned to perform the funeral rites.
Suddenly, blue lotus flowers emerged from atop the coffin, numbering five. (From the *Nianhan Shan Shi Bing Xu Wangsheng Ji*)
Zhuang Guanghuan. His courtesy name was Fuzhen. He was a native of Tongxiang, Jiaxing. In his youth he was a Confucian scholar; later, he studied medicine.

When he was over forty years old, he grew somewhat weary of worldly affairs and consequently devoted himself to the arts of nourishing life (*yangsheng*). After some time, he fell ill and sighed deeply, saying:
"Can I alone not become a man of leisure within this world of heaven and earth? He then constructed a small garden, stacking stones and planting flowering trees, and there he would sing and chant.
One day, beholding the blooming and falling of flowers, he realized the impermanence of the body;

he immediately demolished the garden, closed his door, and sat in meditation, taking up various sutras such as the *Vajracchedikā* to recite them. Once, while traveling to Hangzhou, he encountered an old man with whom he conversed.

He was studying Buddhism. The old man asked, "In your study of Buddhism, whom do you take as your teacher? He replied, "I have not yet found one. The old man said, "Have you not read the writings on the practice of *qi* by Liu Zihou?
There is a Chan Master named Lianchi at Yunqi; he is nearby. Why not go there to take him as your teacher?"
He replied, "Yes," and subsequently traveled on foot to Yunqi to visit Lianchi. Lianchi bestowed upon him the method of reciting the Buddha’s name, whereupon he received the five precepts.
Upon returning home, he daily recited the name of Amitābha Buddha fifty thousand times. Before half a year had passed, his mind became tranquil.
At the age of eighty, he visited Yunqi again to receive the bodhisattva precepts and retired to his home. He often lamented that...
The people of my village were ignorant of the True Dharma and mostly followed heterodox teachings.

I have compiled the essential passages from various sutras and treatises on the Pure Land, entitled the *Pure Land Provisions Collection* (*Jingtu ziliang ji*), in order to guide the faithful. The villagers subsequently followed this example and were transformed by it. (From the *Pure Land Provisions Collection*)
Bao Zongzhao, courtesy name Xingquan, was a native of Shanyin in Shaoxing. His family had followed the Buddhist faith for generations.

Once Zongzhao reached the age of majority, he abstained from meat and alcohol and was able to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* from memory, completing one full cycle each day. His father ordered him to sell paper.
In Jiaxing, he was angered by a financial loss and punished with a prostration for a long time. When he rose, he had already silently finished reciting the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
He had formerly traveled with masters such as Zibo and Sanmu; later, he turned his heart toward Yunqi, where he devoted himself earnestly to the Pure Land practice.
Furthermore, he exerted great effort in studying various texts such as the *Fangshan Heli Lun* and Yongming’s *Zongjing Lu*, until his faith and understanding became thorough and proficient.
He styled himself the Layman Heavenly Drum (Tiāngǔ Jūshì). He authored a work titled *The Heavenly Music Resounds in the Void* (*Tiānyuè Míngkōng*).

At the time of his death, he instructed his son to prepare a vegetarian feast and invited several monastics, including the monk Wang Jichang, to attend. Together, they recited the name of the Buddha of the Western Paradise in unison.
When the sun was setting, he suddenly joined his palms, thanked the assembly, saying, "I bid you all a final farewell," and then passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. (From the *Tiān*)
Lè-míng-kōng-jí). Zāng-yán-zāng-yán. His courtesy name was Píngshū.
A native of Huátíng, Sōngjiāng, he had a profound understanding of the Buddha-dharma. He guided his fellow practitioners, [providing them with] clothing and footwear.
He gave away all his remaining possessions to others. His family consisted of only one son and one daughter-in-law, whom he regarded with utter detachment.

In his leisure time, he composed poetry and short lyrics (*ci*), all of which were refined, remote, and full of resonance. He once composed a *man-ting-fang* tune, the first line of which reads: "Sixty-odd years..."
A fleeting dream of spring; upon awakening, the yellow millet was already cooked. How much true splendor is there in these floating flowers and illusory shadows?

With a cool eye, one lightly pierces through them; quickly turning over, one snaps the silken tether. Let children and grandchildren perform their plays as they will—there is no need to watch to the very end.
A handful of thatch upon the green mountains is my remaining livelihood; let us deliberate on this anew. Simply follow conditions as they arise.
Passing the time. Washing the bowl and burning incense, he first sent his mind back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss to roam at ease.

Amidst the cool serenity of the jewel-trees, there is cause for sorrow. When one turns their head to look back, the ocean of karma is vast and boundless. In the fourth year of the Tianqi era, he passed away in the garden of his friend Hu Zhihao.
Wang Ruosheng of Kunshan recorded these verses as a record of what he had observed over several years of study.
The Daoist master considered Pingshu to be the foremost (from Wang Ruosheng’s *Hezhu ji*).
Huang Chenghui, courtesy name Yuanfu, was a native of Qiantang in Hangzhou. He was a man of upright integrity who did not conform to worldly conventions; he was unable to...
He managed the family's agricultural production and served his paternal grandmother and maternal mother with complete filial piety. He delighted in practicing charity;
whenever a neighbor lacked clothing in the cold, he would take off his own garment to clothe them, and to those who had no food, he emptied the coins from his own purse to give to them.

His wife’s younger brother, upon hearing of Qi Chu’s character, marveled at his purity and austerity, and guided him to visit Master Hong at Yunqi, where he met him in the manner of a disciple. Master Hong named him Jingming.

Thereafter, he contracted a disease of vomiting blood. It persisted for three years without abating and grew increasingly severe. Chenghui had previously been taught by Qichu to recite the Buddha’s name, but while suffering from the agony, he was not mindful of it.
Qichu said in a stern voice, "When the light of your eyes falls to the ground, where will that which currently knows pain ultimately reside?
Chenghui was struck with awe and asked, "What should I do? Qichu replied, "Nothing is better than this."
When Chenghui was reciting the Buddha’s name, he asked, "Are you teaching me to recite the Amitābha of self-nature, or the Amitābha of Sukhāvatī?
Qichu replied, "Do you think there are two? Chenghui suddenly attained realization and invited Dharma Master Huiwen to come.

He set up an image of the Buddha and explained the causes and conditions for the Pure Land to him. Accepting this with joy, he requested the Dharma Master to shave his head and received the śrāmaṇera precepts.

He secluded himself from his family and chanted the name of the Buddha while silently reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for seven days. All the family members smelled the fragrance of the lotus.
Suddenly, [the deceased] smiled and spoke a verse, saying: "Not a single thing is brought here; not a single thing is taken away. High...
"A single autumn moon atop the mountain peak—this is the original, true meaning.

He then instructed his family to prepare a vegetarian feast for the Buddha, invite monks to chant the Buddha’s name, and recite the *Vow Text of Yunqi*. When the text reached the passage: "Amitābha Buddha emits light to welcome and guide;
He lowers His hand to take us by the wrist," he rose from his seat with joy. Gazing intently at the Buddha image, he passed away. (From the *Dream Wandering Collection* of Hanshan Deqing)
Wen Qi was originally named Wen Qichu;
his courtesy name was Zixing, and his Dharma name was Dachi. He was a fellow villager of Chenghui. From his youth, he had been plagued by illness and resolved to transcend birth and death.
Consequently, he went to Yunqi to receive the teachings on the Buddha-recitation method. After Yunqi entered parinirvāṇa, [he went to] Hanshan Qing...
When Master Qing arrived to offer condolences, Huiqi initiated the ritual and spoke, saying, "I wish to shave my hair and become your disciple.

Master Qing said, "The Buddha-nature cannot be constrained by the four great elements; how could mere hair and beard pose an obstacle? Furthermore, you have parents living; this is not yet permissible."
At first, his illness had already subsided. Suddenly, however, it flared up again. Zhiqiu said, "I shall go straight to the Western Land; this illness will not harm me.

When the illness became severe, his spirit and mind grew confused and disordered, and he could no longer sustain himself. Greatly terrified, he urgently ordered his family members to invite a monk to chant the Buddha's name.
After one day had passed, his confusion remained as before. He then started in alarm and said, "The root and trunk of birth and death..."
It was not something others could have extracted for him. He rose immediately, washed his face and hands, and donned his robes.

Facing the Buddha, he burned incense and set his arm on fire, repenting with such bitter grief that he did not show the slightest weariness throughout the entire night. Upon returning to his seat, his spirit was at peace and his mind settled; the Pure Land appeared before him.

Thereupon, he shaved his head, donned the *kāṣāya*, and passed away apart from the assembly. When Master Qing of Mount Han heard of this, he sighed in admiration, saying: "How brave! How brave! (Wencai).
He may truly be called a man of fierce integrity (*liè zhàngfū*). Shen Xian (Shen Xian), courtesy name Zhixian, was a native of Wujiang.
From his youth, he was exceptionally brilliant; having reached the age of twenty, he was enrolled as a *zhusheng* (local student). By nature, he was profoundly filial. His father... [text continues]

His mother passed away in succession, and he was so overcome with grief that he became emaciated until his ribs were visible. While reading by chance the *Amitābha-sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, and other Mahāyāna scriptures, he attained a profound realization.

He went to visit Master Yunqi and, upon returning, renounced meat and pungent flavors. He secluded himself at the Shuixi Hermitage in his home district, dedicating himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
Every day he recited the Buddha’s name fifty thousand times, without ceasing regardless of cold or heat. Furthermore, he beautifully transcribed the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
Jianmu once established a Pure Land association with the monk Yuanjian, and many people in the district were converted by her influence.
One day, she said to her daughter-in-law, "My worldly karmic ties have come to an end; the Buddha of the West has come to welcome me, and I shall follow him back.
Shortly thereafter, she passed away while sitting cross-legged facing west. This was in the thirty-ninth year of the Wanli era. Her son...
Hong also cultivated pure karma. He once transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* using his own blood (as recorded in the biography of Layman Shen by Zhang Mengyi).

Zhu Lu, whose courtesy name was Baimin, was a local student from Wujiang. Possessing brilliant talent from a young age, he abandoned his status as a student upon the death of his parents and devoted himself to study.

Regarding the art of longevity: subsequently, he studied under Master Yunqi Hong to investigate the essential points of the Dharma. After Master Hong passed away, Lü paid homage at his stupa and composed a verse, saying:
"In the past, when I first visited the Master, I asked whether Chan meditation and the recitation of the Buddha’s name could be integrated and practiced together."

The Master’s answers emerged spontaneously from his mouth. "If these were two separate things, how could they be so harmoniously integrated? How wonderful this single phrase is! It brings joy to one's heart and soul.
He would frequently bring it up for others, and it spread everywhere throughout all quarters. Those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name are inexhaustible.
This refers to that which is also inexhaustible: the assembly on Vulture Peak has not yet dispersed, and the lotus pond remains ever-living through its tongue.

With this short verse as an offering, I join my palms before the seamless stupa. Accompanying King Zai-gong, we traveled together to Mount Jing; there he cleared a studio for his residence and studied the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Later, he lived beneath Lotus Peak in Suzhou, where he practiced the samādhi of Buddha-recitation alongside mountain monks. He styled himself [as follows].
The layman Xikong was eighty years old when he composed a verse for his departure from this world;
having bathed and changed his clothes, he passed away (from the *Yunqi Fahui*, the *Wujiang Zhi*, and the *Hanshan Mengyou Ji*).
Wu Zhanlou (吳瞻樓).
His given name has been lost. A native of Taicang (太倉), in his later years he entrusted his household affairs to his two sons and devoted himself earnestly to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.

With single-minded intent directed toward the Western Paradise, he daily recited the Buddha’s name ten thousand times and chanted the Larger and Smaller Amitābha Sūtras, as well as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-vyūha-sūtra*.

He recited the dharanis while simultaneously practicing the visualization of the Western Paradise, never mixing this with other activities. For twelve years, he perceived them as if they were a single day.
The sacred realms of the West appeared repeatedly before his eyes; at times, white lotus flowers as large as mortars would well up from before his bed, which even young children could see.
At over seventy years of age, he sat peacefully and passed away. His descendants continued their family tradition of serving the Buddha (from the *Xianguo suilu*).

Wu Minggong, whose courtesy name was Shubao, was a native of Taicang. His family had long been wealthy, and he was fond of practicing charity; however, he did not have a particularly deep understanding of the Buddha-dharma.
At over sixty years of age, he suddenly took leave of the assembly and bathed. He invited Dharma Master Yinchu of Longfu Temple to receive the Three Refuges and Five Precepts from him.
After calling out "Go forth! twice with a loud voice, he passed away with palms joined. A short while later, he opened his eyes again and said to those around him:
"As soon as I made the vow to forever sever ties with the mundane world and courageously recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, the Lotus World suddenly appeared."

Suddenly manifesting before him, [the deity] asked, "Reflect inwardly upon what good deeds you have performed in your daily life to have obtained this retribution. Speak these words to all the gentlemen; each must exert himself.
Having finished speaking, he requested water, looked at his own reflection, and suddenly attained awakening, saying, "In this life I am Wu Shubao; in my previous life I was Master Xu.
He then cried out, "How wonderful! and passed away. A rare fragrance then issued from the room (*Xianguo suilu*).

Wang Chun, courtesy name Xianmin, was a native of Yangzhou. He traveled extensively through the mountains and waters of Wu and Yue, where he attended upon Chan Master Yiyu and received the Upāsaka precepts.
While dwelling in the mountains, he recited the Lotus Sūtra daily. Subsequently, he returned to Yangzhou and resided at Ciyun Hermitage.
He devoted himself with piety to the cultivation of pure karma and named his residence "Abode of Precious Filaments. At the time of his death, he knew in advance that the hour had come;
sitting cross-legged, he requested monks to circumambulate him while reciting the names of the Buddhas, and thus passed away (from the *Biographies of Wang Xianmin*).
Chen Zhishan, courtesy name Yongzhuo, was a native of Changshu. When he was a child, upon hearing his grandmother recite the names of the Buddhas, his crying would immediately cease.

Later, having entered school, he read the *Analects* until reaching the passage: "If one hears the Way in the morning, it is acceptable to die in the evening. He went home and asked his mother, "When a person dies..."
"Peaceful refuge. His mother could not answer and told his father. His father asked, "What is your intention?
Zhishi replied, "I wish to know of birth and death; must I not hear the Way? His father said, "This child will surely enter the Dharma of non-arising in the future.
When he grew up, he heard of the reputation of Yunqi and admired it; he devoted himself earnestly to the practice of purity and released all living beings. There was a Master Ji...
He succeeded Fayun as abbot. Subsequently, he thatched a hut at Tengxi. Zhishan raised funds to construct a Chan temple there.
One day, Master Ji dreamed that Zhishan, dressed in black robes with a yellow sash, was smiling as they bid farewell.
He hurried to see him and found Zhishan reciting the Buddha’s name, having passed away while lying on his right side (from the *Changshu Zhi*).

Zhang Guangwei, courtesy name Cimin, was a native of Wuxi. At the age of fourteen, he was enrolled as a local student (zhusheng). Following the fall of the Ming dynasty, he abandoned his studies for the civil service examinations.
He taught students at his home. Over fifty years of age, he had lost all his wife and children and lived alone.

Because he devoted his mind to the inner scriptures (Buddhist texts), he styled himself the Layman of the Tranquil Hut (Xi-lu). He followed the teachings of Yunqi; his writings generally took Pure Land as their ultimate refuge.

Daily, he recited the Buddha’s name ten thousand times or more, while simultaneously contemplating Buddhist images. Every evening he prostrated before the Buddha, arranging flower offerings between two lamps.
Sometimes they appeared like pearls, sometimes like grains of millet, sometimes like necklaces, or like clouds of flower garlands.
One night, a lamp on the left suddenly manifested a lotus flower, upon which sat a Buddha in the full-lotus posture; his golden countenance was majestic and his marks and signs were all complete.

After a long while, the light vanished. Guangwei prostrated himself and prayed, vowing to behold him again. Three days later, on the evening of the third day, a standing image of the Buddha appeared above the lamp on the left. To its right...
Above the lamp, a lotus flower also emerged, and the Buddha sat cross-legged upon it; all members of the family witnessed this.
Guangwei received the Upāsaka precepts and regarded the abstention from killing as the foremost principle, cherishing and protecting even a single mosquito or ant.

In his later years, he observed a long fast. For sacrifices to his ancestors and the worship of deities, he used exclusively vegetables and fruit; he made no distinctions regarding food and drink. Whenever he encountered delicacies, he would immediately give them away to others.
He wore the same cap throughout both winter and summer, never changing it for twenty years. At the age of seventy-three, he established his own funeral regulations:
he would not accept condolences from others, nor would he set up a wooden spirit tablet. His burial would not exceed forty-nine days, as he considered himself free from worldly concerns.

He was without attachment and without anger; he simply waited for his life to end with profound equanimity. Before long, he passed away. He left behind the *Jingtu shengyan* (Remnants of Words on the Pure Land), which was carved into woodblocks and circulated in the world.
Among its three chapters on the recitation of the Buddha’s name, those most essential for students are summarized as follows:
The sutras state, "Uphold the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction. Regarding "upholding," it is as if it could be grasped, yet it is not grasped. This is the Confucian...
What is called "earnestly wearing it upon one's breast" is what Zhu Xi glossed as "reverently upholding. The phrase "not losing it," which follows, carries the meaning of "not becoming disordered.
Furthermore, the Confucian term *gùshì* (to look back and take heed) is explained by Zhu Xi as "constantly keeping it before one's eyes";

this is precisely the meaning of "contemplating the Buddha," and it is also the meaning of "not becoming disordered. [This involves] reciting the Buddha’s name with the mouth, contemplating the Buddha’s image with the eyes, and [listening with the ears...]
Listen for yourself: sounds flow from the tongue; the flavor of dhyāna delights the mind; the nose perceives fragrances. Thus one recollects the Buddha, returning the six senses to the One.
How could there be distraction? Now, as I recollect the Buddha, I employ a skillful means: I observe this mind as being like a pure jewel vase. The name of the Buddha is like grain;
following each word and each phrase, it is like grain being poured into the vase, falling down like a string of pearls. Once the grain has entered...

It is inexhaustible; yet the vial is not filled. Without casting out even a single grain, one gazes upon this vial, which is not more than an inch in diameter, and beholds within it Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a hundred billion three-thousandfold world systems—namely, thirty-six trillion, one hundred and eleven thousand, nine thousand five hundred Amitābha Buddhas, all identical in name and title—dwelling peacefully therein.
"In the midst [of this], I shall also join them in one place to enjoy ourselves, feast, and rest;

that alone is where I shall find peace for my body and establish my life. Furthermore, it is said: The verse of Master Shinan states: "When reciting the Buddha’s name, do not greedily seek to recite too much;

simply recite one hundred times with an undistracted mind. If you miss even one of the ninety-nine recitations, you have strayed from mindfulness; turning the prayer beads will then count for nothing. Thus it is.

From one hundred to one thousand, from one thousand to ten thousand, like beads strung together; arrows cannot pierce it, blades cannot penetrate it, and even a million demonic armies must all flee in retreat.
When I was reciting the Buddha’s name in the past, I did so merely by reciting it as a whole mass.
Only now do I realize that every single character must emerge from within the heart, and furthermore, every single character must enter back into the heart. When reciting the Buddha’s name, first...

One must sit upright with eyes closed, concentrating the spirit and stabilizing the thoughts. One must not harbor even a trace of a distracted mind, a restless and competitive mind, or a dull and slothful mind.
When opening the mouth to produce sound, one must ensure that the voice issues from the mind and the mind is transmitted through the mouth.

The breath shall be regulated and the voice harmonized—neither too slow nor too fast—with every syllable distinct and every phrase continuous. If analyzed, each single character may be further divided.
If one penetrates it with a single phrase, then hundreds or thousands of phrases are as direct as that single phrase.
Continuous and dense, from one sound to ten million sounds, and from one moment to twelve hours, there is no interruption and no succession; nothing is deficient and nothing is leaking.

After a long time, [the practice] becomes pure and matured; when the flower blooms, one sees the Buddha. This will be verified at the appointed time, for it certainly does not deceive anyone. It is further said:

"When the recitation of the Buddha's name reaches its ultimate point, one must also cultivate visualization (*vipaśyanā*). Close your eyes and face west; sitting upright, contemplate silently: the spirit separates from the form and proceeds straight toward the west.
Gradually, you will see forests, various waterfowl, and roads demarcated by golden cords with railings interlaced. Proceeding in succession...
I traveled swiftly. Before my eyes appeared jeweled ponds with exquisite lotuses, fragrant altars, and multi-storied pavilions. There, the Tathāgata stood manifest in a body sixteen feet tall;
Avalokiteśvara attended to his left and Mahāsthāmaprāpta to his right. He emitted light from between his brows and extended his hand to welcome us.
I and the assembly of beings from the sea were all gathered within that light and followed it upward. Prostrating at his feet with deep sorrow and earnestness, I suddenly beheld a golden palm.
He stroked my head and sprinkled nectar upon my body. This mind became vast and empty, attaining great peace and stability. Gradually, my spirit returned;
as if emerging from a state of deep concentration, I traveled once around that world. The path for rebirth was now matured, and when the time arrives, I shall not be deluded.
I pray that you convey this to all who practice mindfulness of the Buddha: one must understand that it is the mind that recites, and not merely the mouth. When entering this gate, depart.
The Buddha is not far away (a supplementary remark regarding the Pure Land).
Yuan Lixing, courtesy name Yuansan, was a native of Kunshan. He once resided at Xixi in Hangzhou, and thus styled himself "Xixi."

When the layman was still a youth, he practiced the examination curriculum. One day, hearing his maternal grandmother recite the passage from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* concerning the "four marks," he immediately attained a profound realization.
Subsequently, he encountered Chan Master Yue-shan, under whom he sought the ultimate truth. He redoubled his diligence daily.
It happened that the elder Bai-song came from Xuefeng to Kunshan; after Li-xing had questioned and challenged him repeatedly, he penetrated the truth upon hearing the Master’s words.

Thus, he eventually received the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Thereafter, his spiritual influence spread daily; he guided others according to their capacities, his wisdom and eloquence being unimpeded.

He proclaimed the One Vehicle while simultaneously propagating the Pure Land teachings. At that time, many of his contemporaries were fond of practicing alchemical arts and admired the "withered dhyāna" (the practice of self-mortification), many of whom did not believe in the Pure Land.
Liesheng exhorted them, saying: "The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is perfectly integrated, vast, and great. I..."
Hitherto, I have practiced and realized the secret teachings in seclusion, not daring to speak lightly of them to others. This was not out of secrecy or a refusal to speak;

rather, it was because the time had not yet arrived, and I feared that speaking of them would be of no benefit. As for the profound Dharma-treasury of the Buddhas, even the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Two Vehicles do not believe in it when they hear it.
This is because they abide in the purity of Nirvana and have already realized the wondrous supernatural powers.
Because they do not know that the great ocean of adornments of the Pure Land is manifested and perfected everywhere, the Buddhas rebuke those of the two vehicles as being mistaken,

The treatise on abstaining from killing is titled *The Primary Requisite for Myriad Good Deeds*. Its words are largely earnest, poignant, and deeply moving. He himself stated that whenever he passed by any shrine, he would invariably offer this prayer:

Shen Zhongxu, courtesy name Qibai, was a native of Wu County. In his youth, he was bold and unrestrained, and he took urgent action to relieve the hardships of others.

Wherever he passed—whether at monasteries, street corners, or beneath bridges—he inscribed everywhere the names of the Buddhas of the Western Paradise and words of exhortation, urging people to recite the Buddha’s name.
