After five years had passed, while sitting in meditation one night, he vowed not to attain perfect enlightenment until his task was finished, and he never ceased his efforts.
Suddenly, a sound resonated from his spine; it straightened up like that of a healthy person. Thereupon, he received the five precepts.
While meeting with Master Gōng at a roadside inn, Bìngcháng said, "The myriad phenomena of the world arise and perish without ceasing;
there is only this single phrase, 'Amitābha Buddha,' which is the place of great rest.

He further remarked that the practice of nianfo was especially effective during his illness, such that amidst the torment of various sufferings, his single-minded recollection remained vividly clear, never once faltering. (Qianlong 40)
In the eleventh month of the sixth year, he manifested a slight illness for several days. On the final day of that month, having finished washing and bathing at dawn, his breathing became labored;

he turned his body toward the west, sat in the full lotus position, and recited the Buddha’s name. His wife was by his side, but he gestured for her to leave. Shortly thereafter, he passed away peacefully while sitting.
He left instructions that he be enshrined in a coffin and cremated according to the *caibi* (cremation) rite. His wife also observed a lifelong fast and cultivated the practices of the Pure Land.
Having done so, she left the household life to become a nun (her later residence at Er-lin is recorded in the subsequent collection).
Wang Gong, courtesy name Liyan, was a native of Taicang. By nature he was tranquil and simple, possessing few desires; in his youth, he abandoned his studies for the civil service examinations.
He was fond of composing poetry. His residence, Nan Yuan (South Garden), was formerly the country villa of his late elder uncle, the Duke Wensu.

Surrounded by bamboo and rocks in a cool and serene atmosphere, he would join his various kinsmen and followers in drinking and chanting, finding fulfillment therein. When he reached over fifty years of age, he ceased writing poetry and no longer composed it.

He observed a long fast and cultivated the Pure Land practice, styling himself the Layman "Destroying Existence" (Poyou). One night, he dreamed of traveling to the Pure Land; upon waking, he recorded this experience in verse, beginning with: "No..."

There is much that cannot be deliberated upon. One dreams of entering the Lotus Land, the Great Place of Rest. There, the various superior beings discourse on the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), while each of the celestial Śakras rains down flowers and incense.
The songs of birds and the music of trees resound without ceasing; pearl pavilions and golden terraces all radiate light.
The immortal plains are but a few inches away, never separated by distance—do not let yourself lose the way and sigh like the fisherman. It is also said: "The Old Man of the Snowy Mountains."
My son is most full of feeling; he has pointed out the path home with great clarity. Do not dwell elsewhere—you must dwell right here.

In the midst of non-arising, there is precisely this arising. Once the seed is sown, the sprout soon emerges; once the root is nourished, the fruit naturally forms. Accept this and go straight to Mount Tiantai;
why trouble yourself traveling ten thousand *li* to seek Penglai and Yingzhou? At that time, I was seventy-two years old. His...
In the summer of the following year, he lay ill in the Tan-ying Hall (Tányǐng xuān) within the garden. In front of the hall was a lotus pond;
while the flowers had not yet bloomed, a single medicinal lotus beside a cliff rock opened its petals alone before his bed, its color fresh and beautiful.

After two full days, he recited the names of the Buddha as usual and passed away while forming mudrās with his hands, at which time the flower also withered. This was the fifth month of the forty-seventh year of the Qianlong era.

It was the eighth day. Not long after, there was a person from Liuhe who could summon spirits through spirit-writing (ji). Gong Zichong went to consult him. The spirit-writing board inscribed in large characters:
"I am the master who has shattered existence. When asked where he currently resides, it replied: "Fortunately, I have ascended to the Lotus Realm."
[The master] asked, “Do you perhaps remember your home? [Guchengzhi] replied, “What need is there for thought or anxiety? [The master] asked about his family affairs. He replied, “Namo Buddha.
When pressed further, he again wrote “Namo Buddha. This occurred three times, after which he became silent. (Recorded by Xu Peixiu). The Commentary states:
In my youth, I heard the teachings on the cycle of saṃsāra and its coming and going; I immediately felt sorrow at being adrift through the five turbidities, wandering aimlessly.

Yet there is nothing upon which to rely. Having grown older, I have observed the conduct of such men as Yu Yanbao and Wang Xuzhong, who cast aside worldly glory and set their hearts solely on journeying toward the West;
I truly admire them. A hundred-year lifespan is but a fleeting moment, yet our schemes for body, family, and wife grow ever more entrenched.
The cycles of sorrow and joy, gain and loss, honor and disgrace emerge daily, while death follows close behind.
An ancient said that among all the gates of practice, the single gate of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) is most urgent for laypeople.

Placed amidst the midst of blazing fires and immersed in the sea of afflictions, when a single breath ceases, the iron bed and copper pillar follow immediately; if one does not rely upon the power of the Buddha, how can one withstand this?
There are those who, having examined the legacy of these gentlemen, have stirred themselves to resolute effort.
[They were] such as these. All of them were of the same flesh and bone as those within the lotus womb. My wish is to hold the whip and follow after them.
*Records of the Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land*, Volume Eight;
*Records of the Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land*, Volume Nine.
Section Eight: Miscellaneous Accounts of Rebirth—Zhang Zhongqiu.
Zhang Zhongqiu was a man of the Tang dynasty who lived in Chang’an. He made his living by slaughtering chickens. As he was dying, he saw a person in vermilion robes driving him away.
A flock of chickens arrived and began crying out, "Tuo! Tuo! Each time they pecked upward, blood flowed from both eyes, and the pain was unbearable.
A śramaṇa named Hongdao saw this and set up an image for them, encouraging them to recite the Buddha’s name. Suddenly, he perceived the fragrance of incense filling the room.
The flock of chickens dispersed, and he passed away while sitting upright (*Fozu tongji*).
Zhang Shanhe, also a man of the Tang dynasty, made his living as a butcher of oxen. At the moment of his death, he saw dozens of oxen appearing in human form.
He said, "You have killed me. Shanhe told his wife, "Quickly invite the monks to recite the Buddha's name for me. When the monks arrived, he said to them, "The sutras state:

'If there are sentient beings who have committed unwholesome deeds and ought to fall into the evil realms, yet with a sincere heart complete ten recitations calling upon the name of Amitābha Buddha, they shall eliminate the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death and immediately attain rebirth in the Ultimate [Pure Land].'"

In the World of Bliss, Shanhe said, "The hells are most urgent. He then took a incense burner, held the fire with his left hand and grasped the incense with his right, calling upon the Buddha toward the west with a stern voice.
Before he had completed ten invocations, he suddenly cried out, "The Buddha has come!
He has already given me a jeweled throne. Having finished speaking, he passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Jin Hei and Jin Hei.

Their place of origin is unknown. They made their living as fishermen, but later changed their ways, abstaining from meat and blood and reciting the name of the Buddha ten thousand times a day without ceasing.
One day, he suddenly said to his family: "I see Amitābha Buddha and..."
"Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta have arrived; I shall now return to the Pure Land. On the following day, he spoke again, saying, "A golden lotus flower has come to welcome me.
He sat upright while burning incense, formed mudras with his hands, and passed away. Celestial music and extraordinary fragrances did not dissipate for the entire day.
The incident occurred in the sixth year of the Zhenghe era of the Song dynasty (as recorded in the *Jingtu wen*).

Feng Meng, whose courtesy name was also Feng Meng, was a native of Shangyu. In his youth, he was devoted to hunting. There was a giant serpent that caused distress to the local villagers; Meng killed it. Fearing...

Taking a snake as his enemy, he then turned his heart toward the Buddha-dharma and directed his merit toward the Western Paradise. For ten years, he practiced repentance and recited the names of the Buddhas.

One night, after inviting several companions in pure practice to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* and chant the Buddha’s name together, and having further recited the *Samantabhadra Verses for Repenting Sins and Rebirth*, he sat upright with palms joined and passed away (*Fozu Tongji*).
Wu Qiong, Wu Qiong.
His origins are unknown. He was originally a monk, but later returned to lay life and became a cook.

While slicing meat, he would never cease reciting the names of the Buddhas from his mouth. He frequently instructed the villagers to recite sutras, practice repentance, and chant the name of Amitābha.

He recited the name of Amitābha Buddha. Later, a tumor grew on his eyelid, as large as a chicken egg. Terrified, he sent his wife and children away and built a thatched hut, where he practiced meditation day and night.
In the autumn of the twenty-third year of the Xiangsheng era, he told the villagers, "Tomorrow, at the hour of Xu (7–9 p.m.), I shall depart.
Everyone laughed at him. The following evening, he informed his fellow practitioners, "The time has come."

"Come, let us recite the Buddha's name together. He then pawned his cotton shirt for wine and drank it all. He immediately wrote a verse: "The cup is empty; what need is there to ask about the Zen school?
Be careful today; tomorrow there will be a clear breeze. Sitting upright with palms joined, he called upon the Buddha’s name.
Suddenly, he cried out in a loud voice, "The Buddha has come! and immediately passed away (from the *Jingtu wen*).
Li Yantong was a native of Kuaiji.

He was a blacksmith by trade. Once, while visiting the city, he happened to attend a Buddhist assembly; there, he suddenly realized the impermanence of his life and body and turned his heart toward the Pure Land.
One day, he fell ill and said, "In a dream, I traveled to the Pure Land and saw two gates bolted shut."
The lock was very secure. Just then, he encountered the monk Zongli, who opened the door and led him inside. There, within the pavilions, he beheld the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"I am about to depart," he said. He then invited the two monks Xi and Jingdao to his bedside to exhort them to cultivate pure karma.
He caused his entire family to recite the Buddha’s name together, and he passed away while sitting facing west (*Fozu Tongji*).
Huang Sheng, a native of Tanzhou, made his living by forging iron; every time he was hammering iron, he would call out the name of Amitābha Buddha.
He did not cease his practice for a single day. One day, he dictated a verse to a neighbor to write down, saying: "Ding-ding dang-dang; long refined into steel.
Peace will soon arrive; I am going to the Western Land. He further instructed, "After I have departed, you may circulate this verse."
He widely exhorted others to practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name. He then passed away (from the *Fozu tongji*).
Xu Liugong was a farmer from Jiaxing who maintained a lifelong vegetarian fast and recited the Buddha’s name. He established images for worship in this manner for forty years.

Throughout his life, he frequently dreamed of traveling to the Pure Land. He prepared a burial niche in advance; on the day of his passing, he changed into coarse cloth robes and straw sandals, entered the niche, and sat upright.
After a short while, he said, "The Buddha has come to welcome me," and passed away in serene stillness (*Fozu Tongji*).
Shen Sanlang, Shen Sanlang.
He was a merchant from Lin’an who, in his later years, served the Buddha with great devotion. One day, while suffering from illness, he invited a monk to lecture on the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
He set up an image of the Buddha and gazed toward the west from morning until night. He changed his clothes and passed away; shortly thereafter, his knees slightly bent, as if...
When he wished to rise from his seat, his two sons pulled his legs straight for him. Suddenly, he rose abruptly and sat up. He then moved to a new shrine and was cremated.
A white crane circled in the clouds and flew westward (*Fozu Tongji*).
Shi Zan, Shi Zan.
A native of Yongzhou, he served as a novice monk. At the age of fourteen, he recited the name of the Buddha without ceasing. Suddenly, he fell ill and passed away, but soon thereafter he revived.
He said to his parents, "Amitābha Buddha has come here; I shall follow him. A neighbor witnessed this.
In the sky, a jeweled terrace appeared, emitting five-colored, extraordinary radiance that vanished toward the west (*Fozu Tongji*).
As for the practitioner Ni:

Ni was a native of Renhe who abandoned his home to build a small hermitage. He devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the Buddha’s name, intending to cremate his own body as a substitute for another.
All sentient beings made offerings to the Buddhas. Thereupon, they assembled the multitude and chanted the names of the Buddhas; those who arrived numbered ten thousand.
On the eve of his self-immolation, a golden light suddenly appeared upon that ground, rising about half a foot high. He spoke to the people, saying:
"When I burn my body, there will surely be clouds of two colors—purple and blue—passing from the northeast to the southwest; this is the sign of my rebirth in the Pure Land."
After a while, he lit a torch and sat upright within it; two-colored clouds appeared, and only when the fire was extinguished did they vanish (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Regarding the novice of Dashaan Temple:
the novice of Dashaan Temple constantly followed his master, Shanhui, reciting the names of the Buddhas. One night, he dreamed of a woman holding...
He showed him his prayer beads. The boy said, "I wish to have one string, but I regret that I have no money to buy it.
The woman said, "I shall give it to you; you may open your mouth. She then placed the prayer beads into his mouth. When the boy awoke, he told his teacher. Eihui said:
"This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, who has bestowed upon you the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
After several days, the boy saw two Great Beings who presented him with a flower throne and said, "In seven days, you shall mount this and be reborn in the Pure Land."
The boy immediately told the people, "I shall depart in seven days. When the appointed time arrived, he suddenly cried out, "The Bodhisattva has come!
and passed away while seated (from the *Fozu Tongji*).
Zhang Ai, Zhang Ai.
He was a eunuch during the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty. In his later years, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

After several years of practice, he died of illness and arrived before a king, who said to him, "You ought to receive a conception in the human realm. He replied, "I cherish the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."
"I vow to be reborn in the Pure Land; I do not wish to undergo conception. The King said, "Your merit from upholding the sutra is slight; how can this be?

Dao’ai replied, "I have heard that even ten recitations can achieve success, let alone those performed over a long period. The King said, "Release him for now; let him go to continue his recitation of the sutra."
Having regained consciousness, he departed for Biyun Temple on the Western Mountains, where he devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
After eleven years, one day he assembled his followers and said, "By the power of upholding this sūtra, I shall now depart for the West.
He bathed, changed his robes, sat upright, and passed away (*Jingang xinyi lu*).

Wu Jiaozhu (Wu Who Poured Oil on Candles) lived at Loumen in Suzhou; he made his living by pouring oil over candles, and thus he gained his name. He lived alone without a companion, observing a perpetual fast and reciting the Buddha’s name day and night.
As a man of integrity who never deceived others, candle-sellers vied with one another to welcome him to pour oil for their wicks. Wu [the local official] was so impressed that he... [inclined].
He used one ladle of oil [per day] and invariably made it his custom to recite the name of the Buddha a certain number of times. When he was over seventy years old, he suddenly said to his host:

"I have accumulated some modest wealth, originally intended as a provision for after death. Now that the merit of my mindfulness of the Buddha has been perfected, on such-and-such a day, I shall depart."
"Since you have been reborn in a good realm, there is no need for this; I respectfully offer it to you as a gift. May the host perform meritorious deeds on your behalf.
Wu Xi was then led to a cellar, where a thousand pieces of gold were taken out. The host distributed them among the great monasteries, using the entirety to provide meals for the monks.

When the appointed time arrived, Wu Xi joined his palms in mindfulness of the Buddha and passed away while sitting upright. His remains were enshrined in a coffin according to his final instructions, and the cremation ceremony was subsequently performed.

On that day, there were thousands upon thousands of people who came to see him off. The account is found in the *Xianguo suilu* (Record of Manifest Results) from the seventh year of the Chongzhen era.
Wu Mao, Wu Mao—this was a servant of the Wu family of Qingyang—who regularly observed the fast, recited the Buddha’s name, and cultivated various forms of goodness. Left.

When the soldiers led by Liang Yu crossed the river, the entire Wu family fled to avoid them; only Mao remained alone to guard the house. When the soldiers arrived, he was struck by seven spears and died.
Once the chaos had subsided and the head of the household returned, Mao revived and said: "Due to my past karma, I was destined to receive the body of a pig for seven lifetimes.

Because I have observed the precepts and recited the Buddha’s name in this life, I have dispersed the karmic enmity through these seven spears. Now the Buddha has come to welcome me, and I shall attain rebirth in the Pure Land."

"Go to the western direction. Having finished speaking, he joined his palms and passed away. This account is recorded in the *Guobao Wenjian Lu* (Record of Heard Accounts of Karmic Retribution) under the first year of the Shunzhi era.
Wang Yangquan was a native of Hangzhou who made his living by slaughtering sheep; the number of those killed was beyond counting. Later, while suffering from illness, he saw a multitude...
A sheep was destined for slaughter, and his heart was filled with great fear. When he recovered from his illness, he suddenly and completely changed his occupation.

He observed a lifelong fast and served the Buddha, reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until he had completed three *piṭakas* worth of volumes. In his later years, he also prostrated before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, never tiring day or night.

At the age of eighty-one, he suddenly saw an official bearing a warrant come to summon him. He raised his voice in refusal, saying, "I shall wait for the Buddha to arrive before I depart. Five days later, he indeed saw [the Buddha].
The Buddha manifested a great body, extending his hand to guide him, and passed away with a serene countenance (*Xianguo suilu*).
Liang Weizhou, Liang Weizhou, was a native of Chengxian County in Shaoxing. While serving as a lay practitioner at Longtan Hermitage, he became blind at the age of forty.
He had nothing to eat and wished to die. Sengyun Li stopped him, saying, "Do not die in vain. To the west there is a Buddha named Amitābha.
If you can recite his name with a sincere heart, it will not be difficult to cross over birth and death. Why worry about being blind? He followed this advice.
Sengyun Li raised funds to provide him with meals. Hui Zhou’s recitation of the Buddha’s name was so earnest that after three years, his eyes [were restored].
Fuming lived for half a month before announcing to the assembly, "I am about to depart. Three days later, at noon, he sat facing west and passed away.
This occurred in the thirty-eighth year of the Qianlong era (as recorded by the monk Yunli).

The commentary states: For those who cultivate the practice of Pure Land, it matters not whether they are noble or lowly, nor does one choose between the wise and the foolish; if their faith is deep, they shall enter, provided they accumulate sincerity.

Yet they attained enlightenment—just as Zhong Kui, Shanhe, and others, who were all merely peddlers and butchers. With a single thought of turning the light back within, they suddenly transcended to the other shore.
Thus we know that the power of the mind is inconceivable, and the power of the Buddha is likewise inconceivable.
The ninth woman to attain rebirth was Lady Vaidehī.
Vaidehī was the consort of King Bimbisāra of Śrāvastī. She had a crown prince named Ajātaśatru.
World-Honored One, following the instructions of the evil friend Devadatta, he seized his father, the King, and confined him within seven layers of chambers, forbidding all ministers from entering.
At that time, Vaidehī reverently attended to the Great King;

having bathed and purified herself, she smeared her body with a mixture of ghee, honey, and parched grain flour. She placed grape juice within her various necklaces and offered the honey to the King. The King—
She attained immortality. When Ajātaśatru heard this, he immediately seized a sharp sword, intending to harm his mother.

He was dissuaded by two high ministers, who subsequently confined her in a deep palace and did not allow her to come out again. At that time, having been imprisoned, Vaidehī was distressed and emaciated;
she turned toward Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa from afar, paid homage to the Buddha, and spoke these words: "O Tathāgata of the World..."
“Venerable One, in the past, you always sent Ānanda to come and comfort me. Now I am filled with grief and anxiety;
because of the World-Honored One’s majestic gravity, I have no means by which to see him. I pray that you will send the Venerable Maudgalyāyana and Ānanda so that they may meet with me.

Having spoken these words, he wept bitterly, shedding tears like rain, and paid homage to the Buddha from afar. At that time, the World-Honored One was on Vulture Peak Mountain. Knowing [the situation of] Wei...
As Vaidhī was thus reflecting in her mind, she immediately commanded Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Ānanda to come through the air.
The Buddha then vanished from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and appeared within the royal palace.

When Vaidhī had finished her prostrations, she raised her head and beheld the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni Buddha, his body the color of purple-gold, seated upon a lotus flower made of a hundred jewels, with Maudgalyāyana attending to his left.
Ānanda attended on his right. Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protecting devas were in the void, raining down celestial flowers everywhere.
At that time, Vaidehī, weeping and wailing, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what sins did I commit in my past lives to give birth to such a wicked son?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively explain for me the place free from sorrow and affliction; I shall be reborn there, for I take no pleasure in the turbidity of Jambudvīpa."
This is an evil age. This turbid and wicked place is filled with hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals; it is a mass of many unwholesome things.
I pray that in the future, I may not hear evil sounds nor see evil people. Now, before the World-Honored One, I seek compassion and repent.
I only pray that the Buddha-sun will teach me to contemplate the realm of pure karma. At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from between his eyebrows. Its...
The light was golden in color, illuminating immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.

It returned to the crown of the Buddha’s head and transformed into a golden platform, within which the pure and wondrous lands of all the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared. Having seen this, Vaidehī addressed the Buddha, saying:
Although these Buddha-fields are adorned and pure, and all possess radiance, I now wish to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, in the presence of Amitābha Buddha.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will instruct me in contemplation and instruct me in right concentration. The Buddha said to Vaidehī:
"Amitābha Buddha is not far from here; you should fix your mindfulness and clearly contemplate that land. I now...
I shall explain this extensively for you, so that ordinary persons of the future who cultivate pure karma may be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three types of merit: first, filially supporting one’s parents, serving teachers and elders, practicing compassion by refraining from killing, and cultivating the ten virtuous actions;
second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges and fully observing the various precepts; third, [not...]
Third, to violate the rules of decorum. These three matters are called the primary causes for purifying one's karma.

After the Buddha had further explained the sixteen contemplations to Vaidehī, Vaidehī and her five hundred attendants, having heard what the Buddha taught, immediately beheld the [Amitābha] Land at that very moment.
He beheld the vast and expansive features of the Land of Bliss and saw the Buddha’s body, as well as the two Bodhisattvas.
His heart was filled with joy, and he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Suddenly and completely awakened, he attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Five hundred female attendants resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and vowed to be born in that land. The World-Honored One prophesied for them all that they would indeed be reborn there. Once born in that land...
[In] the country of Vaidiśa, there was a poor old woman who came and spoke [to the Buddha]. At that time, the Buddha was in the country of Vaidiśa;

the place where he stayed was named Rauruka. There was a poor old woman who came and addressed him. (From the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*). "Rauruka": the Buddha was in the country of Vaidiśa; the location where he resided was called Rauruka. There was a poor old woman who came and said:

The Buddha said: "From where do birth, old age, sickness, and death come? To where do they go? Even as for the six consciousnesses, the six sense organs, and the five great elements—from where do they come?
To where do they go? The Buddha said: "Birth, old age, sickness, and death come from nowhere."
When they depart, they go nowhere. Even the six consciousnesses, the six sense organs, and the five great elements come from nowhere and, when they depart, go nowhere.
It is like two pieces of wood: when rubbed together, fire is produced; the fire then consumes the wood, and once the wood is exhausted, the fire is extinguished. All phenomena are likewise:
they are formed through the convergence of causes and conditions, and they perish when causes and conditions disperse. They come from nowhere.

"Departing, there is nowhere to which one goes. He then extensively explained various parables for her. Upon hearing the Dharma, the old woman attained understanding and immediately gained the Dharma-eye.
The Buddha said, "In a previous life when I first resolved to attain Bodhicitta, I was once her son.
This old woman shall, at the end of her life, be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, where she will make offerings to all Buddhas. Sixty billion kalpas hence, she shall..."
She attained Buddhahood; her name was P’u-p’o-kan. Her country was named Hua-chao (The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Old Mother).
She was of the Chi clan—Chi Chi—and was the wife of Ko Chih-chih of Kuei-yung. She lived during the Liu Sung period. Chih-chih was a descendant of Ko Hung.
The family had studied the arts of the immortals for generations, yet Ji alone took pleasure in the Buddha-dharma, maintaining her sincerity without fail.

One day, while she was weaving, she looked up and saw the clouds parting to reveal the bright sun; the sky was clear and serene. Suddenly, precious canopies, banners, and streamers appeared, coming from the west.
In the center sat a Tathāgata, his golden body radiating such brilliance that it illuminated the heights beyond the clouds. Ji paused her shuttle and gazed intently;
her heart leaped with joy as she exclaimed, "The sutras speak of Amitāyus Buddha—is this not he?
She then prostrated herself in worship and led Jizhi there, pointing out the location of the Buddha. Jizhi saw only half the body, along with various banners and canopies; suddenly, they vanished.
[She] passed away. At that time, the elders and children of the village all witnessed and heard of this; consequently, many followed her in taking refuge in the Buddha (*Mingxiang ji*).

As for the daughter of the Wei family: she was a native of Liang Commandery. Both her father and elder brother cultivated the practice of purity, and the daughter likewise resolved her will upon rebirth in the Pure Land. She had no...
"How did you pass away? After seven days, he revived. He immediately ascended a high seat and recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Upon completion, he descended and addressed his father, saying: "When I departed, I went directly to the Land of Immeasurable Life.

Within this precious pond, there is a great lotus flower each for me, for you, and for my elder brother; we shall be born therein. Only my mother alone has none. I cannot bear this grief, and therefore have come to inform you."
Having finished speaking, she closed her eyes and passed away. From that time on, her mother also honored the Dharma (*Mingxiang ji*).
Empress Gudu was a native of Luoyang in Henan; she was the daughter of Guo Xing, the Grand Marshal of the Zhou dynasty and Duke of Henei.
When Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty was not yet illustrious, she married him as his consort; upon his accession to the throne, she was established as Empress.

She was virtuous and wise, offering much counsel and benefit regarding the affairs of state. However, she was somewhat jealous and envious, so that those in the inner palace rarely had the opportunity to attend upon the Emperor.

The Emperor, who greatly protected the Buddha-dharma, issued edicts to all provinces and commanderies to construct spirit-stupas everywhere to enshrine śarīra relics, many of which manifested auspicious responses. The Empress...

She also revered and admired the Mahāyāna and constantly maintained the Buddha’s name. Whenever she recited the name, she would first change into clean robes, chew fragrant aloeswood, and rinse her mouth;
this was her constant practice. On the day of Jiazi in the eighth month of the second year of the Renshou era, she passed away at the Yong’an Palace.
At the age of fifty, a rare fragrance filled the air and celestial music resounded. The Emperor asked the Indian monk Jñānagupta, "What auspicious omen is this?
He replied, "In the Pure Land there is a Buddha named Amitābha; the Empress has been reborn there, and thus these portents have appeared.
